    A Presentation of the Absolute Galois Group of \(\mathbb{Q}_2\)

    David Roe
    Department of Mathematics
    Massachusetts Institute of Technology
    roed@mit.edu
    David Turturean
    Fulcrum*
    davidturturean@gmail.com
    * Incoming, Physical Superintelligence PBC
    Abstract
    We give an explicit profinite presentation of the absolute Galois group \(\notn{GQ}{G_{\mathbb{Q}_2}}\text{,}\) filling a gap left by Jannsen and Wingberg [JW, Thm. 2] (who found a presentation for all \(p\)-adic fields with odd \(p\)) and Diekert [Die, Theorem, p. 152] (who found a presentation for \(2\)-adic fields where adjoining \(i\) is unramified). The presentation has four generators \(\notn{sigma}{\sigma},\notn{tau}{\tau},\notn{x0}{x_0},\notn{x1}{x_1}\text{;}\) the closed normal subgroup generated by \(\notn{x0}{x_0},\notn{x1}{x_1}\) is required to be pro-\(2\text{;}\) and there are two defining relations. The first is the tame relation \(\notn{tau}{\tau}^\notn{sigma}{\sigma}=\notn{tau}{\tau}^2\) and the second is the explicit relation stated in Theorem 1.2.
    🔗
    🔗

    Section 1 Introduction and main theorem

    For odd primes \(p\text{,}\) the absolute Galois group of \(\notn{Qp}{\mathbb{Q}_p}\) admits an explicit four-generator presentation of Jannsen–Wingberg type; see [NSW, Thm. 7.5.14]. Yet both the statement and proof break down for \(p=2\text{.}\) Jarden and Shusterman [JS, Thms. 2.1, 3.4, and 4.4] have since shown that the absolute Galois group of every \(p\)-adic field, including the dyadic ones, is finitely presented, and they computed the minimal numbers of generators and relations; their argument is cohomological and does not produce explicit generators or relations. We give an explicit presentation for \(p=2\) and a new approach that works in the dyadic setting.
    🔗
    Throughout, exponentiation by an element of \(\notn{Zhat}{\Zhat}\) has its usual profinite meaning. Let
    \begin{equation*} \notn{w}{\w}=(1\text{ in }\mathbb{Z}_2,\;0\text{ in }\mathbb{Z}_\ell\text{ for every odd prime }\ell). \end{equation*}
    Thus \(\notn{w}{\w}^2=\notn{w}{\w}\text{.}\)
    🔗
    We use the conventions
    \begin{equation*} x^g=g^{-1}xg, \qquad [x,y]=x^{-1}y^{-1}xy. \end{equation*}
    The unramified coordinate is normalized geometrically throughout: if \(\Phi_{\mathrm{ar}}\) is arithmetic Frobenius and \(\Phi_{\mathrm{geom}}=\Phi_{\mathrm{ar}}^{-1}\text{,}\) then \(\notn{nuur}{\nu_{\mathrm{ur}}}(\Phi_{\mathrm{geom}})=1\text{.}\) With the right-conjugation convention above, a standard tame generator satisfies
    \begin{equation*} \notn{tau}{\tau}^{\Phi_{\mathrm{geom}}}=\notn{tau}{\tau}^q. \end{equation*}
    Thus the displayed relation \(\notn{tau}{\tau}^\notn{sigma}{\sigma}=\notn{tau}{\tau}^2\) means that \(\notn{sigma}{\sigma}\) maps to geometric Frobenius. Put
    \begin{equation} \sigma_2=\notn{sigma}{\sigma}^{\notn{w}{\w}},\qquad u_i=(x_i\notn{tau}{\tau})^{\notn{w}{\w}}\;(i=0,1),\qquad d_0=u_0\notn{x0}{x_0}^{-1},\tag{1.1} \end{equation}
    \begin{equation} z_0=\notn{x0}{x_0}^{\sigma_2}, \qquad c_0=[d_0,z_0], \qquad g_0=\sigma_2^2, \qquad d_g=d_0^{g_0},\tag{1.2} \end{equation}
    \begin{equation} h_c=[d_g,d_0], \qquad h_0=\notn{x0}{x_0}^{g_0}\notn{x0}{x_0}\,d_gd_0d_0^2h_c.\tag{1.3} \end{equation}
    🔗

    Proposition 1.1. Marked dyadic Demushkin normalization.

    Let \(\notn{Dloc}{D_{\mathrm{loc}}}=G_{\Qtwo}(2)\) and let \(\notn{nuur}{\nu_{\mathrm{ur}}}:\notn{Dloc}{D_{\mathrm{loc}}}\twoheadrightarrow\mathbb{Z}_2\) be normalized by sending geometric Frobenius to \(1\text{.}\) There exist topological generators \(a,s,y\) such that
    \begin{equation} \notn{Dloc}{D_{\mathrm{loc}}}\cong \left\langle a,s,y\;\middle|\;a^2s^4[s,y]=1\right\rangle_{\mathrm{pro}-2}, \qquad \notn{nuur}{\nu_{\mathrm{ur}}}(a)=-2,\quad \notn{nuur}{\nu_{\mathrm{ur}}}(s)=1,\quad \notn{nuur}{\nu_{\mathrm{ur}}}(y)=0.\tag{1.4} \end{equation}
    The proof is given in Sections 3.1–3.3.
    🔗
    Lean
    🔗
    With the marked Demushkin normalization available, the main theorem takes the following form.
    🔗

    Theorem 1.2. Presentation theorem.

    The absolute Galois group \(\notn{GQ}{\GQ}\) is isomorphic to the profinite group topologically generated by
    \begin{equation*} \notn{sigma}{\sigma},\notn{tau}{\tau},\notn{x0}{x_0},\notn{x1}{x_1}, \end{equation*}
    for which the closed normal subgroup generated by \(\notn{x0}{x_0},\notn{x1}{x_1}\) is pro-\(2\text{,}\) and which is subject to the two relations
    \begin{equation} \notn{tau}{\tau}^\notn{sigma}{\sigma}=\notn{tau}{\tau}^2\tag{1.5} \end{equation}
    and
    \begin{equation} h_0u_1^{-1}\notn{x1}{x_1}^\notn{sigma}{\sigma} c_0=1,\tag{1.6} \end{equation}
    where the auxiliary words are defined in (1.1)–(1.3).
    🔗
    Lean (literal relators)Lean (counting form)Lean (main)Lean
    🔗
    Explicit presentations of this kind have a substantial history. For odd \(p\text{,}\) the structure of the full group \(G_{\mathbb{Q}_p}\) by generators and relations is due to Jannsen and Wingberg [JW]; see [NSW, Chapter VII] for a systematic account. In residue characteristic two, Zel’venskiĭ [Zel, Theorem 4] described the Galois group of the maximal extension without simple ramification for \(2\)-adic base fields of odd degree, and Diekert [Die, Theorem, p. 152] obtained structure results for absolute Galois groups of dyadic fields under additional hypotheses. More recently, Jarden and Shusterman [JS, Thms. 2.1, 3.4, 4.4] proved that \(G_K\) is finitely presented as a profinite group for every finite extension \(K/\mathbb{Q}_p\text{,}\) with no restriction at \(p=2\text{,}\) and computed the minimal numbers of generators and relations (\([K:\mathbb{Q}_p]+2\) and \([K:\mathbb{Q}_p]+1\)); their proof, via Lubotzky’s cohomological criterion for finite presentability, deliberately produces no explicit generators or relations. The present paper’s contribution is therefore not finite presentability, which is theirs, but the explicit marked presentation: concrete generators tied to the tame–wild structure, concrete word relations, and the finite-quotient characterization on which the counting proof runs. Presentations of local Galois groups also feed anabelian questions about their automorphisms; see for instance [Nis].
    🔗
    Theorem 1.2 is not the only presentation of \(G_{\mathbb{Q}_2}\) that has been proposed. A second four-generator, two-relator candidate, the square-commutator presentation, was written down independently of it and checked against finite-quotient counts; Appendix C proves that it, too, presents \(G_{\mathbb{Q}_2}\text{.}\) It is not obtained from Theorem 1.2 by a change of generators (no triple of words identifies the two maximal pro-\(2\) quotients) and is proved instead by running the argument of this paper over a second source: the interface of Corollary 6.19 is re-verified for the new relator, and the instance of the Demushkin classification needed to identify its maximal pro-\(2\) quotient is proved there rather than quoted. That appendix therefore rests on the same classical inputs as Theorem 1.2 and on no others, and the chain it completes is formalized without gaps.
    🔗
    During preparation of this manuscript, we also learned of independently proposed candidate presentations for \(G_{\mathbb{Q}_2}\) by other researchers. Some may be isomorphic, after changes of generators, to the presentation in Theorem 1.2. At the time of writing, those candidate presentations and the proposed isomorphisms have not been fully validated.
    🔗
    Write \(\notn{GA}{\GA}\) for the profinite group in Theorem 1.2. The condition that the normal closure of \(\notn{x0}{x_0},\notn{x1}{x_1}\) be pro-\(2\) is part of its presentation. For an epimorphism to a finite group \(G\text{,}\) this condition is equivalent to requiring the images of \(\notn{x0}{x_0},\notn{x1}{x_1}\) to lie in the \(2\)-core \(O_2(G)\text{.}\)
    🔗
    We use presentation in the following marked sense. The group \(\notn{GA}{\GA}\) is the quotient of the free profinite group on \(\notn{sigma}{\sigma},\notn{tau}{\tau},\notn{x0}{x_0},\notn{x1}{x_1}\) by the intersection of the kernels of all its admissible finite quotients: those in which the images of the four generators generate, satisfy (1.5) and (1.6), and have \(2\)-group normal closure of the images of \(\notn{x0}{x_0},\notn{x1}{x_1}\text{;}\) the formal construction is (2.1). The pro-\(2\) requirement is thus a condition imposed on every finite quotient alongside the two word relations. It is not itself a word relation, and we do not claim that it follows from the two displayed relators; in particular, \(\notn{GA}{\GA}\) is not asserted to coincide with the quotient of the free profinite group by the closed normal subgroup generated by the two relators alone. This enriched format is the classical one for absolute Galois groups of \(p\)-adic fields: for odd \(p\text{,}\) the Jannsen–Wingberg presentation likewise imposes, alongside its word relations, the condition that the normal closure of the wild generators be pro-\(p\) [JW, Thm. 2]. In the unmarked sense, finite presentability of \(\notn{GQ}{\GQ}\text{,}\) with minimal generator and relation numbers three and two, is the theorem of Jarden and Shusterman [JS, Thms. 2.1, 3.4, and 4.4] recalled above; Theorem 1.2 provides the explicit marked presentation.
    🔗

    Subsection 1.1 Strategy of the proof

    The proof has six stages.
    🔗
    1. The candidate \(\notn{GA}{\GA}\) is constructed from its admissible finite quotients. A reconstruction lemma reduces the theorem to equality of epimorphism counts from \(\notn{GA}{\GA}\) and \(\notn{GQ}{\GQ}\) to every finite group.
      🔗
      🔗
    2. The tame quotient of \(\notn{GA}{\GA}\) is identified with the tame quotient of \(\notn{GQ}{\GQ}\text{.}\) Its maximal pro-\(2\) quotient is identified with \(G_{\Qtwo}(2)\) in a form preserving the full unramified character to \(\mathbb{Z}_2\text{,}\) not merely its reduction modulo \(2\text{.}\)
      🔗
      🔗
    3. The tame and maximal pro-\(2\) maps are combined over their common unramified quotient. Fixing this fibre-product datum turns the comparison into a finite lifting problem with a prescribed tame quotient and a prescribed map to an elementary abelian \(2\)-group.
      🔗
      🔗
    4. For extensions with elementary abelian \(2\)-group kernel, lifts from the candidate are governed by the two defining relators, while lifts from \(\notn{GQ}{\GQ}\) are governed by continuous cohomology. The two theories are shown to have the same obstruction dimensions, lift multiplicities, duality pairings, and connecting maps.
      🔗
      🔗
    5. When a simple coefficient module is self-dual, a scalar central pushout produces a quadratic obstruction. An exact word calculation on the candidate side and the dyadic square-class filtration on the local side give the same quadratic Gauss sum.
      🔗
      🔗
    6. For a finite target, the normal \(2\)-subgroup is reduced through an elementary quotient and a central Frattini layer. Fourier inversion and the partition of homomorphisms according to their image subgroup reduce the count to strictly smaller targets. Strong induction gives equality of all finite epimorphism counts, and profinite reconstruction gives the required isomorphism.
      🔗
      🔗
    The dependence of the argument is therefore
    \begin{equation*} \begin{gathered} \text{marked tame and maximal pro-$2$ quotients} \\ \Downarrow \\ \text{common tame--pro-$2$ data over $\mathbb{Z}_2$} \\ \Downarrow \\ \text{linear lifting comparison and quadratic obstruction comparison} \\ \Downarrow \\ \text{induction on the normal $2$-subgroup of a finite target} \\ \Downarrow \\ |\Sur(\notn{GA}{\GA},G)|=|\Sur(\notn{GQ}{\GQ},G)|\quad\text{for every finite group $G$} \\ \Downarrow \\ \notn{GA}{\GA}\cong\notn{GQ}{\GQ}. \end{gathered} \end{equation*}
    In order, the five arrows are carried by: the marked identifications of Section 3 (Proposition 1.1, Proposition 3.14); the fibre-product boundary of Section 4; the two lifting theories and their numerical comparison in Section 5, Section 6, summarized in the source interface of Corollary 6.19, together with the minimal-block analysis and closed recursion of Section 7, Section 8 (Theorem 8.17) driving the induction of Section 9 (Theorem 4.2); the exhaustion over tame frames of Section 10 (Lemma 10.1, Proposition 2.3); and the one-sided reconstruction lemma (Lemma 2.5). This chain agrees with the formalization’s dependency graph: in Lean, the main theorem consumes exactly Lemma 2.5, Lemma 10.1, Proposition 2.3, Theorem 4.2, with Theorem 8.17 and the source interface feeding Theorem 4.2.
    🔗
    The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 we construct the candidate \(\notn{GA}{\GA}\) as a profinite group and prove the one-sided reconstruction lemma, reducing Theorem 1.2 to the equality of finite epimorphism counts. In Section 3 we identify the tame and maximal pro-\(2\) quotients of \(\notn{GA}{\GA}\) with those of \(\notn{GQ}{\GQ}\) in marked form over the full unramified quotient \(\mathbb{Z}_2\text{,}\) proving Proposition 1.1. In Section 4 we combine the two quotients over their common unramified data and reduce the comparison to a boundary-framed lifting problem. In Section 5 we develop the linear lifting theory on both sides: the evaluated Fox Jacobian complex for \(\notn{GA}{\GA}\text{,}\) and continuous cohomology with local Tate duality for \(\notn{GQ}{\GQ}\text{.}\) In Section 6 we compute the quadratic obstruction that appears for self-dual simple \(\F_2\)-modules, comparing the candidate word calculation with the dyadic Gauss sum. In Section 7 we isolate a minimal non-scalar module layer in the wild kernel, and in Section 8 we invert the resulting lifting-count recursion by finite Fourier analysis. In Section 9 we assemble these ingredients into the inductive proof of the boundary-framed theorem, and in Section 10 we sum over tame boundary frames to complete the proof of Theorem 1.2. A closing section records further questions. The normalized cochain and transfer conventions used throughout are fixed in Appendix A, and the finite Fox–Heisenberg evaluation rules and the word ledger behind the Jacobian and quadratic calculations are recorded in Appendix B. In Appendix C we prove that a second, independently proposed presentation also presents \(\notn{GQ}{\GQ}\text{.}\) A final appendix collects background material.
    🔗

    Subsection 1.2 What is new

    We record the aspects of the argument that we believe are new.
    🔗
    The route to the presentation is enumerative: we match \(|\Sur(\GA,G)|=|\Sur(\GQ,G)|\) for every finite group \(G\) and conclude by a one-sided profinite reconstruction. To our knowledge, this counting comparison has not previously been used to establish a presentation of a local absolute Galois group; the known proofs for odd \(p\) [JW] and the dyadic partial results [Zel], [Die] proceed through embedding-problem solvability and the Demushkin classification.
    🔗
    The reconstruction lemma (Lemma 2.5) is stated in a one-sided form: \(P\) is assumed topologically finitely generated while \(Q\) is an arbitrary profinite group, with equality of the surjection counts \(|\Sur(P,H)|=|\Sur(Q,H)|\) the only hypothesis required for \(P \cong Q\text{.}\) Classical finite-quotient rigidity [DFPR, Theorem 1] (see also [RZ, Prop. 2.5.2]) assumes finite generation on both sides, while for small profinite groups the set of finite quotients is already determining [FJ, Proposition 16.10.7]. Although both sides are known to be finitely generated in the present application, the one-sided form is the natural strength of the argument (it matches the counting data the proof actually produces) and it is the shape required in settings where finite generation of the Galois side is open, such as the restricted-ramification groups \(G_{\mathbb{Q},S}\text{,}\) which are small by Hermite–Minkowski yet not known to be topologically finitely generated.
    🔗
    Lifting problems are controlled by an evaluated Fox–Jacobian three-term complex, with cup products computed in an explicit Heisenberg model. Free differential calculus is an established tool in pro-\(p\) Galois theory [Koc]; the device of evaluating the Jacobian on each finite target to control lifting counts appears to be new here. Finite Fourier inversion over character groups of finite modules is used to invert the lifting-count recursion: a classical enumerative device in the Frobenius tradition, applied inside a Galois-presentation argument.
    🔗
    For self-dual simple \(\F_2\)-modules, the lifting count acquires a quadratic obstruction, computed through Arf invariants and the dyadic filtration of square classes: the count is not determined by the linear duality data alone, in contrast with the odd-\(p\) pattern of [NSW, Chapter VII]. The dyadic obstruction is computed with tools imported from quadratic-form theory and topology: Arf invariants, Stiefel–Whitney classes [Kah], [Gui], the Evens norm from finite-group cohomology [Eve], [Koz], and Gauss-sign computations.
    🔗
    The boundary-framed marked target \(\mathcal Y=(Y,L_Y,\pi_Y,\theta_Y)\) of Definition 4.1 and the exact-image count \(e_\Gamma^{\beta}\) are defined for an arbitrary profinite source with a tame–pro-\(2\) boundary; nothing in the construction is specific to \(\Qtwo\text{.}\) The framework is a candidate approach to presentations of \(G_K\) for other dyadic fields, where only partial results are known [Die], [Sch].
    🔗
    The normalized-cochain ledger of Appendix A carries Shapiro maps, corestriction, and the Evens norm at the level of explicit normalized cochains with transversal bookkeeping, making transfer-level cohomology computations finite and machine-checkable; standard treatments [Bro], [Eve] work at the level of classes.
    🔗
    🔗

    Subsection 1.3 The formalizations and their trust base

    The theorem has been formalized in Lean 4 twice, in separately initiated projects, and the statements in the web edition of this paper link directly to the corresponding Lean declarations. The first author’s formalization proves the literal continuous isomorphism GQ2.main_presentation_literal with no sorry, together with the equivalent finite-counting form; the second author’s formalization was developed separately from the same manuscript, and its completed version incorporates a documented later adaptation of several steps from the first. Beyond checking the argument, the formalization effort sharpened the paper: a number of standing hypotheses, cochain normalizations, and citations were made explicit only when the proofs were machine-checked, and several statements in this revision repeat hypotheses whose necessity the formalization exposed.
    🔗
    Neither formalization is unconditional. Lean verifies the entire argument of this paper down to nine named interfaces with the classical literature, stated as axioms with a citation recorded for each; the kernel then checks everything above them. The nine interfaces are not of equal character, and we classify them accordingly: a direct classical theorem is transcribed from a single published statement; a classical theorem with encoding choices is classical mathematics whose Lean form passes through project normalizations that must be checked against the paper’s conventions; and a composite interface bundles several classical inputs, or a classical input plus a project convention, into one statement. The composite interfaces (B3c, B8, B11a below) are where independent expert attention is most valuable. The list below is generated from the same census as the formalization itself; the literal Lean statements, with links into the API documentation and this paper, are collected on the project’s axioms page.

    Section 2 The candidate as a profinite group

    Starting from the four generators, the two relators, and the requirement on the normal closure of \(\notn{x0}{x_0},\notnfar{x1}{x_1}\text{,}\) we construct the candidate as an inverse limit of finite quotients. The section ends with an exact finite-quotient semantics for this construction and the reconstruction criterion used in Section 10.
    🔗

    Subsection 2.1 The marked quotient construction

    Let \(F\) be the free profinite group on \(\notn{sigma}{\sigma},\notn{tau}{\tau},\notn{x0}{x_0},\notnfar{x1}{x_1}\text{.}\) The finite quotients relevant to the presentation are precisely those in which the four distinguished elements generate, satisfy both relators, and have \(2\)-group wild normal closure. Formally, call an epimorphism
    \begin{equation*} \varphi:F\twoheadrightarrow G \end{equation*}
    to a finite group admissible if the distinguished tuple generates \(G\text{,}\) satisfies (1.5) and (1.6), and the normal closure of \(\varphi(\notn{x0}{x_0}),\varphi(\notnfar{x1}{x_1})\) is a \(2\)-group. Let \(\mathcal Q_A\) be the class of all admissible finite quotients and set
    \begin{equation} \notn{NA}{N_A}=\bigcap_{\varphi\in\mathcal Q_A}\ker\varphi, \qquad \notn{GA}{\GA}=F/\notn{NA}{N_A}.\tag{2.1} \end{equation}
    Let \(\notn{WA}{\WA}\) denote the closed normal subgroup of \(\notn{GA}{\GA}\) generated by \(\notn{x0}{x_0},\notnfar{x1}{x_1}\text{.}\)
    🔗

    Lemma 2.1. Finite subdirect closure.

    If \(F\twoheadrightarrow G_i\) are finitely many admissible quotients and \(Y\) is the image of \(F\) in \(\prod_iG_i\text{,}\) then \(F\twoheadrightarrow Y\) is admissible and its kernel is the intersection of the given kernels.
    🔗
    Lean
    🔗

    Proof.
    The two relations hold coordinatewise. The distinguished tuple generates \(Y\text{.}\) The normal closure of \(\notn{x0}{x_0},\notnfar{x1}{x_1}\) in \(Y\) lies in
    \begin{equation*} Y\cap\prod_i O_2(G_i), \end{equation*}
    which is a finite \(2\)-group. Since \(Y\) is the image of the diagonal map \(F\to\prod_iG_i\text{,}\) one has
    \begin{equation*} \ker(F\to Y)=\bigcap_i\ker(F\to G_i), \end{equation*}
    which proves the assertion about kernels.
    🔗
    🔗
    Two features make the construction usable in counting arguments: every finite quotient of the candidate is itself admissible, and epimorphisms to a finite group admit a purely equational description. We record them in turn.
    🔗

    Lemma 2.2. Cofinality.

    Every finite quotient of \(\notn{GA}{\GA}\) is an admissible marked quotient. In particular, \(\notn{WA}{\WA}\) is pro-\(2\text{.}\)
    🔗
    Lean
    🔗

    Proof.
    Let \(K\triangleleft_{\mathrm{open}}F\) contain \(\notn{NA}{N_A}\text{.}\) For every \(g\notin K\text{,}\) the definition of \(\notn{NA}{N_A}\) gives an admissible quotient whose kernel does not contain \(g\text{.}\) Compactness of \(F\setminus K\) gives finitely many such kernels whose intersection is contained in \(K\text{.}\) By Lemma 2.1, this intersection is itself the kernel of an admissible quotient. Therefore \(F/K\) is a quotient of an admissible quotient, and admissibility passes to quotients. The last assertion follows because every finite image of \(\notn{WA}{\WA}\) is a \(2\)-group.
    🔗
    🔗

    Proposition 2.3. Epimorphic finite-quotient semantics.

    For every finite group \(G\text{,}\) epimorphisms \(\notn{GA}{\GA}\twoheadrightarrow G\) are in natural bijection with generating quadruples \((\notn{sigma}{\sigma},\notn{tau}{\tau},\notn{x0}{x_0},\notnfar{x1}{x_1})\in G^4\) satisfying (1.5), (1.6), and \(\notn{x0}{x_0},\notnfar{x1}{x_1}\in O_2(G)\text{.}\)
    🔗
    Lean (equivalence)Lean (main)Lean
    🔗

    Proof.
    An epimorphism sends \(\notn{WA}{\WA}\) to a normal \(2\)-subgroup of \(G\text{,}\) hence into \(O_2(G)\text{.}\) Conversely, a generating quadruple with \(\notn{x0}{x_0},\notnfar{x1}{x_1}\in O_2(G)\) has normal \(2\)-group closure and defines an admissible quotient in \(\mathcal Q_A\text{.}\)
    🔗
    🔗

    Remark 2.4.

    The corresponding statement for arbitrary, non-surjective homomorphisms into a fixed ambient group is false: the image of \(\notn{WA}{\WA}\) is normal in the image subgroup, but need not lie in the \(2\)-core of the ambient group. This is why the proof below keeps track of exact images and their induced markings.
    🔗
    🔗
    🔗

    Subsection 2.2 A reconstruction lemma

    Lemma 2.5. One-sided profinite reconstruction.

    Let \(P\) be a topologically finitely generated profinite group and let \(Q\) be any profinite group. If
    \begin{equation*} |\Sur(P,H)|=|\Sur(Q,H)| \end{equation*}
    for every finite group \(H\text{,}\) then \(P\cong Q\text{.}\)
    🔗
    Lean (from equal counts)Lean (main)
    🔗

    Proof.
    We construct an epimorphism in each direction from compatible finite quotients and then use Hopficity to identify both maps as isomorphisms.
    🔗
    Since \(P\) is finitely generated, \(\Sur(P,H)\) and hence \(\Sur(Q,H)\) are finite for every finite \(H\text{.}\) The two groups have exactly the same finite quotients.
    🔗
    For \(n\ge1\text{,}\) let \(R_n(P)\) be the intersection of the kernels of all maps from \(P\) to groups of order at most \(n\text{,}\) and put \(P_n=P/R_n(P)\text{.}\) The \(P_n\) form a cofinal inverse system of finite quotients of \(P\text{.}\) Every \(P_n\) is a quotient of \(Q\text{.}\) For any finite set of indices, a sufficiently large \(P_m\) maps onto all corresponding \(P_n\text{;}\) composing an epimorphism \(Q\twoheadrightarrow P_m\) gives a compatible family on that finite set. Compactness of the inverse limit of the finite nonempty sets \(\Sur(Q,P_n)\) yields a compatible family and therefore an epimorphism \(Q\twoheadrightarrow P\text{.}\)
    🔗
    Interchanging the two groups, use the directed system of all finite quotients of \(Q\text{.}\) The sets of epimorphisms from \(P\) to those quotients are finite and have the finite intersection property, so there is an epimorphism \(P\twoheadrightarrow Q\text{.}\) The composite \(P\twoheadrightarrow Q\twoheadrightarrow P\) is a surjective endomorphism of a finitely generated profinite group. Such groups are Hopfian; see, for example, [RZ, Prop. 2.5.2]. Hence the composite is an isomorphism, and so is \(P\twoheadrightarrow Q\text{.}\)
    🔗
    In more detail: the counting hypothesis is used only through finite data. Summing surjection counts over the subgroups of a finite \(H\) converts the hypothesis into \(|\Hom(P,H)|=|\Hom(Q,H)|\) for every finite \(H\text{,}\) and these counts are finite because \(P\) is topologically finitely generated. The formalization also assumes \(Q\) topologically finitely generated: with counts encoded as natural numbers, an infinite homomorphism set would make the count hypothesis vacuous rather than false, so finiteness on both sides is part of the statement’s content. In the application this is harmless: the candidate is finitely generated by construction, and the finite generation of \(\GQ\) is exactly the foundational input B1.
    🔗
    🔗
    The topological finite generation of \(\notn{GQ}{\GQ}\) required in this argument is classical; the direct dyadic reference is [NSW, Ch. VII §7.4, Theorem (7.4.1)], which bounds the number of generators of \(G_k\) for every \(p\)-adic \(k\) with no parity hypothesis; see also [JW]. Reconstruction of profinite groups from their finite quotients goes back to [DFPR, Theorem 1]; the counting refinement used here is a one-sided variant.
    🔗
    🔗
    🔗

    Section 3 The tame and maximal pro-\(2\) quotients

    The candidate construction of Section 2 is now compared with the corresponding tame and maximal pro-\(2\) quotients of \(\notn{GQ}{G_{\Qtwo}}\text{.}\) Besides the abstract quotient identifications, we determine compatible maps to the full unramified quotient \(\mathbb{Z}_2\text{;}\) those marked maps are the input to the fibre product in Section 4.
    🔗
    Let
    \begin{equation*} \notn{TA}{\TA}=\langle \notn{sigma}{\sigma},\notn{tau}{\tau}\mid \notn{tau}{\tau}^\notn{sigma}{\sigma}=\notn{tau}{\tau}^2\rangle_{\mathrm{prof}} \end{equation*}
    denote the finite-quotient tame group.
    🔗

    Lemma 3.1. Finite tame quotients.

    In every finite quotient generated by \(s,t\) with \(t^s=t^2\text{,}\) the element \(t\) has odd order, and the quotient has the form
    \begin{equation*} C_e\rtimes C_n, \qquad e\text{ odd}, \qquad s^{-1}ts=t^2. \end{equation*}
    Every normal \(2\)-subgroup of such a quotient is central and lies in the unramified cyclic direction.
    🔗
    Lean (odd order)Lean (central 2-subgroup)Lean
    🔗

    Proof.
    Conjugation preserves order, whereas \(|t^2|=|t|/\gcd(2,|t|)\text{,}\) so \(|t|\) is odd. Let \(I=\langle t\rangle\) and suppose \(sI\) has order \(n\text{.}\) Then \(s^n=t^m\text{.}\) Since \(s^n\) commutes with \(s\text{,}\) the relation \(t^s=t^2\) gives \(t^m=t^{2m}\text{,}\) hence \(m\equiv0\pmod{|t|}\text{.}\) Thus the extension splits.
    🔗
    If \(N\) is a normal \(2\)-subgroup, then \(N\cap I=1\) and \([N,I]\le N\cap I=1\text{.}\) Hence \(N\) centralizes \(I\text{.}\) It is therefore contained in the \(2\)-primary part of the kernel of the Frobenius action on \(I\text{,}\) which is central and unramified.
    🔗
    🔗
    The first comparison between the two sources happens on tame quotients, where both collapse onto the same explicit group.
    🔗

    Proposition 3.2. Common tame quotient.

    There are canonical isomorphisms
    \begin{equation*} \notn{GA}{\GA}/\notn{WA}{\WA}\cong \notn{TA}{\TA}\cong \notn{GQ}{\GQ}/\notn{WF}{\WF}, \end{equation*}
    where \(\notn{WF}{\WF}\) is wild inertia.
    🔗
    Lean (Γ_A)Lean (local)Lean (structure)Lean
    🔗

    Proof.
    In the quotient by \(\notn{WA}{\WA}\text{,}\) the elements \(\notn{x0}{x_0},\notnfar{x1}{x_1}\) vanish. By Lemma 3.1, \(\notn{tau}{\tau}\) has odd order in every finite quotient, so \(\notn{tau}{\tau}^\notn{w}{\w}=1\text{.}\) Hence \(u_i=d_0=z_0=c_0=d_g=h_c=h_0=1\text{;}\) the words \(\sigma_2\) and \(g_0\) may remain nontrivial, but they only conjugate the identity. The wild relation therefore disappears. For the local group, the tame quotient has pro-prime-to-\(2\) cyclic inertia and procyclic unramified quotient; geometric Frobenius acts on tame inertia by \(x\mapsto x^2\text{.}\) With \(x^g=g^{-1}xg\text{,}\) this is precisely the relation \(\notn{tau}{\tau}^\notn{sigma}{\sigma}=\notn{tau}{\tau}^2\text{.}\)
    🔗
    🔗
    The description of the tame quotient is Iwasawa’s; see [NSW, Theorem (7.5.3)] and [Ser79, Chapter IV].
    🔗

    Lemma 3.3. The wild subgroup is the characteristic \(2\)-core.

    The tame group \(\notn{TA}{\TA}\) has no nontrivial closed normal pro-\(2\) subgroup. Consequently
    \begin{equation*} O_2(\notn{GA}{\GA})=\notn{WA}{\WA}, \qquad O_2(\notn{GQ}{\GQ})=\notn{WF}{\WF}. \end{equation*}
    In particular, the marked wild subgroups of the two sources are characteristic.
    🔗
    Lean (trivial images)Lean (maximality)Lean
    🔗

    Proof.
    Let \(I=\overline{\langle\notn{tau}{\tau}\rangle}\triangleleft\notn{TA}{\TA}\) be tame inertia; it is pro-odd. If \(N\triangleleft\notn{TA}{\TA}\) is pro-\(2\text{,}\) then
    \begin{equation*} N\cap I=1, \qquad [N,I]\le N\cap I=1, \end{equation*}
    so \(N\) centralizes \(I\text{.}\) Its image in \(\notn{TA}{\TA}/I\cong\widehat{\mathbb{Z}}\) lies in the \(2\)-primary factor and has a \(2\)-adic geometric Frobenius coordinate \(a\in\mathbb{Z}_2\text{.}\) For every \(m\ge1\text{,}\) use the finite inertia quotient of order
    \begin{equation*} e_m=2^{2^m}-1. \end{equation*}
    Centrality forces \(2^a\equiv1\pmod {e_m}\text{.}\) The order of \(2\) modulo \(e_m\) is exactly \(2^m\text{,}\) and hence \(a\in2^m\mathbb{Z}_2\) for every \(m\text{.}\) Thus \(a=0\text{,}\) so \(N\le I\text{,}\) and therefore \(N=1\text{.}\)
    🔗
    The subgroup \(\notn{WA}{\WA}\) is normal pro-\(2\) and \(\notn{GA}{\GA}/\notn{WA}{\WA}\cong\notn{TA}{\TA}\text{.}\) Every normal pro-\(2\) subgroup of \(\notn{GA}{\GA}\) maps trivially to \(\notn{TA}{\TA}\) and is contained in \(\notn{WA}{\WA}\text{.}\) This proves \(O_2(\notn{GA}{\GA})=\notn{WA}{\WA}\text{.}\) The identical argument applied to \(1\to\notn{WF}{\WF}\to\notn{GQ}{\GQ}\to\notn{TA}{\TA}\to1\) gives the local assertion.
    🔗
    🔗

    Subsection 3.1 The standard rank-three dyadic Demushkin group

    Labute’s classification identifies \(G_{\Qtwo}(2)\) with the group below as an abstract pro-\(2\) group, but it does not choose an isomorphism preserving the full unramified character. An abstract identification is insufficient because the tame and pro-\(2\) quotients must agree over their common quotient \(\mathbb{Z}_2\text{.}\) The canonical Demushkin orientation supplies the additional rigidity: together with the unramified character, it separates the three summands of the abelianization.
    🔗
    Put
    \begin{equation} \notn{D0}{D_0}= \left\langle \notn{Agen}{A},\notn{Sgen}{S},\notn{Ygen}{Y}\;\middle|\;\notn{Agen}{A}^2\notn{Sgen}{S}^4[\notn{Sgen}{S},\notn{Ygen}{Y}]=1 \right\rangle_{\mathrm{pro}-2}\tag{3.1} \end{equation}
    and
    \begin{equation} \notn{Bab}{B_{\mathrm{ab}}}=\notn{D0}{D_0}^{\mathrm{ab}} =\left\langle \notn{barA}{\bar A},\notn{barS}{\bar S},\notn{barY}{\bar Y}\;\middle|\; 2\notn{barA}{\bar A}+4\notn{barS}{\bar S}=0\right\rangle_{\mathbb{Z}_2}.\tag{3.2} \end{equation}
    Let
    \begin{equation} \notn{tTors}{t}=\notn{barA}{\bar A}+2\notn{barS}{\bar S}, \qquad \notn{eta}{\eta}=(-3)^{-1}\in\mathbb{Z}_2^\times.\tag{3.3} \end{equation}
    Then
    \begin{equation} \notn{Bab}{B_{\mathrm{ab}}}=C_2\notn{tTors}{t}\oplus\mathbb{Z}_2\notn{barS}{\bar S}\oplus\mathbb{Z}_2\notn{barY}{\bar Y}.\tag{3.4} \end{equation}
    🔗

    Lemma 3.4. Standard dyadic group and its orientation.

    The group \(\notn{D0}{D_0}\) is the standard rank-three, \(q=2\) Demushkin group, and \(G_{\Qtwo}(2)\) is abstractly isomorphic to \(\notn{D0}{D_0}\text{.}\) The canonical Demushkin orientation of \(\notn{D0}{D_0}\) factors through \(\notn{Bab}{B_{\mathrm{ab}}}\) and is the character
    \begin{equation} \notn{chi0}{\chi_0}(\notn{tTors}{t})=-1, \qquad \notn{chi0}{\chi_0}(\notn{barS}{\bar S})=1, \qquad \notn{chi0}{\chi_0}(\notn{barY}{\bar Y})=\notn{eta}{\eta}.\tag{3.5} \end{equation}
    Equivalently,
    \begin{equation*} \notn{chi0}{\chi_0}(\notn{barA}{\bar A})=-1, \qquad \notn{chi0}{\chi_0}(\notn{barS}{\bar S})=1, \qquad \notn{chi0}{\chi_0}(\notn{barY}{\bar Y})=(-3)^{-1}. \end{equation*}
    🔗
    🔗

    Proof.
    The presentation (3.1) is the odd-rank dyadic case of Labute’s classification, with parameter \(q=2\) and secondary exponent \(4\text{;}\) see [Lab, Theorem 8]. The canonical character for the odd-rank normal form is computed in [Lab, Theorem 4, case (2)]: for the relation \(\notnfar{x1}{x_1}^2x_2^{2^f}[x_2,x_3]\) it takes the values \(-1,1,(1-2^f)^{-1}\) on \(\notnfar{x1}{x_1},x_2,x_3\text{.}\) With \(f=2\) and the standing commutator convention, this gives \(-1,1,(1-4)^{-1}=(-3)^{-1}\) on \(\notn{Agen}{A},\notn{Sgen}{S},\notn{Ygen}{Y}\text{,}\) respectively. The maximal pro-\(2\) Galois group of \(\notn{Qtwo}{\Qtwo}\) is the rank-three local Demushkin group with these parameters, so the abstract isomorphism follows from the same classification.
    🔗
    🔗

    Lemma 3.5. Marked abelianization, orientation, and initial form.

    Use arithmetic local reciprocity \(\notn{rec}{\rec}\text{,}\) normalized so that \(\notn{rec}{\rec}(2)\) is arithmetic Frobenius, and normalize \(\notn{nuur}{\nu_{\mathrm{ur}}}\) geometrically. Put
    \begin{equation*} \notn{bars}{\bar s}=\notn{rec}{\rec}(2)^{-1}=\notn{rec}{\rec}(1/2),\qquad \bar\epsilon=\notn{rec}{\rec}(-1),\qquad \notn{bary}{\bar y}=\notn{rec}{\rec}(-3),\qquad \notn{bara}{\bar a}=\bar\epsilon\notn{bars}{\bar s}^{-2}=\notn{rec}{\rec}(-4). \end{equation*}
    Then the pro-\(2\) abelianization of \(\notnfar{Dloc}{D_{\mathrm{loc}}}=G_{\Qtwo}(2)\) is identified with \(\notn{Bab}{B_{\mathrm{ab}}}\) by
    \begin{equation*} \notn{barA}{\bar A}\longmapsto\notn{bara}{\bar a}, \qquad \notn{barS}{\bar S}\longmapsto\notn{bars}{\bar s}, \qquad \notn{barY}{\bar Y}\longmapsto\notn{bary}{\bar y}. \end{equation*}
    Under this identification,
    \begin{equation} \notn{nuur}{\nu_{\mathrm{ur}}}(\notn{bara}{\bar a},\notn{bars}{\bar s},\notn{bary}{\bar y})=(-2,1,0), \qquad \notn{chiloc}{\chi_{\mathrm{loc}}}(\notn{bara}{\bar a},\notn{bars}{\bar s},\notn{bary}{\bar y})=(-1,1,(-3)^{-1}),\tag{3.6} \end{equation}
    where \(\notn{chiloc}{\chi_{\mathrm{loc}}}\) is the canonical Demushkin orientation. In the basis of \(H^1(\notnfar{Dloc}{D_{\mathrm{loc}}},\F_2)\) dual to \((\notn{bara}{\bar a},\notn{bars}{\bar s},\notn{bary}{\bar y})\text{,}\) the Demushkin quadratic initial form is
    \begin{equation*} \alpha^2+\beta\gamma+\gamma\beta. \end{equation*}
    Consequently a Demushkin relator for lifts of these classes has the same quadratic initial form as
    \begin{equation*} \notn{r0}{r_0}=\notn{Agen}{A}^2\notn{Sgen}{S}^4[\notn{Sgen}{S},\notn{Ygen}{Y}], \end{equation*}
    namely \(\notn{Agen}{A}^2+[\notn{Sgen}{S},\notn{Ygen}{Y}]\) in degree two. Moreover the pair
    \begin{equation*} (\notn{nuur}{\nu_{\mathrm{ur}}},\notn{chiloc}{\chi_{\mathrm{loc}}}):\notn{Bab}{B_{\mathrm{ab}}}\longrightarrow \mathbb{Z}_2\times\mathbb{Z}_2^\times \end{equation*}
    is injective.
    🔗
    Lean (injectivity)Lean (abelianization)Lean (Hilbert ledger)
    🔗

    Proof.
    We compute successively the unramified character, the cyclotomic orientation, the quadratic initial form, and the injectivity of the two-character marking.
    🔗
    Since \(\notn{nuur}{\nu_{\mathrm{ur}}}\) is normalized by geometric Frobenius while \(\notn{rec}{\rec}(2)\) is arithmetic Frobenius, one has \(\notn{nuur}{\nu_{\mathrm{ur}}}(\notn{rec}{\rec}(2))=-1\text{.}\) Hence
    \begin{equation*} \notn{nuur}{\nu_{\mathrm{ur}}}(\notn{bars}{\bar s})=1, \qquad \notn{nuur}{\nu_{\mathrm{ur}}}(\notn{bary}{\bar y})=0, \qquad \notn{nuur}{\nu_{\mathrm{ur}}}(\notn{bara}{\bar a})=-2. \end{equation*}
    The pro-\(2\) completion of \(\notn{Qtwo}{\Qtwo}^\times\) is
    \begin{equation*} \widehat{\notn{Qtwo}{\Qtwo}^\times}^{(2)} \cong \langle 2\rangle_{\mathbb{Z}_2} \oplus \langle -1\rangle_{C_2} \oplus \langle -3\rangle_{\mathbb{Z}_2}. \end{equation*}
    The single relation among \(\notn{barA}{\bar A},\notn{barS}{\bar S},\notn{barY}{\bar Y}\) is
    \begin{equation*} \notn{bara}{\bar a}^2\notn{bars}{\bar s}^4 =\notn{rec}{\rec}((-4)^2(1/2)^4)=\notn{rec}{\rec}(1)=1, \end{equation*}
    that is, additively, \(2\notn{barA}{\bar A}+4\notn{barS}{\bar S}=0\text{.}\)
    🔗
    For a local Demushkin group the canonical orientation is the \(2\)-adic cyclotomic character. With the reciprocity convention above, local reciprocity gives
    \begin{equation*} \notn{chiloc}{\chi_{\mathrm{loc}}}(\notn{rec}{\rec}(u))=u^{-1}\qquad(u\in\mathbb{Z}_2^\times), \end{equation*}
    while the uniformizer component acts trivially on the totally ramified extension \(\notn{Qtwo}{\Qtwo}(\mu_{2^\infty})/\notn{Qtwo}{\Qtwo}\text{.}\) This proves the orientation row in (3.6).
    🔗
    Modulo squares, the classes are
    \begin{equation*} \notn{bara}{\bar a}\equiv[-1],\qquad \notn{bars}{\bar s}\equiv[2],\qquad \notn{bary}{\bar y}\equiv[-3]. \end{equation*}
    For odd units \(u,v\text{,}\) write
    \begin{equation*} \notn{epsu}{\epsilon}(u)=\frac{u-1}{2}\bmod 2, \qquad \notn{omgu}{\omega}(u)=\frac{u^2-1}{8}\bmod 2. \end{equation*}
    The dyadic Hilbert-symbol formula
    \begin{equation*} (2^\alpha u,2^\beta v)_2 =(-1)^{\notn{epsu}{\epsilon}(u)\notn{epsu}{\epsilon}(v)+\alpha\notn{omgu}{\omega}(v)+\beta\notn{omgu}{\omega}(u)} \end{equation*}
    gives, in the square-class basis \((-1,2,-3)\text{,}\)
    \begin{equation*} (-1,-1)_2=-1, \qquad (2,-3)_2=-1, \end{equation*}
    with all other pairings among these basis elements trivial, up to symmetry. Under Kummer theory, cup product is the Hilbert symbol. Thus the dual basis has Bockstein/cup initial form \(\alpha^2+\beta\gamma+\gamma\beta\text{,}\) which is exactly the degree-two initial form of \(\notn{Agen}{A}^2\notn{Sgen}{S}^4[\notn{Sgen}{S},\notn{Ygen}{Y}]\text{.}\)
    🔗
    Finally, in the decomposition (3.4),
    \begin{equation*} \notn{nuur}{\nu_{\mathrm{ur}}}(\notn{tTors}{t},\notn{barS}{\bar S},\notn{barY}{\bar Y})=(0,1,0), \qquad \notn{chiloc}{\chi_{\mathrm{loc}}}(\notn{tTors}{t},\notn{barS}{\bar S},\notn{barY}{\bar Y})=(-1,1,\notn{eta}{\eta}). \end{equation*}
    The element \(\notn{eta}{\eta}\) topologically generates \(1+4\mathbb{Z}_2\text{,}\) because \(v_2(\notn{eta}{\eta}-1)=2\text{.}\) The two displayed characters therefore detect the three direct summands of (3.4), proving injectivity.
    🔗
    🔗
    The Demushkin classification underlying this normalization goes back to [Ser63] and [Lab]; the local reciprocity inputs are standard, see [NSW, Chapter VII §7.1] and [Ser79, Chapters XI–XIII].
    🔗

    Remark 3.6. Why the orientation cannot be omitted.

    An un-oriented marked-relator normalization with only the abelianized relation and quadratic initial form is false. Let \(F=\langle \notn{Agen}{A},\notn{Sgen}{S},\notn{Ygen}{Y}\rangle_{\mathrm{pro}-2}\) and define
    \begin{equation*} \psi(\notn{Agen}{A})=AY^{-4}, \qquad \psi(\notn{Sgen}{S})=SY^2, \qquad \psi(\notn{Ygen}{Y})=\notn{Ygen}{Y}. \end{equation*}
    This is an automorphism, with inverse \(\notn{Agen}{A}\mapsto AY^4\text{,}\) \(\notn{Sgen}{S}\mapsto SY^{-2}\text{,}\) \(\notn{Ygen}{Y}\mapsto \notn{Ygen}{Y}\text{.}\) For \(\notn{r0}{r_0}=\notn{Agen}{A}^2\notn{Sgen}{S}^4[\notn{Sgen}{S},\notn{Ygen}{Y}]\text{,}\) put \(r=\psi^{-1}(\notn{r0}{r_0})\text{.}\) On the free abelianization,
    \begin{equation*} \psi_{\mathrm{ab}}(2\notn{barA}{\bar A}+4\notn{barS}{\bar S}) =2(\notn{barA}{\bar A}-4\notn{barY}{\bar Y})+4(\notn{barS}{\bar S}+2\notn{barY}{\bar Y}) =2\notn{barA}{\bar A}+4\notn{barS}{\bar S}. \end{equation*}
    Moreover
    \begin{equation*} r=(AY^4)^2(SY^{-2})^4[SY^{-2},\notn{Ygen}{Y}], \end{equation*}
    so, modulo the third Zassenhaus term, its initial form is \(\notn{Agen}{A}^2+[\notn{Sgen}{S},\notn{Ygen}{Y}]\text{.}\) Thus \(r\) has the same abelianized relation and quadratic initial form as \(\notn{r0}{r_0}\text{,}\) and its quotient is abstractly \(\notn{D0}{D_0}\text{.}\) However, under the isomorphism induced by \(\psi\text{,}\) the transported canonical orientation takes \(\notn{Sgen}{S}\) to \(\notn{eta}{\eta}^2\ne1\text{.}\) Therefore no isomorphism from this quotient to \(\notn{D0}{D_0}\) which is the identity on \(\notn{Bab}{B_{\mathrm{ab}}}\) can exist. The orientation-preserving lifting statement Proposition 3.9, rather than the false un-oriented normalization, is the exact structural input needed below.
    🔗
    Lean
    🔗
    🔗

    Subsection 3.2 Automorphisms preserving the orientation

    To correct the action of an abstract isomorphism on \(\notn{Bab}{B_{\mathrm{ab}}}\text{,}\) it is enough to show that every automorphism of \(\notn{Bab}{B_{\mathrm{ab}}}\) preserving \(\notn{chi0}{\chi_0}\) is induced by an automorphism of \(\notn{D0}{D_0}\text{.}\)
    🔗

    Lemma 3.7. Cyclotomic powering of the three peripheral classes.

    Let
    \begin{equation*} \notn{Deltatame}{\Delta}=\langle \notn{Pperi}{P},\notn{Tperi}{T}\rangle_{\mathrm{pro}-2}, \qquad \notn{Cperi}{C}=(PT)^{-1}. \end{equation*}
    For every \(u\in\mathbb{Z}_2^\times\) there are an automorphism \(\notn{varphiu}{\varphi_u}\in\Aut(\notn{Deltatame}{\Delta})\) and elements \(\notn{cP}{c_P},\notn{cT}{c_T},\notn{cC}{c_C}\in\Delta\) such that
    \begin{equation} \notn{varphiu}{\varphi_u}(\notn{Pperi}{P})=\notn{cP}{c_P}^{-1}\notn{Pperi}{P}^u \notn{cP}{c_P}, \qquad \notn{varphiu}{\varphi_u}(\notn{Tperi}{T})=\notn{cT}{c_T}^{-1}\notn{Tperi}{T}^u \notn{cT}{c_T}, \qquad \notn{varphiu}{\varphi_u}(\notn{Cperi}{C})=\notn{cC}{c_C}^{-1}\notn{Cperi}{C}^u \notn{cC}{c_C}.\tag{3.7} \end{equation}
    🔗
    Lean
    🔗

    Proof.
    We obtain the required outer automorphism from the arithmetic Galois action and then choose a representative that realizes the three peripheral conjugacy classes simultaneously.
    🔗
    Identify \(\notn{Deltatame}{\Delta}\) with the maximal pro-\(2\) geometric fundamental group of
    \begin{equation*} X=\mathbb{P}^1_{\mathbb{Q}}\setminus\{0,1,\infty\}, \end{equation*}
    with \(\notn{Pperi}{P},\notn{Tperi}{T},\notn{Cperi}{C}\) the three compatible peripheral inertia generators. The Galois action on the geometric fundamental group gives
    \begin{equation*} G_{\mathbb{Q}}\longrightarrow\operatorname{Out}(\notn{Deltatame}{\Delta}). \end{equation*}
    The \(2\)-adic cyclotomic character is surjective, since
    \begin{equation*} \operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb{Q}(\mu_{2^\infty})/\mathbb{Q}) \cong\mathbb{Z}_2^\times. \end{equation*}
    Each of the three cusps is rational, so its peripheral conjugacy class is preserved. The corresponding decomposition group acts on the procyclic inertia group through the cyclotomic character; see [Sti, Section 3.3 and Definition 37]. Concretely, if \(z\) is a local parameter and a chosen inertia generator sends \(z^{1/2^n}\) to \(\zeta_{2^n}z^{1/2^n}\text{,}\) then the arithmetic action of \(g\) replaces \(\zeta_{2^n}\) by \(\zeta_{2^n}^{\chi_2(g)}\text{.}\) With the opposite convention for representing the outer action, the exponent is \(\chi_2(g)^{-1}\text{.}\) Accordingly choose \(g\) with \(\chi_2(g)=u\) in the first convention and with \(\chi_2(g)=u^{-1}\) in the second. In either convention the resulting outer automorphism sends each peripheral generator to a conjugate of its \(u\)-th power. Choosing a representative of the outer class gives (3.7).
    🔗
    🔗

    Lemma 3.8. Square-root and HNN lifting.

    For every \(u\in\mathbb{Z}_2^\times\) there is an automorphism \(\notn{Psiu}{\Psi_u}\in\Aut(\notn{D0}{D_0})\) such that, on \(\notn{Bab}{B_{\mathrm{ab}}}\text{,}\)
    \begin{equation} \notn{barA}{\bar A}\longmapsto u\notn{barA}{\bar A}, \qquad \notn{barS}{\bar S}\longmapsto u\notn{barS}{\bar S}.\tag{3.8} \end{equation}
    🔗
    Lean (classification)Lean (lift)
    🔗

    Proof.
    The proof first lifts peripheral powering across the square-root relation, then transports the lift to the free pro-\(2\) group on \(\notnfar{Sgen}{S},\notn{Agen}{A}\text{,}\) and finally extends it over the HNN stable letter \(\notn{Ygen}{Y}\text{.}\)
    🔗
    Start with \(\notn{varphiu}{\varphi_u}\) and the conjugators from Lemma 3.7. Consider
    \begin{equation*} \notn{Esq}{E_\square}= \left\langle \notn{Pperi}{P},\notn{Tperi}{T},\notn{Agen}{A}\;\middle|\;PTA^2=1\right\rangle_{\mathrm{pro}-2} \cong\langle \notn{Pperi}{P},\notn{Agen}{A}\rangle_{\mathrm{pro}-2}, \qquad \notn{Cperi}{C}=\notn{Agen}{A}^2. \end{equation*}
    View the words \(\notn{cP}{c_P},\notn{cT}{c_T},\notn{cC}{c_C}\) in \(\notn{Esq}{E_\square}\) via \(\notn{Pperi}{P},\notn{Tperi}{T}\text{,}\) and define
    \begin{equation*} \notn{Pperi}{P}\longmapsto\notn{varphiu}{\varphi_u}(\notn{Pperi}{P}), \qquad \notn{Tperi}{T}\longmapsto\notn{varphiu}{\varphi_u}(\notn{Tperi}{T}), \qquad \notn{Agen}{A}\longmapsto \notn{cC}{c_C}^{-1}\notn{Agen}{A}^u \notn{cC}{c_C}. \end{equation*}
    The defining relation is preserved, because
    \begin{equation*} (\notn{cC}{c_C}^{-1}\notn{Agen}{A}^u \notn{cC}{c_C})^2 =\notn{cC}{c_C}^{-1}\notn{Cperi}{C}^u \notn{cC}{c_C} =\notn{varphiu}{\varphi_u}(\notn{Cperi}{C}) =(\notn{varphiu}{\varphi_u}(\notn{Pperi}{P})\notn{varphiu}{\varphi_u}(\notn{Tperi}{T}))^{-1}. \end{equation*}
    Modulo the Frattini subgroup, the free basis \(\notn{Pperi}{P},\notn{Agen}{A}\) is sent to \(u\bar P,u\notn{barA}{\bar A}\text{,}\) hence to \(\bar P,\notn{barA}{\bar A}\text{.}\) The pro-\(2\) Burnside basis theorem and Hopficity therefore show that this endomorphism is an automorphism; call it \(\notn{thetau}{\theta_u}\text{.}\)
    🔗
    In the free pro-\(2\) group \(\notn{FSA}{F_{S,A}}=\langle \notnfar{Sgen}{S},\notn{Agen}{A}\rangle_{\mathrm{pro}-2}\) put
    \begin{equation*} \notn{Pperi}{P}=\notnfar{Sgen}{S}^3, \qquad \notn{Tperi}{T}=\notnfar{Sgen}{S}^{-3}\notn{Agen}{A}^{-2}. \end{equation*}
    Since \(3\in\mathbb{Z}_2^\times\text{,}\) the pair \(\notn{Pperi}{P},\notn{Agen}{A}\) is again a free basis of \(\notn{FSA}{F_{S,A}}\text{,}\) and \(PTA^2=1\text{.}\) For every odd integer \(m\text{,}\) the power map \(x\mapsto x^m\) is bijective on a pro-\(2\) group, with inverse \(x\mapsto x^{m^{-1}}\) for \(m^{-1}\in\mathbb{Z}_2^\times\text{.}\) Comparing the unique cube roots of the two sides of (3.7) therefore gives
    \begin{equation*} \notn{thetau}{\theta_u}(\notnfar{Sgen}{S})=\notn{cP}{c_P}^{-1}\notnfar{Sgen}{S}^u \notn{cP}{c_P}, \qquad \notn{thetau}{\theta_u}(\notn{Tperi}{T})=\notn{cT}{c_T}^{-1}\notn{Tperi}{T}^u \notn{cT}{c_T}. \end{equation*}
    The relation of \(\notn{D0}{D_0}\) is equivalently
    \begin{equation} \notn{Ygen}{Y}^{-1}SY=\notn{Tperi}{T}, \qquad \notn{Tperi}{T}=\notnfar{Sgen}{S}^{-3}\notn{Agen}{A}^{-2}.\tag{3.9} \end{equation}
    Define an endomorphism of the presentation (3.9) by
    \begin{equation*} \notn{Psiu}{\Psi_u}|_E=\notn{thetau}{\theta_u}, \qquad \notn{Psiu}{\Psi_u}(\notn{Ygen}{Y})=\notn{cP}{c_P}^{-1}\notn{Ygen}{Y}\notn{cT}{c_T}. \end{equation*}
    Then
    \begin{equation*} \notn{Psiu}{\Psi_u}(\notn{Ygen}{Y})^{-1}\notn{Psiu}{\Psi_u}(\notnfar{Sgen}{S})\notn{Psiu}{\Psi_u}(\notn{Ygen}{Y}) =\notn{cT}{c_T}^{-1}\notn{Ygen}{Y}^{-1}\notnfar{Sgen}{S}^uY\notn{cT}{c_T} =\notn{cT}{c_T}^{-1}\notn{Tperi}{T}^u \notn{cT}{c_T} =\notn{Psiu}{\Psi_u}(\notn{Tperi}{T}), \end{equation*}
    so the relation is respected. On the Frattini quotient of \(\notn{D0}{D_0}\text{,}\) the images of \(\notn{Agen}{A},\notnfar{Sgen}{S},\notn{Ygen}{Y}\) form a triangular basis with diagonal entries \(1,1,1\text{.}\) Consequently \(\notn{Psiu}{\Psi_u}\) is surjective and hence an automorphism. Its action on \(\notn{barA}{\bar A},\notn{barS}{\bar S}\) is (3.8).
    🔗
    🔗
    Orientation-preserving automorphisms of the abelianization must now be lifted to the full pro-\(2\) model.
    🔗

    Proposition 3.9. Lifting the orientation-preserving abelian automorphisms.

    The natural map
    \begin{equation} \Aut(\notn{D0}{D_0})\longrightarrow\Aut(\notn{Bab}{B_{\mathrm{ab}}},\notn{chi0}{\chi_0})\tag{3.10} \end{equation}
    is surjective. More explicitly, every element of \(\Aut(\notn{Bab}{B_{\mathrm{ab}}},\notn{chi0}{\chi_0})\) has the unique form
    \begin{equation} \notn{alphaub}{\alpha_{u,b}}: \quad \notn{tTors}{t}\longmapsto \notn{tTors}{t}, \qquad \notn{barS}{\bar S}\longmapsto u\notn{barS}{\bar S}, \qquad \notn{barY}{\bar Y}\longmapsto\notn{barY}{\bar Y}+b\notn{barS}{\bar S},\tag{3.11} \end{equation}
    with \(u\in\mathbb{Z}_2^\times\) and \(b\in\mathbb{Z}_2\text{,}\) and every \(\notn{alphaub}{\alpha_{u,b}}\) lifts to \(\Aut(\notn{D0}{D_0})\text{.}\)
    🔗
    🔗

    Proof.
    We first determine the orientation-preserving automorphisms of the abelianization, then realize their unit-scaling part, and finally realize the remaining shear.
    🔗
    Because \(v_2(\notn{eta}{\eta}-1)=2\text{,}\) the element \(\notn{eta}{\eta}\) topologically generates \(1+4\mathbb{Z}_2\text{.}\) From (3.4) and (3.5) one obtains
    \begin{equation*} \ker\notn{chi0}{\chi_0}=\mathbb{Z}_2\notn{barS}{\bar S}. \end{equation*}
    The torsion subgroup of \(\notn{Bab}{B_{\mathrm{ab}}}\) is the order-two group generated by \(\notn{tTors}{t}\text{.}\) Hence an orientation-preserving automorphism fixes \(\notn{tTors}{t}\text{,}\) sends \(\notn{barS}{\bar S}\) to \(u\notn{barS}{\bar S}\) for a unique unit \(u\text{,}\) and sends \(\notn{barY}{\bar Y}\) to \(\notn{barY}{\bar Y}+b\notn{barS}{\bar S}\) for a unique \(b\text{.}\) Conversely, every map (3.11) is an orientation-preserving automorphism of \(\notn{Bab}{B_{\mathrm{ab}}}\text{.}\)
    🔗
    In more detail: the fact that the coefficient \(u\) is a unit is not an extra assumption in the classification. Applying the same row extraction to an automorphism and to its inverse produces coefficients \(u\) and \(u'\) with \(uu'=1\text{.}\) Preservation of the order-two element \(t=\bar A+2\bar S\) then forces the \(\bar A\)-row once the \(\bar S\)-row is known.
    🔗
    The automorphism \(\notn{Psiu}{\Psi_u}\) of Lemma 3.8 sends \(\notn{barA}{\bar A},\notn{barS}{\bar S}\) to \(u\notn{barA}{\bar A},u\notn{barS}{\bar S}\text{,}\) so it fixes \(\notn{tTors}{t}=\notn{barA}{\bar A}+2\notn{barS}{\bar S}\) and sends \(\notn{barS}{\bar S}\) to \(u\notn{barS}{\bar S}\text{.}\) The canonical orientation is the action on the dualizing module and is therefore preserved by every automorphism of \(\notn{D0}{D_0}\text{.}\) Thus \(\notn{Psiu}{\Psi_u}\) induces \(\alpha_{u,b(u)}\) for some \(b(u)\in\mathbb{Z}_2\text{.}\)
    🔗
    For the lift, the formal proof makes a small coordinate correction explicit. If \(\Psi_u\) sends \(\bar Y\) to \(\bar Y+c(u)\bar S\text{,}\) then composing with a shear of parameter \(b'\) contributes \(ub'\text{,}\) not \(b'\text{,}\) after the unit scaling. Thus one takes \(b'=(b-c(u))u^{-1}\text{.}\) The inverse shear has parameter \(-b'\text{,}\) so this construction gives an automorphism rather than only an endomorphism.
    🔗
    For \(b\in\mathbb{Z}_2\text{,}\) define
    \begin{equation} \notn{Thetab}{\Theta_b}(\notn{Agen}{A})=\notn{Agen}{A}^{\notnfar{Sgen}{S}^b}, \qquad \notn{Thetab}{\Theta_b}(\notnfar{Sgen}{S})=\notnfar{Sgen}{S}, \qquad \notn{Thetab}{\Theta_b}(\notn{Ygen}{Y})=YS^b,\tag{3.12} \end{equation}
    Here \(\notn{Agen}{A}^{\notnfar{Sgen}{S}^b}=(\notnfar{Sgen}{S}^b)^{-1}AS^b\) is conjugation, not the product \(AS^b\text{.}\) This is an automorphism of the free pro-\(2\) group on \(\notn{Agen}{A},\notnfar{Sgen}{S},\notn{Ygen}{Y}\text{,}\) with inverse \(\Theta_{-b}\text{.}\) Moreover
    \begin{equation*} [\notnfar{Sgen}{S},YS^b]=[\notnfar{Sgen}{S},\notn{Ygen}{Y}]^{\notnfar{Sgen}{S}^b}, \end{equation*}
    and therefore
    \begin{equation*} \notn{Thetab}{\Theta_b}(\notn{Agen}{A}^2\notnfar{Sgen}{S}^4[\notnfar{Sgen}{S},\notn{Ygen}{Y}]) =(\notn{Agen}{A}^2)^{\notnfar{Sgen}{S}^b}\notnfar{Sgen}{S}^4[\notnfar{Sgen}{S},\notn{Ygen}{Y}]^{\notnfar{Sgen}{S}^b} =(\notn{Agen}{A}^2\notnfar{Sgen}{S}^4[\notnfar{Sgen}{S},\notn{Ygen}{Y}])^{\notnfar{Sgen}{S}^b}. \end{equation*}
    It therefore descends to an automorphism of \(\notn{D0}{D_0}\text{,}\) inducing \(\alpha_{1,b}\text{.}\) The composite \(\notn{Thetab}{\Theta_{b-b(u)}}\circ\notn{Psiu}{\Psi_u}\) induces \(\notn{alphaub}{\alpha_{u,b}}\text{,}\) proving surjectivity.
    🔗
    🔗
    🔗

    Subsection 3.3 Matching the unramified marking

    The preceding surjectivity permits an arbitrary abstract isomorphism \(G_{\Qtwo}(2)\cong \notn{D0}{D_0}\) to be corrected so that it induces the identity on the marked abelianization \(\notn{Bab}{B_{\mathrm{ab}}}\text{.}\) The unramified character is then preserved integrally, not only after reduction modulo \(2\text{.}\)
    🔗

    Proof of Proposition 1.1.
    By Lemma 3.4, choose an abstract isomorphism
    \begin{equation*} f:\notnfar{Dloc}{D_{\mathrm{loc}}}\xrightarrow{\sim}\notn{D0}{D_0}. \end{equation*}
    Use Lemma 3.5 to identify \(\notnfar{Dloc}{D_{\mathrm{loc}}}^{\mathrm{ab}}\) with \(\notn{Bab}{B_{\mathrm{ab}}}\text{,}\) and use (3.2) for \(\notn{D0}{D_0}^{\mathrm{ab}}\text{.}\) Canonical orientations are functorial under group isomorphisms. The orientation row (3.6) and (3.5) therefore imply
    \begin{equation*} \notn{chi0}{\chi_0}\circ f_{\mathrm{ab}}=\notn{chiloc}{\chi_{\mathrm{loc}}}=\notn{chi0}{\chi_0}. \end{equation*}
    Thus \(f_{\mathrm{ab}}\in\Aut(\notn{Bab}{B_{\mathrm{ab}}},\notn{chi0}{\chi_0})\text{.}\) By Proposition 3.9, choose \(\gamma\in\Aut(\notn{D0}{D_0})\) with
    \begin{equation*} \gamma_{\mathrm{ab}}=f_{\mathrm{ab}}^{-1}. \end{equation*}
    Then
    \begin{equation*} \beta=\gamma\circ f:\notnfar{Dloc}{D_{\mathrm{loc}}}\xrightarrow{\sim}\notn{D0}{D_0} \end{equation*}
    induces the identity on the marked abelianization \(\notn{Bab}{B_{\mathrm{ab}}}\text{.}\)
    🔗
    Set
    \begin{equation*} a=\beta^{-1}(\notn{Agen}{A}), \qquad s=\beta^{-1}(\notnfar{Sgen}{S}), \qquad y=\beta^{-1}(\notn{Ygen}{Y}). \end{equation*}
    These elements topologically generate \(\notnfar{Dloc}{D_{\mathrm{loc}}}\text{,}\) satisfy \(a^2s^4[s,y]=1\text{,}\) and have the prescribed abelianized classes. Hence
    \begin{equation*} \notn{nuur}{\nu_{\mathrm{ur}}}(a,s,y)=(-2,1,0), \end{equation*}
    which proves Proposition 1.1.
    🔗
    🔗
    🔗

    Subsection 3.4 The maximal pro-\(2\) quotient of the candidate

    Proposition 3.10. Maximal pro-\(2\) quotient.

    The maximal pro-\(2\) quotient of \(\notn{GA}{\GA}\) is
    \begin{equation} \notn{Pi}{\Pi}= \left\langle \notn{sigma}{\sigma},\notn{x0}{x_0},\notnfar{x1}{x_1}\;\middle|\; \notn{x0}{x_0}^{\notn{sigma}{\sigma}^2}\notn{x0}{x_0}[\notnfar{x1}{x_1},\notn{sigma}{\sigma}]=1 \right\rangle_{\mathrm{pro-}2}.\tag{3.13} \end{equation}
    The group \(\notn{Pi}{\Pi}\) is abstractly isomorphic to \(G_{\Qtwo}(2)\text{.}\) Equipped with
    \begin{equation} \notn{nu2}{\nu_2}:\notn{Pi}{\Pi}\twoheadrightarrow\mathbb{Z}_2, \qquad \notn{nu2}{\nu_2}(\notn{sigma}{\sigma})=1,\quad \notn{nu2}{\nu_2}(\notn{x0}{x_0})=\notn{nu2}{\nu_2}(\notnfar{x1}{x_1})=0,\tag{3.14} \end{equation}
    it is isomorphic to the fully unramified marked pair \((G_{\Qtwo}(2),\notn{nuur}{\nu_{\mathrm{ur}}})\text{.}\)
    🔗
    Lean (Γ_A, proved)Lean (local, proved)Lean (Γ_A)Lean (local)Lean
    🔗

    Proof.
    In a finite \(2\)-group quotient, Lemma 3.1 forces \(\notn{tau}{\tau}=1\text{,}\) and \(\notn{w}{\w}\) acts as the identity. Hence
    \begin{equation*} u_i=x_i,\qquad d_0=1,\qquad c_0=1,\qquad g_0=\notn{sigma}{\sigma}^2,\qquad d_g=h_c=1, \end{equation*}
    and
    \begin{equation*} h_0=\notn{x0}{x_0}^{\notn{sigma}{\sigma}^2}\notn{x0}{x_0}. \end{equation*}
    Moreover
    \begin{equation*} u_1^{-1}\notnfar{x1}{x_1}^\notn{sigma}{\sigma}=\notnfar{x1}{x_1}^{-1}\notnfar{x1}{x_1}^\notn{sigma}{\sigma}=[\notnfar{x1}{x_1},\notn{sigma}{\sigma}]. \end{equation*}
    Thus (1.6) becomes precisely the relator in (3.13). Conversely, every finite quotient of (3.13) is admissible after setting \(\notn{tau}{\tau}=1\text{.}\) The fully marked local identification is given by Corollary 3.12.
    🔗
    🔗

    Proposition 3.11. Nielsen transform to the pro-\(2\) boundary.

    For any pro-\(2\) group with topological generators \(a,s,y\) and unique defining relation
    \begin{equation} a^2s^4[s,y]=1,\tag{3.15} \end{equation}
    the Nielsen change
    \begin{equation} \notn{sigma}{\sigma}=s,\qquad \notnfar{x1}{x_1}=y,\qquad \notn{x0}{x_0}=s^{-2}a^{-1}\tag{3.16} \end{equation}
    changes the closed normal closure of the relator to that of
    \begin{equation} \notn{x0}{x_0}^{\notn{sigma}{\sigma}^2}\notn{x0}{x_0}[\notnfar{x1}{x_1},\notn{sigma}{\sigma}].\tag{3.17} \end{equation}
    Consequently Proposition 1.1 identifies \(\notn{Dpro2}{D}=G_{\Qtwo}(2)\) abstractly with \(\notn{Pi}{\Pi}\text{.}\)
    🔗
    Lean
    🔗

    Proof.
    Under (3.16), one has \(a=\notn{x0}{x_0}^{-1}\notn{sigma}{\sigma}^{-2}\) and therefore
    \begin{equation*} a^2s^4=\notn{x0}{x_0}^{-1}(\notn{x0}{x_0}^{-1})^{\notn{sigma}{\sigma}^2}. \end{equation*}
    Writing \(P=\notn{x0}{x_0}^{\notn{sigma}{\sigma}^2}\notn{x0}{x_0}\) and \(Q=[\notnfar{x1}{x_1},\notn{sigma}{\sigma}]\text{,}\) the inverse of the standard relator is \(QP\text{.}\) The words \(QP\) and \(PQ\) are cyclic conjugates, so they have the same closed normal closure. This proves the assertion.

    Corollary 3.12. Fully marked form.

    The generators furnished by Proposition 1.1 and transformed by (3.16) satisfy
    \begin{equation*} \notn{nuur}{\nu_{\mathrm{ur}}}(\notn{sigma}{\sigma})=1, \qquad \notn{nuur}{\nu_{\mathrm{ur}}}(\notn{x0}{x_0})=\notn{nuur}{\nu_{\mathrm{ur}}}(\notnfar{x1}{x_1})=0, \end{equation*}
    and (3.17) is the unique defining relation. Hence \((\notn{Dpro2}{D},\notn{nuur}{\nu_{\mathrm{ur}}})\cong(\notn{Pi}{\Pi},\notn{nu2}{\nu_2})\text{.}\)
    🔗
    Lean
    🔗

    Proof.
    The relation is Proposition 3.11. The values follow directly from (1.4):
    \begin{equation*} \notn{nuur}{\nu_{\mathrm{ur}}}(\notn{x0}{x_0}) =-2\notn{nuur}{\nu_{\mathrm{ur}}}(s)-\notn{nuur}{\nu_{\mathrm{ur}}}(a)=0. \end{equation*}

    Remark 3.13. The integral marking is not detected by the mod-\(2\) cup form.

    The more familiar unmarked Labute relator
    \begin{equation*} \notn{x0}{x_0}^2\notnfar{x1}{x_1}^4[\notnfar{x1}{x_1},\notn{sigma}{\sigma}] \end{equation*}
    has the same quadratic initial form \(b^2+ac+ca\) as (3.17). It does not, however, admit the marking

The Nielsen transformation (3.16) replaces that relator by (3.17). It has the same mod-\(2\) two-jet; its full unramified marking follows from Proposition 1.1.

    Section 4 The common tame–pro-\(2\) boundary and the global induction

    The compatible quotient maps obtained in Section 3 are assembled here into a single boundary condition. This produces the epimorphisms \(\notn{bGamma}{b_\Gamma}:\notn{GammaSrc}{\Gamma}\twoheadrightarrow\notn{bdry}{\bdry}\) and the finite targets on which the induction of Section 9 is carried out.
    🔗
    The tame quotient and the maximal pro-\(2\) quotient share the full unramified pro-\(2\) quotient:
    \begin{equation} \notnfar{TA}{\TA}\xrightarrow{\,\nu_{\mathrm t}\,}\mathbb{Z}_2 \xleftarrow{\,\notn{nu2}{\nu_2}\,}\notn{Pi}{\Pi}, \qquad \notn{bdry}{\bdry}=\notnfar{TA}{\TA}\times_{\mathbb{Z}_2}\notn{Pi}{\Pi}.\tag{4.1} \end{equation}
    The fibre product records the requirement that the two quotient maps have the same unramified coordinate. Thus their markings cannot be chosen independently, or merely matched after reduction modulo \(2\text{.}\) For \(\notn{GammaSrc}{\Gamma}\in\{\notn{GA}{\GA},\notn{GQ}{\GQ}\}\text{,}\) the compatible tame and maximal pro-\(2\) maps of Proposition 3.14 combine to an epimorphism
    \begin{equation} \notn{bGamma}{b_\Gamma}:\notn{GammaSrc}{\Gamma}\twoheadrightarrow\notn{bdry}{\bdry}.\tag{4.2} \end{equation}
    Surjectivity follows from profinite Goursat. Any common quotient of \(\notnfar{TA}{\TA}\) and the pro-\(2\) group \(\notn{Pi}{\Pi}\) is a pro-\(2\) quotient of \(\notnfar{TA}{\TA}\text{,}\) hence a quotient of its maximal pro-\(2\) quotient \(\mathbb{Z}_2\text{;}\) Proposition 3.14 shows that the full \(\mathbb{Z}_2\) quotient occurs.
    🔗
    Fix a finite tame quotient \(\notn{Htarget}{H}\text{,}\) an epimorphism \(\alpha:\notnfar{TA}{\TA}\twoheadrightarrow \notn{Htarget}{H}\text{,}\) an elementary abelian \(2\)-group \(\notn{Etarget}{E}\text{,}\) and a homomorphism \(\bar\psi:\notn{Pi}{\Pi}\to \notn{Etarget}{E}\text{.}\) They define
    \begin{equation} \beta:\notn{bdry}{\bdry}\longrightarrow \notn{Htarget}{H}\times \notn{Etarget}{E}, \qquad \beta(t,p)=(\alpha(t),\bar\psi(p)).\tag{4.3} \end{equation}
    🔗
    We compare only surjections that induce the fixed map to \(\notn{Htarget}{H}\) and the fixed elementary decoration in \(\notn{Etarget}{E}\text{.}\) A finite target carrying these two prescribed pieces of data will be called boundary-framed.
    🔗

    Definition 4.1. Boundary-framed marked target.

    Keep the frame data fixed above: the finite tame quotient \(\notn{Htarget}{H}\) with \(\alpha:\notnfar{TA}{\TA}\twoheadrightarrow \notn{Htarget}{H}\text{,}\) and the decoration group \(\notn{Etarget}{E}\text{,}\) an elementary abelian \(2\)-group (abelian of exponent dividing \(2\)), with \(\bar\psi:\notn{Pi}{\Pi}\to \notn{Etarget}{E}\text{.}\) A boundary-framed marked target is a tuple
    \begin{equation*} \notn{calY}{\mathcal Y}=(\notn{Ytarget}{Y},\notn{LY}{L_Y},\notn{piY}{\pi_Y},\notn{thetaY}{\theta_Y}) \end{equation*}
    where \(\notn{LY}{L_Y}\triangleleft \notn{Ytarget}{Y}\) is a finite \(2\)-group, \(\notn{piY}{\pi_Y}:\notn{Ytarget}{Y}\twoheadrightarrow \notn{Htarget}{H}\) has kernel \(\notn{LY}{L_Y}\text{,}\) and \(\notn{thetaY}{\theta_Y}:\notn{Ytarget}{Y}\to \notn{Etarget}{E}\) is a homomorphism. Put
    \begin{equation*} \notn{qY}{q_Y}=(\notn{piY}{\pi_Y},\notn{thetaY}{\theta_Y}):\notn{Ytarget}{Y}\longrightarrow \notn{Htarget}{H}\times \notn{Etarget}{E}. \end{equation*}
    For \(\notn{GammaSrc}{\Gamma}\in\{\notn{GA}{\GA},\notn{GQ}{\GQ}\}\) define
    \begin{equation} \notn{eGamma}{e_\Gamma}^\beta(\notn{calY}{\mathcal Y}) =\#\{f:\notn{GammaSrc}{\Gamma}\twoheadrightarrow \notn{Ytarget}{Y}:q_Yf=\beta \notn{bGamma}{b_\Gamma}\}.\tag{4.4} \end{equation}
    🔗
    Lean
    🔗
    The tuple \(\notn{calY}{\mathcal Y}\) therefore fixes, on the same finite target, both the tame quotient \(\notn{Ytarget}{Y}/\notn{LY}{L_Y}\cong \notn{Htarget}{H}\) and the homomorphism \(\notn{Ytarget}{Y}\to \notn{Etarget}{E}\text{.}\) The equation \(q_Yf=\beta \notn{bGamma}{b_\Gamma}\) counts surjections inducing both prescribed maps. Since the wild subgroup is the kernel of the tame quotient, it also forces \(\notnfar{WA}{\WA}\) or \(\notnfar{WF}{\WF}\) into \(\notn{LY}{L_Y}\text{.}\)
    🔗
    An exact-image stratum consists of maps whose image is a specified subgroup \(J\text{,}\) rather than maps that merely land in \(J\text{.}\) If \(J\le \notn{Ytarget}{Y}\) projects onto \(\notn{Htarget}{H}\text{,}\) then
    \begin{equation*} \mathcal J=(J,J\cap \notn{LY}{L_Y},\notn{piY}{\pi_Y}|_J,\notn{thetaY}{\theta_Y}|_J) \end{equation*}
    inherits the same structure. Consequently, partitioning maps according to their image subgroup produces targets of the same form.
    🔗

    Theorem 4.2. Boundary-framed exact-image theorem.

    For every boundary-framed marked target \(\notn{calY}{\mathcal Y}\text{,}\)
    \begin{equation*} e_{\notn{GA}{\GA}}^\beta(\notn{calY}{\mathcal Y})=e_{\notn{GQ}{\GQ}}^\beta(\notn{calY}{\mathcal Y}). \end{equation*}
    The same equality holds for every exact-image target \(\mathcal J\) defined above.
    🔗
    Lean (main)Lean (stratum)Lean
    🔗
    The proof is a global induction over all boundary-framed marked targets, ordered by \(|\notn{LY}{L_Y}|\text{.}\) Auxiliary central covers need not lie inside the original ambient group, which is why the induction is stated globally.

    Section 5 Linear lifting theory and duality

    This section starts with a lower map and an elementary kernel and extracts the linear information needed by the target induction. The candidate and local cochain theories remain distinct; their common numerical and duality content is stated in Corollary 5.17.
    🔗
    Fix a finite group \(\notn{Cfin}{C}\text{,}\) a boundary-compatible epimorphism \(\notn{rhoEpi}{\rho}:\notn{GammaSrc}{\Gamma}\twoheadrightarrow \notn{Cfin}{C}\text{,}\) and a finite elementary \(\F_2[\notn{Cfin}{C}]\)-module \(\notn{Amod}{A}\text{.}\) Here boundary-compatible means that \(\notn{Cfin}{C}\) is the underlying group of a boundary-framed marked target \((\notn{Cfin}{C},L_C,\pi_C,\theta_C)\) as in Definition 4.1 and that \(\notn{rhoEpi}{\rho}\) induces the fixed frame: \((\pi_C,\theta_C)\circ\rho=\beta\circ \notn{bGamma}{b_\Gamma}\) with \(\beta\) as in (4.3). The marking of \(\notn{Cfin}{C}\) is thus compatible with the fixed boundary frame, and all comparisons in this section are between the two sources over this common frame. Here elementary means that the additive group of \(\notn{Amod}{A}\) is a finite-dimensional \(\F_2\)-vector space; no semisimplicity assumption is made. A lifting datum over \(\notn{rhoEpi}{\rho}\) is an extension
    \begin{equation*} 1\longrightarrow \notn{Amod}{A}\longrightarrow \widetilde C \xrightarrow{\,\pi\,} \notn{Cfin}{C}\longrightarrow1 \end{equation*}
    inducing the prescribed \(\notn{Cfin}{C}\)-action on \(\notn{Amod}{A}\text{.}\) In either source theory it has a degree-two obstruction
    \begin{equation*} o_{\Gamma,\notn{rhoEpi}{\rho}}(\widetilde C)\in \notn{HGr}{H^2_{\Gamma,\rho}}(\notn{Amod}{A}). \end{equation*}
    The obstruction vanishes exactly when \(\notn{rhoEpi}{\rho}\) lifts to \(\widetilde C\text{;}\) after one lift is fixed, every other lift is obtained uniquely by multiplication by an element of \(\notn{Z1Gr}{Z^1_{\Gamma,\rho}}(\notn{Amod}{A})\text{.}\) Thus a nonempty lift set is a principal homogeneous space under \(\notn{Z1Gr}{Z^1_{\Gamma,\rho}}(\notn{Amod}{A})\text{.}\) Only the obstruction dimensions, torsor cardinalities, perfect pairings, and connecting homomorphisms will be compared; no map between the two cochain complexes or their degree-one cohomology spaces is used.
    🔗
    For \(\notn{GammaSrc}{\Gamma}=\notn{GA}{\GA}\text{,}\) varying the four distinguished generators through an extension by \(\notn{Amod}{A}\) gives the finite word complex
    \begin{equation} C_{\rho,\notn{Amod}{A}}^\bullet: 0\longrightarrow \notn{Amod}{A}\xrightarrow{d^0_{\rho,\notn{Amod}{A}}}\notn{Amod}{A}^4 \xrightarrow{d^1_{\rho,\notn{Amod}{A}}}\notn{Amod}{A}^2\longrightarrow0.\tag{5.1} \end{equation}
    Write \(\notn{opS}{\mathsf S},\notn{opT}{\mathsf T},\notn{opX0}{\mathsf X_0},\notn{opX1}{\mathsf X_1}\) for the actions of the four lower values on \(\notn{Amod}{A}\text{.}\) With the lift convention \((a,g)\) in a semidirect product, simultaneous infinitesimal conjugation gives
    \begin{equation} d^0_{\rho,\notn{Amod}{A}}(v)=((\notn{opS}{\mathsf S}-1)v,(\notn{opT}{\mathsf T}-1)v,(\notn{opX0}{\mathsf X_0}-1)v,(\notn{opX1}{\mathsf X_1}-1)v).\tag{5.2} \end{equation}
    The map \(d^1_{\rho,\notn{Amod}{A}}\) is the ordered pair of the exact tame- and wild-relator defects. Concretely, if the lower map has values in \(\notn{Cfin}{C}\) and a lift to \(\notn{Cfin}{C}\ltimes \notn{Amod}{A}\) is written
    \begin{equation*} (\notn{rhoEpi}{\rho}(\notn{sigma}{\sigma}),a),\quad (\notn{rhoEpi}{\rho}(\notn{tau}{\tau}),b),\quad (\notn{rhoEpi}{\rho}(\notn{x0}{x_0}),c),\quad (\notn{rhoEpi}{\rho}(\notnfar{x1}{x_1}),d), \end{equation*}
    then \(d^1_{\rho,\notn{Amod}{A}}(a,b,c,d)\) is the coefficient of \(\notn{Amod}{A}\) in the evaluated tame and wild relators. This construction is functorial in the \(\notn{Cfin}{C}\)-module \(\notn{Amod}{A}\) because it is obtained by evaluating the same two finite words in semidirect products. Its degree-one kernel is denoted \(Z^1_{A,\notn{rhoEpi}{\rho}}(\notn{Amod}{A})\) and its cohomology by \(H^i_{A,\notn{rhoEpi}{\rho}}(\notn{Amod}{A})\text{.}\)
    🔗
    The pro-\(2\) normal-closure condition contributes no additional linear equation. The elementary kernel \(\notn{Amod}{A}\) lies in the marked normal \(2\)-subgroup of the target, so multiplying any of the four chosen lifts by an element of \(\notn{Amod}{A}\) preserves the marked condition; the only defects are the two displayed relators.

    Subsection 5.1 The evaluated Fox Jacobian

    Let \(\notn{opS}{\mathsf S},\notn{opT}{\mathsf T}\) denote the actions of \(\notn{rhoEpi}{\rho}(\notn{sigma}{\sigma}),\notn{rhoEpi}{\rho}(\notn{tau}{\tau})\) on \(\notn{Amod}{A}\text{.}\) If \(e=|\notn{opT}{\mathsf T}|\) is odd, put
    \begin{equation*} \notn{Pnorm}{P}=1+\notn{opT}{\mathsf T}+\cdots+\notn{opT}{\mathsf T}^{e-1}. \end{equation*}
    The following calculation is valid for any finite coefficient module after replacing \(\notn{w}{\w}\) by an integer representative modulo the exponent of the finite semidirect products used in the calculation.
    🔗

    Lemma 5.1. Finite-exponent independence.

    Suppose \(\nu\) and \(\nu'\) represent \(\notn{w}{\w}\) modulo the exponent of every finite semidirect and Heisenberg group occurring in a fixed first- or second-order calculation. Replacing every \(\notn{w}{\w}\)-power in the relators by \(\nu\) or by \(\nu'\) gives the same first derivative and the same mixed second derivative.
    🔗
    Lean
    🔗

    Proof.
    The two ordinary powers define the same element in each finite group in which the relator is evaluated. First and mixed derivatives are, by definition, the noncentral and central coordinates of those finite evaluations. They are therefore identical. The representative may be chosen separately for each finite coefficient calculation; no global coherent integer is required.
    🔗
    🔗

    Lemma 5.2. Exact class-two identity.

    Let
    \begin{equation*} 1\longrightarrow Z\longrightarrow\widetilde V\longrightarrow V\longrightarrow1 \end{equation*}
    be a central extension in which \(V\) and \(Z\) are elementary abelian \(2\)-groups, and let \(\phi\) be an automorphism of \(\widetilde V\) fixing \(Z\text{.}\) For \(X,D\in\widetilde V\text{,}\) put
    \begin{equation*} \mathfrak h_\phi(X,D) =\phi(X)X\,\phi(D)D\,D^2[\phi(D),D]. \end{equation*}
    Then
    \begin{equation} \mathfrak h_\phi(X,D)=\phi(X)X D^{-1}\phi(D).\tag{5.3} \end{equation}
    Consequently:
    🔗
    1. if \(D\) and \(X\) have the same image in \(V\text{,}\) then \(\mathfrak h_\phi(X,D)=X^2\text{;}\)
      🔗
      🔗
    2. if \(\phi\) is the identity, then \(\mathfrak h_\phi(X,D)=X^2\) for every \(D\text{.}\)
      🔗
      🔗
    Lean (core)Lean (identity)Lean (identity, id case)Lean
    🔗

    Proof.
    The group \(\widetilde V\) has class at most two, every commutator has order at most two, and every element has fourth power one. Put \(\notn{Amod}{A}=\phi(\notn{Dfox}{D})\text{,}\) \(B=\notn{Dfox}{D}\text{,}\) and \(k=[\notn{Amod}{A},B]\text{.}\) With our commutator convention \(AB=BAk\text{;}\) since \(k\) is central of order at most two and \(B^2\) is central,
    \begin{equation*} ABB^2k=BAB^2=B^3\notn{Amod}{A}=B^{-1}\notn{Amod}{A}. \end{equation*}
    This proves (5.3).
    🔗
    If \(\notn{Dfox}{D}=Xz\) with \(z\in Z\text{,}\) then \(\phi(z)=z\) and \(\notn{Dfox}{D}^{-1}\phi(\notn{Dfox}{D})=X^{-1}\phi(X)\text{.}\) Hence \(\mathfrak h_\phi(X,\notn{Dfox}{D})=\phi(X)^2=X^2\text{,}\) because \(X^2\in Z\) and \(\phi\) fixes \(Z\text{.}\) If \(\phi=1\text{,}\) (5.3) gives the second assertion directly.

    🔗

    Lemma 5.3. The elementary and class-two shadow of \(h_0\).

    Let \(\notn{Vhead}{V}\) be either the trivial module or a nontrivial simple tame \(\F_2[\notn{Cfin}{C}]\)-module. For an arbitrary lower map, the marked wild subgroup acts trivially on every simple factor, so the evaluated simple-factor derivatives are the same as those of the induced tame lower map. At that tame map:
    🔗
    1. the first derivative of \(h_0\) is the first derivative of \(\notn{x0}{x_0}^2\text{,}\) namely zero;
      🔗
      🔗
    2. on the normalized degree-one representatives supported on \(\notn{x0}{x_0}\text{,}\) the mixed Heisenberg and extraspecial central coordinates of \(h_0\) are respectively those of \(\notn{x0}{x_0}^2\text{.}\)
      🔗
      🔗
    Thus \(h_0\) may replace \(\notn{x0}{x_0}^2\) in every linear, cup-product, and determinant calculation used below.

    Lean
    🔗

    We first compute the linear variation of \(h_0\) and then treat its class-two central coordinate separately in the cases \(\notn{Pnorm}{P}=0\) and \(\notn{Pnorm}{P}=1\text{.}\)
    🔗
    Let \(\notn{opU}{\mathsf U}=\notn{opS}{\mathsf S}^\notn{w}{\w}\text{.}\) If the first-order variations of \(\notn{tau}{\tau}\) and \(\notn{x0}{x_0}\) are \(b\) and \(c\text{,}\) then
    \begin{equation*} Dd_0=\notn{Pnorm}{P} b+(\notn{Pnorm}{P}+1)c, \qquad \notn{Dfox}{D}\notn{x0}{x_0}=c. \end{equation*}
    The variation of \(g_0\) affects only terms of order at least two, because the base values of \(\notn{x0}{x_0}\) and \(d_0\) at the tame map are both the identity. If \(\notn{Pnorm}{P}=0\text{,}\) then \(Dd_0=c=\notn{Dfox}{D}\notn{x0}{x_0}\text{,}\) and the four linear terms in \(\mathfrak h_{g_0}(\notn{x0}{x_0},d_0)\) cancel. If \(\notn{Pnorm}{P}=1\text{,}\) then \(\notn{opT}{\mathsf T}=1\) and the \(2\)-primary part \(\notn{opU}{\mathsf U}\) acts trivially on a simple characteristic-\(2\) module; again the four linear terms cancel. This proves (i).
    🔗
    For the normalized cohomology representatives used in the mixed and quadratic calculations, only \(\notn{x0}{x_0}\) varies. If \(\notn{Pnorm}{P}=0\text{,}\) the two elements \(d_0\) and \(\notn{x0}{x_0}\) have the same image \(c\) in \(\notn{Vhead}{V}\text{,}\) so Lemma 5.2(i) applies. If \(\notn{Pnorm}{P}=1\text{,}\) then \(Dd_0=0\) and \(\notn{opT}{\mathsf T}=1\text{.}\) The \(2\)-primary operator \(\notn{opU}{\mathsf U}\) acts trivially on the simple quotient \(\notn{Vhead}{V}\text{.}\) Its lift to a Heisenberg or extraspecial coefficient group is therefore a central automorphism. Such an automorphism has order at most \(2\text{,}\) because it is determined by a homomorphism from the elementary quotient to the central involution. Hence \(g_0=\sigma_2^2\) acts trivially on the full coefficient group, and Lemma 5.2(ii) applies. For the trivial module, \(\notn{opT}{\mathsf T}=\notn{opU}{\mathsf U}=1\text{,}\) so the second case applies without modification. Taking the mixed Heisenberg central kernel gives the square diagonal \(\lambda(c)\text{;}\) taking the extraspecial central kernel gives \(q(c)\text{.}\) This proves (ii).

    Lemma 5.4. Full finite-word ledger.

    At a tame lower map, write first-order variations of \((\notn{sigma}{\sigma},\notn{tau}{\tau},\notn{x0}{x_0},\notnfar{x1}{x_1})\) as \((a,b,c,d)\text{.}\) Let \(\notn{opS}{\mathsf S},\notn{opT}{\mathsf T}\) be the lower actions of \(\notn{sigma}{\sigma},\notn{tau}{\tau}\text{,}\) put \(\notn{opU}{\mathsf U}=\notn{opS}{\mathsf S}^\notn{w}{\w}\text{,}\) and let \(\notn{Pnorm}{P}=1+\notn{opT}{\mathsf T}+\cdots+\notn{opT}{\mathsf T}^{e-1}\) for the odd order \(e\) of \(\notn{opT}{\mathsf T}\text{.}\) The raw finite Fox rules give

    \begin{equation*} \begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{factor}&\text{$\notn{Vhead}{V}$-coordinate}&\text{central coordinate}\\ \hline h_0&0&\lambda(c)\text{ in }\mathcal H(\notn{Vhead}{V}),\; q(c)\text{ for }\notn{kappaq0}{\kappa_q^0}\\ u_1^{-1}&0&0\\ \notnfar{x1}{x_1}^\notn{sigma}{\sigma}&0&0\\ d_0=(\notn{x0}{x_0}\notn{tau}{\tau})^\notn{w}{\w} \notn{x0}{x_0}^{-1}&(\notn{Pnorm}{P}+1)c&\ast\\ z_0=\notn{x0}{x_0}^{\sigma_2}&\notn{opU}{\mathsf U}^{-1}c&\ast\\ {[d_0,z_0]}&0&b_{\mathrm{cl}}((\notn{Pnorm}{P}+1)c,\notn{opU}{\mathsf U}^{-1}c). \end{array} \end{equation*}
    The symbols \(\ast\) are irrelevant because \(d_0\) and \(z_0\) enter the relator only through their commutator. The safety of replacing \(h_0\) by \(\notn{x0}{x_0}^2\) in these ledgers is exactly Lemma 5.3: the variation of \(g_0=\sigma_2^2\) starts in order at least two; when \(\notn{Pnorm}{P}=0\) one has \(Dd_0=\notn{Dfox}{D}\notn{x0}{x_0}\text{,}\) so Lemma 5.2(i) applies; when \(\notn{Pnorm}{P}=1\text{,}\) the lift of \(\notn{opU}{\mathsf U}\) to the class-two coefficient group is a central automorphism of order at most two, so \(g_0\) acts trivially and Lemma 5.2(ii) applies.

    Differentiating the relator words in these ledgers linearizes the lifting problem; the resulting Jacobian can be evaluated on each simple tame module.

    Lemma 5.5. Evaluated Jacobian.

    Write the lift variables on \((\notn{sigma}{\sigma},\notn{tau}{\tau},\notn{x0}{x_0},\notnfar{x1}{x_1})\) as \((a,b,c,d)\in \notn{Amod}{A}^4\text{.}\) On a simple tame module the actual relation differential is
    \begin{equation} d^1_{\rho,\notn{Amod}{A}}= \begin{pmatrix} \notn{opS}{\mathsf S}^{-1}(1+\notn{opT}{\mathsf T})&\notn{opS}{\mathsf S}^{-1}+1+\notn{opT}{\mathsf T}&0&0\\ 0&\notn{Pnorm}{P}&0&\notn{Pnorm}{P}+\notn{opS}{\mathsf S}^{-1} \end{pmatrix}.\tag{5.4} \end{equation}
    Equivalently,
    \begin{align} L_{\mathrm t} &=\notn{opS}{\mathsf S}^{-1}(1+\notn{opT}{\mathsf T})a+(\notn{opS}{\mathsf S}^{-1}+1+\notn{opT}{\mathsf T})b,\tag{5.5}\\ L_{\mathrm w} &=Pb+(\notn{Pnorm}{P}+\notn{opS}{\mathsf S}^{-1})d.\tag{5.6} \end{align}
    Postcomposing the tame defect coordinate by \(\notn{opS}{\mathsf S}\) gives the row-normalized expression
    \begin{equation*} (1+\notn{opT}{\mathsf T})a+\bigl(1+\notn{opS}{\mathsf S}(1+\notn{opT}{\mathsf T})\bigr)b, \end{equation*}
    which may be used for rank calculations only. The word complex, the mixed derivative, and the endpoint maps below use the unnormalized row (5.5).
