    Proof.
    Use \((u,g)(v,h)=(u+gv,gh)\) in \(\notn{Amod}{A}\rtimes \notn{Cfin}{C}\text{.}\) A direct calculation gives
    \begin{equation*} \notn{Dfox}{D}(\notn{tau}{\tau}^\notn{sigma}{\sigma}\notn{tau}{\tau}^{-2})(a,b) =\notn{opS}{\mathsf S}^{-1}(\notn{opT}{\mathsf T}-1)a+\bigl(\notn{opS}{\mathsf S}^{-1}-(1+\notn{opT}{\mathsf T})\bigr)b. \end{equation*}
    Over \(\F_2\) this is exactly (5.5).

    For an odd-order \(\notn{opT}{\mathsf T}\)-orbit, differentiation of a \(\notn{w}{\w}\)-power gives the norm projector \(\notn{Pnorm}{P}\text{.}\) By Lemma 5.3, the word \(h_0\) has the first-order value of \(\notn{x0}{x_0}^2\text{,}\) hence zero. The remaining wild factors give

    Their sum is (5.6). Without the simplicity assumption, the same finite Fox rules define the word complex; the displayed reduction is the simple-factor calculation used in the devissage.

    Here and below, the duality inputs on the Galois side are local Tate duality and the Euler–Poincaré characteristic; see [NSW, Theorems (7.2.6) and (7.3.1)] and [Mil, Chapter I].

    Subsection 5.2 The Fox–Heisenberg cup calculation

    For an elementary module \(\notn{Amod}{A}\text{,}\) set
    \begin{equation*} \mathcal H(\notn{Amod}{A})=\notn{Amod}{A}\times \notn{Amod}{A}^\vee\times\F_2, \end{equation*}
    with multiplication
    \begin{equation*} (a,\lambda,z)(a',\lambda',z') =(a+a',\lambda+\lambda',z+z'+\lambda(a')). \end{equation*}
    The \(\notn{Cfin}{C}\)-action is diagonal. If a finite word has evaluated coordinates
    \begin{equation*} (\bar u,D_u,D_u^\vee,\beta_u), \end{equation*}
    then multiplication and inversion obey
    \begin{align} D_{uv}&=D_u+\bar uD_v,& D_{uv}^\vee&=D_u^\vee+\bar uD_v^\vee,\tag{5.7}\\ \beta_{uv}&=\beta_u+\beta_v+(D_u^\vee)(\bar uD_v),& \beta_{u^{-1}}&=\beta_u+(\bar u^{-1}D_u^\vee)(\bar u^{-1}D_u).\tag{5.8} \end{align}
    These are the finite Fox recursion formulas. The Stokes identities below are proved directly by conjugation in the finite Heisenberg group; no cellular diagonal approximation is used. All identities in this subsection are identities of finite word evaluations before cohomology. In particular, coefficient functoriality and the later passage to nonsplit elementary modules are proved at the level of complexes and mapping cones; no semisimple decomposition of the \(\notn{Cfin}{C}\)-module \(\notn{Amod}{A}\) is used.
    🔗

    Lemma 5.6. Strict coefficient naturality.

    For every \(\notn{Cfin}{C}\)-module map \(f:\notn{Amod}{A}\to A'\text{,}\) the mixed derivatives satisfy
    \begin{equation*} \beta^{A'}_{\rho,r}(f_*a,\lambda') =\beta^A_{\rho,r}(a,f^\vee\lambda'). \end{equation*}
    🔗
    LeanLean
    🔗

    Proof.
    Evaluate the same finite relator in the mixed Heisenberg group
    \begin{equation*} \notn{Amod}{A}\times A'^\vee\times\F_2, \qquad (a,\lambda,z)(a',\lambda',z') =(a+a',\lambda+\lambda',z+z'+\lambda(f(a'))). \end{equation*}
    Its two natural images in \(\mathcal H(A')\) and \(\mathcal H(\notn{Amod}{A})\) have the same central coordinate. This gives the identity before passage to cohomology.
    🔗
    🔗

    Lemma 5.7. Finite-word Stokes formula.

    Let \(F_n=\langle g_1,\dots,g_n\rangle\) be a free group, let \(\rho:F_n\to \notn{Cfin}{C}\) be a homomorphism to a finite group, and write \(c_i=\rho(g_i)\text{.}\) Let \(r\in F_n\) be an ordinary finite word with \(\rho(r)=1\text{,}\) and let \(\epsilon_i(r)\in\F_2\) be the total exponent of \(g_i\) in \(r\text{,}\) reduced modulo \(2\text{.}\)
    🔗
    For \(x=(x_i)\in \notn{Amod}{A}^n\) and \(y=(y_i)\in(\notn{Amod}{A}^\vee)^n\text{,}\) evaluate \(r\) after replacing \(g_i\) by \((x_i,y_i,0;c_i)\in\mathcal H(\notn{Amod}{A})\rtimes \notn{Cfin}{C}\text{.}\) Write the result as
    \begin{equation*} \bigl(L_r^\notn{Amod}{A}(x),L_r^{\notn{Amod}{A}^\vee}(y),\beta_r(x,y);1\bigr). \end{equation*}
    Then, for \(a\in \notn{Amod}{A}\) and \(\lambda\in \notn{Amod}{A}^\vee\text{,}\)
    \begin{align} \beta_r(d^0a,y) &=\langle a,L_r^{\notn{Amod}{A}^\vee}(y)\rangle +\sum_{i=1}^n\epsilon_i(r)\,y_i(c_i a),\tag{5.9}\\ \beta_r(x,d^0\lambda) &=\langle L_r^\notn{Amod}{A}(x),\lambda\rangle +\sum_{i=1}^n\epsilon_i(r)\,\lambda(x_i),\tag{5.10} \end{align}
    where
    \begin{equation*} d^0a=((c_i-1)a)_i, \qquad d^0\lambda=((c_i-1)\lambda)_i. \end{equation*}
    Consequently, for words \(r_1,\dots,r_m\) and coefficients \(t_j\in\F_2\) satisfying
    \begin{equation} \sum_{j=1}^m t_j\epsilon_i(r_j)=0 \qquad(1\le i\le n),\tag{5.11} \end{equation}
    the corresponding traced mixed coordinate satisfies the two Stokes identities without correction terms.
    🔗
    Lean (left)Lean (right)
    🔗

    Proof.
    The two identities follow from conjugating by a primal and a dual coefficient, after which the total exponent vector records the central correction contributed by each generator.
    🔗
    Put
    \begin{equation*} p_a=(a,0,0;1),\qquad p_\lambda=(0,\lambda,0;1), \qquad \mathbf z(t)=(0,0,t;1). \end{equation*}
    A direct multiplication in \(\mathcal H(\notn{Amod}{A})\rtimes \notn{Cfin}{C}\) gives
    \begin{align*} p_a^{-1}(0,y_i,0;c_i)p_a &=((c_i-1)a,y_i,0;c_i)\,\mathbf z\bigl(y_i(c_i a)\bigr),\\ p_\lambda^{-1}(x_i,0,0;c_i)p_\lambda &=(x_i,(c_i-1)\lambda,0;c_i)\,\mathbf z\bigl(\lambda(x_i)\bigr). \end{align*}
    The elements \(\mathbf z(t)\) are central of order at most two. Therefore, on evaluating an ordinary word, the extra central factor attached to the \(i\)th generator occurs exactly \(\epsilon_i(r)\) times.
    🔗
    If only the dual variables \(y_i\) are present, the value of \(r\) is \((0,L_r^{\notn{Amod}{A}^\vee}(y),0;1)\text{.}\) Conjugating this value by \(p_a\) contributes the central coordinate \(L_r^{\notn{Amod}{A}^\vee}(y)(a)\text{.}\) Adding the generatorwise central corrections gives (5.9). Repeating this conjugation calculation with \(p_\lambda\) starts from \((L_r^\notn{Amod}{A}(x),0,0;1)\) and gives (5.10). Condition (5.11) cancels the correction terms. Every step is functorial in \(\notn{Amod}{A}\text{.}\)
    🔗
    🔗
    The finite-word identity acquires its useful form after tracing.
    🔗

    Proposition 5.8. Traced finite-word Stokes identity.

    Let \(\beta_{\mathrm t}\) and \(\beta_{\mathrm w}\) be the mixed central coordinates obtained from the tame and wild relators, and set
    \begin{equation*} \mathcal B_{\rho,\notn{Amod}{A}}=\beta_{\mathrm t}+\beta_{\mathrm w}. \end{equation*}
    Let \(L_{\mathrm t}\) and \(L_{\mathrm w}\) denote the two unnormalized first relation differentials. Then, before passage to cohomology,
    \begin{align} \mathcal B_{\rho,\notn{Amod}{A}}(d^0_{\rho,\notn{Amod}{A}}a,y) &=\langle a, L_{\mathrm t}^{\notn{Amod}{A}^\vee}(y)+L_{\mathrm w}^{\notn{Amod}{A}^\vee}(y)\rangle,\tag{5.12}\\ \mathcal B_{\rho,\notn{Amod}{A}}(x,d^0_{\rho,\notn{Amod}{A}^\vee}\lambda) &=\langle L_{\mathrm t}^{\notn{Amod}{A}}(x)+L_{\mathrm w}^{\notn{Amod}{A}}(x),\lambda\rangle.\tag{5.13} \end{align}
    The identities are natural in \(\notn{Amod}{A}\text{.}\) They are assertions about the sum of the two relator coordinates; in general they are false for either relator separately.
    🔗
    Lean (left)Lean (right)Lean
    🔗

    Proof.
    We compute the two relators’ mod-\(2\) exponent vectors, apply the finite-word Stokes formula to their sum, and then invoke finite-exponent independence and coefficient naturality.
    🔗
    Choose an odd ordinary integer representative of \(\notn{w}{\w}\) which is valid in every finite semidirect-Heisenberg group in the calculation, and replace the two profinite relators by the resulting ordinary words \(r_{\mathrm t}\) and \(r_{\mathrm w}\text{.}\) In the ordered generator list \((\notn{sigma}{\sigma},\notn{tau}{\tau},\notn{x0}{x_0},\notnfar{x1}{x_1})\) their mod-\(2\) exponent vectors are
    \begin{equation*} \notn{epsu}{\epsilon}(r_{\mathrm t})=(0,1,0,0), \qquad \notn{epsu}{\epsilon}(r_{\mathrm w})=(0,1,0,0). \end{equation*}
    Indeed, \(r_{\mathrm t}=\notn{tau}{\tau}^\notn{sigma}{\sigma}\notn{tau}{\tau}^{-2}\) has odd total \(\notn{tau}{\tau}\)-exponent. For \(r_{\mathrm w}=h_0u_1^{-1}\notnfar{x1}{x_1}^\notn{sigma}{\sigma} c_0\text{,}\) the commutator \(c_0\) has zero exponent vector. The word \(h_0\) also has zero exponent vector: the two \(\notn{x0}{x_0}\)-terms cancel modulo \(2\text{,}\) the two occurrences of \(d_0\) cancel, \(d_0^2\) has even exponent vector, and \(h_c\) is a commutator. Finally, \(u_1^{-1}\) contributes \(\notnfar{x1}{x_1}+\notn{tau}{\tau}\) and \(\notnfar{x1}{x_1}^\notn{sigma}{\sigma}\) contributes \(\notnfar{x1}{x_1}\text{.}\) Thus the sum of the two exponent vectors is zero.
    🔗
    Apply Lemma 5.7 with trace coefficients \((1,1)\text{.}\) The correction terms in (5.9) cancel and give (5.12); the correction terms in (5.10) cancel and give (5.13). Independence of the chosen integer representative is Lemma 5.1, and strict coefficient naturality is Lemma 5.6.

    Remark 5.9. The trace is essential.

    There is a small explicit regression test. Take \(\notn{Cfin}{C}=\GL_2(\F_2)\) with
    \begin{equation*} \notn{opS}{\mathsf S}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \notn{opT}{\mathsf T}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \notn{opS}{\mathsf S}^{-1}\notn{opT}{\mathsf T}\notn{opS}{\mathsf S}=\notn{opT}{\mathsf T}^2, \end{equation*}
    and let \(\notn{Amod}{A}=\F_2^2\) be the natural module. For \(a=e_2\) and the dual variation supported on \(\notn{tau}{\tau}\) with value \(e_2^\vee\text{,}\) the tame relator alone has mixed central value \(0\text{,}\) whereas pairing its dual first derivative with \(a\) gives \(1\text{.}\) The wild relator supplies the compensating value. Thus a relator-by-relator Stokes formula would assert \(0=1\text{,}\) while the traced formula above is exact.
    🔗
    🔗
    For \(x\in \notn{Amod}{A}^4\) and \(y\in(\notn{Amod}{A}^\vee)^4\text{,}\) let
    \begin{equation*} \mathcal B_{\rho,\notn{Amod}{A}}(x,y) =\beta_{\rho,r_{\mathrm t}}(x,y) +\beta_{\rho,r_{\mathrm w}}(x,y) \end{equation*}
    be the sum of the two mixed central coordinates. The following proposition constructs the chain map used below, including its degree-zero and degree-two components.
    🔗

    Proposition 5.10. The Fox–Heisenberg chain map.

    Under the canonical identifications
    \begin{equation*} \Hom((\notn{Amod}{A}^\vee)^2,\F_2)\cong \notn{Amod}{A}^2, \qquad \Hom((\notn{Amod}{A}^\vee)^4,\F_2)\cong \notn{Amod}{A}^4, \qquad \Hom(\notn{Amod}{A}^\vee,\F_2)\cong \notn{Amod}{A}, \end{equation*}
    define
    \begin{align} \notn{Dfox}{D}^0_{\rho,\notn{Amod}{A}}(a)&=(a,a),\tag{5.14}\\ \langle \notn{Dfox}{D}^1_{\rho,\notn{Amod}{A}}(x),y\rangle&=\mathcal B_{\rho,\notn{Amod}{A}}(x,y),\tag{5.15}\\ \notn{Dfox}{D}^2_{\rho,\notn{Amod}{A}}(u_{\mathrm t},u_{\mathrm w})&=u_{\mathrm t}+u_{\mathrm w}.\tag{5.16} \end{align}
    Then \(D_{\rho,\notn{Amod}{A}}=(\notn{Dfox}{D}^0,\notn{Dfox}{D}^1,\notn{Dfox}{D}^2)\) is a natural chain map
    \begin{equation} D_{\rho,\notn{Amod}{A}}:C_{\rho,\notn{Amod}{A}}^\bullet \longrightarrow \Hom_{\F_2}(C_{\rho,\notn{Amod}{A}^\vee}^\bullet,\F_2)[-2].\tag{5.17} \end{equation}
    More explicitly,
    \begin{align} \notn{Dfox}{D}^1_{\rho,\notn{Amod}{A}}d^0_{\rho,\notn{Amod}{A}} &=(d^1_{\rho,\notn{Amod}{A}^\vee})^\vee \notn{Dfox}{D}^0_{\rho,\notn{Amod}{A}},\tag{5.18}\\ \notn{Dfox}{D}^2_{\rho,\notn{Amod}{A}}d^1_{\rho,\notn{Amod}{A}} &=(d^0_{\rho,\notn{Amod}{A}^\vee})^\vee \notn{Dfox}{D}^1_{\rho,\notn{Amod}{A}}.\tag{5.19} \end{align}
    🔗
    Lean
    🔗

    Proof.
    The endpoint maps are induced by the scalar trace \(\operatorname{tr}(y_{\mathrm t},y_{\mathrm w})=y_{\mathrm t}+y_{\mathrm w}\text{.}\) Equations (5.12) and (5.13), proved by the direct finite-word calculation of Lemma 5.7, are exactly (5.18) and (5.19), respectively. Strict naturality in \(\notn{Amod}{A}\) is Lemma 5.6, Proposition 5.8. Hence (5.17) is a natural chain map in all three degrees.

    Lemma 5.11. Exact cone dévissage.

    For an elementary \(\F_2[\notn{Cfin}{C}]\)-module \(\notn{Amod}{A}\text{,}\) put
    \begin{equation} K(\notn{Amod}{A})=\Cone\!\left( D_{\rho,\notn{Amod}{A}}:\notn{Cfin}{C}^\bullet_{\rho,\notn{Amod}{A}}\longrightarrow \Hom_{\F_2}(\notn{Cfin}{C}^\bullet_{\rho,\notn{Amod}{A}^\vee},\F_2)[-2] \right).\tag{5.20} \end{equation}
    For every short exact sequence of finite \(\F_2[\notn{Cfin}{C}]\)-modules
    \begin{equation*} 0\longrightarrow A'\longrightarrow \notn{Amod}{A}\longrightarrow A''\longrightarrow0, \end{equation*}
    there is a degreewise short exact sequence of complexes
    \begin{equation} 0\longrightarrow K(A')\longrightarrow K(\notn{Amod}{A})\longrightarrow K(A'') \longrightarrow0.\tag{5.21} \end{equation}
    Consequently, if two of \(K(A')\text{,}\) \(K(\notn{Amod}{A})\text{,}\) and \(K(A'')\) are acyclic, then so is the third. In particular, acyclicity for all simple modules implies acyclicity for every elementary module, including nonsplit and nonsemisimple modules.
    🔗
    Lean (main)Lean (two-of-three)Lean
    🔗

    Proof.
    We verify exactness for the word complexes, then for their duals, and finally for the associated mapping cones.
    🔗
    The finite-word construction is additive and exact in the coefficient module, so the source complexes form a degreewise short exact sequence
    \begin{equation} 0\longrightarrow \notn{Cfin}{C}^\bullet_{\rho,A'} \longrightarrow \notn{Cfin}{C}^\bullet_{\rho,\notn{Amod}{A}} \longrightarrow \notn{Cfin}{C}^\bullet_{\rho,A''}\longrightarrow0.\tag{5.22} \end{equation}
    Dualizing the coefficient sequence gives
    \begin{equation*} 0\longrightarrow A''^\vee\longrightarrow \notn{Amod}{A}^\vee \longrightarrow A'^\vee\longrightarrow0. \end{equation*}
    Applying the same finite-word complex and then \(\Hom_{\F_2}(-,\F_2)\) reverses this sequence once more, and yields
    \begin{equation} \begin{split} 0\longrightarrow&\ \Hom_{\F_2}(\notn{Cfin}{C}^\bullet_{\rho,A'^\vee},\F_2)[-2] \longrightarrow \Hom_{\F_2}(\notn{Cfin}{C}^\bullet_{\rho,\notn{Amod}{A}^\vee},\F_2)[-2]\\ \longrightarrow&\ \Hom_{\F_2}(\notn{Cfin}{C}^\bullet_{\rho,A''^\vee},\F_2)[-2] \longrightarrow0. \end{split}\tag{5.23} \end{equation}
    For compactness write
    \begin{equation*} \notn{Cfin}{C}^\dagger(\notn{Amod}{A})=\Hom_{\F_2}(\notn{Cfin}{C}^\bullet_{\rho,\notn{Amod}{A}^\vee},\F_2)[-2]. \end{equation*}
    Strict coefficient naturality of the Heisenberg central coordinate gives the commutative diagram
    \begin{equation*} \begin{array}{ccccc} \notn{Cfin}{C}^\bullet_{\rho,A'}&\longrightarrow&\notn{Cfin}{C}^\bullet_{\rho,\notn{Amod}{A}} &\longrightarrow&\notn{Cfin}{C}^\bullet_{\rho,A''}\\ \downarrow D_{\rho,A'}&&\downarrow D_{\rho,\notn{Amod}{A}}&&\downarrow D_{\rho,A''}\\ \notn{Cfin}{C}^\dagger(A')&\longrightarrow&\notn{Cfin}{C}^\dagger(\notn{Amod}{A})&\longrightarrow&\notn{Cfin}{C}^\dagger(A''). \end{array} \end{equation*}
    Here the rows are the nonzero portions of (5.22) and (5.23), and commutativity is Lemma 5.6, Proposition 5.10. Mapping cones are formed degree by degree, so this diagram gives (5.21). The associated long exact cohomology sequence proves the two-out-of-three assertion. Applying it successively to a composition series of \(\notn{Amod}{A}\) proves the final statement.

    🔗

    Lemma 5.12. Simple characteristic-two modules are tame.

    Let \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\) be a simple \(\F_2[\notn{Cfin}{C}]\)-module occurring in the induction. Then the marked normal \(2\)-subgroup of \(\notn{Cfin}{C}\) acts trivially on \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\text{.}\) Hence \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\) factors through the finite tame quotient of \(\notn{Cfin}{C}\text{.}\)

    LeanLean
    🔗

    Proof.
    A finite \(2\)-group acting on a nonzero vector space over \(\F_2\) has a nonzero fixed vector. Since the \(2\)-subgroup is normal in \(\notn{Cfin}{C}\text{,}\) the fixed subspace is a nonzero \(\notn{Cfin}{C}\)-submodule. Simplicity forces this fixed subspace to be all of \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\text{.}\)

    🔗

    Lemma 5.13. Normal forms for nontrivial simple modules.

    Let \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\) be a nontrivial simple tame \(\F_2[\notn{Cfin}{C}]\)-module. Every class in \(H^1_{A,\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}}(\notnfar{Vhead}{V})\) has a unique representative supported on \(\notn{x0}{x_0}\text{:}\)
    \begin{equation} (a,b,c,d)\sim(0,0,c,0).\tag{5.24} \end{equation}
    More precisely, the two possible inertia cases are as follows.

    1. If \(\notn{opT}{\mathsf T}=1\text{,}\) then \(\notn{Pnorm}{P}=1\text{,}\) \(1+\notn{opS}{\mathsf S}^{-1}\) is invertible, and
      \begin{equation*} Z^1_{A,\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}}(\notnfar{Vhead}{V})=\{(a,0,c,0):a,c\in \notnfar{Vhead}{V}\},\qquad B^1_{A,\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}}(\notnfar{Vhead}{V})=\{((\notn{opS}{\mathsf S}-1)v,0,0,0):v\in \notnfar{Vhead}{V}\}. \end{equation*}
      🔗
      🔗
    2. If \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}^{\notn{opT}{\mathsf T}}=0\text{,}\) then \(\notn{Pnorm}{P}=0\) and \(\notn{opT}{\mathsf T}-1=1+\notn{opT}{\mathsf T}\) is invertible. The wild row first forces \(d=0\text{.}\) Subtracting the coboundary of \(v=(\notn{opT}{\mathsf T}-1)^{-1}b\) kills \(b\text{,}\) and the tame row then forces \(a=0\text{.}\)
      🔗
      🔗
    Under the representatives (5.24), the degree-one pairing with the corresponding representative \(\lambda\in \notnfar{Vhead}{V}^\vee\) is
    \begin{equation} (c,\lambda)\longmapsto \begin{cases} \lambda(c),&\notn{opT}{\mathsf T}=1,\\[1mm] \lambda((1+\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}+\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}^{-1})c),&\notnfar{Vhead}{V}^{\notn{opT}{\mathsf T}}=0. \end{cases}\tag{5.25} \end{equation}
    Both operators in (5.25) are invertible.

    Proof.

    🔗
    Because tame inertia is normal, \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}^{\notn{opT}{\mathsf T}}\) is a \(\notn{Cfin}{C}\)-submodule; simplicity gives either \(\notn{opT}{\mathsf T}=1\) and \(\notn{Pnorm}{P}=1\text{,}\) or \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}^{\notn{opT}{\mathsf T}}=0\) and \(\notn{Pnorm}{P}=0\text{.}\)

The same argument shows that \(\notn{opS}{\mathsf S}-1\) is invertible, so each class has a unique representative \((0,0,c,0)\text{.}\)
    🔗
    If \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}^{\notn{opT}{\mathsf T}}=0\text{,}\) then \(1+\notn{opT}{\mathsf T}\) is invertible. The wild row is \(\notn{opS}{\mathsf S}^{-1}d=0\text{,}\) hence \(d=0\text{.}\) For a cocycle \((a,b,c,0)\text{,}\) subtract the coboundary of \(v=(\notn{opT}{\mathsf T}-1)^{-1}b\text{.}\) The new representative has \(b=0\text{,}\) and its tame row is \(\notn{opS}{\mathsf S}^{-1}(1+\notn{opT}{\mathsf T})a=0\text{,}\) so \(a=0\text{.}\) Uniqueness follows because a coboundary with zero \(\notn{opT}{\mathsf T}\)-coordinate has \((\notn{opT}{\mathsf T}-1)v=0\text{,}\) hence \(v=0\text{.}\)
    🔗
    The pairing formula is Lemma 5.14. In the ramified case \(\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}\) has \(2\)-power order, so its minimal polynomial divides a power of \(X+1\text{.}\) Since \(X^2+X+1\) is coprime to \(X+1\text{,}\)
    \begin{equation*} 1+\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}+\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}^{-1}=\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}^{-1}(\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}^2+\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}+1) \end{equation*}
    is invertible. The unramified operator is the identity.
    🔗
    🔗

    Lemma 5.14. Mixed Hessian calculation.

    Let \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\) be a nontrivial simple tame module, put \(\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}=\notn{opS}{\mathsf S}^\notn{w}{\w}\text{,}\) and represent a class in \(H^1_{A,\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}}(\notnfar{Vhead}{V})\) by the cocycle supported on \(\notn{x0}{x_0}\) with value \(c\text{.}\) Represent the dual class similarly by \(\lambda\in \notnfar{Vhead}{V}^\vee\text{.}\) The mixed central contributions are
    \begin{equation*} \begin{array}{c|cc} \text{word contribution}&\notn{opT}{\mathsf T}=1&\notnfar{Vhead}{V}^{\notn{opT}{\mathsf T}}=0\\ \hline r_{\mathrm t}&0&0\\ h_0&\lambda(c)&\lambda(c)\\ {[d_0,z_0]}&0&\lambda(\mathsf Uc)+\lambda(\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}^{-1}c)\\ \text{all other factors of }r_{\mathrm w}&0&0. \end{array} \end{equation*}
    Consequently the degree-one pairing is induced by
    \begin{equation} \begin{cases} 1,&\notn{opT}{\mathsf T}=1,\\ 1+\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}+\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}^{-1},&\notnfar{Vhead}{V}^{\notn{opT}{\mathsf T}}=0. \end{cases}\tag{5.26} \end{equation}
    🔗
    Lean
    🔗

    Proof.
    The representative exists by the row reduction of (5.4). By Lemma 5.3, the word \(h_0\) contributes exactly the usual Heisenberg square diagonal \(\lambda(c)\text{.}\) In the ramified case the first derivatives on the \(\notn{x0}{x_0}\)-coordinate are
    \begin{equation*} Dd_0(c)=c, \qquad Dz_0(c)=\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}^{-1}c, \end{equation*}
    whereas on the dual coordinate they are
    \begin{equation*} Dd_0(\lambda)=\lambda, \qquad Dz_0(\lambda)=\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}^\vee\lambda. \end{equation*}
    Applying (5.7)–(5.8) to the commutator gives
    \begin{equation*} \lambda(\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}^{-1}c)+(\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}^\vee\lambda)(c) =\lambda((\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}^{-1}+\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U})c). \end{equation*}
    The remaining factors have either zero first derivative on the normalized representatives or no mixed central term. Adding the \(h_0\) contribution proves the table.
    🔗
    🔗
    Assembled, these computations say that the candidate’s lifting complex satisfies a two-dimensional duality.
    🔗

    Proposition 5.15. Candidate deformation duality.

    For every elementary \(\F_2[\notn{Cfin}{C}]\)-module \(\notn{Amod}{A}\text{,}\) the chain map (5.17) is a quasi-isomorphism. Hence
    \begin{equation} H^2_{A,\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}}(\notn{Amod}{A})^\vee\cong (\notn{Amod}{A}^\vee)^\notn{Cfin}{C}, \qquad \dim Z^1_{A,\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}}(\notn{Amod}{A})=2\dim \notn{Amod}{A}+\dim(\notn{Amod}{A}^\vee)^\notn{Cfin}{C}.\tag{5.27} \end{equation}
    The induced pairings
    \begin{equation*} H^i_{A,\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}}(\notn{Amod}{A})\times H^{2-i}_{A,\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}}(\notn{Amod}{A}^\vee)\to\F_2 \end{equation*}
    are perfect and natural in \(\notn{Amod}{A}\text{.}\)
    🔗
    Lean (simple case)Lean (split)Lean (ramified)Lean (main)Lean
    🔗

    Proof.
    We treat the trivial simple module, then the nontrivial simple modules, and finally pass to arbitrary elementary modules by exact cone dévissage.
    🔗
    For \(\notn{Amod}{A}=\F_2\text{,}\) all lower actions are trivial, so \(d^0=0\) and the actual Jacobian is
    \begin{equation*} d^1(a,b,c,d)=(b,b). \end{equation*}
    Thus \(\dim H^0=1\text{,}\) \(\dim H^1=3\text{,}\) and \(\dim H^2=1\text{.}\) On the basis of \(H^1\) represented by the coordinates \((\notn{sigma}{\sigma},\notn{x0}{x_0},\notnfar{x1}{x_1})\text{,}\) the traced Fox–Heisenberg form is
    \begin{equation*} ((a,c,d),(a',c',d'))\longmapsto ad'+da'+cc', \end{equation*}
    with matrix
    \begin{equation*} \begin{pmatrix} 0&0&1\\ 0&1&0\\ 1&0&0 \end{pmatrix}. \end{equation*}
    It is nonsingular, and the endpoint trace gives a nonzero \(H^0\)–\(H^2\) pairing. This is exactly the scalar cup–Bockstein table (3.18).
    🔗
    For a nontrivial simple module, Lemma 5.12 makes the action tame, and Lemma 5.13 gives a unique degree-one representative supported on \(\notn{x0}{x_0}\text{.}\) The Jacobian is surjective, so \(H^0=H^2=0\) and \(\dim H^1=\dim \notn{Amod}{A}\text{.}\) On the unique normal forms the degree-one pairing is exactly (5.25), and is nonsingular by the final assertion of Lemma 5.13. Hence the cone \(K(\notn{Amod}{A})\) is acyclic for every simple module, including the trivial simple module treated above.
    🔗
    In more detail: in the split case, fixed-point-freeness of \(\mathsf S-1\) makes this operator bijective and supplies the unique \(x_0\)-supported normal form on both \(A\) and \(A^\vee\text{.}\) In the ramified case the analogous argument uses \(\mathsf T^{-1}-1\text{,}\) while the perfect pairing is reduced to the bijectivity of \(1+\mathsf U+\mathsf U^{-1}\text{.}\) Its injectivity comes from the unipotence of the \(2\)-primary operator \(\mathsf U\text{;}\) finiteness then gives surjectivity.
    🔗
    For a general elementary module, choose a composition series. The degreewise short exact cone sequence (5.21) and its long exact cohomology sequence give acyclicity at each extension step. Thus \(D_{\rho,\notn{Amod}{A}}\) is a quasi-isomorphism for every elementary, possibly nonsplit and nonsemisimple, module \(\notn{Amod}{A}\text{.}\) The numerical formula follows from duality and the Euler characteristic of (5.1).
    🔗
    The dévissage is a strong induction on \(|A|\text{,}\) rather than an appeal to semisimplicity. If \(A\) is neither zero nor simple, choose a proper nonzero \(C\)-stable subgroup \(W\text{.}\) Both \(W\) and \(A/W\) have strictly smaller cardinality, inherit the exponent-two action, and fit into the exact cone sequence of Lemma 5.11. The two-out-of-three property for that sequence therefore propagates duality through arbitrary nonsplit extensions.
    🔗
    🔗
    The Galois side satisfies the same duality, with the local cup product and invariant map supplying the pairing.
    🔗

    Proposition 5.16. Local lifting duality.

    For every elementary \(\F_2[\notn{Cfin}{C}]\)-module \(\notn{Amod}{A}\text{,}\)
    \begin{equation} H^2_{F,\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}}(\notn{Amod}{A})^\vee\cong (\notn{Amod}{A}^\vee)^\notn{Cfin}{C}, \qquad \dim Z^1_{F,\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}}(\notn{Amod}{A})=2\dim \notn{Amod}{A}+\dim(\notn{Amod}{A}^\vee)^\notn{Cfin}{C}.\tag{5.28} \end{equation}
    The local cup product and invariant map give perfect pairings
    \begin{equation*} H^i_{F,\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}}(\notn{Amod}{A})\times H^{2-i}_{F,\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}}(\notn{Amod}{A}^\vee)\to\F_2. \end{equation*}
    🔗
    Lean (bundle)Lean (main)Lean
    🔗

    Proof.
    This is local Tate duality, with the mod-\(2\) cyclotomic twist trivial, together with the local Euler–Poincaré formula for \(\notn{Qtwo}{\Qtwo}\text{;}\) see [NSW, Thms. (7.2.6) and (7.3.1)]. Since the action factors through \(\notn{Cfin}{C}\text{,}\) the invariant space is \((\notn{Amod}{A}^\vee)^\notn{Cfin}{C}\text{.}\) Finally
    \begin{equation*} \dim Z^1=\dim H^1+\dim B^1 =\dim H^1+\dim \notn{Amod}{A}-\dim \notn{Amod}{A}^\notn{Cfin}{C}, \end{equation*}
    and the Euler characteristic gives the stated expression.

    Section 6 Quadratic determinant obstructions

    The Evens norm and the Stiefel–Whitney comparison used throughout this section follow [Eve], [Kah], and [Koz]; for the computation of Stiefel–Whitney classes see also [Gui].
    🔗
    The linear interface of Section 5 does not determine the scalar central pushouts attached to self-dual simple modules, because their lifting obstruction is quadratic. We construct a normalized equivariant base class, compute the resulting form on the candidate and local sides, compare their Gauss sums, and then restore the affine terms required in the finite-target recursion.
    🔗
    Determinant obstruction. Let
    \begin{equation*} 1\longrightarrow \notn{Rcent}{R}\longrightarrow \widetilde M \longrightarrow \notn{Mmid}{M}\longrightarrow1 \end{equation*}
    be a \(\notn{Cfin}{C}\)-equivariant central extension with \(\widetilde M\) of class at most two and with \(\notn{Rcent}{R}\) and \(\notn{Mmid}{M}\) elementary abelian, and let \(\lambda\in(\notn{Rcent}{R}^\vee)^\notn{Cfin}{C}\text{.}\) Pushing out along \(\lambda:\notn{Rcent}{R}\to\F_2\) gives a central double cover of \(\notn{Mmid}{M}\text{.}\) Its square map
    \begin{equation*} \notn{qlambda}{q_\lambda}(m)=\lambda(\widetilde m^{\,2})\in\F_2 \end{equation*}
    is quadratic, with polar form given by the commutator pairing. The scalar degree-two obstruction obtained by pulling back this cover is called the determinant obstruction. In the application, its restriction to the nontrivial simple head \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\) is a nonzero nonsingular quadratic form; this is proved in Proposition 7.4.
    🔗
    The notation used for the quadratic and affine terms is as follows.

    Subsection 6.1 The normalized equivariant base class

    A \(\notn{Cfin}{C}\)-invariant quadratic form on \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\) need not admit a \(\notn{Cfin}{C}\)-invariant factor set for a chosen section \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\to E\text{.}\) The correction terms in the lifted \(\notn{Cfin}{C}\)-action are therefore included in the equivariant central extension class.
    🔗

    Lemma 6.1. Equivariant extraspecial connecting cocycle.

    Let \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\) be an elementary \(\F_2[\notn{Cfin}{C}]\)-module, let \(q:\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\to\F_2\) be a \(\notn{Cfin}{C}\)-invariant quadratic form with polar form \(\notn{bq}{b_q}\text{,}\) and let
    \begin{equation*} f:\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\times \notnfar{Vhead}{V}\to\F_2, \qquad f(v,v)=q(v),\qquad f(v,w)+f(w,v)=\notn{bq}{b_q}(v,w), \end{equation*}
    be a normalized factor set for the central extension
    \begin{equation*} E_f=\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\times\F_2, \qquad (v,z)(w,t)=(v+w,z+t+f(v,w)). \end{equation*}
    When an equivariant lift is chosen, its action in the normalized section is written by functions \(m_c:\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\to\F_2\) satisfying
    \begin{equation} m_c(v+w)+m_c(v)+m_c(w)=f(cv,cw)+f(v,w)\tag{6.1} \end{equation}
    and
    \begin{equation} m_{cd}(v)=m_c(dv)+m_d(v),\qquad m_1=0.\tag{6.2} \end{equation}
    Equivalently,
    \begin{equation*} c\cdot(v,z)=(cv,z+m_c(v)) \end{equation*}
    defines an action by automorphisms of \(E_f\text{.}\) The associated normalized base central cocycle on \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\rtimes \notn{Cfin}{C}\) is
    \begin{equation} \notnfar{kappaq0}{\kappa_q^0}((v,c),(w,d))=f(v,cw)+m_c(w).\tag{6.3} \end{equation}
    Consequently, for a source \(\notnfar{GammaSrc}{\Gamma}\text{,}\) a lower map \(\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}:\notnfar{GammaSrc}{\Gamma}\to \notn{Cfin}{C}\text{,}\) and a normalized \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\)-valued \(1\)-cocycle \(b\text{,}\) the base connecting cocycle is
    \begin{equation} (b,\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho})^*\notnfar{kappaq0}{\kappa_q^0}(g,h) =f(b(g),\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}(g)b(h))+m_{\rho(g)}(b(h)).\tag{6.4} \end{equation}
    🔗
    If \(\kappa\) is another normalized central cocycle on \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\rtimes \notn{Cfin}{C}\) whose restriction to \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\) is the same quadratic form \(q\text{,}\) then, after replacing \(\kappa\) by a cohomologous normalized cocycle and changing the normalized section, the following is an equality of normalized \(2\)-cochains:
    \begin{equation} \kappa=\notnfar{kappaq0}{\kappa_q^0}+\Gamma_\gamma+ \operatorname{inf}_C^{\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\rtimes \notn{Cfin}{C}}\delta,\tag{6.5} \end{equation}
    where
    \begin{equation} \Gamma_\gamma((v,c),(w,d))=\gamma(c)(cw), \qquad \gamma\in Z^1(\notn{Cfin}{C},\notnfar{Vhead}{V}^\vee),\quad \delta\in Z^2(\notn{Cfin}{C},\F_2).\tag{6.6} \end{equation}
    After graph pullback and application of the source functional \(\notn{iotaGamma}{\iota_\Gamma}\text{,}\) the corresponding scalar quadratic obstruction is
    \begin{equation} Q_{\kappa,\notnfar{GammaSrc}{\Gamma},\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}}(b) =Q^0_{\Gamma,\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}}(b) +\langle b,\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}^*\gamma\rangle_\Gamma +\notn{iotaGamma}{\iota_\Gamma}(\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}^*\delta),\tag{6.7} \end{equation}
    where
    \begin{equation*} Q^0_{\Gamma,\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}}(b)= \notn{iotaGamma}{\iota_\Gamma}\bigl((b,\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho})^*\notnfar{kappaq0}{\kappa_q^0}\bigr). \end{equation*}
    Its polarization is the source pairing transported by \(\notn{bq}{b_q}\text{.}\)
    🔗
    Lean
    🔗

    Proof.
    We verify the equivariant central extension, identify the filtration-one and inflated difference terms, and then compute the polarization.
    🔗
    Equation (6.1) is exactly the condition that \((v,z)\mapsto(cv,z+m_c(v))\) preserve the multiplication in \(E_f\text{;}\) equation (6.2) says that these automorphisms form a genuine \(\notn{Cfin}{C}\)-action. Multiplication in the semidirect product attached to this lifted action is
    \begin{equation} (v,c,z)(w,d,t)= (v+cw,cd,z+t+f(v,cw)+m_c(w)),\tag{6.8} \end{equation}
    which gives (6.3). Pulling back this cocycle by the graph of a \(1\)-cocycle \(b\) gives (6.4). This is the term which would be missing if one incorrectly assumed that the section \(v\mapsto(v,0)\) were \(\notn{Cfin}{C}\)-equivariant.
    🔗
    For the difference statement, the quotient \(\kappa-\notnfar{kappaq0}{\kappa_q^0}\) restricts trivially to \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\times \notnfar{Vhead}{V}\text{.}\) In the normalized Lyndon–Hochschild–Serre filtration for the split extension \(1\to \notnfar{Vhead}{V}\to \notnfar{Vhead}{V}\rtimes \notn{Cfin}{C}\to \notn{Cfin}{C}\to1\text{,}\) such a class has only a filtration-one part in \(Z^1(\notn{Cfin}{C},\notnfar{Vhead}{V}^\vee)\) and an inflated scalar part in \(Z^2(\notn{Cfin}{C},\F_2)\text{.}\) The normalized representative is exactly (6.6); the cocycle condition for it is the condition that \(\gamma\) be a \(1\)-cocycle. Pullback along \((b,\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho})\) gives (6.7). Polarization of the base term is obtained by adding the formulas for \(b+b'\text{,}\) \(b\text{,}\) and \(b'\text{;}\) the \(m_c\)-contribution cancels because each \(m_c\) has polar form \(f(c-,c-)+f(-,-)\text{,}\) and the remaining term is \(\notn{bq}{b_q}(b\smile b')\text{.}\) The difference terms in (6.7) are linear or inflated scalar terms and therefore do not change the polar form.
    🔗
    🔗

    Lemma 6.2. Explicit involution-orbit cocycle.

    Let \(H\) be a finite group, let \(g\in H\) have order \(2\text{,}\) and let \(M=\F_2[H]\) with left-regular action
    \begin{equation*} (c x)_h=x_{c^{-1}h}. \end{equation*}
    Choose a set \(\mathcal R\subset H\) of representatives for the right cosets \(u\langle g\rangle\text{.}\) For \(c\in H\) and \(u\in\mathcal R\text{,}\) write uniquely
    \begin{equation} c^{-1}u=\pi_c(u)g^{\epsilon_c(u)}, \qquad \pi_c(u)\in\mathcal R, \quad \epsilon_c(u)\in\F_2.\tag{6.9} \end{equation}
    Define
    \begin{align} q_g(x)&=\sum_{u\in\mathcal R}x_u x_{ug},\tag{6.10}\\ f_g(x,y)&=\sum_{u\in\mathcal R}x_u y_{ug},\tag{6.11}\\ m_c^g(x)&=\sum_{u\in\mathcal R} \epsilon_c(u)x_{\pi_c(u)}x_{\pi_c(u)g}.\tag{6.12} \end{align}
    Then
    \begin{align} m_c^g(x+y)+m_c^g(x)+m_c^g(y) &=f_g(cx,cy)+f_g(x,y),\tag{6.13}\\ m_{cd}^g(x)&=m_c^g(dx)+m_d^g(x), \qquad m_1^g=0.\tag{6.14} \end{align}
    Consequently
    \begin{equation} \kappa_g^{\mathcal R}((x,c),(y,d)) =f_g(x,cy)+m_c^g(y)\tag{6.15} \end{equation}
    is a normalized \(2\)-cocycle on \(M\rtimes H\text{.}\) It vanishes on the zero section \(H\hookrightarrow M\rtimes H\text{,}\) and its restriction to \(M\) has square map \(q_g\text{.}\)
    🔗
    🔗

    Proof.
    We first compute the transition functions for the right-coset action, then verify the quadratic correction, and finally apply the general equivariant extension formula.
    🔗
    From (6.9) one obtains
    \begin{equation} \pi_{cd}=\pi_d\circ\pi_c, \qquad \epsilon_{cd}(u)=\epsilon_c(u)+\epsilon_d(\pi_c(u)).\tag{6.16} \end{equation}
    Moreover,
    \begin{equation*} f_g(cx,cy) =\sum_{u\in\mathcal R} x_{\pi_c(u)g^{\epsilon_c(u)}} y_{\pi_c(u)g^{\epsilon_c(u)+1}}. \end{equation*}
    For \(\epsilon_c(u)=0\) this is the summand of \(f_g(x,y)\) indexed by \(\pi_c(u)\text{;}\) for \(\epsilon_c(u)=1\) its orientation is reversed. Therefore
    \begin{equation*} f_g(cx,cy)+f_g(x,y) =\sum_{u\in\mathcal R}\epsilon_c(u) \bigl(x_{\pi_c(u)}y_{\pi_c(u)g} +x_{\pi_c(u)g}y_{\pi_c(u)}\bigr), \end{equation*}
    which is exactly the polarization of (6.12). This proves (6.13).
    🔗
    The product \(x_vx_{vg}\) is unchanged when \(v\) is replaced by \(vg\text{.}\) Hence
    \begin{equation*} m_c^g(dx) =\sum_{u\in\mathcal R}\epsilon_c(u) x_{\pi_d(\pi_c(u))}x_{\pi_d(\pi_c(u))g}. \end{equation*}
    Adding \(m_d^g(x)\) and using (6.16) gives (6.14). The cocycle assertion now follows directly from Lemma 6.1. Finally, \(f_g(x,x)=q_g(x)\) and \(m_1^g=0\text{,}\) proving the restriction and normalization claims.
    🔗
    🔗

    Lemma 6.3. Base equivariant determinant class.

    Let \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\) be a nontrivial simple self-dual tame \(\F_2[\notn{Cfin}{C}]\)-module, let \(H=H_V\) be its faithful tame image, and let \(q:\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\to\F_2\) be a nonzero \(H\)-invariant nonsingular quadratic form. There is a normalized base class
    \begin{equation*} \notnfar{kappaq0}{\kappa_q^0}\in Z^2(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\rtimes H,\F_2) \end{equation*}
    whose restriction to \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\) has square map \(q\text{.}\)
    🔗
    Choose an \(H\)-split pair
    \begin{equation*} \notnfar{Vhead}{V}\xrightarrow{i}W=\F_2[H]^N\xrightarrow{p}\notnfar{Vhead}{V}, \qquad pi=1, \end{equation*}
    and put \(q_W=q\circ p\text{.}\) In the left-regular coordinates \(X_{j,h}\) of \(W\text{,}\) the unique algebraic normal form of the \(H\)-invariant quadratic map \(q_W\) is a sum of orbit polynomials of the following three types:
    \begin{align*} S_j&=\sum_{h\in H}X_{j,h}^2,\\ C_{j,k,g}&=\sum_{h\in H}X_{j,h}X_{k,hg} \quad\text{when the corresponding unordered pair has trivial stabilizer},\\ E_{j,g}&=\sum_{u\in\mathcal R_g}X_{j,u}X_{j,ug}, \qquad g^2=1,\ g\ne1, \end{align*}
    where \(\mathcal R_g\) is any set of representatives for the right cosets of \(\langle g\rangle\) in \(H\text{.}\) For a square orbit use the \(H\)-invariant factor set
    \begin{equation} f_{S_j}(x,y)=\sum_{h\in H}x_{j,h}y_{j,h}, \qquad m_c=0.\tag{6.17} \end{equation}
    For a free orbit use
    \begin{equation} f_{C_{j,k,g}}(x,y)=\sum_{h\in H}x_{j,h}y_{k,hg}, \qquad m_c=0.\tag{6.18} \end{equation}
    For an involution-stabilized orbit use the cocycle (6.15) of Lemma 6.2 on the \(j\)th regular summand, with \(\mathcal R=\mathcal R_g\text{.}\) Let \(\kappa_{q_W}^0\) be the sum of the cocycles corresponding to the orbit polynomials occurring in \(q_W\text{,}\) and put
    \begin{equation} \notnfar{kappaq0}{\kappa_q^0}=(i\rtimes1)^*\kappa_{q_W}^0.\tag{6.19} \end{equation}
    Then \(\notnfar{kappaq0}{\kappa_q^0}\) vanishes on the zero section and \(\operatorname{res}_V(\notnfar{kappaq0}{\kappa_q^0})\) has square map \(q\text{.}\) If a lower target has quotient \(\notn{Cfin}{C}\) acting through \(H\text{,}\) we inflate this class along \(\notn{Cfin}{C}\to H\) and keep the same notation.
    🔗
    Lean
    🔗

    Proof.
    We construct the class on a split regular module by the three possible orbit types of quadratic monomials and then pull it back to \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\text{.}\)
    🔗
    If \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\) is ramified, \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\) is projective over \(\F_2[H]\) by Lemma 6.11; if \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\) is unramified, the \(2\)-primary subgroup of the cyclic unramified image acts trivially on every simple characteristic-\(2\) module, so the faithful image \(H\) has odd order and Maschke’s theorem applies. Thus the split pair exists.
    🔗
    The algebraic normal form of a quadratic map over \(\F_2\) is determined by its values on the coordinate vectors and by its polar form. \(H\)-invariance makes its coefficients constant on the orbits of unordered degree-two coordinate monomials. Since the action on each regular coordinate set is free, the stabilizer of an unordered pair is either trivial or has order two and exchanges the two entries. The latter possibility is exactly \(j=k\) with a nontrivial involution \(g\text{,}\) and gives \(E_{j,g}\text{.}\)
    🔗
    The factor sets (6.17) and (6.18) are \(H\)-invariant, vanish on the zero section, and have square maps \(S_j\) and \(C_{j,k,g}\text{,}\) respectively. By Lemma 6.2, the explicit cocycle for \(E_{j,g}\) has square map \(E_{j,g}\) and also vanishes on the zero section. Their sum is therefore an actual normalized equivariant central cocycle on \(W\rtimes H\) with fibre square map \(q_W\text{.}\) Pullback along \(i\rtimes1\) gives fibre square map \(q_W(iv)=q(v)\) and preserves zero-section normalization.
    🔗
    🔗

    Lemma 6.4. Uniqueness and isometry invariance of the normalized base class.

    Let \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\text{,}\) \(H=H_V\text{,}\) and \(q\) be as in Lemma 6.3. Then
    \begin{equation} H^1(H,\notnfar{Vhead}{V}^\vee)=0.\tag{6.20} \end{equation}
    Any two classes in \(H^2(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\rtimes H,\F_2)\) which restrict to the class with square map \(q\) on \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\) and restrict trivially along the zero section \(H\hookrightarrow \notnfar{Vhead}{V}\rtimes H\) are equal. Consequently, changing the normalized factor set, the correction functions \(m_c\text{,}\) the half-orbit transversals, or the \(H\)-split regular embedding and retraction changes \(\notnfar{kappaq0}{\kappa_q^0}\) only by a normalized coboundary. In particular the base quadratic obstruction \(Q^0_{\Gamma,\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}}\) is well-defined.
    🔗
    Moreover, every \(H\)-equivariant isometry \(u\) of \((\notnfar{Vhead}{V},q)\) fixes the normalized base class:
    \begin{equation} (u\rtimes1)^*[\notnfar{kappaq0}{\kappa_q^0}]=[\notnfar{kappaq0}{\kappa_q^0}].\tag{6.21} \end{equation}
    🔗
    🔗

    Proof.
    We first prove the required cohomology vanishing, then use the low-degree Lyndon–Hochschild–Serre sequence for uniqueness, and finally deduce choice-independence and isometry invariance.
    🔗
    If \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\) is unramified, its faithful image \(H\) has odd order: the \(2\)-primary subgroup of the cyclic unramified image acts trivially on every simple characteristic-\(2\) module. Hence positive-degree \(\F_2[H]\)-cohomology vanishes by averaging.
    🔗
    Assume that \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\) is ramified, and let \(I\triangleleft H\) be the odd tame-inertia subgroup. The fixed space \((\notnfar{Vhead}{V}^\vee)^I\) is an \(H\)-submodule. It is zero, because \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\) is simple and inertia acts nontrivially. Since \(|I|\) is odd, \(H^j(I,\notnfar{Vhead}{V}^\vee)=0\) for \(j>0\text{.}\) The Hochschild–Serre spectral sequence for \(1\to I\to H\to H/I\to1\) therefore gives [Bro, Ch. VII, §6]
    \begin{equation*} H^n(H,\notnfar{Vhead}{V}^\vee)=0\qquad(n\ge0). \end{equation*}
    In particular (6.20) holds in both cases.
    🔗
    Put \(G=\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\rtimes H\text{.}\) For an elementary abelian \(2\)-group \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\text{,}\) the square-map correspondence
    \begin{equation*} H^2(\notnfar{Vhead}{V},\F_2)\xrightarrow{\sim} \{\text{quadratic maps }\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\to\F_2\} \end{equation*}
    is an isomorphism: the polarization recovers the commutator form, and the square and commutator data determine the central extension class. Thus two classes with square map \(q\) have the same fibre restriction.
    🔗
    The low-degree Lyndon–Hochschild–Serre sequence for \(1\to \notnfar{Vhead}{V}\to G\to H\to1\) contains the exact segment [Bro, Cor. VII.6.4]
    \begin{equation} H^2(H,\F_2)\xrightarrow{\operatorname{inf}} \ker\!\left(H^2(G,\F_2)\longrightarrow H^2(\notnfar{Vhead}{V},\F_2)\right) \xrightarrow{\operatorname{edge}}H^1(H,\notnfar{Vhead}{V}^\vee).\tag{6.22} \end{equation}
    Let \(\xi\) be the difference of two classes with the stated normalizations. Its fibre restriction is zero. By (6.20) and exactness of (6.22), \(\xi=\operatorname{inf}(\delta)\) for some \(\delta\in H^2(H,\F_2)\text{.}\) Pullback along the zero section is a left inverse to inflation, while both classes vanish there. Hence \(\delta=0\) and \(\xi=0\text{.}\)
    🔗
    At the filtration-one level one can see the same cancellation directly. If \(\gamma=dh\) for \(h\in \notnfar{Vhead}{V}^\vee\text{,}\) then the normalized \(1\)-cochain
    \begin{equation} \ell_h(v,c)=h(v)\tag{6.23} \end{equation}
    on \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\rtimes H\) satisfies \(d\ell_h=\Gamma_{dh}\text{,}\) with \(\notnfar{GammaSrc}{\Gamma}\) as in (6.6).
    🔗
    If normalized cocycle representatives are used, their difference is \(da\) for a normalized \(1\)-cochain \(a\text{.}\) Since the difference vanishes on \(H\times H\text{,}\) \(a|_H\) is a \(1\)-cocycle. Subtracting its inflation makes \(a\) vanish on the zero section without changing \(da\text{.}\) Thus all choices in Lemma 6.3 give isomorphic normalized central extensions, and transport of lifts through that isomorphism leaves both the candidate relator obstruction and the local pullback class unchanged. This proves the choice-independence of \(Q^0_{\Gamma,\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}}\text{.}\)
    🔗
    Finally, \((u\rtimes1)^*\notnfar{kappaq0}{\kappa_q^0}\) has the same fibre square map and the same zero-section restriction as \(\notnfar{kappaq0}{\kappa_q^0}\text{,}\) so uniqueness proves (6.21).
    🔗
    The uniqueness assertion is deliberately made over the faithful image \(H_V\text{.}\) After inflation to a larger quotient \(\notn{Cfin}{C}\) acting through \(H_V\text{,}\) the group \(H^1(\notn{Cfin}{C},\notnfar{Vhead}{V}^\vee)\) need not vanish; its contribution is precisely the filtration-one term \(\Gamma_\gamma\) in (6.5), and it remains part of the target-side affine data.
    🔗
    🔗
    🔗

    Subsection 6.2 Candidate-side calculation

    Let \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\) be a nontrivial self-dual simple tame module, let \(q:\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\to\F_2\) be invariant and nonsingular, let \(\notnfar{bq}{b_q}\) be its polar form, and let \(\notnfar{kappaq0}{\kappa_q^0}\) be the base equivariant determinant class of Lemma 6.3. The candidate determinant calculation below is made in the lifted semidirect product (6.8); thus all \(m_c\)-terms are included.
    🔗

    Proposition 6.5. Complete base second-order word expansion.

    With \(\notn{opS}{\mathsf S},\notn{opT}{\mathsf T},\notn{Pnorm}{P},\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}=\notn{opS}{\mathsf S}^\notn{w}{\w}\) as above, evaluation of the actual relator (1.6) for the base class \(\notnfar{kappaq0}{\kappa_q^0}\) gives
    \begin{equation} Q_A^0(c)=q(c)+\notnfar{bq}{b_q}((\notn{Pnorm}{P}+1)c,\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}^{-1}c).\tag{6.24} \end{equation}
    Equivalently,
    \begin{equation} Q_A^0(c)= \begin{cases} q(c),&\notn{opT}{\mathsf T}=1,\\ q(c)+\notnfar{bq}{b_q}(c,\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}^{-1}c),&\notnfar{Vhead}{V}^{\notn{opT}{\mathsf T}}=0. \end{cases}\tag{6.25} \end{equation}
    Its ramified polar form is
    \begin{equation} b_A(c,c')=\notnfar{bq}{b_q}(c,(1+\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}+\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}^{-1})c').\tag{6.26} \end{equation}
    For a general determinant class \(\kappa=\notnfar{kappaq0}{\kappa_q^0}+\Gamma_{\gamma_\kappa}+\operatorname{inf}\delta_\kappa\text{,}\) one has
    \begin{equation} Q_{A,\kappa,\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}}(c)=Q_A^0(c) +\langle c,\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}^*\gamma_\kappa\rangle_A +\iota_A(\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}^*\delta_\kappa).\tag{6.27} \end{equation}
    🔗
    Lean
    🔗

    Proof.
    We evaluate the square contribution of \(h_0\text{,}\) the commutator contribution of \(d_0\) and \(z_0\text{,}\) and then polarize the resulting quadratic expression.
    🔗
    Normalize a cohomology representative so that only \(\notn{x0}{x_0}\) varies, by \(c\text{.}\) In terms of (6.8), the complete base contribution ledger is
    \begin{equation*} \begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{factor}&\text{$\notnfar{Vhead}{V}$-coordinate}&\text{central coordinate}\\ \hline h_0&0&q(c)\\ u_1^{-1}&0&0\\ \notnfar{x1}{x_1}^\notn{sigma}{\sigma}&0&0\\ d_0=(\notn{x0}{x_0}\notn{tau}{\tau})^\notn{w}{\w} \notn{x0}{x_0}^{-1}&(\notn{Pnorm}{P}+1)c&\ast\\ z_0=\notn{x0}{x_0}^{\notn{sigma}{\sigma}^\notn{w}{\w}}&\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}^{-1}c&\ast\\ {[d_0,z_0]}&0&\notnfar{bq}{b_q}((\notn{Pnorm}{P}+1)c,\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}^{-1}c)\\ \end{array} \end{equation*}
    The starred entries contain ordinary \(f\)-terms and the \(m\)-terms of the lifted \(\notn{Cfin}{C}\)-action. They occur only as central coordinates of \(d_0\) and \(z_0\text{,}\) and central coordinates do not affect the commutator. Since the lower values of \(d_0\) and \(z_0\) at the tame map are both the identity, the commutator contribution is exactly the polar form of their \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\)-coordinates, \(\notnfar{bq}{b_q}((\notn{Pnorm}{P}+1)c,\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}^{-1}c)\text{.}\)
    🔗
    The first line is the extraspecial case of Lemma 5.3, but we recall why it remains valid with the \(m\)-terms present. The class-two identity Lemma 5.2 uses only that the lift of the relevant tame operator is an automorphism of the central extension and fixes the centre; it does not assume that the chosen section is equivariant. If \(\notn{Pnorm}{P}=0\text{,}\) then \(d_0\) and \(\notn{x0}{x_0}\) have the same image in \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\text{,}\) so the identity gives the square of \(\notn{x0}{x_0}\text{,}\) namely \(q(c)\text{.}\) If \(\notn{Pnorm}{P}=1\text{,}\) then \(\notn{opT}{\mathsf T}=1\) and the lift of \(\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}\) is a central automorphism of order at most \(2\text{,}\) so \(g_0=\sigma_2^2\) acts trivially on the class-two coefficient group and the same identity applies.
    🔗
    The factors \(u_1^{-1}\) and \(\notnfar{x1}{x_1}^\notn{sigma}{\sigma}\) have zero \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\)-coordinate on the normalized representative, and hence no quadratic central contribution. Multiplying the table gives (6.24). Polarizing and using the \(\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}\)-invariance of \(\notnfar{bq}{b_q}\) gives (6.26); the operator is invertible by the same polynomial argument used in Proposition 5.15. Finally, (6.27) is exactly (6.7) on the candidate source.
    🔗
    🔗

    Subsubsection 6.2.1 The Arf invariant of the candidate form

    Lemma 6.6. Wall doubling.
    Let \((\notnfar{Vhead}{V},q)\) be nonsingular over \(\F_2\text{,}\) with polar form \(\notnfar{bq}{b_q}\text{,}\) and let \(\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}\in O(\notnfar{Vhead}{V},q)\) have \(2\)-power order. Put
    \begin{equation*} q_{\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}}(x)=q(x)+\notnfar{bq}{b_q}(x,\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}^{-1}x). \end{equation*}
    Then \(q_{\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}}\) is nonsingular and
    \begin{equation} \notn{Arf}{\Arf}(q_{\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}})=\notn{Arf}{\Arf}(q)+\operatorname{rank}(1+\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U})\pmod2.\tag{6.28} \end{equation}
    🔗
    Lean (nonsingularity)Lean (main)
    🔗
    Proof.
    Let \(N=1+\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}\text{,}\) \(R=NV\text{,}\) and \(K=\ker N\text{.}\) Since \(q(\mathsf Ux)=q(x)\text{,}\)
    \begin{equation*} \notnfar{bq}{b_q}(x,\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}^{-1}x)=\notnfar{bq}{b_q}(x,\mathsf Ux)=q(Nx), \end{equation*}
    so \(q_{\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}}(x)=q(x)+q(Nx)\text{.}\) Define the nondegenerate Wall form on \(R\) by
    \begin{equation*} \notn{omgu}{\omega}(Nx,u)=\notnfar{bq}{b_q}(x,u). \end{equation*}
    In \((\notnfar{Vhead}{V},q_{\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}})\perp(\notnfar{Vhead}{V},q)\text{,}\) the diagonal \(\{(k,k):k\in K\}\) is totally singular. Its orthogonal quotient is \(R\oplus R\) with quadratic form
    \begin{equation*} \Phi_\omega(v,u)=\notn{omgu}{\omega}(v,v)+\notn{omgu}{\omega}(u,u)+\notn{omgu}{\omega}(v,u). \end{equation*}
    If \(v\mapsto\notn{omgu}{\omega}(v,v)\) is nonzero, split an anisotropic plane from \(\Phi_\omega\text{;}\) if \(\omega\) is alternating, split a symplectic plane from \(R\text{,}\) which contributes a hyperbolic four-space. Induction gives \(\notn{Arf}{\Arf}(\Phi_\omega)=\dim R\pmod2\text{,}\) proving (6.28).
    🔗
    🔗
    Lemma 6.7. Invariant quadratic forms on a hermitian line.
    Let \(F/F_0\) be a quadratic extension of finite fields of characteristic \(2\text{,}\) write \(x\mapsto x^*\) for its involution, and let \(\mathcal U_1=\{u\in F^\times:uu^*=1\}\text{.}\) Let \(W\) be a one-dimensional \(F\)-space. Every nonsingular \(\mathcal U_1\)-invariant quadratic form \(Q:W\to\F_2\) is uniquely of the form
    \begin{equation*} Q(x)=\Tr_{F_0/\F_2}(a xx^*) \qquad (a\in F_0^\times). \end{equation*}
    🔗
    Lean
    🔗
    Proof.
    Choose a generator \(u_0\) of the cyclic group \(\mathcal U_1\text{.}\) Since \(2^m\equiv-1\pmod{2^m+1}\) and no smaller positive power of \(2\) is \(1\) modulo \(2^m+1\text{,}\) the element \(u_0\) has degree \(2m\) over \(\F_2\text{;}\) hence \(\F_2[u_0]=F\text{.}\) Invariance gives
    \begin{equation*} b_Q(dx,y)=b_Q(x,d^*y)\qquad(d\in F). \end{equation*}
    Putting \(\ell(y)=b_Q(1,y)\text{,}\) we obtain \(b_Q(x,y)=\ell(x^*y)\text{.}\) Write \(\ell(z)=\Tr_{F/\F_2}(cz)\) for the unique \(c\in F\text{.}\) Symmetry of \(b_Q\) forces \(c=c^*\text{,}\) hence \(c\in F_0\text{,}\) and therefore
    \begin{equation*} b_Q(x,y)=\Tr_{F_0/\F_2} \bigl(c(xy^*+x^*y)\bigr). \end{equation*}
    Conversely these forms are alternating, and they are nonsingular exactly when \(c\ne0\text{.}\) The quadratic form \(q_c(x)=\Tr_{F_0/\F_2}(cxx^*)\) has this polarization. Hence \(Q-q_c\) is a \(\mathcal U_1\)-invariant linear form. Writing such a form as \(x\mapsto\Tr_{F/\F_2}(bx)\text{,}\) invariance under \(u_0\) gives \(b(u_0-1)=0\text{,}\) so \(b=0\text{.}\) Thus \(Q=q_c\text{,}\) uniquely, and nonsingularity gives \(c\in F_0^\times\text{.}\)
    🔗
    🔗
    Lemma 6.8. Ramified Hermitian model and Frobenius fixed space.
    Let \(I=\langle \notn{opT}{\mathsf T}\rangle\) be tame inertia, let \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\) be a simple ramified self-dual \(\F_2[H_V]\)-module, and write
    \begin{equation*} \notnfar{Vhead}{V}|_I\cong W^{\oplus s}, \qquad f=\dim_{\F_2}W=2^a r, \qquad r\text{ odd},\quad a\ge1. \end{equation*}
    Let \(q\) be an \(H_V\)-invariant nonsingular quadratic form with polar form \(\notnfar{bq}{b_q}\text{.}\) Then
    \begin{equation} \notn{Arf}{\Arf}(q)\equiv s\pmod2.\tag{6.29} \end{equation}
    For \(\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}=\notn{opS}{\mathsf S}^{\omega_2}\) one also has
    \begin{equation} \dim_{\F_2}\notnfar{Vhead}{V}^{\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}}=rs, \qquad \operatorname{rank}(1+\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U})=rs(2^a-1)\equiv s\pmod2.\tag{6.30} \end{equation}
    Consequently the ramified candidate base form of (6.25) has \(\notn{Arf}{\Arf}(Q_A^0)=0\text{.}\)
    🔗
    Lean (Arf vanishing)Lean (Arf = s)Lean (main)
    🔗
    Proof.
    We identify the invariant quadratic form with a Hermitian form, compute its Arf invariant one Hermitian line at a time, and then determine the fixed space of the \(2\)-primary Frobenius operator.
    🔗
    Put
    \begin{equation*} F_V=\End_I(W)\cong\F_{2^f}. \end{equation*}
    Choose an inertia character \(\zeta\) over \(\overline{\F}_2\text{;}\) then \(W\) is the additive group of \(F_V\) and \(\notn{opT}{\mathsf T}\) acts by multiplication by \(\zeta\text{.}\) Since \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}|_I\) has only the irreducible isomorphism type \(W\) and \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\cong \notnfar{Vhead}{V}^\vee\text{,}\) the inverse character \(\zeta^{-1}\) lies in the Frobenius orbit of \(\zeta\text{.}\) The character is nontrivial of odd order, so this orbit has even length and
    \begin{equation*} \zeta^{-1}=\zeta^{2^{f/2}}. \end{equation*}
    Set
    \begin{equation*} F_{V,0}=\F_{2^{f/2}}, \qquad x^*=x^{2^{f/2}}. \end{equation*}
    After an \(I\)-module identification \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\cong F_V^s\text{,}\) the nondegenerate \(I\)-invariant form \(\notnfar{bq}{b_q}\) is uniquely expressible as
    \begin{equation} \notnfar{bq}{b_q}(x,y)=\Tr_{F_V/\F_2}(x^{*t}\mathsf H y), \qquad \mathsf H\in\GL_s(F_V),\quad \mathsf H^{*t}=\mathsf H.\tag{6.31} \end{equation}
    Indeed, invariance under multiplication by \(\zeta\text{,}\) nondegeneracy of the trace pairing, and symmetry identify the adjoint involution with \(*\) and force the matrix to be Hermitian.
    🔗
    Define
    \begin{equation} q_{\mathsf H}(x)=\Tr_{F_{V,0}/\F_2}(x^{*t}\mathsf H x).\tag{6.32} \end{equation}
    The scalar \(x^{*t}\mathsf Hx\) lies in \(F_{V,0}\text{,}\) and
    \begin{align*} q_{\mathsf H}(x+y)+q_{\mathsf H}(x)+q_{\mathsf H}(y) &=\Tr_{F_{V,0}/\F_2}(x^{*t}\mathsf Hy+y^{*t}\mathsf Hx)\\ &=\Tr_{F_V/\F_2}(x^{*t}\mathsf Hy)=\notnfar{bq}{b_q}(x,y). \end{align*}
    Thus \(q-q_{\mathsf H}\) is linear. It is \(I\)-invariant, while \((\notnfar{Vhead}{V}^\vee)^I=0\) because the inertia action is nontrivial and \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\) is simple. Hence \(q=q_{\mathsf H}\text{.}\)
    🔗
    Hermitian diagonalization over the finite field extension \(F_V/F_{V,0}\) gives
    \begin{equation*} \mathsf H\sim\operatorname{diag}(a_1,\dots,a_s), \qquad a_i\in F_{V,0}^\times. \end{equation*}
    Therefore \(q\) is an orthogonal sum of the \(s\) Hermitian-line forms
    \begin{equation*} q_{a_i}(x)=\Tr_{F_{V,0}/\F_2}(a_i xx^*). \end{equation*}
    Write \(m=f/2\text{.}\) The norm \(F_V^\times\to F_{V,0}^\times\) is surjective with fibres of size \(2^m+1\text{,}\) and the trace-zero subspace of \(F_{V,0}\) contains \(2^{m-1}-1\) nonzero elements. Hence
    \begin{equation*} \#q_{a_i}^{-1}(0) =1+(2^m+1)(2^{m-1}-1) =2^{2m-1}-2^{m-1}. \end{equation*}
    Each Hermitian line has Arf invariant \(1\text{.}\) Additivity of the Arf invariant proves (6.29).
    🔗
    It remains to compute the fixed space of \(\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}\text{.}\) Over \(\overline{\F}_2\text{,}\) the \(f\) inertia weights form one Frobenius cycle, each weight space having multiplicity \(s\text{.}\) Let \(e_\omega\) be the residue modulo \(f=2^ar\) of an integer representing \(\omega_2\text{.}\) By the defining congruences of \(\omega_2\text{,}\)
    \begin{equation*} e_\omega\equiv1\pmod{2^a}, \qquad e_\omega\equiv0\pmod r. \end{equation*}
    Thus translation by \(e_\omega\) on \(\mathbb{Z}/f\mathbb{Z}\) has \(r\) cycles, each of length \(2^a\text{.}\) On one cycle write the successive maps as
    \begin{equation*} E_0\xrightarrow{A_0}E_1\xrightarrow{A_1}\cdots \xrightarrow{A_{2^a-1}}E_0, \qquad \dim E_i=s. \end{equation*}
    The product \(A_{2^a-1}\cdots A_0\) is the action of \(\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}^{2^a}\) on \(E_0\text{.}\) The shift by \(2^ae_\omega\) is trivial modulo \(f\text{,}\) so \(\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}^{2^a}\) centralizes inertia; it also commutes with \(\notn{opS}{\mathsf S}\text{,}\) being a power of \(\notn{opS}{\mathsf S}\text{.}\) Hence it is a central \(2\)-element of the faithful tame image. A cyclic \(2\)-group acting in characteristic \(2\) has nonzero fixed vectors, and centrality makes its fixed space an \(H_V\)-submodule. Simplicity therefore forces \(\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}^{2^a}=1\) on \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\text{.}\) Consequently a \(\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}\)-fixed vector on a cycle is uniquely determined by its component in \(E_0\text{,}\) and that cycle contributes dimension \(s\text{.}\) There are \(r\) cycles, proving (6.30).
    🔗
    Finally, Lemma 6.6 gives
    \begin{equation*} \notn{Arf}{\Arf}(Q_A^0)=\notn{Arf}{\Arf}(q)+\operatorname{rank}(1+\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U})=s+s=0 \quad\text{in }\F_2. \end{equation*}
    🔗
    🔗
    These determinant computations combine into the candidate-side zero count.
    🔗
    Proposition 6.9. Candidate base determinant zero count.
    If \(d=\dim \notnfar{Vhead}{V}\text{,}\) then
    \begin{equation} \#(Q_A^0)^{-1}(0)= \begin{cases} 2^{d-1}-2^{d/2-1},&\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\text{ unramified},\\ 2^{d-1}+2^{d/2-1},&\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\text{ ramified}. \end{cases}\tag{6.33} \end{equation}
    🔗
    Lean (unramified, free)Lean (unramified, abelian)Lean (unramified, cyclic)Lean (unramified)Lean (ramified)Lean

    Proof.
    We determine the unramified and ramified signs separately, using the Hermitian-line count in the first case and Lemma 6.8 in the second.
    🔗
    If \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\) is unramified, \(\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}=1\) and \(Q_A^0=q\text{.}\) Put \(F_V=\End_{H_V}(\notnfar{Vhead}{V})\cong\F_{2^{2m}}\) and let \(F_{V,0}\cong\F_{2^m}\) be the fixed field of the adjoint involution \(d\mapsto d^*\) defined by the polar form \(\notnfar{bq}{b_q}\text{.}\) The simple cyclic module \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\) is a one-dimensional \(F_V\)-space. The norm-one group
    \begin{equation*} \mathcal U=\{u\in F_V^\times:uu^*=1\} \end{equation*}
    preserves \(\notnfar{bq}{b_q}\text{.}\) For \(u\in\mathcal U\text{,}\) the function \(x\mapsto q(ux)+q(x)\) is therefore linear. It is \(H_V\)-invariant because \(u\) commutes with \(H_V\) and \(q\) is \(H_V\)-invariant. Since \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\) is nontrivial simple, \((\notnfar{Vhead}{V}^\vee)^{H_V}=0\text{,}\) so the function is zero. Thus \(\mathcal U\le O(\notnfar{Vhead}{V},q)\text{.}\)
    🔗
    By Lemma 6.7,
    \begin{equation*} q(x)=\Tr_{F_{V,0}/\F_2}(a xx^*),\qquad a\in F_{V,0}^\times. \end{equation*}
    The norm fibres have size \(2^m+1\text{,}\) so the number of zeros is \(2^{2m-1}-2^{m-1}\) and the Arf invariant is \(1\text{.}\)
    🔗
    Assume \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\) is ramified. The complete Hermitian and fixed-space calculation is Lemma 6.8; in particular \(\notn{Arf}{\Arf}(Q_A^0)=0\text{.}\) For a nonsingular quadratic form of dimension \(d\text{,}\) the identity
    \begin{equation*} \#Q^{-1}(0)=2^{d-1}+(-1)^{\notn{Arf}{\Arf}(Q)}2^{d/2-1} \end{equation*}
    now gives (6.33).
