    Subsection 6.3 Local calculation

    This subsection uses the unit-filtration structure of dyadic local fields [Ser79, Chapter IV §2], the norm criteria for quadratic extensions [Ser79, Chapter V §2 and Chapter XIV §2], and local Tate duality [NSW, Theorem (7.2.6)].
    🔗
    Let \(q:\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\to\F_2\) be the invariant nonsingular quadratic form under consideration, and let \(\notnfar{kappaq0}{\kappa_q^0}\) be the base equivariant determinant class of Lemma 6.3. For a local cocycle \(b:\notnfar{GQ}{G_{\Qtwo}}\to \notnfar{Vhead}{V}\) with lower map \(\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}\text{,}\) put
    \begin{equation} Q^0_{\mathrm{loc}}([b])= \inv_{\Qtwo}\bigl[(b,\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho})^*\notnfar{kappaq0}{\kappa_q^0}\bigr].\tag{6.34} \end{equation}
    This is the base quadratic connecting map. For a general determinant pushout class \(\kappa=\notnfar{kappaq0}{\kappa_q^0}+\Gamma_{\gamma_\kappa}+\operatorname{inf}\delta_\kappa\text{,}\) the actual local obstruction is obtained from (6.34) by the difference formula (6.7); the affine terms are not folded into the base Gauss sum.
    🔗
    Let \(H_V\) be the faithful tame image on \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\) and let \(K/\notn{Qtwo}{\Qtwo}\) be its tame splitting field. Put \(M_K=K^\times/K^{\times2}\) and let \(U_i\) be the image of \(1+\mathfrak p_K^i\text{.}\) If \(e=v_K(2)\text{,}\) then
    \begin{equation} \gr_iM_K\cong \begin{cases} k_K,&1\le i<2e\text{ odd},\\ 0,&1\le i<2e\text{ even}, \end{cases}\tag{6.35} \end{equation}
    and
    \begin{equation} U_i^\perp=U_{2e-i+1}, \qquad -1\in U_e.\tag{6.36} \end{equation}
    These are the standard dyadic square-class filtration and Hilbert-symbol orthogonality relations; see [Ser79, Chapter XIV, Sections 2--3].
    🔗

    Lemma 6.10. The middle unit layer is unramified.

    Assume \(K/\notn{Qtwo}{\Qtwo}\) is tame and put \(e=v_K(2)\text{.}\) Then \(e\) is odd, and tame inertia acts trivially on the middle graded piece
    \begin{equation*} U_e/U_{e+1}. \end{equation*}
    Consequently a ramified simple tame module does not occur in that graded piece.
    🔗
    🔗

    Proof.
    The ramification index of a tame extension of \(\notn{Qtwo}{\Qtwo}\) is odd and equals the order of tame inertia. On the odd-depth piece \(\gr_jM_K\text{,}\) an inertia element represented by \(\zeta\) acts through the character \(\zeta\mapsto\zeta^j\text{.}\) At \(j=e\) this character is trivial. A ramified simple module has nontrivial inertia, so its isotypic multiplicity at the middle depth is zero.
    🔗
    🔗

    Lemma 6.11. Faithful-image projectivity.

    If \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\) is ramified, then \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\) and \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}^\vee\) are projective \(\F_2[H_V]\)-modules.
    🔗
    Lean (tame pair case)Lean (main)
    🔗

    Proof.
    We use Clifford theory over an algebraic closure to describe the inertia weights, prove regularity on Sylow-\(2\) weight blocks, and then descend projectivity to \(\F_2\text{.}\)
    🔗
    Let \(\overline{\F}_2\) be an algebraic closure, let \(I\triangleleft H_V\) be tame inertia, and choose an absolutely irreducible constituent \(W_0\) of \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\otimes_{\F_2}\overline{\F}_2\text{.}\) Since \(|I|\) is odd, \(W_0|_I\) is semisimple. Choose a nontrivial inertia character \(\chi\) occurring in it, and let \(H_\chi\) be its stabilizer. Clifford theory expresses \(W_0\) as the induction of a simple \(H_\chi\)-module on which \(I\) acts through \(\chi\text{.}\) The quotient \(H_\chi/I\) is cyclic. Since \(\chi\) is \(H_\chi\)-invariant and \(\overline{\F}_2\) contains all roots needed to satisfy the single cyclic relation, \(\chi\) extends to a one-dimensional character of \(H_\chi\text{.}\) After twisting by that extension, the inducing module factors through the cyclic quotient. Over \(\overline{\F}_2\) every simple module for a cyclic group is one-dimensional, and its \(2\)-primary subgroup acts trivially. Thus every \(\chi\)-weight space in \(W_0\) is one-dimensional.
    🔗
    Let the Frobenius orbit of \(\chi\) have length \(f=2^a r\) with \(r\) odd, and let \(\notn{Pnorm}{P}\) be a Sylow \(2\)-subgroup of \(H_V\text{.}\) The image of \(\notn{Pnorm}{P}\) in the cyclic quotient \(H_V/I\) is cyclic. Its action on the orbit of \(\chi\) has \(2\)-power orbit length \(2^a\text{.}\) If an element of \(\notn{Pnorm}{P}\) stabilizes \(\chi\text{,}\) it acts on the one-dimensional \(\chi\)-weight space by a scalar of \(2\)-power order, hence trivially because \(\overline{\F}_2^\times\) has no nontrivial \(2\)-power torsion. By conjugacy it then acts trivially on all inertia-weight spaces of \(W_0\text{,}\) and on every Galois conjugate constituent as well. Faithfulness of the image \(H_V\) therefore shows that this stabilizer is trivial. Consequently \(|\notn{Pnorm}{P}|=2^a\text{,}\) and \(\notn{Pnorm}{P}\) acts freely on the weights in blocks of size \(2^a\text{.}\)
    🔗
    On each block, transport a nonzero vector around the \(\notn{Pnorm}{P}\)-orbit. Because the generator of \(\notn{Pnorm}{P}\) has order \(2^a\text{,}\) the transported vectors form a regular \(\overline{\F}_2[\notn{Pnorm}{P}]\)-basis. Hence the restriction of every absolutely irreducible constituent, and therefore of \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\otimes_{\F_2}\overline{\F}_2\text{,}\) is a direct sum of regular \(\overline{\F}_2[\notn{Pnorm}{P}]\)-modules. It is projective over \(\overline{\F}_2[\notn{Pnorm}{P}]\text{.}\)
    🔗
    Projectivity descends along the faithfully flat extension \(\F_2\subset\overline{\F}_2\text{,}\) so \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}|_P\) is projective over \(\F_2[\notn{Pnorm}{P}]\text{.}\) The Sylow criterion for modular projectivity now gives projectivity over \(\F_2[H_V]\text{.}\) Replacing every inertia character by its inverse gives the identical Sylow restriction calculation for \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}^\vee\text{,}\) and hence proves projectivity of the dual module.
    🔗
    🔗

    Remark 6.12. Why the faithful image is required.

    Projectivity is asserted only for the faithful image \(H_V\text{.}\) A larger tame quotient may contain an additional unramified \(2\)-power subgroup acting trivially on \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\text{,}\) and projectivity over that larger group can fail. The base determinant connecting map depends only on \(H_V\text{;}\) information involving the extra kernel belongs to the inflated and filtration-one components separated from the base determinant calculation.
    🔗
    🔗
    Normalized-cochain conventions. From this point through Lemma 6.15, all coefficient modules are left modules and all cochains are normalized inhomogeneous cochains. The differential, cup product, semidirect-product convention, Shapiro map, corestriction, and all changes of sections and transversals are fixed in Appendix A. In particular, “equal as normalized cochains” means literal equality in the indicated cochain group; when a choice changes a formula, the corresponding normalized coboundary is the one displayed in Subsection A.7.
    🔗

    Lemma 6.13. Universal two-point normalization and the index-two Evens norm.

    Let
    \begin{equation*} J=\langle s\rangle\cong C_2, \qquad E_2=\F_2e_1\oplus\F_2e_s, \qquad s(\notnfar{x1}{x_1},x_s)=(x_s,\notnfar{x1}{x_1}), \end{equation*}
    and put
    \begin{equation*} q_{\mathrm{hyp}}(\notnfar{x1}{x_1},x_s)=x_1x_s, \qquad f_J(x,y)=x_1y_s, \qquad m_1=0, \qquad m_s(y)=y_1y_s. \end{equation*}
    Then
    \begin{equation} \kappa_J((x,c),(y,d))=f_J(x,cy)+m_c(y)\tag{6.37} \end{equation}
    is a normalized \(2\)-cocycle on \(E_2\rtimes J\text{.}\) It restricts to the quadratic map \(q_{\mathrm{hyp}}\) on \(E_2\) and to zero on the zero section \(J\text{.}\) Its fibre extension is the dihedral group \(D_8\text{:}\) the two coordinate lifts are involutions, their commutator is the central involution, and their product has square equal to that involution. Moreover
    \begin{equation} [\kappa_J]=N_{E_2}^{E_2\rtimes J,\mathrm{Ev}}(e_1^\vee) \quad\text{in }H^2(E_2\rtimes J,\F_2).\tag{6.38} \end{equation}
    🔗
    Now let \(N\triangleleft G\) have index \(2\text{,}\) identify \(G/N\) with \(J\text{,}\) and let \(\alpha\in Z^1(N,\F_2)\text{.}\) Choose lifts \(\widetilde1=1\) and \(\widetilde s\in G\text{,}\) and define the normalized Shapiro cocycle
    \begin{equation} b(\gamma)_u= \alpha\!\left(\widetilde u^{-1}\gamma \widetilde{\bar\gamma^{-1}u}\right), \qquad u\in J.\tag{6.39} \end{equation}
    This is the degree-one normalized Shapiro map (A.12). The graph pullback of (6.37) is
    \begin{equation} \nu_\alpha(\gamma,\eta) =b(\gamma)_1b(\eta)_{\bar\gamma^{-1}s} +\varepsilon(\bar\gamma)b(\eta)_1b(\eta)_s,\tag{6.40} \end{equation}
    where \(\varepsilon(1)=0\) and \(\varepsilon(s)=1\text{.}\) Its class is the index-two Evens norm:
    \begin{equation} [\nu_\alpha]=N_N^{G,\mathrm{Ev}}([\alpha])\in H^2(G,\F_2).\tag{6.41} \end{equation}
    Equivalently, the normalization is
    \begin{equation*} N_N^G(1+[\alpha]) =1+\operatorname{cor}_N^G[\alpha] +N_N^{G,\mathrm{Ev}}([\alpha]). \end{equation*}
    🔗
    Finally, if \(g\in H\) is an involution, \(M=\F_2[H]\text{,}\) \(J=\langle g\rangle\text{,}\) and \(\pi:M\to\F_2[J]\) selects the coordinates indexed by \(1\) and \(g\text{,}\) then for every right-coset transversal \(\mathcal R\text{,}\)
    \begin{equation} [\kappa_g^{\mathcal R}] =\operatorname{cor}_{M\rtimes J}^{M\rtimes H} (\pi\rtimes1)^*[\kappa_J].\tag{6.42} \end{equation}
    🔗
    Lean (dihedral)Lean (Evens)
    🔗

    Proof.
    We verify the universal cocycle and its fibre extension, identify its class with the Evens norm, pull it back to a general index-two inclusion, and then compare the regular-module half-orbit transfer.
    🔗
    Expanding \(m_s\) on the two coordinates gives the two identities required in Lemma 6.1: for \(v,w\in E_2\text{,}\)
    \begin{equation*} m_s(v+w)+m_s(v)+m_s(w)=f_J(sv,sw)+f_J(v,w), \qquad m_s(sv)+m_s(v)=0. \end{equation*}
    Thus (6.37) is a normalized cocycle. Its square map is \(x_1x_s\text{,}\) and it vanishes when both fibre coordinates are zero. If \(\widetilde e_1,\widetilde e_s\) are the coordinate lifts, then \(\widetilde e_1^2=\widetilde e_s^2=1\text{,}\) their commutator is the central generator, and \((\widetilde e_1\widetilde e_s)^2\) is that generator; hence the fibre extension is \(D_8\text{.}\)
    🔗
    For the swap module,
    \begin{equation} H^1(J,E_2^\vee)=\frac{\ker(1+s)}{\operatorname{im}(1+s)}=0.\tag{6.43} \end{equation}
    The low-degree exact sequence (6.22) therefore says that a class on \(E_2\rtimes J\) is determined by its restriction to \(E_2\) and its restriction to the zero section. Mackey’s formula for the standard Evens norm gives
    \begin{equation*} \res_{E_2} N_{E_2}^{E_2\rtimes J,\mathrm{Ev}}(e_1^\vee)=e_1^\vee e_s^\vee, \qquad \res_J N_{E_2}^{E_2\rtimes J,\mathrm{Ev}}(e_1^\vee)=0. \end{equation*}
    These are exactly the two restrictions of \([\kappa_J]\text{,}\) proving (6.38). Equivalently, this class is the degree-two component of the relative Stiefel–Whitney class \(w(\operatorname{Ind}\ell)/w(\operatorname{Ind}1)\) under the Evens–Kahn normalization; see [Eve, Thm. 1], [Kah, Théorèmes 1--2], [Koz, Thm. 1.1].
    🔗
    For the general index-two inclusion, the graph
    \begin{equation*} \Phi_\alpha:G\longrightarrow E_2\rtimes J, \qquad \gamma\longmapsto(b(\gamma),\bar\gamma) \end{equation*}
    has inverse image of \(E_2\) equal to \(N\text{,}\) and the pullback of \(e_1^\vee\) to \(N\) is \(\alpha\text{.}\) Naturality of the Evens norm in this pullback square and (6.38) give (6.41). Direct substitution of (6.39) into (6.37) gives (6.40) term by term. This is also the degree-two term in Evens’s normalized bar construction [Eve, §§4--5]. If \(\widetilde s\) is replaced by \(\widetilde s a\) with \(a\in N\text{,}\) then (A.25) gives the exact change of the Shapiro cocycle, and (A.36) gives the resulting normalized \(1\)-cochain whose boundary is the change in (6.40). Thus the lift dependence is controlled at cochain level, not only in cohomology.
    🔗
    For (6.42), Mackey restriction of the right side to \(\notnfar{Mmid}{M}\) is
    \begin{equation*} \sum_{u\in H/J}x_u x_{ug}, \end{equation*}
    and its zero-section restriction is zero. The explicit class \([\kappa_g^{\mathcal R}]\) has the same two restrictions. Moreover \(H^1(H,\notnfar{Mmid}{M}^\vee)=0\) by Shapiro’s lemma, since \(\notnfar{Mmid}{M}^\vee\) is coinduced. The same low-degree uniqueness argument proves equality. More precisely, (A.30) identifies the two representatives as normalized cochains for the chosen transversal, and (A.32) displays the normalized \(1\)-cochain whose boundary is the change under an arbitrary new transversal.
    🔗
    🔗

    Lemma 6.14. Regular-module realization of the base local connecting map.

    With notation as in Lemma 6.3, the base local determinant form satisfies, for every \(x\in H^1(\notn{Qtwo}{\Qtwo},\notnfar{Vhead}{V})\text{,}\)
    \begin{equation} Q^0_{\mathrm{loc},q}(x)=Q^0_{\mathrm{loc},q_W}(i_*x).\tag{6.44} \end{equation}
    Under Kummer theory and the normalized Shapiro cochain map, the right side is obtained by applying the orbit operations of Lemma 6.15 to the scalar Shapiro coordinates. Thus the regular-module computation evaluates the actual base equivariant central class \(\notnfar{kappaq0}{\kappa_q^0}\text{,}\) including the \(m_c\)-terms; it is not merely a polynomial with the same polarization.
    🔗
    Lean
    🔗

    Proof.
    The equality of classes is the pullback identity \(\notnfar{kappaq0}{\kappa_q^0}=(i\rtimes1)^*\kappa_{q_W}^0\) from (6.19). Pulling that identity back along a Galois graph cocycle gives equality of normalized central \(2\)-cocycles over \(\notnfar{GQ}{G_{\Qtwo}}\text{,}\) hence (6.44) after applying the local invariant map.
    🔗
    For the second assertion, use the explicit representatives in (6.17), (6.18), and (6.15). Direct substitution of the normalized Shapiro cocycle gives the square and free-orbit corestriction formulas. For a half-orbit, the correction term \(m_c^g\) records exactly whether the action on a right coset of \(\langle g\rangle\) preserves or reverses the chosen orientation of its two coordinates. Thus the graph pullback is the normalized corestriction of the two-point graph cocycle (6.40); by Lemma 6.13 that two-point class is the index-two Evens norm. The full cochain calculation is written out in Lemma 6.15.
    🔗
    🔗

    Lemma 6.15. Quadratic orbit–stabilizer Shapiro.

    Let \(W=\F_2[H]^N\) have coordinates \(X_{r,h}\) with \(H\) acting by left translation on \(h\text{.}\) If \(K/F\) is the \(H\)-extension and \(\alpha_r\in H^1(K,\F_2)\) is the scalar Shapiro coordinate, then the orbit classes of Lemma 6.3 evaluate as follows. For \(g\in H\text{,}\) choose any lift \(\widetilde g\in G_F\) and use the convention
    \begin{equation*} (g\alpha_s)(n)=\alpha_s(\widetilde g^{-1}n\widetilde g) \qquad(n\in G_K). \end{equation*}
    This is independent of the chosen lift and is the convention fixed in (A.13):
    \begin{align} S_r&\longmapsto \cor_{K/F}(\alpha_r^2),\tag{6.45}\\ C_{r,s,g}&\longmapsto \cor_{K/F}(\alpha_r\smile g\alpha_s),\tag{6.46}\\ E_{r,g}&\longmapsto \cor_{K_0/F}\Evens_{K/K_0}(\alpha_r), \qquad K_0=K^{\langle g\rangle}.\tag{6.47} \end{align}
    🔗
    Lean (square)Lean (free)Lean (involution)Lean (free, aux)Lean (involution, aux)
    🔗

    Proof.
    We treat square orbits, free orbits, and involution-stabilized orbits in that order, recording at each stage whether the identity is literal at cochain level or only after passage to cohomology.
    🔗
    Choose lifts \(\widetilde h\in G_F\) of \(h\in H\text{,}\) and write \(\bar\gamma\) for the image of \(\gamma\in G_F\) in \(H\text{.}\) With the left-regular convention used here, the normalized Shapiro map is
    \begin{equation*} b_r(\gamma)_h =\operatorname{Sh}(\alpha_r)(\gamma)_h =\alpha_r\!\left(\widetilde h^{-1}\gamma \widetilde{\bar\gamma^{-1}h}\right). \end{equation*}
    For scalar cocycles \(\alpha,\beta\) on \(G_K\text{,}\) direct substitution into the normalized bar corestriction gives
    \begin{equation} \sum_{h\in H} \operatorname{Sh}(\alpha)(\gamma)_h\, \operatorname{Sh}(\beta)(\eta)_{\bar\gamma^{-1}h} =\operatorname{cor}_{K/F}(\alpha\smile\beta)(\gamma,\eta).\tag{6.48} \end{equation}
    The factor set (6.17) therefore gives (6.45). For the free orbit, the coordinate appearing in the monomial is the right shift \(\mathsf R_g\operatorname{Sh}(\alpha_s)\text{.}\) By (A.15) this differs from \(\operatorname{Sh}(g\alpha_s)\) by the explicit coboundary \(dq_{\alpha_s,g}\text{,}\) and (A.16) displays the resulting normalized boundary after taking the cup product and trace. Therefore (6.46) holds in cohomology; it is a literal cochain identity whenever the chosen section is right-\(g\)-equivariant.
    🔗
    Now let \(J=\langle g\rangle\text{,}\) let \(\mathcal R\) be right-coset representatives for \(H/J\text{,}\) and put \(K_0=K^J\text{.}\) For \(c\in H\) and \(u\in\mathcal R\text{,}\) use the notation
    \begin{equation*} c^{-1}u=\pi_c(u)g^{\epsilon_c(u)} \end{equation*}
    of Lemma 6.2. Let \(\rho_0:G_{K_0}\twoheadrightarrow J\) be the quotient map. The graph pullback of the explicit half-orbit cocycle (6.15) is
    \begin{align} &\sum_{u\in\mathcal R} b_r(\gamma)_u\, b_r(\eta)_{\bar\gamma^{-1}ug}\notag\\ &\qquad+ \sum_{u\in\mathcal R}\epsilon_{\bar\gamma}(u) b_r(\eta)_{\pi_{\bar\gamma}(u)} b_r(\eta)_{\pi_{\bar\gamma}(u)g}.\tag{6.49} \end{align}
    For completeness, choose the lifts compatibly so that \(\widetilde{ug}=\widetilde u\,\widetilde g\) for \(u\in\mathcal R\text{,}\) and put
    \begin{equation*} \ell_u(\gamma)= \widetilde u^{-1}\gamma\, \widetilde{\pi_{\bar\gamma}(u)} \in G_{K_0}. \end{equation*}
    Its image in \(J\) is \(g^{\epsilon_{\bar\gamma}(u)}\text{.}\) In these conventions the normalized corestriction of a \(2\)-cochain \(\nu\) on \(G_{K_0}\) is
    \begin{equation} (\operatorname{cor}_{K_0/F}\nu)(\gamma,\eta) = \sum_{u\in\mathcal R} \nu\!\left( \ell_u(\gamma), \ell_{\pi_{\bar\gamma}(u)}(\eta) \right).\tag{6.50} \end{equation}
    Let \(b_J=\operatorname{Sh}_{K/K_0}(\alpha_r)\text{.}\) Compatibility of the transversals gives
    \begin{equation*} b_J(\ell_u(\gamma))_1=b_r(\gamma)_u \end{equation*}
    and, for \(j\in\{1,g\}\text{,}\)
    \begin{equation*} b_J\!\left(\ell_{\pi_{\bar\gamma}(u)}(\eta)\right)_j = b_r(\eta)_{\pi_{\bar\gamma}(u)j}. \end{equation*}
    Substituting the explicit two-point cocycle (6.40) into (6.50) gives exactly (6.49): its first summand is the oriented factor-set term, and its second summand is the orientation-reversal correction. Consequently
    \begin{equation} (b_r,\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho})^*\kappa_g^{\mathcal R} =\operatorname{cor}_{K_0/F} \left((\operatorname{Sh}_{K/K_0}\alpha_r,\rho_0)^*\kappa_J\right)\tag{6.51} \end{equation}
    as normalized cochains. By Lemma 6.13, the inner graph class is \(N_{G_K}^{G_{K_0},\mathrm{Ev}}(\alpha_r)\text{,}\) which is denoted \(\Evens_{K/K_0}(\alpha_r)\) in field notation. Equation (6.47) follows. With the compatible nested transversals just chosen, (6.51) is literal equality of normalized cochains. For arbitrary choices, (A.32) and (A.34) give the two explicit normalized \(1\)-cochains whose boundaries account for the change. Hence the formulas evaluate the actual orbit classes used in \(\kappa_{q_W}^0\text{,}\) including all \(m_c\)-terms, without an unspecified convention-dependent ambiguity.
    🔗
    🔗

    Lemma 6.16. Deep-unit Evens norm.

    Let \(L/k\) be an unramified quadratic extension of finite dyadic local fields and put \(e=v_k(2)\text{.}\) Then
    \begin{equation} \Evens_{L/k}(\alpha)=0 \qquad(\alpha\in U_{e+1}(L)\subset L^\times/L^{\times2}).\tag{6.52} \end{equation}
    🔗
    Lean
    🔗

    Proof.
    We translate the Evens norm into the degree-two Evens–Kahn identity, reduce the trace forms to Hilbert symbols, and then cancel the remaining terms by norm and Steinberg relations.
    🔗
    By Lemma 6.13, the Evens norm is represented by the explicit two-point graph cocycle (6.40). The index-two Evens–Kahn formula identifies this normalization with the degree-two term in the relative Stiefel–Whitney identity [Kah, Théorèmes 1--2], [Koz, Thm. 1.1]
    \begin{equation} w(\Tr_{L/k}\langle a\rangle)= w(\Tr_{L/k}\langle1\rangle) \bigl(1+\cor_{L/k}[a]+\Evens_{L/k}([a])\bigr).\tag{6.53} \end{equation}
    🔗
    Take a class in \(U_{e+1}(L)\) and choose from the outset a representative
    \begin{equation*} a=1+2b,\qquad b\in\mathfrak p_L. \end{equation*}
    Write \(L=k(\sqrt d)\text{,}\) where \(d\) is the unramified quadratic square class, and write
    \begin{equation*} a=u+v\sqrt d,\qquad n=N_{L/k}(a)=u^2-dv^2. \end{equation*}
    If
    \begin{equation*} t=\Tr_{L/k}(b),\qquad m=N_{L/k}(b), \end{equation*}
    then
    \begin{equation} u=1+t\in\mathcal O_k^\times, \qquad n=1+2t+4m.\tag{6.54} \end{equation}
    In particular the divisions by \(u\) below are legitimate. The trace forms diagonalize as
    \begin{equation*} \Tr_{L/k}\langle a\rangle\simeq \left\langle2u,\frac{2dn}{u}\right\rangle, \qquad \Tr_{L/k}\langle1\rangle\simeq\langle2,2d\rangle. \end{equation*}
    Taking degree two in (6.53) first gives
    \begin{equation*} \Evens_{L/k}([a])=(2u,2dn/u)+(2,2d)+(d,n). \end{equation*}
    We now keep every Hilbert-symbol cancellation visible. Bilinearity and \((x,x)=(x,-1)\) give
    \begin{align*} (2u,2dn/u) &=(2u,2)+(2u,d)+(2u,n)+(2u,u),\\ (2u,2)+(2u,u)&=(2u,2u)=(2u,-1),\\ (2,2d)&=(2,-1)+(2,d). \end{align*}
    Consequently
    \begin{align*} \Evens_{L/k}([a]) &= (u,-1)+(u,d)+(2u,n)+(d,n)\\ &= (u,-d)+(2du,n). \end{align*}
    Thus
    \begin{equation} \Evens_{L/k}([a])=(u,-d)+(2du,n).\tag{6.55} \end{equation}
    🔗
    In more detail: the Kummer coordinates are part of the proof, not additional arithmetic hypotheses. Since the residue characteristic is not the field characteristic, an unramified quadratic extension has a presentation \(L=k(\delta)\) with \(\delta^2=d\in k^\times\text{,}\) and every deep unit can be written uniquely as \(a=u+v\delta\text{.}\) The index-two condition ensures \(\delta\notin k\text{;}\) together with \(a\ne0\text{,}\) this shows that \(n=u^2-dv^2\) is nonzero and that the divisions in the displayed diagonalization are legitimate.
    🔗
    Because \(L/k\) is unramified and \(b\in\mathfrak p_L\text{,}\) one has \(v_k(m)\ge2\text{.}\) From (6.54),
    \begin{equation} \frac{n}{2u-1} =1+\frac{4m}{2u-1}\in U_{2e+2}(k).\tag{6.56} \end{equation}
    Here \(2u-1\) is a unit and \(v_k(4m)\ge2e+2>2v_k(2)\text{.}\) Hensel’s lemma, applied to \(X^2-n/(2u-1)\) at \(X=1\text{,}\) therefore gives \(U_{2e+2}(k)\subset k^{\times2}\text{.}\) Thus \(n\) and \(2u-1\) have the same square class.
    🔗
    Unramifiedness is used here in two distinct ways. Equality of value groups gives the depth estimate that makes \(n/(2u-1)\) a square by Hensel’s lemma. In the remaining line, surjectivity of the norm on units kills the symbols involving \(d\text{;}\) the Steinberg relation then reduces the answer to two copies of \((u,-1)\text{,}\) which cancel in characteristic two.
    🔗
    Every unit of \(k\) is a norm from its unramified quadratic extension, and \(n=N_{L/k}(a)\text{.}\) Hence
    \begin{equation*} (u,d)=0,\qquad(d,n)=0. \end{equation*}
    Formula (6.55) becomes
    \begin{equation*} (u,-1)+(2u,2u-1). \end{equation*}
    The Steinberg relation gives \((2u,2u-1)=(2u,-1)\text{.}\) Finally \((2,-1)=0\text{:}\) if \(i\in k\text{,}\) then \(-1\) is a square; otherwise \(2=N_{k(i)/k}(1+i)\text{.}\) Consequently \((2u,-1)=(u,-1)\text{,}\) and the two terms cancel.
    🔗
    🔗

    Lemma 6.17. The deep half is totally singular.

    Assume \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\) is ramified and put
    \begin{equation*} X_+=\Hom_{H_V}(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}^\vee,U_{e+1})\subset H^1(\notn{Qtwo}{\Qtwo},\notnfar{Vhead}{V}). \end{equation*}
    Then
    \begin{equation*} \dim X_+=\frac12\dim H^1(\notn{Qtwo}{\Qtwo},\notnfar{Vhead}{V}), \qquad Q^0_{\mathrm{loc}}|_{X_+}=0. \end{equation*}
    🔗
    Lean (dim, ext+duality)Lean (dim, duality)Lean (dim, residue lift)Lean (dimension)Lean (vanishing)
    🔗

    Proof.
    We first count the contributing unit-filtration layers and then prove vanishing on the deep half by checking square, free, and involution orbits.
    🔗
    By Hochschild–Serre and Kummer theory,
    \begin{equation*} H^1(\notn{Qtwo}{\Qtwo},\notnfar{Vhead}{V})\cong\Hom_{H_V}(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}^\vee,M_K), \end{equation*}
    and \(\Hom_{H_V}(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}^\vee,-)\) is exact on the unit filtration. Hilbert duality pairs the depth-\(j\) and depth-\((2e-j)\) graded pieces, and self-duality of \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\) gives equal \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\)-isotypic multiplicities in each pair. The only unpaired depth is \(j=e\text{;}\) by Lemma 6.10 it has trivial inertia and contains no ramified copy of \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\text{.}\) Hence exactly one member of every contributing pair lies above \(e\text{,}\) proving the dimension statement.
    🔗
    In more detail: the dimension assertion is proved in the formalization as the cardinal identity \(|X_+|^2=|H^1(\Qtwo,V)|\text{.}\) The regular-module embedding is constructed for both \(V\) and \(V^\vee\text{;}\) inverse Shapiro maps extend families from the regular module, while local duality identifies the deep part for one module with the quotient part for the other. A residue-trivial lift of tame inertia is what makes this comparison respect the middle unit layer. Since that layer is inertia-trivial, it contains no copy of the ramified simple module.
    🔗
    By Lemma 6.14, compute the base connecting map after an \(H_V\)-split embedding into a regular module, and apply Lemma 6.15 to the complete invariant monomial expansion of \(q\circ p\text{.}\) For a class in \(X_+\) every scalar coordinate \(\alpha_r\) lies in \(U_{e+1}(K)\text{.}\) Free orbits vanish by (6.36). Square orbits vanish because \(\alpha_r^2=\alpha_r\smile(-1)\) and \(-1\in U_e\text{.}\) For an involution orbit, tame inertia has odd order, so \(K/K_0\) in (6.47) is unramified quadratic. The depth parameter is unchanged in an unramified subextension, and Lemma 6.16 makes the Evens norm vanish before corestriction. Every orbit contribution is therefore zero.
    🔗
    For the involution orbits, one needs slightly more than the abstract fact that the relevant subgroup has index two. The tame reciprocity orientation identifies the corresponding quadratic extension as unramified; only then does the deep-unit Evens norm vanish by Lemma 6.16. Thus the square, free, and involution orbit calculations use respectively the depth pairing, ordinary cup-product vanishing, and the oriented unramified norm calculation.
    🔗
    🔗
    🔗

    Subsection 6.4 Comparison of the Gauss signs

    Proposition 6.18. Dyadic base determinant theorem.

    If \(d=\dim \notnfar{Vhead}{V}\text{,}\) then
    \begin{equation} \#(Q^0_{\mathrm{loc}})^{-1}(0)= \begin{cases} 2^{d-1}-2^{d/2-1},&\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\text{ unramified},\\ 2^{d-1}+2^{d/2-1},&\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\text{ ramified}. \end{cases}\tag{6.57} \end{equation}
    Equivalently, the base local Gauss sum is negative in the unramified case and positive in the ramified case. The candidate base form \(Q_A^0\) has the same Gauss sum by Proposition 6.9.
    🔗
    Lean (vanishing core)Lean (ramified)Lean (unramified)Lean
    🔗

    Proof.
    The ramified and unramified cases are treated separately: the first follows from the half-dimensional totally singular subspace, while the second is determined by the invariant Hermitian-line classification.
    🔗
    In the ramified case, local Euler–Poincaré and Tate duality give \(\dim H^1(\notn{Qtwo}{\Qtwo},\notnfar{Vhead}{V})=d\text{.}\) By Lemma 6.17, the nonsingular base local quadratic space contains a totally singular subspace of dimension \(d/2\text{,}\) so it is hyperbolic.
    🔗
    In more detail: the two conclusions of Lemma 6.17 are used as a Lagrangian criterion. The local determinant form is first shown to be nonsingular, and simplicity together with \(|V|=2^{2m}\) supplies the exponent-two structure. A totally singular subgroup whose square has the cardinality of the whole quadratic space is maximal totally singular; hence the Arf invariant is zero, and the plus-type zero count follows without choosing a symplectic basis.
    🔗
    In the unramified case, the faithful image is cyclic of odd order. Put \(F_V=\End_{H_V}(\notnfar{Vhead}{V})\text{.}\) Self-duality equips \(F_V\cong\F_{2^{2m}}\) with the involution \(x\mapsto x^*=x^{2^m}\) and fixed field \(F_{V,0}\cong\F_{2^m}\text{.}\) Inflation–restriction and the local Euler characteristic identify \(H^1(\notn{Qtwo}{\Qtwo},\notnfar{Vhead}{V})\) with a one-dimensional \(F_V\)-space. The norm-one group
    \begin{equation*} \mathcal U=\{u\in F_V^\times:uu^*=1\} \end{equation*}
    preserves the polar form of \(q\text{.}\) For \(u\in\mathcal U\text{,}\) the function \(x\mapsto q(ux)+q(x)\) is linear and \(H_V\)-invariant. Since \((\notnfar{Vhead}{V}^\vee)^{H_V}=0\text{,}\) it vanishes; hence every \(u\in\mathcal U\) is an \(H_V\)-equivariant \(q\)-isometry. By (6.21), \((u\rtimes1)^*[\notnfar{kappaq0}{\kappa_q^0}]=[\notnfar{kappaq0}{\kappa_q^0}]\text{.}\) Functoriality of graph pullback therefore gives
    \begin{equation*} Q^0_{\mathrm{loc}}(u_*x)=Q^0_{\mathrm{loc}}(x) \qquad(u\in\mathcal U). \end{equation*}
    Thus Lemma 6.7 applies to the base local form, and it is
    \begin{equation*} Q(x)=\Tr_{F_{V,0}/\F_2}(a xx^*), \qquad a\in F_{V,0}^\times. \end{equation*}
    The norm map \(F_V^\times\to F_{V,0}^\times\) has fibres of size \(2^m+1\text{.}\) Among the nonzero elements of \(F_{V,0}\text{,}\) exactly \(2^{m-1}-1\) have trace \(0\text{.}\) Hence
    \begin{equation*} \#Q^{-1}(0)=1+(2^m+1)(2^{m-1}-1) =2^{2m-1}-2^{m-1}, \end{equation*}
    which is the minus-type number in (6.57).
    🔗
    Here one must also justify that the norm-one scalars act by isometries of the local form. The formal proof does not treat this as a literal equality of the chosen factor sets: naturality changes the graph cocycle by an explicit normalized coboundary, which is enough to preserve its cohomology class and therefore \(Q^0_{\mathrm{loc}}\text{.}\) After this descent, \(H^1(\Qtwo,V)\) is a one-dimensional space over the Schur field \(F_V\text{,}\) and the Hermitian trace model applies.
    🔗
    🔗
    Thus the candidate and local base determinant problems have the same Gauss sum. For an arbitrary determinant pushout class, the edge term \(\gamma_\kappa\) and the inflated scalar term \(\delta_\kappa\) remain in the obstruction formula; their behavior under transgression and shear is described in Subsection 6.5.
    🔗

    Corollary 6.19. Complete source interface.

    Call a source a topologically finitely generated profinite group \(\notnfar{GammaSrc}{\Gamma}\text{,}\) marked by four generators \(\notn{sigma}{\sigma},\notn{tau}{\tau},\notn{x0}{x_0},\notnfar{x1}{x_1}\text{,}\) whose compatible tame and maximal pro-\(2\) quotient maps assemble as in (4.2) into an epimorphism \(\notnfar{bGamma}{b_\Gamma}:\notnfar{GammaSrc}{\Gamma}\twoheadrightarrow\notnfar{bdry}{\bdry}\text{.}\) Say that a source \(\notnfar{GammaSrc}{\Gamma}\) meets the source interface if, for every finite lower quotient, every lower exact-image map, and every elementary characteristic-\(2\) coefficient module, \(\notnfar{GammaSrc}{\Gamma}\) and \(\notnfar{GQ}{\GQ}\) have:
    🔗
    1. the same obstruction-space dimension and the same number of lifts when the obstruction vanishes;
      🔗
      🔗
    2. natural perfect pairings for all short exact coefficient sequences, with adjoint connecting homomorphisms;
      🔗
      🔗
    3. the same scalar cup–Bockstein form for the trivial module;
      🔗
      🔗
    4. for every nonzero invariant nonsingular quadratic form on a simple self-dual head, the same base determinant Gauss sum for the class \(\notnfar{kappaq0}{\kappa_q^0}\text{.}\)
      🔗
      🔗
    Then \(\notnfar{GA}{\GA}\) meets the source interface.
    🔗
    Together with the marked maximal pro-\(2\) identification in Proposition 3.10, these are the source-side inputs supplied to the target induction, and they are the only ones: after Section 5 the argument never differentiates the wild word again, so it applies verbatim to any source that meets the interface and carries the tame and pro-\(2\) data of Section 3. That is exactly what a further presentation has to supply, and Appendix C supplies it for a second one, the square-commutator presentation; the statement above is used there in this abstract form, at a source other than \(\notnfar{GA}{\GA}\text{.}\) This corollary is not by itself a determinacy statement: equality of base Gauss sums is used only after Fourier expansion. For a general pushout class
    \begin{equation*} \kappa=\notnfar{kappaq0}{\kappa_q^0}+\Gamma_{\gamma_\kappa}+ \operatorname{inf}\delta_\kappa, \end{equation*}
    the terms \(\gamma_\kappa\) and \(\delta_\kappa\) enter only through the scalar classes obtained by completing the square in Proposition 8.8. The corresponding signed sums are expressed as exact-image counts in central double covers of the lower target.
    🔗
    Lean (the interface)Lean (Γ_A meets it)Lean (induction over a source)Lean
    🔗

    Proof.
    Items (i)–(iii) are Proposition 5.15, Proposition 5.16, Corollary 5.17 and (3.18); item (iv) is Proposition 6.9, Proposition 6.18. The later operations are restrictions, pushouts, exact-image partitions, finite Fourier transforms, and central-cover constructions internal to the finite target. The determinacy of those operations is isolated in Theorem 8.17 and then executed in Section 9; the central-cover identity (8.22) supplies the remaining affine information.

    Subsection 6.5 Affine terms: transgression and shear

    Lemma 6.20. No square-only invariant.

    Let \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\) be a nontrivial simple \(\F_2[\notn{Cfin}{C}]\)-module. Every nonzero element of \(H^0(\notn{Cfin}{C},\operatorname{Sym}^2\notnfar{Vhead}{V}^\vee)\) has nonzero, hence nonsingular, polar form.
    🔗
    Lean
    🔗

    Proof.
    The zero-polar submodule is the Frobenius-square copy of \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}^\vee\text{,}\) whose fixed subspace is zero. The radical of a nonzero invariant polar form is a submodule of the simple module \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\text{.}\)
    🔗
    🔗

    Lemma 6.21. Determinant transgression relative to the fixed equivariant class.

    Let \(q\) be a nonsingular \(\notn{Cfin}{C}\)-invariant quadratic form on \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\text{,}\) and assume that a zero-section-normalized equivariant class
    \begin{equation*} \notnfar{kappaq0}{\kappa_q^0}\in H^2(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\rtimes \notn{Cfin}{C},\F_2) \end{equation*}
    restricting to \(q\) on \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\) has been fixed. Let
    \begin{equation*} 1\to \notnfar{Vhead}{V}\to G_\eta\to \notn{Cfin}{C}\to1 \end{equation*}
    have extension class \(\eta\in H^2(\notn{Cfin}{C},\notnfar{Vhead}{V})\text{.}\) Relative to the fixed equivariant lift \(\notnfar{kappaq0}{\kappa_q^0}\text{,}\) the obstruction to extending the fibre class over \(G_\eta\) is
    \begin{equation} d_2(q)=\notnfar{bq}{b_q}^\flat{}_*\eta\in H^2(\notn{Cfin}{C},\notnfar{Vhead}{V}^\vee).\tag{6.58} \end{equation}
    Consequently, if \(q\) is the restriction of an actual class in \(H^2(G_\eta,\F_2)\text{,}\) then \(\eta=0\) and \(G_\eta\cong \notnfar{Vhead}{V}\rtimes \notn{Cfin}{C}\) over \(\notn{Cfin}{C}\text{.}\)
    🔗
    LeanLean
    🔗

    Proof.
    We choose sections for the extension, compare the induced automorphisms of the fibre extension, and identify their discrepancy with the transgressed class \(\notnfar{bq}{b_q}^\flat{}_*(\eta)\text{.}\)
    🔗
    Let
    \begin{equation*} 1\longrightarrow\F_2\longrightarrow E_q\longrightarrow \notnfar{Vhead}{V}\longrightarrow1 \end{equation*}
    be the central extension represented by \(\notnfar{kappaq0}{\kappa_q^0}|_V\text{.}\) Central automorphisms of \(E_q\) inducing the identity on \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\) are canonically \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}^\vee\text{.}\) If \(\widehat v\) is a lift of \(v\in \notnfar{Vhead}{V}\text{,}\) inner conjugation by \(\widehat v\) is the central automorphism
    \begin{equation} w\longmapsto \notnfar{bq}{b_q}(v,w)=\notnfar{bq}{b_q}^\flat(v)(w).\tag{6.59} \end{equation}
    Choose the zero-section-normalized representative of \(\notnfar{kappaq0}{\kappa_q^0}\text{.}\) Its preimage of \(\notn{Cfin}{C}\) is split, so conjugation by the chosen lifts of \(c\in \notn{Cfin}{C}\) supplies coherent automorphisms
    \begin{equation*} \alpha_c\in\Aut(E_q), \qquad \alpha_c\alpha_d=\alpha_{cd}, \end{equation*}
    lifting the prescribed \(\notn{Cfin}{C}\)-action on \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\text{.}\)
    🔗
    Choose a normalized section \(s:\notn{Cfin}{C}\to G_\eta\) and write
    \begin{equation} s(c)s(d)=\eta(c,d)s(cd).\tag{6.60} \end{equation}
    In a putative central extension of \(G_\eta\) restricting to \(E_q\text{,}\) lifts of the section elements would satisfy
    \begin{equation*} \widehat s(c)\widehat s(d) =z(c,d)\widehat{\eta(c,d)}\widehat s(cd) \end{equation*}
    for a scalar factor \(z(c,d)\in\F_2\text{.}\) Compare the induced automorphisms of \(E_q\text{.}\) The left side induces \(\alpha_c\alpha_d=\alpha_{cd}\text{,}\) whereas the right side induces
    \begin{equation*} \operatorname{Int}(\widehat{\eta(c,d)})\alpha_{cd}. \end{equation*}
    By (6.59), their discrepancy is the \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}^\vee\)-valued normalized \(2\)-cocycle
    \begin{equation} (c,d)\longmapsto \notnfar{bq}{b_q}^\flat(\eta(c,d)).\tag{6.61} \end{equation}
    Changing the section \(s\) changes \(\eta\) by a coboundary and changes (6.61) by the corresponding \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}^\vee\)-coboundary. Changing the coherent lifts \(\alpha_c\) by central automorphisms \(\gamma(c)\in \notnfar{Vhead}{V}^\vee\) changes the discrepancy by \(d\gamma\text{.}\) Hence the cohomology class of the obstruction is exactly \(\notnfar{bq}{b_q}^\flat{}_*[\eta]\text{.}\) This is the \(d_2^{0,2}\) differential after the intrinsic equivariance obstruction has been trivialized by the fixed split class \(\notnfar{kappaq0}{\kappa_q^0}\text{,}\) proving (6.58).
    🔗
    If an actual class on \(G_\eta\) restricts to \(q\text{,}\) the obstruction vanishes. Since \(q\) is nonsingular, \(\notnfar{bq}{b_q}^\flat:\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\xrightarrow{\sim}\notnfar{Vhead}{V}^\vee\) is an isomorphism of \(\notn{Cfin}{C}\)-modules. Therefore \([\eta]=0\text{,}\) so the extension splits over \(\notn{Cfin}{C}\text{.}\)
    🔗
    🔗
    For a split group \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\rtimes \notn{Cfin}{C}\text{,}\) fix the base determinant class \(\notnfar{kappaq0}{\kappa_q^0}\) of Lemma 6.3. After replacing a representative by a cohomologous normalized cocycle and changing the normalized section, every central class with restriction \(q\) admits the following equality of normalized \(2\)-cochains:
    \begin{equation} \kappa=\notnfar{kappaq0}{\kappa_q^0}+\Gamma_\gamma+ \operatorname{inf}_C^{\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\rtimes \notn{Cfin}{C}}\delta,\tag{6.62} \end{equation}
    where \(\gamma\in Z^1(\notn{Cfin}{C},\notnfar{Vhead}{V}^\vee)\text{,}\) \(\delta\in Z^2(\notn{Cfin}{C},\F_2)\text{,}\) and \(\Gamma_\gamma\) is given by (6.6).
    🔗

    Lemma 6.22. Marking-preserving shear of the difference data.

    Let \(a\in Z^1(\notn{Cfin}{C},\notnfar{Vhead}{V})\) and define
    \begin{equation*} s_a(v,c)=(v+a(c),c). \end{equation*}
    If \(\kappa=\notnfar{kappaq0}{\kappa_q^0}+\Gamma_\gamma+\operatorname{inf}\delta\text{,}\) then, in cohomology,
    \begin{equation} s_a^*\kappa= \notnfar{kappaq0}{\kappa_q^0}+ \Gamma_{\gamma+\notnfar{bq}{b_q}^\flat a}+ \operatorname{inf}\bigl(\delta+ \Theta_q^0(a)+\gamma\smile a\bigr),\tag{6.63} \end{equation}
    where
    \begin{equation} \Theta_q^0(a)=(a,\id_C)^*\notnfar{kappaq0}{\kappa_q^0}\in Z^2(\notn{Cfin}{C},\F_2)\tag{6.64} \end{equation}
    and
    \begin{equation} (\gamma\smile a)(c,d)=\gamma(c)(c a(d)).\tag{6.65} \end{equation}
    In particular, if \(q\ne0\text{,}\) a unique cohomology class \(a\) kills the edge \(\gamma\text{,}\) and the scalar phase then becomes \(\delta+\Theta_q^0(a)+\gamma\smile a\text{.}\)
    🔗
    Lean
    🔗

    Proof.
    The cocycle identity for \(a\) is exactly the condition that \(s_a\) be an automorphism over \(\notn{Cfin}{C}\text{.}\) Substitute \(v+a(c)\) and \(w+a(d)\) into the normalized representative (6.62). The terms linear in \(v\) or \(w\) change the edge by the polar map \(\notnfar{bq}{b_q}^\flat a\text{.}\) The term containing only the base class and the graph \(a\) is \(\Theta_q^0(a)\text{.}\) The old edge also contributes the scalar term \(\gamma(c)(c a(d))\text{,}\) namely (6.65). All remaining changes are normalized coboundaries. Since \(\notnfar{bq}{b_q}^\flat\) is an isomorphism, the edge can be killed uniquely in cohomology.
    🔗
    The shear fixes the quotient \(\notn{Cfin}{C}\text{.}\) A marked subgroup containing \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\) is the full inverse image of its image in \(\notn{Cfin}{C}\text{,}\) so it is preserved. Scalar decorations kill the nontrivial simple module \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\text{,}\) and are therefore preserved as well.

    Section 7 A minimal non-scalar module layer in the wild kernel

    Given a finite target whose marked \(2\)-kernel has a nontrivial composition factor, this section isolates the first such factor and the minimal normal subgroup that realizes it. The resulting quotient tower separates the elementary lifting stage from the final Frattini obstruction and shows that every nonzero scalar pushout induces a nonsingular quadratic form on the simple head.
    🔗
    Let \(\notnfar{calY}{\mathcal Y}=(\notnfar{Ytarget}{Y},\notnfar{LY}{L_Y},\notnfar{piY}{\pi_Y},\notnfar{thetaY}{\theta_Y})\) be a boundary-framed target, so that \(\notnfar{LY}{L_Y}=\ker(\notnfar{piY}{\pi_Y})\) is a finite \(2\)-group and \(\notnfar{Htarget}{H}=\notnfar{Ytarget}{Y}/\notnfar{LY}{L_Y}\text{.}\) For a finite \(2\)-group \(\notn{Kker}{K}\text{,}\) write
    \begin{equation*} \notn{Frattini}{\Phi}(\notn{Kker}{K})=\notn{Kker}{K}^2[\notn{Kker}{K},\notn{Kker}{K}] \end{equation*}
    for its Frattini subgroup. A chief factor is scalar when the tame quotient acts on it trivially. Thus, formally, a chief factor of \(\notnfar{LY}{L_Y}\) is called scalar when it is the trivial \(\F_2[\notnfar{Htarget}{H}]\)-module.
    🔗
    Assume that \(\notnfar{LY}{L_Y}\) has a non-scalar chief factor. Choose \(\notnfar{Ytarget}{Y}\)-normal subgroups
    \begin{equation*} S\triangleleft P\le \notnfar{LY}{L_Y}, \qquad P/S\cong \notnfar{Vhead}{V}, \end{equation*}
    where all chief factors below \(S\) are scalar and \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\) is the first non-scalar simple factor. Choose \(\notn{Kker}{K}\triangleleft \notnfar{Ytarget}{Y}\text{,}\) \(\notn{Kker}{K}\le P\text{,}\) minimal subject to \(KS=P\text{,}\) and set
    \begin{equation*} \notn{Rrad}{R}=\notn{Frattini}{\Phi}(\notn{Kker}{K}),\qquad \notnfar{Mmid}{M}=\notn{Kker}{K}/\notn{Rrad}{R},\qquad \notn{Tsub}{T}=(\notn{Kker}{K}\cap S)/\notn{Rrad}{R}, \end{equation*}
    \begin{equation*} \notn{Bmid}{B}=\notnfar{Ytarget}{Y}/\notn{Rrad}{R},\qquad \notn{Cfin}{C}=\notnfar{Ytarget}{Y}/\notn{Kker}{K},\qquad \notnfar{Htarget}{H}=\notnfar{Ytarget}{Y}/\notnfar{LY}{L_Y},\qquad H_V=\im(\notn{Cfin}{C}\to\GL(\notnfar{Vhead}{V})). \end{equation*}
    The quotient tower and the elementary module layer are
    \begin{equation} \notnfar{Ytarget}{Y}\twoheadrightarrow \notn{Bmid}{B}=\notnfar{Ytarget}{Y}/\notn{Rrad}{R}\twoheadrightarrow \notn{Cfin}{C}=\notnfar{Ytarget}{Y}/\notn{Kker}{K} \twoheadrightarrow \notnfar{Htarget}{H}=\notnfar{Ytarget}{Y}/\notnfar{LY}{L_Y}, \qquad 0\longrightarrow \notn{Tsub}{T}\longrightarrow \notnfar{Mmid}{M}\longrightarrow \notnfar{Vhead}{V}\longrightarrow0.\tag{7.1} \end{equation}
    Write \(L_B=\notnfar{LY}{L_Y}/\notn{Rrad}{R}\) and \(L_C=\notnfar{LY}{L_Y}/\notn{Kker}{K}\text{.}\) The four quotient levels used below are
    🔗
    🔗
    Level Role
    \(\notnfar{Htarget}{H}\) fixed tame quotient and boundary frame
    \(\notn{Cfin}{C}\) lower target for elementary \(\notnfar{Mmid}{M}\)-lifting, connecting maps, and scalar phase classes
    \(\notn{Bmid}{B}\) quotient on which the final \(\notn{Rrad}{R}\)-valued obstruction and its scalar pushouts are evaluated
    \(H_V\) faithful image used only for the pure quadratic-form calculation on the simple head \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\)

    Lemma 7.1. Simple head.

    There is an exact sequence of \(\F_2[\notn{Cfin}{C}]\)-modules
    \begin{equation*} 0\to \notn{Tsub}{T}\to \notnfar{Mmid}{M}\to \notnfar{Vhead}{V}\to0, \end{equation*}
    and
    \begin{equation*} \notn{Tsub}{T}=\rad_{\F_2[\notn{Cfin}{C}]}\notnfar{Mmid}{M}, \qquad \notnfar{Mmid}{M}/\notn{Tsub}{T}\cong \notnfar{Vhead}{V}, \qquad (\notnfar{Mmid}{M}^\vee)^\notn{Cfin}{C}=0. \end{equation*}
    🔗
    Lean (head)Lean (radical)Lean (dual)Lean
    🔗

    Proof.
    Since \(\notn{Kker}{K}/(\notn{Kker}{K}\cap S)\cong \notnfar{Vhead}{V}\) is elementary abelian, \(\notn{Rrad}{R}\le \notn{Kker}{K}\cap S\text{.}\) The displayed sequence follows. Since the quotient is simple, \(\rad \notnfar{Mmid}{M}\le \notn{Tsub}{T}\text{.}\) If a maximal submodule \(X<\notnfar{Mmid}{M}\) failed to contain \(\notn{Tsub}{T}\text{,}\) then \(X+\notn{Tsub}{T}=\notnfar{Mmid}{M}\text{,}\) so \(X\) would map onto \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\text{.}\) Writing \(K_X\) for the inverse image of \(X\) in \(\notn{Kker}{K}\text{,}\) the subgroup \(K_X\) would be proper and \(\notnfar{Ytarget}{Y}\)-normal while still satisfying \(K_XS=P\text{,}\) contradicting minimality. Thus every maximal submodule contains \(\notn{Tsub}{T}\text{.}\) The assertion about dual invariants follows because a nonzero map \(\notnfar{Mmid}{M}\to\F_2\) would give a trivial simple quotient, whereas the unique simple head is \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\text{.}\)
    🔗
    🔗

    Lemma 7.2. Frattini–centralizer collapse.

    The subgroup \(\notn{Rrad}{R}\) is central elementary abelian in \(\notn{Kker}{K}\text{,}\) and \(\notn{Kker}{K}^4=1\text{.}\)
    🔗
    LeanLean
    🔗

    Proof.
    We first prove that \(\notn{Kker}{K}\) centralizes its Frattini subgroup, then show that the fourth-power homomorphism vanishes, and finally identify \(\notn{Rrad}{R}\) as central and elementary abelian.
    🔗
    Let \(H_2\) be the maximal \(2\)-quotient of the finite tame group \(\notnfar{Htarget}{H}\text{,}\) let \(N=\ker(\notnfar{Htarget}{H}\to H_2)\text{,}\) and choose an odd Hall lift \(\widetilde N\) in the preimage of \(N\) in \(\notnfar{Ytarget}{Y}\text{.}\) Along a chief series for \(S\text{,}\) the action of \(\widetilde N\) on every factor is trivial; coprime action gives
    \begin{equation*} [S,\widetilde N]=1. \end{equation*}
    Since \(\notn{Rrad}{R}\le \notn{Kker}{K}\cap S\text{,}\) \(\widetilde N\) centralizes \(\notn{Rrad}{R}\text{.}\)
    🔗
    Put \(\mathcal C_R=C_K(\notn{Rrad}{R})\text{.}\) It is characteristic in \(\notn{Kker}{K}\) and hence normal in \(\notnfar{Ytarget}{Y}\text{.}\) The three-subgroup lemma gives \([\notn{Kker}{K},\widetilde N]\le\mathcal C_R\text{.}\) The group \(N\) acts nontrivially on \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\text{:}\) otherwise the action would factor through the \(2\)-group \(\notnfar{Htarget}{H}/N\text{,}\) whose only simple module in characteristic \(2\) is trivial. Hence \([\notnfar{Vhead}{V},N]=\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\text{,}\) so
    \begin{equation*} [\notn{Kker}{K},\widetilde N]S=P. \end{equation*}
    Thus \(\mathcal C_RS=P\text{,}\) and minimality of \(\notn{Kker}{K}\) gives \(\mathcal C_R=\notn{Kker}{K}\text{.}\) Therefore \(\notn{Rrad}{R}\le Z(\notn{Kker}{K})\text{.}\)
    🔗
    Since \(\notn{Kker}{K}/\notn{Rrad}{R}\) is elementary abelian, squares lie in \(\notn{Rrad}{R}\) and commutators have order at most \(2\text{.}\) The fourth-power map
    \begin{equation*} f:\notn{Kker}{K}\to \notn{Rrad}{R}, \qquad f(k)=k^4, \end{equation*}
    is a \(\notnfar{Ytarget}{Y}\)-equivariant homomorphism. The subgroup \(\widetilde N\) fixes \(\notn{Rrad}{R}\text{,}\) so \(f([k,n])=1\) for \(k\in \notn{Kker}{K}\text{,}\) \(n\in\widetilde N\text{.}\) The \(\notnfar{Ytarget}{Y}\)-normal closure of \([\notn{Kker}{K},\widetilde N]\) still maps onto \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\) modulo \(S\text{,}\) hence equals \(\notn{Kker}{K}\) by minimality. Thus \(f=1\) and \(\notn{Kker}{K}^4=1\text{.}\) Finally
    \begin{equation*} \notn{Rrad}{R}=\notn{Frattini}{\Phi}(\notn{Kker}{K})=\notn{Kker}{K}^2[\notn{Kker}{K},\notn{Kker}{K}] \end{equation*}
    is central of exponent \(2\text{.}\)
    🔗
    🔗

    Lemma 7.3. Decorations vanish on the block.

    Every homomorphism from \(\notnfar{Ytarget}{Y}\) to an elementary abelian \(2\)-group vanishes on \(\notn{Kker}{K}\text{.}\)
    🔗
    LeanLean
    🔗

    Proof.
    It kills \(\notn{Rrad}{R}=\notn{Kker}{K}^2[\notn{Kker}{K},\notn{Kker}{K}]\) and therefore induces a \(\notn{Cfin}{C}\)-module map \(\notnfar{Mmid}{M}\to \notnfar{Etarget}{E}\text{.}\) By Lemma 7.1, \(\Hom_C(\notnfar{Mmid}{M},\F_2)=0\text{,}\) so this map is zero.
    🔗
    🔗

    Subsection 7.1 The determinant pushout on the simple head

    Put
    \begin{equation*} \notn{calX}{\mathcal X_R}=(\notn{Rrad}{R}^\vee)^\notn{Bmid}{B}=(\notn{Rrad}{R}^\vee)^\notn{Cfin}{C}. \end{equation*}
    For \(0\ne\lambda\in \notn{calX}{\mathcal X_R}\text{,}\) the pushout \(K_\lambda=\notn{Kker}{K}/\ker\lambda\) is a central extension
    \begin{equation*} 1\to\F_2\to K_\lambda\to \notnfar{Mmid}{M}\to1. \end{equation*}
    Let \(\notn{qlambda}{q_\lambda}:\notnfar{Mmid}{M}\to\F_2\) be its square map and \(\notn{blambda}{b_\lambda}\) its polar form.
    🔗

    Proposition 7.4. Simple-head determinant.

    Keep the minimal-block data of (7.1): \(\notnfar{Mmid}{M}=K/R\) with radical submodule \(\notn{Tsub}{T}=(K\cap S)/R\) and simple head \(\notnfar{Mmid}{M}/\notn{Tsub}{T}\cong \notnfar{Vhead}{V}\text{,}\) all acted on by the finite quotient \(\notn{Cfin}{C}=Y/K\) arising from the chosen minimal block; by Lemma 5.12, the action on \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\) factors through the finite tame quotient \(H\text{.}\) For every \(0\ne\lambda\in \notn{calX}{\mathcal X_R}\text{,}\)
    \begin{equation*} \notn{qlambda}{q_\lambda}|_{T}=0, \qquad \notn{blambda}{b_\lambda}(\notn{Tsub}{T},\notnfar{Mmid}{M})=0. \end{equation*}
    Hence \(\notn{qlambda}{q_\lambda}\) descends to a nonzero nonsingular \(\notn{Cfin}{C}\)-invariant quadratic form
    \begin{equation*} \ol q_\lambda:\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\to\F_2. \end{equation*}
    🔗
    Lean (main)Lean (commutator vanishing)Lean
    🔗

    Proof.
    We identify the polar radical, rule out a nonzero restriction to \(\notn{Tsub}{T}\text{,}\) and then prove that the descended form on \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\) is nonzero and nonsingular.
    🔗
    The adjoint \(\notn{blambda}{b_\lambda}^\flat:\notnfar{Mmid}{M}\to \notnfar{Mmid}{M}^\vee\) is \(\notn{Cfin}{C}\)-linear. Since \(\notn{Tsub}{T}\) has only trivial composition factors while \(\soc(\notnfar{Mmid}{M}^\vee)\cong \notnfar{Vhead}{V}^\vee\) is nontrivial simple, \(\Hom_C(\notn{Tsub}{T},\notnfar{Mmid}{M}^\vee)=0\text{.}\) Thus \(\notn{blambda}{b_\lambda}(\notn{Tsub}{T},\notnfar{Mmid}{M})=0\text{.}\)
    🔗
    The restriction \(\notn{qlambda}{q_\lambda}|_{T}\) is therefore a \(\notn{Cfin}{C}\)-invariant linear functional. Suppose it is nonzero. Quotienting \(\notn{Tsub}{T}\) by its kernel yields a \(\notn{Cfin}{C}\)-module extension
    \begin{equation*} 0\to\F_2t\to\ol M\to \notnfar{Vhead}{V}\to0, \end{equation*}
    with \(t\) in the polar radical and \(\notn{qlambda}{q_\lambda}(t)=1\text{.}\) The kernel of \(\notn{Cfin}{C}\to H_V\) acts on \(\ol M\) by possible shears
    \begin{equation*} m\longmapsto m+f(\ol m)t. \end{equation*}
    Quadratic invariance and \(\notn{qlambda}{q_\lambda}(t)=1\) force every such \(f\) to vanish, so the extension factors through \(H_V\text{.}\) If \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\) is ramified, its odd inertia subgroup has no fixed vectors and \(H^*(H_V,\notnfar{Vhead}{V}^\vee)=0\) by Hochschild–Serre. If \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\) is unramified, \(H_V\) is cyclic of odd order and the same vanishing follows from Maschke’s theorem. Hence
    \begin{equation*} H^1(H_V,\notnfar{Vhead}{V}^\vee)=0, \end{equation*}
    so the extension splits. Projection to the scalar summand gives a nonzero \(\notn{Cfin}{C}\)-map \(\notnfar{Mmid}{M}\to\F_2\text{,}\) contradicting \((\notnfar{Mmid}{M}^\vee)^\notn{Cfin}{C}=0\text{.}\) Therefore \(\notn{qlambda}{q_\lambda}|_{T}=0\text{.}\)
    🔗
    In more detail: the vanishing of \(q_\lambda\) on \(T\) is the one part of the argument that uses the boundary frame, rather than only the abstract minimal block. If \(q_\lambda(t)=1\text{,}\) conjugation on the extension \(0\to\F_2t\to\bar M\to V\to0\) could a priori contain shears by elements of \(V^\vee\text{.}\) Quadratic invariance kills the shears coming from the kernel of the action, so the extension is controlled by the faithful acting image \(H_V\text{.}\) It is important here to pass to \(H_V\text{,}\) not to make a normal-odd-inertia assertion about the original group \(C\text{.}\) The framed tame quotient makes \(H_V\) either cyclic of odd order or an extension with odd inertia, and in both cases \(H^1(H_V,V^\vee)=0\text{.}\) The resulting splitting yields an invariant functional on \(M\text{,}\) contradicting the simple-head construction.
    🔗
    The descended form is nonzero. Otherwise \(K_\lambda\) would be elementary abelian, whereas
    \begin{equation*} \notn{Frattini}{\Phi}(K_\lambda)=\notn{Rrad}{R}/\ker\lambda\ne1. \end{equation*}
    Its polar radical is a submodule of the simple module \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\text{;}\) if the radical were all of \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\text{,}\) the form would be invariant linear, impossible. Thus it is nonsingular.
    🔗
    🔗
    🔗
    🔗

    Section 8 Central covers, affine fibres, and Fourier inversion

    Using the target tower of Section 7 and the source comparison from Section 5, Section 6, this section converts the lifting count into scalar Fourier coefficients and exact-image counts for smaller targets. The result is the closed recursion of Theorem 8.17.
    🔗
    Retain the tower and module sequence (7.1).
    🔗
    The induction repeatedly separates maps according to the subgroup they generate. The notation below retains only maps whose image is exactly the lower target.
    🔗

    Definition 8.1. Exact-image lower maps.

    For a boundary-framed lower target \(\notn{Cfin}{C}\text{,}\) let \(\notn{XGamma}{X_\Gamma}(\notn{Cfin}{C})\) denote the finite set of boundary-framed exact-image epimorphisms \(\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}:\notnfar{GammaSrc}{\Gamma}\twoheadrightarrow \notn{Cfin}{C}\) at the current lower stage. All sums over \(\notn{XGamma}{X_\Gamma}(\notn{Cfin}{C})\) are over exact-image lower maps; proper-image contributions are subtracted separately by induction.
    🔗
    Lean
    🔗
    Before the transform can be compared across the two sources, the scalar characters entering it must agree; they do, with the same count on both sides.
    🔗

    Lemma 8.2. Common scalar character group.

    For both sources \(\notnfar{GammaSrc}{\Gamma}\in\{\notnfar{GA}{\GA},\notnfar{GQ}{\GQ}\}\) one has
    \begin{equation*} |\Hom_{\mathrm{cont}}(\notnfar{GammaSrc}{\Gamma},\F_2)|=8. \end{equation*}
    Moreover scalar twisting by any such character preserves the boundary-framed condition for the central double covers used below.
    🔗
    Lean (Γ_A)Lean (local)Lean
    🔗

    Proof.
    For the candidate, every map to \(\F_2\) kills \(\notn{tau}{\tau}\) because the tame relation forces the tame inertia generator to have odd order in finite quotients; hence it factors through the maximal pro-\(2\) quotient \(\notnfar{Pi}{\Pi}\text{.}\) For the local source, the same assertion follows from the characteristic wild subgroup and the common marked maximal pro-\(2\) quotient. The quotient \(\notnfar{Pi}{\Pi}\) has three mod-\(2\) generators, represented by \(\notn{sigma}{\sigma},\notn{x0}{x_0},\notnfar{x1}{x_1}\text{,}\) and one Demushkin relator with no linear mod-\(2\) part, so
    \begin{equation*} H^1(\notnfar{Pi}{\Pi},\F_2)\cong\F_2^3. \end{equation*}
    Thus the scalar character group has order \(2^3=8\) for both sources. The central covers used in the induction have central kernel killed by the fixed boundary and decoration, so multiplying a lift by a scalar character changes only the central coordinate and leaves the boundary-framed data unchanged.
    🔗
    🔗

    Lemma 8.3. Central-cover exact-image transform.

    Let \(\notnfar{calY}{\mathcal Y}=(\notnfar{Ytarget}{Y},\notnfar{LY}{L_Y},\notnfar{piY}{\pi_Y},\notnfar{thetaY}{\theta_Y})\) be boundary-framed and let
    \begin{equation*} p:\widetilde Y\twoheadrightarrow \notnfar{Ytarget}{Y} \end{equation*}
    be a central double cover. Give it the pulled-back structure
    \begin{equation*} \widetilde L=p^{-1}(\notnfar{LY}{L_Y}), \qquad \widetilde\pi=\pi_Yp, \qquad \widetilde\theta=\theta_Yp, \end{equation*}
    and assume the central kernel lies in \(\ker(\widetilde\pi,\widetilde\theta)\text{.}\) Fix an exact-image subgroup \(J\le \notnfar{Ytarget}{Y}\) projecting onto \(\notnfar{Htarget}{H}\text{.}\) If \(u_\Gamma^\beta(p,J)\) counts boundary-framed exact-image maps to \(J\) whose pullback cover is split, then
    \begin{equation} 8u_\Gamma^\beta(p,J) =\sum_{\substack{\widetilde J\le p^{-1}(J)\\p(\widetilde J)=J}} \notnfar{eGamma}{e_\Gamma}^\beta(\widetilde J,\widetilde J\cap\widetilde L, \widetilde\pi|_{\widetilde J}, \widetilde\theta|_{\widetilde J}).\tag{8.1} \end{equation}
    Every term on the right is therefore an ordinary exact-image object in the same global boundary-framed category.
    🔗
    LeanLean
    🔗

    Proof.
    An unobstructed map \(f:\notnfar{GammaSrc}{\Gamma}\twoheadrightarrow J\) has a lift, and the set of all lifts is a torsor under \(\Hom(\notnfar{GammaSrc}{\Gamma},\F_2)\text{.}\) By Lemma 8.2, this group has order \(8\) for both sources, and scalar twisting preserves the boundary-framed condition. Twisting a lift changes only the new central coordinate. Because that coordinate lies in the kernel of both the tame marking and the decoration, every twist still satisfies the identical boundary equation. The exact image of a lift is a subgroup \(\widetilde J\le p^{-1}(J)\) mapping onto \(J\text{,}\) and every such exact-image lift occurs in precisely one summand. This is a literal partition of the eight lifts, proving (8.1); it also proves exact-image and decoration compatibility without an equidistribution assumption.
    🔗
    🔗
    The transform is inverted by a finite Fourier average.
    🔗

    Lemma 8.4. Fourier inversion.

    Let \(\Lambda\) be the character group of a finite \(\F_2\)-obstruction space and let \(o:X\to \Lambda^\vee\text{.}\) If
    \begin{equation*} m_\lambda=\#\{x\in X:\langle\lambda,o(x)\rangle=0\}, \end{equation*}
    then
    \begin{equation} \#\{x:o(x)=0\} =\frac1{|\Lambda|}\sum_{\lambda\in \Lambda}(2m_\lambda-|X|).\tag{8.2} \end{equation}
    🔗
    LeanLean
    🔗

    Proof.
    Use \(1_{o=0}=|\Lambda|^{-1}\sum_{\lambda\in \Lambda}(-1)^{\langle\lambda,o\rangle}\text{.}\)
    🔗
    🔗

    Lemma 8.5. Constrained quadratic Gauss transform.

    Let \(W,E\) be finite \(\F_2\)-vector spaces, let \(L:W\twoheadrightarrow E\text{,}\) and let \(Q:W\to\F_2\) be nonsingular with polar form \(b_Q\text{.}\) For \(\kappa\in E\) and \(\epsilon\in\F_2\text{,}\) put
    \begin{equation*} N(\kappa,\epsilon)=\#\{x\in W:Lx=\kappa,\ Q(x)=\epsilon\}. \end{equation*}
    For \(\chi\in E^\vee\text{,}\) let \(a_\chi\) be uniquely determined by
    \begin{equation*} b_Q(a_\chi,x)=\chi(Lx). \end{equation*}
    Then
    \begin{equation} N(\kappa,\epsilon) =\frac1{2|E|}\left( |W|+G(Q)\sum_{\chi\in E^\vee} (-1)^{\chi(\kappa)+\epsilon+Q(a_\chi)} \right),\tag{8.3} \end{equation}
    where \(G(Q)=\sum_{x\in W}(-1)^{Q(x)}\text{.}\)
    🔗
    Lean (aggregated)Lean (main)Lean
    🔗

    Proof.
    Expand both conditions with additive characters. Surjectivity of \(L\) kills the nontrivial characters in the nonquadratic sum. In the quadratic sum, complete the square:
    \begin{equation*} Q(x)+b_Q(a_\chi,x)=Q(x+a_\chi)+Q(a_\chi). \end{equation*}
    This gives (8.3).
    🔗
    🔗
    We now record the two pieces that replace an unrestricted count on all of \(H^1(\notnfar{Vhead}{V})\text{.}\)
    🔗
    The preimage of \(\notn{Tsub}{T}\) in a scalar double cover need not have a normal complement to the new central involution. The cohomology class measuring that failure, and equivalently the variation of the scalar obstruction under \(\notn{Tsub}{T}\)-twists, is called the radical edge.
    🔗

    Lemma 8.6. Radical edge, variation formula, and descent.

    Let \(0\to \notn{Tsub}{T}\to \notnfar{Mmid}{M}\to \notnfar{Vhead}{V}\to0\) be the simple-head sequence, and let
    \begin{equation*} p:\widetilde B\twoheadrightarrow \notnfar{Bmid}{B} \end{equation*}
    be a central double cover whose restriction to \(\notnfar{Mmid}{M}\) has quadratic form with polar radical \(\notn{Tsub}{T}\) and whose restriction to \(\notn{Tsub}{T}\) is zero. The cover determines a canonical edge class
    \begin{equation*} [\varepsilon]\in H^1(\notnfar{Bmid}{B}/\notn{Tsub}{T},\notn{Tsub}{T}^\vee). \end{equation*}
    Its restriction to \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\) is zero, so it is inflated from a unique class
    \begin{equation*} [\bar\varepsilon]\in H^1(\notn{Cfin}{C},\notn{Tsub}{T}^\vee). \end{equation*}
    For every lower exact-image epimorphism \(\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}:\notnfar{GammaSrc}{\Gamma}\twoheadrightarrow \notn{Cfin}{C}\) and every unrestricted \(\notnfar{Mmid}{M}\)-lift \(f\text{,}\) twisting by \(u\in \notn{Z1Gr}{Z^1_{\Gamma,\rho}}(\notn{Tsub}{T})\) changes the scalar obstruction by
    \begin{equation} \operatorname{ob}(f_u)=\operatorname{ob}(f) +\bigl\langle [u],\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}^*[\bar\varepsilon]\bigr\rangle_\Gamma.\tag{8.4} \end{equation}
    If \([\bar\varepsilon]\ne0\text{,}\) the free \(\notn{Z1Gr}{Z^1_{\Gamma,\rho}}(\notn{Tsub}{T})\)-action partitions the unrestricted \(\notnfar{Mmid}{M}\)-lifts into orbits in each of which exactly one half satisfy the central relation. If \([\bar\varepsilon]=0\text{,}\) the cover descends to a central double cover of \(\notnfar{Bmid}{B}/\notn{Tsub}{T}\text{;}\) conversely, descent forces the edge class to vanish.
    🔗
    Lean (torsor, Γ_A)Lean (torsor, local)Lean (Γ_A)Lean (local)Lean (data)Lean
    🔗

    Proof.
    We construct the edge cocycle, descend it from \(\notnfar{Bmid}{B}/\notn{Tsub}{T}\) to \(\notn{Cfin}{C}\text{,}\) derive the exact variation formula, and then analyze the nonzero and zero edge cases.
    🔗
    Let \(z\) generate \(\ker p\text{.}\) Since both the square and commutator forms vanish on \(\notn{Tsub}{T}\text{,}\) the preimage \(\widetilde T=p^{-1}(\notn{Tsub}{T})\) is elementary abelian. Choose a linear complement \(s(\notn{Tsub}{T})\) to \(\langle z\rangle\) in \(\widetilde T\text{.}\)
    🔗
    For \(\bar b\in \notnfar{Bmid}{B}/\notn{Tsub}{T}\text{,}\) choose a lift \(\widehat b\in\widetilde B\) and define \(\varepsilon(\bar b)\in \notn{Tsub}{T}^\vee\) by
    \begin{equation} \widehat b\,s(t)\,\widehat b^{-1} =s({}^{\bar b}t)\, z^{\varepsilon(\bar b)({}^{\bar b}t)}.\tag{8.5} \end{equation}
    The definition is independent of the chosen lift \(\widehat b\text{.}\) Applying (8.5) successively to two elements shows
    \begin{equation*} \varepsilon(\bar b_1\bar b_2) =\varepsilon(\bar b_1)+{}^{\bar b_1}\varepsilon(\bar b_2), \end{equation*}
    so \(\varepsilon\) is a \(1\)-cocycle. Replacing \(s(t)\) by \(s(t)z^{\ell(t)}\) changes it by the coboundary \(d\ell\text{;}\) hence its class is canonical.
    🔗
    If \(\bar b\in \notnfar{Vhead}{V}=\notnfar{Mmid}{M}/\notn{Tsub}{T}\text{,}\) the exponent in (8.5) is the commutator pairing between a lift of \(\bar b\) and \(t\text{.}\) This is the polar form of the restricted quadratic form, and it is zero because \(\notn{Tsub}{T}\) is the polar radical. Hence \(\res_V[\varepsilon]=0\text{.}\) The group \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}=\notnfar{Mmid}{M}/\notn{Tsub}{T}\) acts trivially on \(\notn{Tsub}{T}\text{,}\) since \(\notnfar{Mmid}{M}\) is elementary abelian. Inflation–restriction for \(1\to \notnfar{Vhead}{V}\to \notnfar{Bmid}{B}/\notn{Tsub}{T}\to \notn{Cfin}{C}\to1\) therefore gives a unique \([\bar\varepsilon]\in H^1(\notn{Cfin}{C},\notn{Tsub}{T}^\vee)\) inflating to \([\varepsilon]\text{.}\) Choose a normalized cocycle representative \(\bar\varepsilon\) of this class. The difference between \(\varepsilon\) and its inflation is a coboundary \(d\ell\) for some \(\ell\in \notn{Tsub}{T}^\vee\text{;}\) changing the complement \(s(\notn{Tsub}{T})\) by \(\ell\) therefore lets us assume from now on that \(\varepsilon=\operatorname{inf}(\bar\varepsilon)\) as cocycles.
    🔗
    Fix a lower exact-image epimorphism \(\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}:\notnfar{GammaSrc}{\Gamma}\twoheadrightarrow \notn{Cfin}{C}\text{,}\) an \(\notnfar{Mmid}{M}\)-lift \(f:\notnfar{GammaSrc}{\Gamma}\to \notnfar{Bmid}{B}\text{,}\) and lifts \(\widehat f(g)\in\widetilde B\text{.}\) For \(u\in \notn{Z1Gr}{Z^1_{\Gamma,\rho}}(\notn{Tsub}{T})\) put
    \begin{equation*} f_u(g)=u(g)f(g),\qquad \widehat f_u(g)=s(u(g))\widehat f(g). \end{equation*}
    Let \(\omega_f\) and \(\omega_{f_u}\) be the scalar central defects. Using (8.5), the cocycle identity \(u(gh)=u(g)+\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}(g)u(h)\text{,}\) and the fact that \(s(\notn{Tsub}{T})\) is elementary abelian gives the exact identity
    \begin{equation} \omega_{f_u}(g,h)=\omega_f(g,h) +\bar\varepsilon(\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}(g))\bigl(\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}(g)u(h)\bigr).\tag{8.6} \end{equation}
    For the local source, applying the invariant map identifies the second term with the ordinary cup pairing. For the candidate source, its evaluation on the two relation defects is the adjoint pairing supplied by the direct finite-word Fox–Heisenberg chain map of Proposition 5.10. Thus (8.6) yields (8.4) in either source theory.
    🔗
    If \([\bar\varepsilon]\ne0\text{,}\) then \(\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}^*[\bar\varepsilon]\ne0\text{.}\) Indeed, a pulled-back coboundary gives the same coboundary formula on every element of \(\notn{Cfin}{C}\) because \(\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}\) is surjective. Perfect degree-one duality therefore makes
    \begin{equation*} [u]\longmapsto \bigl\langle[u],\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}^*[\bar\varepsilon]\bigr\rangle_\Gamma \end{equation*}
    a nonzero linear functional on \(\notn{HGr}{H^1_{\Gamma,\rho}}(\notn{Tsub}{T})\text{,}\) and hence on \(\notn{Z1Gr}{Z^1_{\Gamma,\rho}}(\notn{Tsub}{T})\text{.}\) This group acts freely on each fibre of the map from \(\notnfar{Mmid}{M}\)-lifts to their quotient modulo \(\notn{Tsub}{T}\text{.}\) Equation (8.4) is one affine equation with nonzero linear part on every such orbit, so exactly half of its elements satisfy the scalar central relation.
    🔗
    In more detail: the half-count is a statement about a finite affine torsor, not merely about cohomology classes. Coboundaries lie in the kernel of the variation functional, so nonvanishing is detected on \(H^1\text{;}\) perfect degree-one duality makes the functional nonzero, and a nonzero functional on a finite \(\F_2\)-space has fibres of equal size. The formal proof checks this separately for the two sources: local Tate duality supplies the nonzero class for \(\GQ\text{,}\) while the finite-word obstruction map supplies it for \(\GA\text{.}\) In both cases the scalar obstruction group has two elements, so precisely one half of each twist orbit satisfies the central relation.

    \begin{equation*} \widetilde B/s(\notn{Tsub}{T})\twoheadrightarrow \notnfar{Bmid}{B}/\notn{Tsub}{T} \end{equation*}
    is a central double cover. Conversely, a descended cover supplies a normal complement to the preimage of \(\notn{Tsub}{T}\text{,}\) so the edge class vanishes.

    Vanishing is first used to change the chosen linear complement of the central kernel so that the edge cocycle itself, not only its class, is zero. That complement is then normal, and quotienting by it produces the descended double cover of \(B/T\text{.}\) This normalization is what makes the two alternatives in the later recursion genuinely exhaustive.

By Lemma 6.21, the quotient \(\notnfar{Bmid}{B}/\notn{Tsub}{T}\) is identified with \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\rtimes \notnfar{Cfin}{C}\text{.}\) For the scalar pushout class under consideration, choose the base determinant class \(\notnfar{kappaq0}{\kappa_q^0}\) attached to the descended nonsingular form on \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\text{.}\) After a normalized change of section, write the descended class by the following equality of normalized \(2\)-cocycles:

    Lemma 8.7. Affine \(\notn{Tsub}{T}\)-lifting equation.

    Choose the splitting \(\notnfar{Bmid}{B}/\notn{Tsub}{T}\cong \notnfar{Vhead}{V}\rtimes \notnfar{Cfin}{C}\) above and let

    be the class obtained by pulling \(\notnfar{Bmid}{B}\to \notnfar{Vhead}{V}\rtimes \notnfar{Cfin}{C}\) back along the zero section \(\notnfar{Cfin}{C}\to \notnfar{Vhead}{V}\rtimes \notnfar{Cfin}{C}\text{.}\) For a lower exact-image map \(\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}:\notnfar{GammaSrc}{\Gamma}\twoheadrightarrow \notnfar{Cfin}{C}\text{,}\) a class
    \begin{equation*} c\in \notn{HGr}{H^1_{\Gamma,\rho}}(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}) \end{equation*}
    is the \(\notnfar{Vhead}{V}\)-coordinate of an actual \(\notnfar{Mmid}{M}\)-lift if and only if
    \begin{equation} \partial_{\Gamma,\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}}(c)=\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}^*e \quad\text{in }\notn{HGr}{H^2_{\Gamma,\rho}}(\notn{Tsub}{T}).\tag{8.8} \end{equation}
    For every such class, the number of raw lifts above it is
    \begin{equation} \mu=|B^1_{\Gamma,\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}}(\notnfar{Vhead}{V})|\,|\notn{Z1Gr}{Z^1_{\Gamma,\rho}}(\notn{Tsub}{T})|,\tag{8.9} \end{equation}

    Proposition 8.8. Completed-square phase identity.

    For either source, every lower exact-image map \(\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}\text{,}\) every \(b\in \notn{HGr}{H^1_{\Gamma,\rho}}(\notnfar{Vhead}{V})\text{,}\) and every \(\chi\in \notnfar{calX}{\mathcal X_T}\text{,}\)

    Proof.
    By Corollary 5.17,
    \begin{equation*} \langle\partial_{\Gamma,\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}}b,\chi\rangle =\langle b,\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}^*\gamma_\chi\rangle_\Gamma. \end{equation*}
    Using (6.7), the left side of (8.12) is
    \begin{equation*} Q^0_{\Gamma,\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}}(b) +\langle b,\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}^*(\gamma_\kappa+\gamma_\chi)\rangle_\Gamma +\notn{iotaGamma}{\iota_\Gamma}(\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}^*\delta_\kappa) +\notn{iotaGamma}{\iota_\Gamma}(\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}^*(\chi_*e)). \end{equation*}

    \begin{equation*} Q^0(b)+\notnfar{bq}{b_q}(b,\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}^*a_{\chi,\kappa}) =Q^0(b+\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}^*a_{\chi,\kappa}) +\notn{iotaGamma}{\iota_\Gamma}\bigl(\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}^*\Theta_q^0(a_{\chi,\kappa})\bigr). \end{equation*}
    Adding the two inflated scalar terms proves (8.12). The class \(\notn{DeltaChiKappa}{\Delta_{\chi,\kappa}}\) is defined on the finite target \(\notnfar{Cfin}{C}\text{;}\) no comparison map between the two source \(H^1\)-spaces is involved.

    Subsection 8.1 The exact-image recursion

    Fix a boundary-framed target \(\notnfar{calY}{\mathcal Y}=(\notnfar{Ytarget}{Y},\notnfar{LY}{L_Y},\notnfar{piY}{\pi_Y},\notnfar{thetaY}{\theta_Y})\) whose marked kernel has a non-scalar simple head, and retain the notation (7.1). Abbreviate \(\notnfar{eGamma}{e_\Gamma}(\notnfar{Ytarget}{Y})=\notnfar{eGamma}{e_\Gamma}^\beta(\notnfar{calY}{\mathcal Y})\text{,}\) with the same convention for inherited exact-image subgroups and central covers. The successive finite operations are
    \begin{equation*} \begin{gathered} \notnfar{Cfin}{C}\ \rightsquigarrow\ \text{$\notnfar{Mmid}{M}$-lifts} \ \rightsquigarrow\ \text{proper-image subtraction}\\ \rightsquigarrow\ \text{scalar tests of the $\notnfar{Rcent}{R}$-obstruction} \ \rightsquigarrow\ \text{phase covers} \ \rightsquigarrow\ \notnfar{Ytarget}{Y}. \end{gathered} \end{equation*}
    The elementary stage counts all \(\notnfar{Mmid}{M}\)-lifts over \(\notnfar{Cfin}{C}\) and removes their proper images. The remaining \(\notnfar{Rcent}{R}\)-valued obstruction is separated by invariant scalar pushouts; in the zero-edge case, completing the resulting quadratic sums replaces their scalar phases by central covers before the final Fourier inversion.
    🔗

    Lemma 8.9. Elementary lifting and exact-image subtraction.

    For every \(\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}\in \notnfar{XGamma}{X_\Gamma}(\notnfar{Cfin}{C})\text{,}\)
    \begin{equation*} \notn{HGr}{H^2_{\Gamma,\rho}}(\notnfar{Mmid}{M})=0, \qquad |\notn{Z1Gr}{Z^1_{\Gamma,\rho}}(\notnfar{Mmid}{M})|=2^{2\dim \notnfar{Mmid}{M}}. \end{equation*}
    Consequently
    \begin{equation} \notnfar{eGamma}{e_\Gamma}(\notnfar{Bmid}{B})=2^{2\dim \notnfar{Mmid}{M}}\notnfar{eGamma}{e_\Gamma}(\notnfar{Cfin}{C}) -\sum_{\substack{J<\notnfar{Bmid}{B}\\J\twoheadrightarrow \notnfar{Cfin}{C}}}\notnfar{eGamma}{e_\Gamma}(J),\tag{8.13} \end{equation}
    where each \(J\) has the boundary-framed structure induced from \(\notnfar{Bmid}{B}\text{.}\) For every proper \(J<\notnfar{Bmid}{B}\) occurring in this sum,
    \begin{equation} |J\cap L_B|=|J\cap \notnfar{Mmid}{M}|\,|L_C| \le \frac{|\notnfar{Mmid}{M}|}{2}|L_C| =\frac{|L_B|}{2}<|\notnfar{LY}{L_Y}|.\tag{8.14} \end{equation}
    🔗
    Lean (main)Lean (conditional)Lean (auxiliary)Lean
    🔗

    Proof.
    The unique simple head of \(\notnfar{Mmid}{M}\) is nontrivial, so \((\notnfar{Mmid}{M}^\vee)^\notnfar{Cfin}{C}=0\) by Lemma 7.1. Candidate deformation duality and local Tate duality therefore give the displayed vanishing and lift multiplicity. Every relation-compatible \(\notnfar{Mmid}{M}\)-lift has an exact image \(J\le \notnfar{Bmid}{B}\) mapping onto \(\notnfar{Cfin}{C}\text{;}\) partitioning by that exact image gives (8.13). If \(J<\notnfar{Bmid}{B}\text{,}\) then \(J\cap \notnfar{Mmid}{M}\) is a proper subgroup of the elementary abelian group \(\notnfar{Mmid}{M}\text{,}\) and the exact sequence
    \begin{equation*} 1\longrightarrow J\cap \notnfar{Mmid}{M}\longrightarrow J\cap L_B \longrightarrow L_C\longrightarrow1 \end{equation*}
    gives (8.14).

    🔗

    Lemma 8.10. Scalar pushouts separate the complete obstruction.

    Put
    \begin{equation*} \notnfar{calX}{\mathcal X_R}=(\notn{Rrad}{R}^\vee)^\notnfar{Bmid}{B}=(\notn{Rrad}{R}^\vee)^\notnfar{Cfin}{C}. \end{equation*}
    For either source, \(\notnfar{calX}{\mathcal X_R}\) is canonically the dual of the \(\notn{Rrad}{R}\)-valued obstruction space. If \(o\) is an \(\notn{Rrad}{R}\)-valued lifting obstruction, then
    \begin{equation*} o=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \lambda_*o=0\text{ for every }\lambda\in\notnfar{calX}{\mathcal X_R}. \end{equation*}
    For \(0\ne\lambda\in\notnfar{calX}{\mathcal X_R}\text{,}\) the corresponding scalar pushout is the central double cover
    \begin{equation*} p_\lambda:B_\lambda=\notnfar{Ytarget}{Y}/\ker\lambda\twoheadrightarrow \notnfar{Bmid}{B}. \end{equation*}
    🔗
    Lean
    🔗

    Proof.
    By Lemma 7.2, \(\notnfar{Rcent}{R}\) is elementary abelian and \(\notn{Kker}{K}\) centralizes \(\notnfar{Rcent}{R}\text{,}\) so the \(\notnfar{Ytarget}{Y}\)-action on \(\notnfar{Rcent}{R}\) factors through \(\notnfar{Cfin}{C}\text{.}\) The two duality theorems give
    \begin{equation*} H^2_{A,\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}}(\notnfar{Rcent}{R})^\vee\cong(\notnfar{Rcent}{R}^\vee)^\notnfar{Cfin}{C}, \qquad H^2_{F,\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}}(\notnfar{Rcent}{R})^\vee\cong(\notnfar{Rcent}{R}^\vee)^\notnfar{Cfin}{C}. \end{equation*}
    For \(\lambda\in(\notnfar{Rcent}{R}^\vee)^\notnfar{Cfin}{C}\text{,}\) the subgroup \(\ker\lambda\) is normal in \(\notnfar{Ytarget}{Y}\) and \(\notnfar{Cfin}{C}\) acts trivially on \(\notnfar{Rcent}{R}/\ker\lambda\text{.}\) Thus \(\notnfar{Ytarget}{Y}/\ker\lambda\to \notnfar{Ytarget}{Y}/\notnfar{Rcent}{R}\) is a central double cover, and its obstruction is the pairing with \(\lambda\text{.}\) Perfectness proves the equivalence.

    Separating the obstruction makes the final Frattini layer accessible to the same inversion.

    Proposition 8.11. Fourier inversion for the final Frattini obstruction.

    Assume \(\notnfar{Rcent}{R}\ne1\) and put
    \begin{equation*} z_R=|\notn{Z1Gr}{Z^1_{\Gamma,\rho}}(\notnfar{Rcent}{R})| =2^{2\dim \notnfar{Rcent}{R}+\dim\notnfar{calX}{\mathcal X_R}}. \end{equation*}
    For \(\lambda\in\notnfar{calX}{\mathcal X_R}\text{,}\) let \(m_{\Gamma,\lambda}(\notnfar{Bmid}{B})\) be the number of exact-image maps to \(\notnfar{Bmid}{B}\) for which the scalar pushout \(\lambda_*o_R\) vanishes. Then \(m_{\Gamma,0}(\notnfar{Bmid}{B})=\notnfar{eGamma}{e_\Gamma}(\notnfar{Bmid}{B})\) and
    \begin{equation} \boxed{ \notnfar{eGamma}{e_\Gamma}(\notnfar{Ytarget}{Y})=\frac{z_R}{|\notnfar{calX}{\mathcal X_R}|} \sum_{\lambda\in\notnfar{calX}{\mathcal X_R}} \bigl(2m_{\Gamma,\lambda}(\notnfar{Bmid}{B})-\notnfar{eGamma}{e_\Gamma}(\notnfar{Bmid}{B})\bigr).}\tag{8.15} \end{equation}

    Proof.

    Proposition 8.14. The zero radical-edge case.

    \begin{equation*} s_\Gamma(\zeta)= \sum_{\rho\in \notnfar{XGamma}{X_\Gamma}(\notnfar{Cfin}{C})} (-1)^{\notn{iotaGamma}{\iota_\Gamma}(\notnfar{rhoEpi}{\rho}^*\zeta)}. \end{equation*}
