    Lemma 8.16. Strict decrease of recursive targets.

    Every target occurring on the right sides of (8.13), (8.16), (8.17), and (8.22) has marked \(2\)-kernel strictly smaller than \(|\notnfar{LY}{L_Y}|\text{.}\) More precisely,
    \begin{equation*} |L_C|=\frac{|\notnfar{LY}{L_Y}|}{|\notn{Kker}{K}|}<|\notnfar{LY}{L_Y}|, \end{equation*}
    \begin{equation} 2|J\cap L_B|\le |L_B|<|\notnfar{LY}{L_Y}|\tag{8.23} \end{equation}
    for a proper scalar-cover stratum, and
    \begin{equation} |L_{C_\zeta}|=2|L_C| =\frac{2|\notnfar{LY}{L_Y}|}{|\notn{Kker}{K}|}<|\notnfar{LY}{L_Y}|.\tag{8.24} \end{equation}
    The proper-image bound in the elementary stage is (8.14).
    🔗
    Lean
    🔗

    Proof.
    The first two inequalities follow from \(\notnfar{Rcent}{R}<\notn{Kker}{K}\) and from the fact that a proper subgroup of the elementary abelian group \(\notnfar{Mmid}{M}=\notn{Kker}{K}/\notnfar{Rcent}{R}\) has index at least two. A scalar double cover of a proper \(J<\notnfar{Bmid}{B}\) has marked kernel \(2|J\cap L_B|\text{,}\) giving (8.23). Since the non-scalar simple head has dimension at least two, \(|\notn{Kker}{K}|\ge4\text{;}\) hence a phase cover has marked kernel as in (8.24).
    🔗
    🔗
    Strict decrease of the marked \(2\)-kernel is what closes the recursion: every count reduces to boundary data and exact-image counts for smaller targets.
    🔗

    Theorem 8.17. Closed exact-image recursion.

    Let \(\notnfar{calY}{\mathcal Y}=(\notnfar{Ytarget}{Y},\notnfar{LY}{L_Y},\notnfar{piY}{\pi_Y},\notnfar{thetaY}{\theta_Y})\) be a boundary-framed marked target (Definition 4.1) and suppose \(\notnfar{LY}{L_Y}\) has a non-scalar simple head, with the minimal-block tower (7.1) chosen as above. When \(\notnfar{Rcent}{R}\ne1\text{,}\) the recursion uses, for each nonzero scalar functional \(\lambda\in\notnfar{calX}{\mathcal X_R}\text{,}\) the descended nonsingular \(C\)-invariant form \(\ol q_\lambda\) on \(V\) of Proposition 7.4, its fixed equivariant base determinant class \(\kappa^0_{\ol q_\lambda}\) of Lemma 6.3, and the radical data \(T\) with its edge class \([\bar\varepsilon]\) of Lemma 8.6. The exact-image count \(\notnfar{eGamma}{e_\Gamma}(\notnfar{Ytarget}{Y})\) is obtained from (8.13) and, when \(\notnfar{Rcent}{R}\ne1\text{,}\) from (8.15)–(8.22). Every exact-image count on the right-hand sides belongs to a boundary-framed target with strictly smaller marked \(2\)-kernel. Hence the count is determined by the source interface of Corollary 6.19 and the exact-image counts for smaller targets.
    🔗
    Lean
    🔗

    Proof.
    The elementary stage is Lemma 8.9. If \(\notnfar{Rcent}{R}=1\text{,}\) then \(\notnfar{Bmid}{B}=\notnfar{Ytarget}{Y}\text{.}\) Otherwise Lemma 8.10, Proposition 8.11 reduce the final \(\notnfar{Rcent}{R}\)-obstruction to its scalar pushouts. Proper images are removed by Lemma 8.12. The unrestricted scalar count is given by Proposition 8.13 when the radical edge is nonzero and by Proposition 8.14 when it vanishes. The signed scalar phases in the latter formula are exact-image counts by Lemma 8.15. Strict decrease is Lemma 8.16.
    🔗
    🔗
    🔗
    🔗

    Section 9 Proof of the boundary-framed theorem

    The terminal fibre-product description and the closed recursion of Theorem 8.17 cover all finite boundary-framed targets. We prove Theorem 4.2 by strong induction on \(|\notnfar{LY}{L_Y}|\text{,}\) simultaneously for all such targets; every recursive target carries the same map to \(\notnfar{Htarget}{H}\times \notnfar{Etarget}{E}\text{.}\)
    🔗

    Lemma 9.1. Coprime-kernel subdirect products.

    Let \(A\twoheadrightarrow C\) and \(B\twoheadrightarrow C\) be finite epimorphisms whose kernels have coprime orders. If a subgroup \(J\le A\times_C B\) projects onto both \(A\) and \(B\text{,}\) then \(J=A\times_C B\text{.}\)
    🔗
    Lean
    🔗

    Proof.
    The kernel of \(J\to A\) is a subgroup of \(\ker(\notnfar{Bmid}{B}\to \notnfar{Cfin}{C})\text{,}\) and the kernel of \(J\to \notnfar{Bmid}{B}\) is a subgroup of \(\ker(A\to \notnfar{Cfin}{C})\text{.}\) Comparing the two order formulas for \(J\) shows that both kernels have their full possible orders, because the two ambient kernel orders are coprime. Thus \(J\) contains both kernels and is the full fibre product.
    🔗
    🔗

    Subsection 9.1 The terminal case: only trivial module factors

    Lemma 9.2. Targets with only trivial module factors.

    Suppose every chief factor of \(\notnfar{LY}{L_Y}\) is a trivial \(\notnfar{Htarget}{H}\)-module. Let \(H_2\) be the maximal \(2\)-quotient of \(\notnfar{Htarget}{H}\) and let \(N=\ker(\notnfar{Htarget}{H}\to H_2)\text{.}\) Then \(N\) has odd order, has a unique normal lift \(\widetilde N\triangleleft \notnfar{Ytarget}{Y}\) centralizing \(\notnfar{LY}{L_Y}\text{,}\) and
    \begin{equation} \notnfar{Ytarget}{Y}\cong \notnfar{Htarget}{H}\times_{H_2}Q, \qquad Q=\notnfar{Ytarget}{Y}/\widetilde N\text{ a finite $2$-group}.\tag{9.1} \end{equation}
    Projection to \(Q\) identifies exact-image subgroups of \(\notnfar{Ytarget}{Y}\) projecting onto \(\notnfar{Htarget}{H}\) with subgroups \(Q'\le Q\) that map onto \(H_2\text{.}\)
    🔗
    LeanLean
    🔗

    Proof.
    We construct and characterize the odd-order complement, identify \(\notnfar{Ytarget}{Y}\) as a fibre product, and then classify the exact-image subgroups.
    🔗
    The kernel \(N\) has odd order by Lemma 3.1. Let \(\notn{Pnorm}{P}\) be its inverse image in \(\notnfar{Ytarget}{Y}\text{.}\) Schur–Zassenhaus gives a complement \(\widetilde N\le \notn{Pnorm}{P}\text{.}\) Along a \(\notnfar{Ytarget}{Y}\)-chief series
    \begin{equation*} 1=L_0\triangleleft L_1\triangleleft\cdots\triangleleft L_m=\notnfar{LY}{L_Y}, \end{equation*}
    triviality of every factor gives \([L_i,\widetilde N]\le L_{i-1}\text{.}\) Hence \([\notnfar{LY}{L_Y},{}_m\widetilde N]=1\text{.}\) Coprime action gives
    \begin{equation*} [\notnfar{LY}{L_Y},\widetilde N]=[\notnfar{LY}{L_Y},\widetilde N,\widetilde N] =\cdots=[\notnfar{LY}{L_Y},{}_m\widetilde N]=1. \end{equation*}
    Thus \(\notn{Pnorm}{P}=\notnfar{LY}{L_Y}\times\widetilde N\text{.}\) Schur–Zassenhaus conjugacy says that all complements are \(\notnfar{LY}{L_Y}\)-conjugate; since \(\notnfar{LY}{L_Y}\) centralizes \(\widetilde N\text{,}\) the complement is unique and therefore normal in \(\notnfar{Ytarget}{Y}\text{.}\)
    🔗
    In more detail: every element of the inverse image of \(N\) has a commuting factorization \(\tilde n\ell\text{,}\) with \(\tilde n\) of odd order and \(\ell\) of \(2\)-power order. Coprimality shows that such a product has odd order exactly when \(\ell=1\text{.}\) Thus \(\widetilde N\) is intrinsically the set of odd-order elements in this subgroup. This characterization is preserved by conjugation, giving normality and uniqueness at once.
    🔗
    The quotient \(Q=\notnfar{Ytarget}{Y}/\widetilde N\) is a \(2\)-group. The two quotient maps define
    \begin{equation*} \notnfar{Ytarget}{Y}\longrightarrow \notnfar{Htarget}{H}\times_{H_2}Q. \end{equation*}
    Its kernel lies in both \(\notnfar{LY}{L_Y}\) and \(\widetilde N\text{,}\) hence is trivial, and the two groups have the same order. This proves (9.1).
    🔗
    The same parity separation explains the decoration: every homomorphism to the exponent-two group \(E\) kills \(\widetilde N\text{,}\) so the decoration descends to \(Q\text{.}\) A subgroup of the resulting fibre product that surjects to both factors has kernels of coprime orders; the coprime subdirect-product lemma therefore forces it to be the whole fibre product.
    🔗
    If \(J\le \notnfar{Ytarget}{Y}\) projects onto \(\notnfar{Htarget}{H}\) and \(Q'=\operatorname{pr}_Q(J)\text{,}\) then \(Q'\twoheadrightarrow H_2\text{.}\) Inside \(\notnfar{Htarget}{H}\times_{H_2}Q'\text{,}\) the subgroup \(J\) projects onto both factors. The two kernels have odd and \(2\)-power orders, so Lemma 9.1 gives \(J=\notnfar{Htarget}{H}\times_{H_2}Q'\text{.}\) Conversely, for every subgroup \(Q'\le Q\) mapping onto \(H_2\text{,}\) the fibre product \(\notnfar{Htarget}{H}\times_{H_2}Q'\) is a subgroup of \(\notnfar{Ytarget}{Y}\) projecting onto \(\notnfar{Htarget}{H}\text{.}\)
    🔗
    🔗
    Let \(q:Q\twoheadrightarrow H_2\) be the quotient map. The tame frame \(\alpha:\notnfar{TA}{\TA}\twoheadrightarrow \notnfar{Htarget}{H}\) induces, through the full unramified marking of Proposition 3.14, a map
    \begin{equation*} \alpha_2:\notnfar{Pi}{\Pi}\twoheadrightarrow H_2. \end{equation*}
    Every boundary decoration kills the odd group \(\widetilde N\) and factors through a map \(\bar\theta:Q\to \notnfar{Etarget}{E}\text{.}\)
    🔗
    For either source, the universal property of the pullback gives a bijection between maps \(f:\notnfar{GammaSrc}{\Gamma}\to \notnfar{Ytarget}{Y}\) with fixed tame frame and maps \(g:\notnfar{Pi}{\Pi}\to Q\) satisfying
    \begin{equation} qg=\alpha_2, \qquad \bar\theta g=\bar\psi.\tag{9.2} \end{equation}
    This uses the full \(\mathbb{Z}_2\) marking: if \(H_2=C_{2^m}\text{,}\) the first equation fixes the reduction of the unramified character modulo \(2^m\text{,}\) not merely its parity.
    🔗
    The kernels of \(\notnfar{Htarget}{H}\to H_2\) and \(Q\to H_2\) have coprime orders, so Lemma 9.1 applies to the pullback \(\notnfar{Htarget}{H}\times_{H_2}Q\text{:}\) the map \(f\) is surjective exactly when \(g\) is, and projection to \(Q\) identifies every exact-image subgroup of \(\notnfar{Ytarget}{Y}\) projecting onto \(\notnfar{Htarget}{H}\) with a subgroup of \(Q\) satisfying (9.2). Thus the terminal exact-image problems are genuinely identical for the two sources, by the fully marked isomorphism of their maximal pro-\(2\) quotients.
    🔗
    🔗

    Subsection 9.2 The inductive step

    The cohomological count in this step rests on the local Euler–Poincaré characteristic [NSW, Theorem (7.3.1)]; see also [Mil, Theorem I.2.8].
    🔗
    Assume that \(\notnfar{LY}{L_Y}\) has a non-scalar simple head. The target tower and module sequence are those of (7.1). By Lemma 8.9, Lemma 8.16, the elementary lifting stage expresses \(\notnfar{eGamma}{e_\Gamma}(\notnfar{Bmid}{B})\) in terms of \(\notnfar{eGamma}{e_\Gamma}(\notnfar{Cfin}{C})\) and exact-image counts with smaller marked kernels. If \(\notnfar{Rcent}{R}=1\text{,}\) then \(\notnfar{Bmid}{B}=\notnfar{Ytarget}{Y}\) and the induction closes at this stage.
    🔗
    Suppose \(\notnfar{Rcent}{R}\ne1\text{.}\) The closed recursion of Theorem 8.17 expresses \(\notnfar{eGamma}{e_\Gamma}(\notnfar{Ytarget}{Y})\) through the common lift multiplicities and Gauss signs of Corollary 6.19, together with exact-image counts for the smaller targets listed in Lemma 8.16. The induction hypothesis makes every such count equal for \(\notnfar{GA}{\GA}\) and \(\notnfar{GQ}{\GQ}\text{.}\) Thus
    \begin{equation*} e_{\notnfar{GA}{\GA}}^\beta(\notnfar{Ytarget}{Y})=e_{\notnfar{GQ}{\GQ}}^\beta(\notnfar{Ytarget}{Y}), \end{equation*}
    which completes the inductive step and proves Theorem 4.2.
    🔗
    🔗
    🔗

    Section 10 Passage to all finite quotients

    The fixed-frame equality is now summed over the possible tame quotient maps of an arbitrary finite group. This gives equality of all finite epimorphism counts, to which the reconstruction lemma applies.
    🔗

    Lemma 10.1. Exhaustion by tame boundary frames.

    Let \(G\) be finite and put \(L=O_2(G)\text{.}\) For either source \(\notnfar{GammaSrc}{\Gamma}\text{,}\) every epimorphism \(f:\notnfar{GammaSrc}{\Gamma}\twoheadrightarrow G\) determines a unique tame boundary frame
    \begin{equation*} \notnfar{TA}{\TA}\twoheadrightarrow G/L. \end{equation*}
    Conversely, with decoration \(\notnfar{Etarget}{E}=0\text{,}\) a boundary-framed epimorphism to \(G\) with a fixed tame frame is exactly an ordinary epimorphism to \(G\) inducing that frame. Distinct tame frames give disjoint sets of epimorphisms.
    🔗
    Lean (main)Lean (count identity)Lean
    🔗

    Proof.
    The characteristic marked wild subgroup maps into \(O_2(G)=L\text{,}\) so every epimorphism has a well-defined quotient map to \(G/L\text{.}\) The descended map \(\notnfar{TA}{\TA}\to G/L\) is continuous: the projection \(\Gamma\twoheadrightarrow\notnfar{TA}{\TA}\) is a continuous surjection from a compact profinite group onto a Hausdorff quotient, hence a topological quotient map, and the composite \(\Gamma\to G/L\) is continuous. By Proposition 3.2, this quotient map is a tame frame. Conversely, when \(\notnfar{Etarget}{E}=0\) there is no extra decoration, and the boundary-framed condition records only the induced tame quotient map and the marked \(2\)-kernel. Thus a boundary-framed epimorphism with target \(G\) is precisely an ordinary epimorphism inducing the chosen frame. The induced quotient map \(\notnfar{TA}{\TA}\to G/L\) is unique, so the fixed-frame sets are disjoint as the frame varies.
    🔗
    🔗
    Let \(G\) be finite and put \(L=O_2(G)\text{.}\) By Lemma 10.1, the ordinary surjection set is the disjoint union of the fixed-frame surjection sets over all tame frames \(\notnfar{TA}{\TA}\twoheadrightarrow G/L\text{.}\) Applying Theorem 4.2 to each frame with \(\notnfar{Etarget}{E}=0\text{,}\) summing over the finite set of frames, and using Proposition 2.3, gives
    \begin{equation} |\Sur(\notnfar{GA}{\GA},G)|=|\Sur(\notnfar{GQ}{\GQ},G)|\tag{10.1} \end{equation}
    for every finite group \(G\text{.}\)
    🔗
    The candidate is topologically generated by four elements. The one-sided reconstruction lemma Lemma 2.5 applied to (10.1) gives \(\notnfar{GA}{\GA}\cong\notnfar{GQ}{\GQ}\text{,}\) proving Theorem 1.2.
    🔗
    🔗

    Section 11 Further questions

    The presentation, the counting route behind it, and the formalization each suggest continuations. We record the questions we consider most tractable or most consequential.
    🔗
    A natural continuation of the formalization is to drive the census of external interfaces (nine at the time of writing; see Subsection 1.3) to zero and to upstream the reusable theory. The project has already discharged several earlier assumptions internally: the dyadic Hilbert-symbol formula, Kummer surjectivity, and the unit-filtration counts are now theorems of the repository. Each remaining interface (local Euler characteristic, local Tate duality, local reciprocity, the oriented Demushkin classification [Lab], and the rest of the list in Subsection 1.3) is a well-scoped target, so the paper induces a prioritized worklist for formalizing local class field theory at \(p=2\text{.}\)
    🔗
    1. Uniformity across dyadic fields. Extend Theorem 1.2 to every finite extension \(K/\Qtwo\) without rebuilding the proof field by field. The boundary formalism and counting induction are already uniform, while the marked Demushkin group [Lab], its cyclotomic orientation, and the quadratic comparison vary through the standard local data \([K:\Qtwo]\text{,}\) the image of the cyclotomic character, and the filtered square-class group with its Hilbert pairing. The central question is whether the candidate relator and the quadratic Gauss-sign calculation can be formulated once over this package of invariants. A positive answer would give a uniform theorem for all dyadic fields; a negative answer should identify the additional invariant and reduce the problem to finitely many structural types, rather than one calculation per field. The seven quadratic extensions of \(\Qtwo\text{,}\) which lie outside Diekert’s hypotheses [Die], are a useful stress test for such a uniform formulation; Schneider’s partial structural results [Sch] provide a second comparison point.
      🔗
      🔗
    2. Constraints on Jannsen–Wingberg-type presentations. Classify the allowable wild relator in a dyadic analogue of the Jannsen–Wingberg presentation. Here Jannsen–Wingberg shape means the structural ansatz of [NSW, Theorem 7.5.14]: tame generators \(\sigma,\tau\) with \(\sigma\tau\sigma^{-1}=\tau^q\text{;}\) wild generators whose closed normal subgroup is pro-\(p\text{;}\) and one further relation expressing \(x_0^\sigma\) as a cyclotomic norm word in \(x_0,\tau\text{,}\) a \(p\)-power, and commutators whose partners are constrained by the tame cyclotomic action. Determine, modulo boundary-preserving changes of wild generators, which \(2\)-adic analogues of this ansatz can present \(G_{\Qtwo}\text{.}\) Low central quotients, the evaluated Fox Jacobian, and the quadratic Gauss sums should give necessary constraints on the relator. Constraints of this kind would also give criteria for evaluating the independently proposed candidate presentations mentioned in the introduction.
      🔗
      🔗
    3. Deformation rings from the presentation. Compute universal deformation rings of residual representations \(\bar\rho:G_{\Qtwo}\to\mathrm{GL}_d(k)\) directly from the presentation. Substitute universal framed matrices into the two relator words and complete at \(\bar\rho\text{;}\) the evaluated Fox Jacobian is the linearization of these equations, matching Mazur’s description of the tangent space by \(H^1(G_{\Qtwo},\operatorname{ad}\bar\rho)\) and of the relation ideal by an obstruction map into \(H^2\) [Maz, Section 1.6, Proposition 2], while higher Fox terms retain the full power-series equations. Compare the resulting completed rings, and their quotients imposing Hodge conditions, with the formal completions of the Emerton–Gee stack and its crystalline or semistable substacks [EG, Section 1.1 and Theorem 1.2.4]. This would turn the local geometry of their moduli spaces at \(G_{\Qtwo}\)-representations into explicit word calculus: first recover known two-dimensional crystalline deformation rings as a consistency check, then compute new \(p=2\) examples.
      🔗
      🔗
    4. Explicit counting formulas. Extract from the Fourier-inversion stage an explicit algorithm, ideally a closed form, for \(|\Sur(G_{\Qtwo},G)|\) for an arbitrary finite group \(G\text{,}\) refined by inertia and higher ramification data. The quotient \(|\Sur(G_{\Qtwo},G)|/|\operatorname{Aut}(G)|\) counts \(G\)-Galois extensions, whereas Monge’s formula [Mon, Theorem 1] counts isomorphism classes of extensions with prescribed ramification index \(e\) and inertia degree \(f\text{,}\) equivalently conjugacy classes of the corresponding open subgroups. Find an explicit passage between these counts using subgroup and normalizer data, and reconcile it with the Krasner–Serre mass-formula tradition [Ser78]; then refine the comparison by discriminant and upper ramification breaks. Tables for small \(G\text{,}\) cross-linked to the LMFDB’s \(2\)-adic fields data and a machine-readable form of the presentation, would make both kinds of enumeration computable from the same source.
      🔗
      🔗
    5. Ramification filtration and canonical wild generators. Give the wild generators \(x_0,x_1\) a canonical Galois-theoretic characterization up to conjugacy, and locate the ramification filtration in upper numbering word-theoretically in the presentation. The presentation retains only the tame–wild dichotomy; recovering the filtration would connect it to the local anabelian results [Moc], in which the filtration is the essential extra datum.
      🔗
      🔗
    6. The outer automorphism group. Compute \(\operatorname{Out}(G_{\Qtwo})\text{,}\) or at least its action on the marked tame–pro-\(2\) data, directly from the presentation. Automorphism groups of \(2\)-adic local Galois groups are studied in [Nis]; a finite presentation plus the Fox toolkit makes this a concrete word problem.
      🔗
      🔗
    7. The counting route as a general technique. Establish the counting route as a general profinite technique. The pipeline (a candidate assembled from admissible finite quotients, the one-sided reconstruction lemma, a lifting-theory comparison, and Fourier induction) uses nothing specific to \(\Qtwo\) before the quadratic stage. Test cases: a machine-checkable re-proof of the odd-\(p\) theorem [JW], and maximal pro-\(p\) Galois groups with restricted ramification, where Koch-type presentations supply candidates. Separately: is there an a priori bound on the induction, turning the count comparison into a finite decision procedure?
      🔗
      🔗
    🔗

    Appendix A Normalized cochains, Shapiro maps, corestriction, and the Evens norm

    The formulas in Lemma 6.13, Lemma 6.15 depend on choices of left action, coset representatives, and normalized sections. This appendix fixes those conventions at cochain level and gives the explicit normalized boundaries produced by every change of section or transversal.
    🔗
    The general bar and transfer constructions are standard; compare [Bro, Chapter III and Chapter VII] and [Eve].
    🔗

    Subsection A.1 Normalized inhomogeneous cochains

    All coefficient modules are left modules. If \(G\) is profinite and \(M\) is a finite discrete continuous left \(G\)-module, then \(C^n(G,M)\) denotes the group of continuous normalized inhomogeneous \(n\)-cochains. Thus a cochain of positive degree vanishes whenever one of its arguments is \(1\text{,}\) and \(C^0(G,M)=M\text{.}\) In additive notation the differential is
    \begin{align} (df)(g_1,\ldots,g_{n+1}) &=g_1f(g_2,\ldots,g_{n+1}) +\sum_{i=1}^{n}(-1)^i f(g_1,\ldots,g_ig_{i+1},\ldots,g_{n+1})\notag\\ &\qquad+(-1)^{n+1}f(g_1,\ldots,g_n),\tag{A.1} \end{align}
    and, in degree zero,
    \begin{equation} (dm)(g)=gm-m.\tag{A.2} \end{equation}
    All coefficient groups in the normalization-sensitive calculations of Lemma 6.13, Lemma 6.15 are \(\F_2\)-vector spaces, so the minus signs in (A.1) disappear there.
    🔗
    Let \(\mu:A\times B\to C\) be a \(G\)-equivariant bilinear pairing of left \(G\)-modules. Our cup-product convention is
    \begin{equation} (f\smile g)(g_1,\ldots,g_{p+q}) =\mu\!\left( f(g_1,\ldots,g_p), (g_1\cdots g_p)g(g_{p+1},\ldots,g_{p+q}) \right).\tag{A.3} \end{equation}
    In particular, for trivial scalar coefficients, \((\alpha\smile\beta)(n_1,n_2)=\alpha(n_1)\beta(n_2)\text{.}\)
    🔗
    We use the following three levels of assertion.
    🔗
    1. “Equal as normalized cochains” means equality in \(C^n(G,M)\text{.}\)
      🔗
      🔗
    2. “Equal up to the displayed normalized coboundary” means \(f-g=dh\) for the particular normalized cochain \(h\) that is written down.
      🔗
      🔗
    3. “Equal in cohomology” means only \([f]=[g]\) in \(H^n(G,M)\text{.}\)
      🔗
      🔗
    No cochain-level assertion in the main text is intended to pass silently from one of these levels to another.
    🔗
    🔗

    Subsection A.2 Conjugation and semidirect products

    The group-theoretic exponent convention remains
    \begin{equation*} x^g=g^{-1}xg. \end{equation*}
    It is distinct from the notation \(gm\) for the given left action of \(G\) on a module \(M\text{.}\) We write the semidirect product as \(M\rtimes G\text{,}\) with elements \((m,g)\) and multiplication
    \begin{equation} (m,g)(n,h)=(m+gn,gh), \qquad (m,g)^{-1}=(-g^{-1}m,g^{-1}).\tag{A.4} \end{equation}
    Consequently
    \begin{equation*} (0,g)(m,1)(0,g)^{-1}=(gm,1), \qquad (m,1)^{(0,g)}=(g^{-1}m,1). \end{equation*}
    Thus the manuscript’s right-conjugation notation acts on the normal module by \(g^{-1}\text{,}\) whereas the semidirect-product law uses the specified left action by \(g\text{.}\)
    🔗
    Let \(\rho:\Gamma\to G\) and \(b:\Gamma\to M\text{.}\) The graph map
    \begin{equation} \Phi_{b,\rho}:\Gamma\longrightarrow M\rtimes G, \qquad \gamma\longmapsto(b(\gamma),\rho(\gamma))\tag{A.5} \end{equation}
    is a homomorphism if and only if
    \begin{equation} b(\gamma\eta)=b(\gamma)+\rho(\gamma)b(\eta).\tag{A.6} \end{equation}
    This is the graph-pullback convention used in (6.4), (6.40), and (6.51).
    🔗
    🔗

    Subsection A.3 The left-regular coordinate convention

    For a finite group \(H\) we identify \(\F_2[H]\) with the functions \(x=(x_h)_{h\in H}\) and use the left-regular action
    \begin{equation} (cx)_h=x_{c^{-1}h}.\tag{A.7} \end{equation}
    Hence
    \begin{equation*} (\bar\gamma x)_h=x_{\bar\gamma^{-1}h}. \end{equation*}
    This is the source of the index \(\bar\gamma^{-1}h\) in the Shapiro cocycle and in the cup/corestriction formula. Right multiplication of the coordinate index is a different operator:
    \begin{equation} (\mathsf R_gx)_h=x_{hg}.\tag{A.8} \end{equation}
    The operators \(\mathsf R_g\) commute with the left-regular \(H\)-action. The monomial \(x_ux_{ug}\) is therefore naturally indexed by cosets written \(u\langle g\rangle\text{,}\) which explains the right multiplication by \(g\) and the coset convention in Lemma 6.2.
    🔗
    🔗

    Subsection A.4 The normalized Shapiro cochain map

    Let
    \begin{equation*} 1\longrightarrow N\longrightarrow G\xrightarrow{\;\pi\;}H\longrightarrow1 \end{equation*}
    be exact with \(H\) finite. Choose a normalized section \(h\mapsto\widetilde h\text{,}\) with \(\widetilde1=1\text{,}\) and write \(\bar\gamma=\pi(\gamma)\text{.}\) Define the transition element
    \begin{equation} \lambda_h(\gamma) =\widetilde h^{-1}\gamma \widetilde{\bar\gamma^{-1}h}\in N.\tag{A.9} \end{equation}
    It is normalized and satisfies
    \begin{equation} \lambda_h(\gamma\eta) =\lambda_h(\gamma)\lambda_{\bar\gamma^{-1}h}(\eta).\tag{A.10} \end{equation}
    For a normalized scalar cochain \(f\in C^n(N,\F_2)\) put
    \begin{equation} \bigl(\operatorname{Sh}_{\widetilde H}^n f\bigr) (\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_n)_h =f\bigl( \lambda_{h_0}(\gamma_1),\ldots, \lambda_{h_{n-1}}(\gamma_n) \bigr), \quad h_i=\overline{\gamma_1\cdots\gamma_i}^{\,-1}h.\tag{A.11} \end{equation}
    Equation (A.10) gives \(d\operatorname{Sh}_{\widetilde H} =\operatorname{Sh}_{\widetilde H}d\) directly. Thus (A.11) fixes a full normalized cochain map, although the main text uses it only in degree one, together with the degree-two corestriction formula below.
    🔗
    For \(\alpha\in Z^1(N,\F_2)\) this specializes to
    \begin{equation} \operatorname{Sh}_{\widetilde H}(\alpha)(\gamma)_h =\alpha\!\left( \widetilde h^{-1}\gamma \widetilde{\bar\gamma^{-1}h} \right).\tag{A.12} \end{equation}
    Indeed, by (A.10),
    \begin{align*} \operatorname{Sh}(\alpha)(\gamma\eta)_h &=\operatorname{Sh}(\alpha)(\gamma)_h +\operatorname{Sh}(\alpha)(\eta)_{\bar\gamma^{-1}h}\\ &=\operatorname{Sh}(\alpha)(\gamma)_h +(\bar\gamma\operatorname{Sh}(\alpha)(\eta))_h, \end{align*}
    which is exactly the left-module cocycle identity. Formula (6.39) is (A.12) for \(H=C_2\text{.}\)
    🔗
    🔗

    Subsection A.5 The convention for \(g\alpha\)

    Let \(g\in H\text{,}\) choose its section lift \(\widetilde g\text{,}\) and let \(\alpha\in Z^1(N,\F_2)\text{.}\) We define
    \begin{equation} (g\alpha)(n)=\alpha(\widetilde g^{-1}n\widetilde g) \qquad(n\in N).\tag{A.13} \end{equation}
    Because \(\alpha\) has trivial scalar coefficients, this does not depend on replacing \(\widetilde g\) by another lift. It is the usual left \(H\)-action on \(H^1(N,\F_2)\) expressed in the manuscript’s conjugation convention.
    🔗
    For \(h\in H\) put
    \begin{equation} a_h^{(g)}=\widetilde{hg}^{-1}\widetilde h\widetilde g\in N, \qquad q_{\alpha,g}(h)=\alpha(a_h^{(g)}).\tag{A.14} \end{equation}
    If \(k=\bar\gamma^{-1}h\text{,}\) then
    \begin{equation*} \lambda_{hg}(\gamma) =a_h^{(g)}\, \widetilde g^{-1}\lambda_h(\gamma)\widetilde g\, (a_k^{(g)})^{-1}. \end{equation*}
    Applying \(\alpha\) gives the exact normalized-cochain identity
    \begin{equation} \operatorname{Sh}(g\alpha) =\mathsf R_g\operatorname{Sh}(\alpha)+dq_{\alpha,g},\tag{A.15} \end{equation}
    where \((dq_{\alpha,g})(\gamma)_h =q_{\alpha,g}(h)+q_{\alpha,g}(\bar\gamma^{-1}h)\text{.}\) If the section is right-\(g\)-equivariant, namely \(\widetilde{hg}=\widetilde h\widetilde g\) for all relevant \(h\text{,}\) then \(q_{\alpha,g}=0\) and (A.15) is strict:
    \begin{equation*} \operatorname{Sh}(g\alpha)(\gamma)_h =\operatorname{Sh}(\alpha)(\gamma)_{hg}. \end{equation*}
    No such equivariance is assumed silently when it is unavailable.
    🔗
    For later use, let \(A=\operatorname{Sh}(\alpha)\) and \(B=\operatorname{Sh}(\beta)\text{.}\) With the \(H\)-invariant trace pairing \(\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_hx_hy_h\text{,}\) the free-orbit cochain formed with the right-shifted coordinate \(\mathsf R_gB\) differs from the cochain formed with \(\operatorname{Sh}(g\beta)\) by the displayed boundary
    \begin{equation} \operatorname{tr}\bigl(A\smile R_gB\bigr) -\operatorname{tr}\bigl(A\smile\operatorname{Sh}(g\beta)\bigr) =d\mathfrak b_{\alpha,\beta,g},\tag{A.16} \end{equation}
    where
    \begin{equation} \mathfrak b_{\alpha,\beta,g}(\gamma) =\sum_{h\in H} A(\gamma)_h\, q_{\beta,g}(\bar\gamma^{-1}h).\tag{A.17} \end{equation}
    This follows from (A.3), (A.15), and the Leibniz rule. It is the precise cochain correction behind (6.46).
    🔗
    🔗

    Subsection A.6 Corestriction in degrees one and two

    Let \(K\leq G\) have finite index and let \(\Omega=G/K\text{,}\) with cosets written \(t_\omega K\text{.}\) Choose a normalized transversal \(\{t_\omega\}_{\omega\in\Omega}\) and define
    \begin{equation} \ell_\omega(\gamma) =t_\omega^{-1}\gamma t_{\gamma^{-1}\omega}\in K.\tag{A.18} \end{equation}
    Then
    \begin{equation} \ell_\omega(\gamma\eta) =\ell_\omega(\gamma)\ell_{\gamma^{-1}\omega}(\eta).\tag{A.19} \end{equation}
    For scalar normalized cochains, the bar-corestriction map is
    \begin{equation} (\operatorname{cor}_{\mathcal T}^n f)(\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_n) =\sum_{\omega\in\Omega} f\bigl( \ell_{\omega_0}(\gamma_1),\ldots, \ell_{\omega_{n-1}}(\gamma_n) \bigr), \quad \omega_i=(\gamma_1\cdots\gamma_i)^{-1}\omega.\tag{A.20} \end{equation}
    In degrees one and two this reads
    \begin{align} (\operatorname{cor}_{\mathcal T}\alpha)(\gamma) &=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}\alpha(\ell_\omega(\gamma)),\tag{A.21}\\ (\operatorname{cor}_{\mathcal T}\nu)(\gamma,\eta) &=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega} \nu\bigl(\ell_\omega(\gamma), \ell_{\gamma^{-1}\omega}(\eta)\bigr).\tag{A.22} \end{align}
    Equation (A.19) gives
    \begin{equation} d\operatorname{cor}_{\mathcal T} =\operatorname{cor}_{\mathcal T}d.\tag{A.23} \end{equation}
    Equivalently, when \(K=N\triangleleft G\) and \(H=G/N\text{,}\) corestriction is the coordinate-sum map after the Shapiro map.
    🔗
    In particular, for \(\alpha,\beta\in Z^1(N,\F_2)\text{,}\)
    \begin{equation} \operatorname{cor}_N^G(\alpha\smile\beta)(\gamma,\eta) =\sum_{h\in H} \operatorname{Sh}(\alpha)(\gamma)_h\, \operatorname{Sh}(\beta)(\eta)_{\bar\gamma^{-1}h}.\tag{A.24} \end{equation}
    This is the exact normalized-cochain identity used in (6.48).
    🔗
    For (6.50), take \(G=G_F\text{,}\) \(K=G_{K_0}\text{,}\) \(\Omega=H/J\text{,}\) and representatives written \(uJ\text{.}\) The relation \(\bar\gamma^{-1}u=\pi_{\bar\gamma}(u)g^{\epsilon_{\bar\gamma}(u)}\) means that \(\gamma^{-1}(uJ)=\pi_{\bar\gamma}(u)J\text{,}\) so (A.22) becomes exactly (6.50).
    🔗
    🔗

    Subsection A.7 Changing sections and transversals

    We first record the degree-one Shapiro correction. Let \(\widetilde h'=\widetilde h a_h\) with \(a_h\in N\) and \(a_1=1\text{.}\) Then
    \begin{equation*} \lambda_h'(\gamma)=a_h^{-1}\lambda_h(\gamma) a_{\bar\gamma^{-1}h}. \end{equation*}
    For \(\alpha\in Z^1(N,\F_2)\) define the normalized \(0\)-cochain \(q_\alpha\in\F_2[H]\) by \(q_\alpha(h)=\alpha(a_h)\text{.}\) Then
    \begin{equation} \operatorname{Sh}_{\widetilde H'}(\alpha) -\operatorname{Sh}_{\widetilde H}(\alpha) =dq_\alpha \quad\text{in }C^1(G,\F_2[H]).\tag{A.25} \end{equation}
    Thus the change of Shapiro lift is not left as an unspecified cohomology ambiguity.
    🔗
    For all degrees there is an explicit prism homotopy. Let \(K\leq G\) be as in Subsection A.6, and let \(t_\omega'=t_\omega a_\omega\text{,}\) \(a_\omega\in K\text{,}\) be a second normalized transversal indexed by the same coset set \(\Omega\text{.}\) For a normalized \(n\)-cochain \(f\) on \(K\text{,}\) write
    \begin{equation*} f^{\mathrm h}(y_0,\ldots,y_n) =f(y_0^{-1}y_1,\ldots,y_{n-1}^{-1}y_n) \end{equation*}
    whenever all consecutive ratios lie in \(K\text{.}\) Given \(\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_{n-1}\in G\text{,}\) put
    \begin{equation*} p_i=\gamma_1\cdots\gamma_i, \qquad \omega_i=p_i^{-1}\omega, \qquad y_i=p_i t_{\omega_i}, \qquad y_i'=p_i t_{\omega_i}'=y_i a_{\omega_i}. \end{equation*}
    Define
    \begin{equation} \bigl(\mathfrak c_{\mathcal T,\mathcal T'}^n f\bigr) (\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_{n-1}) =\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} f^{\mathrm h}(y_0,\ldots,y_i,y_i',\ldots,y_{n-1}').\tag{A.26} \end{equation}
    Over general coefficients the inner sum has the usual signs \((-1)^i\text{;}\) over \(\F_2\) they are all \(+1\text{.}\) The simplicial prism identity gives
    \begin{equation} \operatorname{cor}_{\mathcal T'}f -\operatorname{cor}_{\mathcal T}f =d\mathfrak c_{\mathcal T,\mathcal T'}f +\mathfrak c_{\mathcal T,\mathcal T'}(df).\tag{A.27} \end{equation}
    This is the promised cochain-level change-of-transversal formula.
    🔗
    For a normalized \(2\)-cochain \(\nu\text{,}\) the degree-one transition cochain in (A.26) is especially concrete. Write \(\ell_\omega,\ell_\omega'\) for the transition elements associated to the two transversals. Then
    \begin{equation} \begin{split} \bigl(\mathfrak c_{\mathcal T,\mathcal T'}\nu\bigr)(\gamma) =\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}\bigl(& \nu(a_\omega,\ell_\omega'(\gamma))\\ &+\nu(\ell_\omega(\gamma),a_{\gamma^{-1}\omega}) \bigr). \end{split}\tag{A.28} \end{equation}
    It is normalized. If \(d\nu=0\text{,}\) then
    \begin{equation} \operatorname{cor}_{\mathcal T'}\nu -\operatorname{cor}_{\mathcal T}\nu =d\bigl(\mathfrak c_{\mathcal T,\mathcal T'}\nu\bigr).\tag{A.29} \end{equation}
    The same prism without the outer sum over \(\Omega\) gives the corresponding homotopy between the two Shapiro cochain maps; in degree one it is precisely (A.25).
    🔗
    We now specialize these formulas to the two cocycles used in the manuscript. Let \(J=\langle g\rangle\text{,}\) \(M=\F_2[H]\text{,}\) and write \(p:M\to\F_2[J]\) for the projection to the coordinates \(1,g\text{.}\) Put
    \begin{equation*} \theta_g=(p\rtimes1)^*\kappa_J \in Z^2(M\rtimes J,\F_2). \end{equation*}
    For a transversal \(\mathcal R\) of the cosets \(uJ\text{,}\) represented in \(M\rtimes H\) by \(\widehat u=(0,u)\text{,}\) direct substitution into (A.22) gives the literal cochain equality
    \begin{equation} \kappa_g^{\mathcal R} =\operatorname{cor}_{\mathcal R}\theta_g.\tag{A.30} \end{equation}
    Indeed, the transition element for \((x,c)\in M\rtimes H\) is
    \begin{equation*} \widehat u^{-1}(x,c)\widehat{\pi_c(u)} =\bigl(u^{-1}x,g^{\epsilon_c(u)}\bigr), \end{equation*}
    and its two selected coordinates are \(x_u,x_{ug}\text{;}\) the two terms of \(\kappa_J\) reproduce (6.11) and (6.12).
    🔗
    Let \(\mathcal R'\) be a second transversal, indexed so that \(u'=uj_u\) with \(j_u\in J\text{,}\) and put \(A_u=(0,j_u)\in M\rtimes J\text{.}\) Formula (A.28) therefore gives the explicit normalized \(1\)-cochain
    \begin{equation} \begin{split} \Lambda^g_{\mathcal R,\mathcal R'}(x,c) =\sum_{u\in\mathcal R}\bigl(& \theta_g(A_u,\ell_u'(x,c))\\ &+\theta_g(\ell_u(x,c),A_{\pi_c(u)}) \bigr) \end{split}\tag{A.31} \end{equation}
    for which
    \begin{equation} \kappa_g^{\mathcal R'}-\kappa_g^{\mathcal R} =d\Lambda^g_{\mathcal R,\mathcal R'}.\tag{A.32} \end{equation}
    Thus the half-orbit change of transversal has a specified boundary, not only an abstract uniqueness argument.
    🔗
    Likewise, in the field-theoretic situation of Lemma 6.15, put
    \begin{equation*} \theta_\alpha =\bigl(\operatorname{Sh}_{K/K_0}(\alpha),\rho_0\bigr)^*\kappa_J \in Z^2(G_{K_0},\F_2) \end{equation*}
    and define \(\nu_{\alpha,\mathcal R}=\operatorname{cor}_{\mathcal R}\theta_\alpha\text{.}\) If the lifts of the representatives change from \(\widetilde u\) to \(\widetilde u'=\widetilde u a_u\) with \(a_u\in G_{K_0}\text{,}\) then
    \begin{equation} \begin{split} \Lambda^\alpha_{\mathcal R,\mathcal R'}(\gamma) =\sum_{u\in\mathcal R}\bigl(& \theta_\alpha(a_u,\ell_u'(\gamma))\\ &+\theta_\alpha(\ell_u(\gamma),a_{\pi_{\bar\gamma}(u)}) \bigr) \end{split}\tag{A.33} \end{equation}
    satisfies
    \begin{equation} \nu_{\alpha,\mathcal R'}-\nu_{\alpha,\mathcal R} =d\Lambda^\alpha_{\mathcal R,\mathcal R'}.\tag{A.34} \end{equation}
    With the compatible nested transversals chosen in the proof of Lemma 6.15, equation (6.51) is a literal equality of normalized cochains. Equations (A.32) and (A.34) give the correction for arbitrary choices.
    🔗
    Finally, consider the index-two formula itself. If the lift \(\widetilde s\) is replaced by \(\widetilde s'=\widetilde s a\text{,}\) \(a\in N\text{,}\) then (A.25) gives \(b'=b+dq\) with \(q_1=0\) and \(q_s=\alpha(a)\text{.}\) Put \(A=(q,1)\in E\rtimes J\) and
    \begin{equation*} \Phi_b(\gamma)=(b(\gamma),\bar\gamma), \qquad \Phi_{b'}(\gamma)=(b'(\gamma),\bar\gamma). \end{equation*}
    Then
    \begin{equation*} \Phi_{b'}(\gamma)=A^{-1}\Phi_b(\gamma)A. \end{equation*}
    For \(p\in E\rtimes J\) define
    \begin{equation} r_A(p)= \kappa_J(A^{-1},A) +\kappa_J(A^{-1},p) +\kappa_J(A^{-1}p,A).\tag{A.35} \end{equation}
    This is the central coordinate of conjugation by the canonical lift of \(A\) in the extension represented by \(\kappa_J\text{.}\) Therefore
    \begin{equation} \nu_{\alpha,\widetilde s'}-\nu_{\alpha,\widetilde s} =d\bigl(r_A\circ\Phi_b\bigr).\tag{A.36} \end{equation}
    This displays the normalized boundary asserted after (6.40).
    🔗
    🔗

    Subsection A.8 The index-two specialization and the Evens normalization

    Let \(J=\langle s\rangle\cong C_2\) act on \(E_2=\F_2e_1\oplus\F_2e_s\) by swapping the two coordinates. Put
    \begin{equation*} q_{\mathrm{hyp}}(\notnfar{x1}{x_1},x_s)=x_1x_s, \qquad f_J(x,y)=x_1y_s, \qquad m_1=0, \qquad m_s(y)=y_1y_s, \end{equation*}
    and
    \begin{equation} \kappa_J((x,c),(y,d))=f_J(x,cy)+m_c(y).\tag{A.37} \end{equation}
    The identities
    \begin{align*} m_s(v+w)+m_s(v)+m_s(w)&=f_J(sv,sw)+f_J(v,w),\\ m_s(sv)+m_s(v)&=0 \end{align*}
    show directly, after expanding \(d\kappa_J((x,c),(y,d),(z,e))\text{,}\) that \(d\kappa_J=0\text{.}\) The cochain is normalized. On the zero section it is zero, and on the fibre
    \begin{equation*} \kappa_J((x,1),(x,1))=f_J(x,x)=x_1x_s, \end{equation*}
    so its square map is \(q_{\mathrm{hyp}}\text{.}\) The lifts of \(e_1,e_s\) are involutions, their commutator is the central involution, and their product has nontrivial square; the fibre extension is therefore \(D_8\text{.}\)
    🔗
    We normalize the homogeneous index-two Evens norm by requiring
    \begin{equation} N_N^G(1+[\alpha]) =1+\operatorname{cor}_N^G[\alpha] +N_N^{G,\mathrm{Ev}}([\alpha])\tag{A.38} \end{equation}
    for \([\alpha]\in H^1(N,\F_2)\text{.}\) For the universal inclusion \(E_2\leq E_2\rtimes J\text{,}\) Mackey restriction gives
    \begin{equation*} \operatorname{res}_{E_2} N_{E_2}^{E_2\rtimes J,\mathrm{Ev}}(e_1^\vee) =e_1^\vee e_s^\vee, \qquad \operatorname{res}_J N_{E_2}^{E_2\rtimes J,\mathrm{Ev}}(e_1^\vee)=0. \end{equation*}
    Since
    \begin{equation*} H^1(J,E_2^\vee)=\ker(1+s)/\operatorname{im}(1+s)=0, \end{equation*}
    the low-degree sequence for \(1\to E_2\to E_2\rtimes J\to J\to1\) shows that these two restrictions determine the class. They are precisely the fibre and zero-section restrictions of (A.37); hence
    \begin{equation} [\kappa_J]=N_{E_2}^{E_2\rtimes J,\mathrm{Ev}}(e_1^\vee).\tag{A.39} \end{equation}
    🔗
    Now let \(N\triangleleft G\) have index two and let \(b=\operatorname{Sh}(\alpha)\) be the cocycle (A.12). By Subsection A.2, the graph \(\gamma\mapsto(b(\gamma),\bar\gamma)\) is a homomorphism. Pulling back (A.37) gives, literally,
    \begin{equation} \nu_\alpha(\gamma,\eta) =b(\gamma)_1b(\eta)_{\bar\gamma^{-1}s} +\varepsilon(\bar\gamma)b(\eta)_1b(\eta)_s,\tag{A.40} \end{equation}
    where \(\varepsilon(1)=0\) and \(\varepsilon(s)=1\text{.}\) Naturality of the Evens norm in this pullback square and (A.39) give
    \begin{equation*} [\nu_\alpha]=N_N^{G,\mathrm{Ev}}([\alpha]). \end{equation*}
    For profinite Galois groups, every cochain in this construction factors through a finite quotient, and the displayed finite-group normalization is applied there.
    🔗
    The convention (A.38) is also the one used in the Evens–Kahn formula: for a quadratic extension \(L/k\text{,}\) the degree-two term in the relative total Stiefel–Whitney identity is
    \begin{equation*} w(\operatorname{Tr}_{L/k}\langle a\rangle) =w(\operatorname{Tr}_{L/k}\langle1\rangle) \bigl(1+\operatorname{cor}_{L/k}[a] +N_{L/k}^{\mathrm{Ev}}([a])\bigr). \end{equation*}
    Thus the normalization in this appendix is exactly the normalization used in (6.53); no additional sign or inverse convention enters Lemma 6.16.
    🔗
    🔗
