    Appendix B Finite Fox–Heisenberg rules and word ledger

    This appendix starts from the finite semidirect, Heisenberg, and extraspecial groups used in the first- and second-order calculations. It records the literal word-evaluation identities that supply the Jacobian, mixed pairing, and candidate quadratic form in Section 5, Section 6.
    🔗
    The rules below are those used in Lemma 5.4, Lemma 5.5, Lemma 5.14, Proposition 6.5. They are identities of finite word evaluations before passage to cohomology; no formal Fox calculus over an infinite completed group is invoked. For each finite coefficient calculation one may replace \(\omega_2\) by any ordinary integer representative modulo the exponent of the finite semidirect, Heisenberg, or extraspecial group being evaluated; Lemma 5.1 then shows that the resulting first and mixed second derivatives are independent of the representative.
    🔗
    Let \(G\) act on \(\notn{Amod}{A}\) and \(\notn{Amod}{A}^\vee\text{,}\) and evaluate a word in
    \begin{equation*} G\ltimes(\notn{Amod}{A}\times \notn{Amod}{A}^\vee\times\F_2). \end{equation*}
    If \(\bar u\) is its base value, \(D_u,D_u^\vee\) are its two first derivatives, and \(\beta_u\) is its mixed central coordinate, then direct multiplication in the finite Heisenberg group gives
    \begin{align} D_{uv}&=D_u+\bar uD_v, &D_{u^{-1}}&=-\bar u^{-1}D_u,\tag{B.1}\\ D_{u^g}&=\bar g^{-1}D_u+\bar g^{-1}(\bar u-1)D_g, &D_{u^n}&=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\bar u^jD_u,\notag\\ \beta_{uv}&=\beta_u+\beta_v+(D_u^\vee)(\bar uD_v), &\beta_{u^{-1}}&=\beta_u+(\bar u^{-1}D_u^\vee)(\bar u^{-1}D_u).\tag{B.2} \end{align}
    The formulas for conjugates, commutators, and powers follow recursively. When \(\bar u\) has odd order \(e\) and the exponent is the \(2\)-primary idempotent, the power sum is the norm projector
    \begin{equation*} \notn{Pnorm}{P}=1+\bar u+\cdots+\bar u^{e-1}. \end{equation*}
    🔗
    We now spell out the first-order ledger at a tame lower map. Write \(\notn{opS}{\mathsf S},\notn{opT}{\mathsf T}\) for the lower actions of \(\notn{sigma}{\sigma},\notn{tau}{\tau}\text{,}\) put \(\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}=\notn{opS}{\mathsf S}^{\omega_2}\text{,}\) and let \((a,b,c,d)\) be the lift variables on \((\notn{sigma}{\sigma},\notn{tau}{\tau},\notn{x0}{x_0},\notnfar{x1}{x_1})\text{.}\) The \(\omega_2\)-power rule gives
    \begin{equation} \notn{Dfox}{D}(u_i)=\notn{Pnorm}{P}(Dx_i+\notn{Dfox}{D}\notn{tau}{\tau}),\tag{B.3} \end{equation}
    and hence
    \begin{equation} \notn{Dfox}{D}(d_0)=\notn{Pnorm}{P} b+(\notn{Pnorm}{P}+1)c, \qquad \notn{Dfox}{D}(z_0)=\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}^{-1}c.\tag{B.4} \end{equation}
    The tame relator gives the unnormalized row
    \begin{equation} \notn{Dfox}{D}(\notn{tau}{\tau}^\notn{sigma}{\sigma}\notn{tau}{\tau}^{-2}) =\notn{opS}{\mathsf S}^{-1}(1+\notn{opT}{\mathsf T})a+(\notn{opS}{\mathsf S}^{-1}+1+\notn{opT}{\mathsf T})b.\tag{B.5} \end{equation}
    The wild relator has the following first-order table:
    \begin{equation*} \begin{array}{c|cccc} \toprule \text{factor} & a&b&c&d\\ \midrule h_0&0&0&0&0\\ u_1^{-1}&0&\notn{Pnorm}{P}&0&\notn{Pnorm}{P}\\ \notnfar{x1}{x_1}^\notn{sigma}{\sigma}&0&0&0&\notn{opS}{\mathsf S}^{-1}\\ {[d_0,z_0]}&0&0&0&0\\ \bottomrule \end{array} \end{equation*}
    Thus
    \begin{equation} L_w=\notn{Pnorm}{P} b+(\notn{Pnorm}{P}+\notn{opS}{\mathsf S}^{-1})d.\tag{B.6} \end{equation}
    Together, (B.5) and (B.6) are the Jacobian displayed in Lemma 5.5.
    🔗
    The only non-obvious entry in this ledger is the first line. The variation of \(g_0=\sigma_2^2\) contributes only in order at least two, because the lower values of \(\notn{x0}{x_0}\) and \(d_0\) at the tame map are both \(1\text{.}\) If \(\notn{Pnorm}{P}=0\text{,}\) then \(Dd_0=\notn{Dfox}{D}\notn{x0}{x_0}=c\text{,}\) and the exact class-two identity of Lemma 5.2 shows that \(h_0\) has the same elementary and central shadow as \(\notn{x0}{x_0}^2\text{.}\) If \(\notn{Pnorm}{P}=1\text{,}\) then \(\notn{opT}{\mathsf T}=1\) and the \(2\)-primary operator \(\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}\) acts trivially on the simple characteristic-\(2\) quotient; its lift to the Heisenberg or extraspecial coefficient group is a central automorphism of order at most \(2\text{,}\) so \(g_0=\sigma_2^2\) acts trivially on the full coefficient group. Again Lemma 5.2 applies. This is the precise reason that \(h_0\) may be replaced by \(\notn{x0}{x_0}^2\) in the linear, mixed cup, and determinant calculations.
    🔗
    Write \(b_{\mathrm{cl}}\) for the bilinear commutator pairing of the chosen class-two coefficient group. For the mixed Heisenberg and extraspecial calculations on normalized representatives supported on \(\notn{x0}{x_0}\text{,}\) the ledger (stated inline in Section 5 and repeated here as part of the appendix’s complete record) is
    \begin{equation*} \begin{array}{c|c|c} \toprule \text{factor} & \notnfar{Vhead}{V}\text{-coordinate} & \text{central coordinate}\\ \midrule h_0&0&\lambda(c)\text{ in }H(\notn{Amod}{A})\text{, or }q(c)\text{ for }\notnfar{kappaq0}{\kappa_q^0}\\ u_1^{-1}&0&0\\ \notnfar{x1}{x_1}^\notn{sigma}{\sigma}&0&0\\ d_0=(\notn{x0}{x_0}\notn{tau}{\tau})^{\omega_2}\notn{x0}{x_0}^{-1}&(\notn{Pnorm}{P}+1)c&*\\ z_0=\notn{x0}{x_0}^{\sigma_2}&\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}^{-1}c&*\\ {[d_0,z_0]}&0&b_{\mathrm{cl}}((\notn{Pnorm}{P}+1)c,\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}^{-1}c)\\ \bottomrule \end{array} \end{equation*}
    The starred central coordinates of \(d_0\) and \(z_0\) are immaterial because these words occur only inside the commutator. The table gives both the mixed Hessian in Lemma 5.14 and the exact base determinant word expansion
    \begin{equation*} Q_A^0(c)=q(c)+\notnfar{bq}{b_q}((\notn{Pnorm}{P}+1)c,\notnfar{opU}{\mathsf U}^{-1}c) \end{equation*}
    of Proposition 6.5. The starred entries may contain the non-diagonal action corrections \(m_c\) from Lemma 6.1; they are central coordinates of \(d_0\) and \(z_0\) and hence do not affect the commutator. No relator-by-relator Stokes identity is used: the correction terms in the finite-word Stokes formula cancel only after summing the tame and wild relators, exactly as in Proposition 5.8.
    🔗
    🔗

    Appendix C The square-commutator presentation

    A second four-generator, two-relator presentation of \(\notnfar{GQ}{\GQ}\) was proposed independently of the one proved in Theorem 1.2. This appendix proves that it, too, presents \(\notnfar{GQ}{\GQ}\text{.}\)
    🔗
    The proof is not an identification of the two presentations. No Nielsen or Tietze transformation carrying one to the other is known, and Proposition C.6 shows that none of the expected kind exists: already their maximal pro-\(2\) quotients cannot be matched by any triple of words. What is reused instead is the argument, through the interface isolated in Corollary 6.19. Three of the interface’s four inputs are computations of the kind carried out in Section 5 and Section 6, with the new word in place of (1.6). The fourth input, the fully marked maximal pro-\(2\) quotient, is genuinely different: the new pro-\(2\) quotient is not the boundary group \(\notnfar{Pi}{\Pi}\) of Proposition 3.10 but a differently presented Demushkin group, and identifying it needs the classification of Demushkin groups at one instance rather than the explicit Nielsen change of (3.16). That instance is proved in Subsection C.5 rather than quoted.
    🔗

    Subsection C.1 The presentation and the theorem

    The conventions of Section 1 remain in force throughout: \(x^g=g^{-1}xg\text{,}\) \([x,y]=x^{-1}y^{-1}xy\text{,}\) and \(\notn{w}{\w}\in\notn{Zhat}{\Zhat}\) is the idempotent that extracts the \(2\)-primary component. Put
    \begin{equation} \sigma_2=\notn{sigma}{\sigma}^{\notn{w}{\w}}, \qquad a=(\notn{x0}{x_0}^{-3}\notn{tau}{\tau})^{\notn{w}{\w}}, \qquad y_1=\notnfar{x1}{x_1}^{\sigma_2}, \qquad c=[\notnfar{x1}{x_1},y_1].\tag{C.1} \end{equation}
    🔗
    Definition C.1. The square-commutator candidate.
    Let \(F\) be the free profinite group on \(\notn{sigma}{\sigma},\notn{tau}{\tau},\notn{x0}{x_0},\notnfar{x1}{x_1}\text{.}\) Call an epimorphism \(\varphi:F\twoheadrightarrow G\) to a finite group square-commutator admissible if the distinguished tuple generates \(G\text{,}\) satisfies (1.5) and
    \begin{equation} (\notn{x0}{x_0}^{\notn{sigma}{\sigma}})^{-1}\,a\,\notnfar{x1}{x_1}^2\,c=1,\tag{C.2} \end{equation}
    and the normal closure of \(\varphi(\notn{x0}{x_0}),\varphi(\notnfar{x1}{x_1})\) is a \(2\)-group. Let \(\mathcal Q_R\) be the class of all such quotients and set
    \begin{equation} N_R=\bigcap_{\varphi\in\mathcal Q_R}\ker\varphi, \qquad \Gamma_R=F/N_R.\tag{C.3} \end{equation}
    For a finite group \(G\) write \(\mathrm{ac}_R(G)\) for the number of square-commutator admissible markings of \(G\text{,}\) that is, of generating quadruples in \(G^4\) satisfying (1.5) and (C.2) whose last two entries lie in the \(2\)-core, as in Proposition 2.3.
    🔗
    Lean (relator word)Lean (relation)Lean (the group)Lean (marking count)
    🔗
    This is the construction of Section 2 with (C.2) in place of (1.6). Nothing in Lemma 2.1, Lemma 2.2 or Proposition 2.3 uses any property of the wild relator beyond its being a word in the four generators, so all three hold verbatim for \(\Gamma_R\text{:}\) finitely many admissible quotients have admissible subdirect product, every finite quotient of \(\Gamma_R\) is again admissible, and epimorphisms \(\Gamma_R\twoheadrightarrow G\) correspond to square-commutator admissible markings of \(G\text{.}\) In particular \(\Gamma_R\) is topologically generated by four elements, so Lemma 2.5 applies to it.
    🔗
    Remark C.2.
    The name records the shape of (C.2): the relator closes with the literal block \(\notnfar{x1}{x_1}^2c\text{,}\) a square times a commutator, where the relator (1.6) of Theorem 1.2 closes with the class-two collector word \(h_0\) and the commutator \(c_0\text{.}\) The two presentations share their generators, their tame relation (1.5) and their pro-\(2\) condition; only the wild relator differs.
    🔗
    🔗
    Theorem C.3. Replacement theorem.
    \(\Gamma_R\cong\notnfar{GQ}{\GQ}\text{.}\) Equivalently,
    \begin{equation} |\Sur(\Gamma_R,G)|=|\Sur(\notnfar{GQ}{\GQ},G)|\tag{C.4} \end{equation}
    for every finite group \(G\text{;}\) equivalently again, \(\mathrm{ac}_R(G)=|\Sur(\notnfar{GQ}{\GQ},G)|\) for every finite group \(G\text{.}\) Consequently the two candidates present the same group, and their marking counts agree: \(\mathrm{ac}_R(G)=\mathrm{ac}(G)\) for every finite \(G\text{.}\)
    🔗
    Lean (literal relators)Lean (counting form)Lean (fixed-frame equality)Lean (counts agree)
    🔗
    Proof.
    By Proposition C.5 the source interface of Corollary 6.19 holds for \(\Gamma_R\text{,}\) so Theorem 4.2 and its proof apply with \(\Gamma_R\) in place of \(\notnfar{GA}{\GA}\text{.}\) Summing over tame boundary frames as in Lemma 10.1 gives (C.4). Since \(\Gamma_R\) is topologically generated by four elements, Lemma 2.5 converts (C.4) into an isomorphism. The last assertion combines (C.4) with (10.1) and Proposition 2.3.
    🔗
    🔗
    Remark C.4.
    The counts \(\mathrm{ac}_R(G)\) were computed and compared with \(|\Sur(\notnfar{GQ}{\GQ},G)|\) for small \(G\) long before any proof: for \(C_2,C_4,V_4,D_4,Q_8\) both sides are \(7,24,42,144,144\text{.}\) Such agreement is evidence and not proof; Theorem C.3 upgrades it to an identity valid for every finite group.
    🔗
    🔗
    🔗

    Subsection C.2 What is reused, and what has to be redone

    The induction of Sections 7–10 takes place entirely inside the finite target: it manipulates lower quotients, exact-image partitions, pushouts, finite Fourier transforms and central double covers, and after Section 5 it never differentiates the wild word again. Its dependence on the source is confined to the items listed in Corollary 6.19 together with the tame and pro-\(2\) data of Section 3. Replacing the source therefore amounts to re-verifying a fixed, finite list.
    🔗
    Proposition C.5. The interface at the square-commutator relator.
    The source \(\Gamma_R\) satisfies every item of Corollary 6.19, and in addition:
    🔗
    1. its tame quotient is \(\notnfar{TA}{\TA}\text{,}\) with the unramified marking of Proposition 3.2 and Proposition 3.14;
      🔗
      🔗
    2. its fully marked maximal pro-\(2\) quotient is \((G_{\Qtwo}(2),\notn{nuur}{\nu_{\mathrm{ur}}})\text{.}\)
      🔗
      🔗
    Lean (the interface)Lean (induction over a source)Lean (deformation duality)Lean (base quadratic form)
    🔗
    Proof.
    Item (i) is the argument of Proposition 3.2 verbatim: in the quotient by the wild subgroup the elements \(\notn{x0}{x_0},\notnfar{x1}{x_1}\) vanish, and Lemma 3.1 gives \(\notn{tau}{\tau}^{\notn{w}{\w}}=1\text{,}\) so \(a=1\) and (C.2) disappears exactly as (1.6) does. Item (ii) is Proposition C.12, proved in Subsection C.4.
    🔗
    For the remaining items the calculations of Section 5 and Section 6 are repeated with (C.2) in place of (1.6), using the word ledgers of Appendix B, which are statements about evaluation in the finite semidirect, Heisenberg and extraspecial groups and are available for any word. The first-order calculation is the shortest of these: the evaluated wild row of the Fox Jacobian of Lemma 5.5 for (C.2) is the row of (1.6) with its two wild columns interchanged. Consequently the lifting complex has the same dimensions, and the argument of Proposition 5.15 gives items (i) and (ii) of Corollary 6.19 unchanged; the trivial-module collapse and the Stokes endpoint of Proposition 5.8 give item (iii); and the second-order expansion of Proposition 6.5, applied to (C.2), produces a base quadratic form with the zero counts of Proposition 6.9, hence item (iv).
    🔗
    The square-commutator relator is the shorter word at every seam, and the calculations are correspondingly shorter: it has no analogue of the auxiliary words \(h_0,d_0,z_0,g_0\) of (1.1)–(1.3), its square block is the bare \(\notnfar{x1}{x_1}^2\text{,}\) and its ramified base evaluation lands on the Wall form of Lemma 6.6 without the telescoping corrections that (1.6) requires; several auxiliary hypotheses used in the main text are correspondingly unnecessary here. In the formalization the independence of the induction from the source is made literal: the interface is a structure, the induction is proved once over an abstract instance of it, and the two sources are two instantiations.
    🔗
    🔗
    🔗

    Subsection C.3 No identification by words

    For the source of Theorem 1.2 the maximal pro-\(2\) quotient is identified with the standard dyadic Demushkin group by the explicit Nielsen change (3.16). The corresponding step for \(\Gamma_R\) cannot be taken that way. Write
    \begin{equation} \notn{D0}{D_0}=\angles{\notn{Agen}{A},S,Y\;\middle|\;\notn{Agen}{A}^2S^4[S,Y]}_{\mathrm{pro}-2}\tag{C.5} \end{equation}
    for the group of (1.4), and let \(D_R\) be the maximal pro-\(2\) quotient of \(\Gamma_R\text{,}\) computed in Lemma C.8 below.
    🔗
    Proposition C.6. Obstruction to a word identification.
    Let \(G,H\in\{\notn{D0}{D_0},D_R\}\text{.}\)
    🔗
    1. Every continuous epimorphism \(G\twoheadrightarrow H\) is an isomorphism.
      🔗
      🔗
    2. Every continuous isomorphism intertwines the canonical orientations of the two groups.
      🔗
      🔗
    3. There is no triple of words in the generators of \(\notn{D0}{D_0}\) whose images generate \(D_R\) and satisfy its relation, and none in the generators of \(D_R\) for \(\notn{D0}{D_0}\text{.}\) The same holds for words in the four generators of \(\notnfar{GA}{\GA}\) or of \(\Gamma_R\text{.}\)
      🔗
      🔗
    🔗
    Proof.
    Both groups have \(\dim_{\F_2}H^1(-,\F_2)=3\) and \(\dim_{\F_2}H^2(-,\F_2)=1\text{.}\) Let \(f:G\twoheadrightarrow H\) be continuous with \(K=\ker f\neq1\text{.}\) Inflation is injective on \(H^1\text{,}\) hence bijective by equality of dimensions, so the restriction \(H^1(G)\to H^1(K)^G\) is zero. The five-term exact sequence then makes transgression injective on \(H^1(K)^G\text{,}\) which is nonzero because \(K\) is a nontrivial pro-\(2\) group; so transgression is onto \(H^2(H)\cong\F_2\text{,}\) and exactness makes inflation \(H^2(H)\to H^2(G)\) vanish. But the cup product on \(H^1(G)\) is the inflation of the cup product on \(H^1(H)\text{,}\) and would therefore be zero, contradicting the nondegeneracy recorded in Lemma C.9 and in Proposition 1.1. Hence \(K=1\text{,}\) which is (i). Assertion (ii) holds because the dualizing module of a Demushkin group is unique and \(\Aut(\mathbb{Z}_2)\) is abelian, so the orientation character is canonical.
    🔗
    For (iii), a word triple as described would define an epimorphism, hence by (i) an isomorphism, hence by (ii) one intertwining the orientations. By Proposition C.10 the orientation of \(D_R\) takes the values \(S,X,Y\) on its generators; these are units of the cubic field \(K=\mathbb{Q}(X)\) of discriminant \(-59\text{,}\) with
    \begin{equation*} N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(X)=-1, \qquad N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(S)=1/4, \qquad N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(Y)=-1, \end{equation*}
    so the orientation value of any word in the generators of \(D_R\) has norm in \(\pm4^{\mathbb{Z}}\text{.}\) An isomorphism \(\notn{D0}{D_0}\to D_R\) would have to carry \(Y\) to an element of orientation value \(\notn{eta}{\eta}=(-3)^{-1}\text{,}\) of norm \(-1/27\text{;}\) impossible. In the other direction the orientation of \(\notn{D0}{D_0}\) takes the rational values \(-1,1,\notn{eta}{\eta}\) on its generators, so every word value is rational, whereas \(X\) is a cubic irrational. Finally, in any pro-\(2\) quotient the tame generator dies and exponentiation by \(\notn{w}{\w}\) is the identity, so words in the four generators factor through words in the three pro-\(2\) generators and the same obstruction applies.
    🔗
    🔗
    Remark C.7.
    Proposition C.6 is an obstruction and not the report of an unsuccessful search, and it is worth recording why a search would not have settled the question. The orientation congruences that a word triple must satisfy are solvable modulo \(2^k\) for every \(k\text{,}\) because \(X\) topologically generates \(1+4\mathbb{Z}_2\text{,}\) and the exponent sums forced at depth \(k\) grow like \(2^{k-3}\text{.}\) A lifting search therefore produces approximate solutions of unbounded length indefinitely, and no finite computation distinguishes that from a solution just out of reach. Unlike the rest of this appendix, the proposition is not part of the formalized chain: it motivates the route taken below but is not used in the proof of Theorem C.3.
    🔗
    🔗
    🔗

    Subsection C.4 The maximal pro-\(2\) quotient and its marking

    Lemma C.8. Pro-\(2\) quotient of the square-commutator candidate.
    The maximal pro-\(2\) quotient of \(\Gamma_R\) is
    \begin{equation} D_R=\angles{s,x,y\;\middle|\;(x^s)^{-1}x^{-3}y^2[y,y^s]}_{\mathrm{pro}-2},\tag{C.6} \end{equation}
    where \(s,x,y\) are the images of \(\notn{sigma}{\sigma},\notn{x0}{x_0},\notnfar{x1}{x_1}\text{.}\)
    🔗
    Lean
    🔗
    Proof.
    In a finite \(2\)-group quotient Lemma 3.1 forces \(\notn{tau}{\tau}=1\text{,}\) and \(\notn{w}{\w}\) acts as the identity. Hence \(\sigma_2=\notn{sigma}{\sigma}\text{,}\) \(a=\notn{x0}{x_0}^{-3}\text{,}\) \(y_1=\notnfar{x1}{x_1}^{\notn{sigma}{\sigma}}\) and \(c=[\notnfar{x1}{x_1},\notnfar{x1}{x_1}^{\notn{sigma}{\sigma}}]\text{,}\) so (C.2) becomes exactly the relator of (C.6). Conversely every finite quotient of (C.6) is square-commutator admissible once \(\notn{tau}{\tau}\) is set to \(1\text{.}\)
    🔗
    🔗
    Lemma C.9. Demushkin invariants of \(D_R\).
    \(D_R\) is a Demushkin pro-\(2\) group of rank \(3\) with \(q(D_R)=2\text{.}\) In the basis of \(H^1(D_R,\F_2)\) dual to \((s,x,y)\text{,}\) the Gram matrix of the cup–Bockstein form is
    \begin{equation} \begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\1&0&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix},\tag{C.7} \end{equation}
    which is nonsingular.
    🔗
    Lean (Demushkin)Lean (rank)Lean (the invariant q)
    🔗
    Proof.
    The presentation has three generators and one relator, so \(\dim H^1=3\) and \(\dim H^2\le1\text{.}\) From \(x^s=x[x,s]\) and \(y^s=y[y,s]\) one gets \([y,y^s]=[y,[y,s]]\) and hence
    \begin{equation*} (x^s)^{-1}x^{-3}y^2[y,y^s]=[x,s]^{-1}\,x^{-4}\,y^2\,[y,[y,s]]. \end{equation*}
    Both \(x^{-4}\) and \([y,[y,s]]\) lie in the third step of the filtration (C.9), so the initial form of the relator is \(y^2[x,s]\text{.}\) This reads off (C.7): the squared generator contributes the diagonal Bockstein entry at \(y\text{,}\) and the commutator contributes the off-diagonal pair at \((s,x)\text{.}\) The matrix is nonsingular, so \(\dim H^2=1\) and the cup product \(H^1\times H^1\to H^2\) is a perfect pairing, which is the Demushkin condition. Finally the exponent sums of the relator on \((s,x,y)\) are \((0,-4,2)\text{,}\) so
    \begin{equation*} D_R^{\mathrm{ab}}\cong\mathbb{Z}_2^2\times\mathbb{Z}/2, \end{equation*}
    and \(q(D_R)\text{,}\) the order of the torsion subgroup of the abelianization, is \(2\text{.}\)
    🔗
    At \(p=2\) the cup square \(u\smile u\) equals the Bockstein \(\beta(u)\) and is additive in \(u\text{,}\) so (C.7) is the Gram matrix of a symmetric bilinear form carrying the Bockstein on its diagonal, not the polar form of a quadratic form; invariants of quadratic type must not be read off from it.
    🔗
    🔗
    Proposition C.10. The orientation of \(D_R\).
    \(D_R\) carries a unique continuous character \(\chi_R:D_R\to\mathbb{Z}_2^\times\) describing its action on the dualizing module. Its values on the generators are
    \begin{equation} \chi_R(s)=S,\qquad \chi_R(x)=X,\qquad \chi_R(y)=Y=-X^2,\tag{C.8} \end{equation}
    where \(X\in\mathbb{Z}_2\) is the unique root of \(Z^3+2Z^2+1\) with \(X\equiv1\pmod2\text{,}\) and \(S=-X^3/(X^2+X+1)\text{;}\) numerically \(X\equiv5\) and \(S\equiv13\pmod{16}\text{.}\) Moreover \(\chi_R\) is surjective, with image \(\{\pm1\}\times(1+4\mathbb{Z}_2)=\mathbb{Z}_2^\times\text{.}\)
    🔗
    Lean (the character)Lean (orientation)Lean (image)
    🔗
    Proof.
    The orientation of a Demushkin group is characterized by the property that every \(\chi\)-crossed derivation of the free pro-\(2\) group kills the relator; see [Ser63, no. 9.3, pp. 153--154]. Evaluating the crossed derivations valued in \(\mathbb{Z}_2(\chi)\rtimes\mathbb{Z}_2^\times\) on the relator of (C.6) gives three coordinate equations, together with the relation \(Y^2=X^4\) forced by the exponent sums. The branch \(Y=+X^2\) is excluded, because it forces \((X-1)(X^2-X-1)=0\) with \(X^2-X-1\) a unit, while \(X=1\) is inconsistent with the remaining equation. On the branch \(Y=-X^2\) the system reduces to \(X^3+2X^2+1=0\text{,}\) which has a unique root congruent to \(1\) modulo \(2\) by Hensel’s lemma, and then \(S=-X^3/(X^2+X+1)\text{.}\) Surjectivity follows from Burnside’s basis theorem applied to the image, together with the fact that \(X\) is not a square modulo \(8\text{.}\)
    🔗
    🔗
    Proposition C.11. Demushkin classification at rank \(3\) and \(q=2\).
    Let \(D\) be a Demushkin pro-\(2\) group of rank \(3\) with \(q(D)=2\text{,}\) carrying a continuous surjective character \(\chi:D\to\mathbb{Z}_2^\times\) that is an orientation of \(D\text{.}\) Then \(D\cong \notn{D0}{D_0}\) as topological groups.
    🔗
    Lean (statement)Lean (theorem)Lean (levelwise limit)Lean (Hopficity)
    🔗
    Proof.
    This is the instance \(n=3\text{,}\) \(q=2\) of the classification of Demushkin groups, [Lab, Thms. 4(2) and 8]. The surjectivity hypothesis pins the remaining invariant: for a Demushkin group of this shape the image of the orientation is \(\{\pm1\}\times(1+2^f\mathbb{Z}_2)\text{,}\) and surjectivity says \(f=2\text{.}\) The instance is proved directly in Subsection C.5.
    🔗
    🔗
    Proposition C.12. Marked identification of the pro-\(2\) quotient.
    Let \(\nu_R:D_R\twoheadrightarrow\mathbb{Z}_2\) be defined by \(\nu_R(s)=1\) and \(\nu_R(x)=\nu_R(y)=0\text{.}\) Then the marked pairs \((G_{\Qtwo}(2),\notn{nuur}{\nu_{\mathrm{ur}}})\) and \((D_R,\nu_R)\) are isomorphic.
    🔗
    Lean
    🔗
    Proof.
    By Lemma C.9 and Proposition C.10 the group \(D_R\) satisfies the hypotheses of Proposition C.11, so \(D_R\cong \notn{D0}{D_0}\text{;}\) and \(\notn{D0}{D_0}\cong G_{\Qtwo}(2)\) is Proposition 1.1. It remains to match the markings. By Proposition C.6(ii) every continuous isomorphism intertwines the orientations, so the composite \(G_{\Qtwo}(2)\to D_R\) is determined on the abelianization up to those automorphisms of \(\notn{D0}{D_0}\) that preserve its orientation. Expressing the unramified character of the target in the coordinates of (C.6) leaves a pair of unknowns, and these are solved by a generation argument modulo \(2\) together with a parity computation for the \(s\)-coordinate modulo \(16\text{,}\) using the values (C.8). Composing with the resulting automorphism gives an isomorphism carrying \(\notn{nuur}{\nu_{\mathrm{ur}}}\) to \(\nu_R\text{.}\)
    🔗
    🔗
    🔗

    Subsection C.5 The classification instance

    This subsection proves Proposition C.11. The argument does not invoke the uniqueness statement of the classification. It re-runs the classification at the single instance needed, by constructing continuous epimorphisms in both directions level by level along a central tower and closing with Hopficity, exactly as in Lemma 2.5. Only the two relators
    \begin{equation*} \notn{r0}{r_0}=\notn{Agen}{A}^2S^4[S,Y], \qquad r_2=(x^s)^{-1}x^{-3}y^2[y,y^s] \end{equation*}
    occur, and the two directions are mirror images of one another.
    🔗
    For a pro-\(2\) group \(G\) put
    \begin{equation} \lambda_1=G, \qquad \lambda_{k+1}=\lambda_k^2[\lambda_k,G], \qquad Q_k=G/\lambda_k, \qquad Z_k=\lambda_k/\lambda_{k+1}.\tag{C.9} \end{equation}
    This is the filtration used in [Ser63, Section 6]. Its steps are open and characteristic, their intersection is trivial when \(G\) is topologically finitely generated, each \(Z_k\) is elementary abelian, and \(Z_k\) is central in \(Q_{k+1}\text{.}\) The following consequences of \([\lambda_a,\lambda_b]\subseteq\lambda_{a+b}\) hold for \(k\ge3\) and are used throughout: \([\lambda_{k-1},\lambda_{k-1}]\subseteq\lambda_{k+1}\text{;}\) squaring induces an \(\F_2\)-linear map \(Z_{k-1}\to Z_k\text{;}\) and, for \(v\in\lambda_{k-1}\text{,}\) the element \([v,g]\) depends only on the classes of \(v\) and \(g\) and is central of order at most \(2\) modulo \(\lambda_{k+1}\text{.}\) At \(k=2\) these fail, which is why every statement below carries the hypothesis \(k\ge3\) and the level \(k=3\) is treated as a base case rather than by the calculus.
    🔗
    Definition C.13. Defect and defect homomorphism.
    Let \(k\ge3\text{,}\) let \(D\) be the group in which we work, and let \(T\) be a triple of elements of \(Q_k\) that generates \(Q_k\) and at which the tested relator evaluates to \(1\text{.}\) Lift \(T\) to \(Q_{k+1}\) and evaluate the relator there; the result lies in \(Z_k\) and is independent of the lift, because all three exponent sums of each relator are even. Call it the defect \(\delta_k(T)\in Z_k\text{.}\) Modifying \(T\) slotwise by \(w\in(\lambda_{k-1})^3\) preserves both clauses and shifts the defect by the defect homomorphism, given in additive notation on \(Z_k\) by
    \begin{equation} \bar d_k(w_1,w_2,w_3)=w_1^2+[w_1,\notn{Agen}{A}]+[w_2,\notn{Ygen}{Y}]+[w_3,\notnfar{Sgen}{S}]\tag{C.10} \end{equation}
    for \(\notn{r0}{r_0}\text{,}\) and by
    \begin{equation} \bar d_k(u,v,w)=w^2+[w,y]+[u,x]+[v,s]\tag{C.11} \end{equation}
    for \(r_2\text{.}\)
    🔗
    Lean (the filtration)Lean (defect)Lean (defect homomorphism)
    🔗
    In (C.10) the factor \(S^4\) is inert, its whole contribution being a square of an element of \(\lambda_k\text{;}\) the factor \(\notn{Agen}{A}^2\) contributes the diagonal term \(w_1^2+[w_1,\notn{Agen}{A}]\text{,}\) and \([S,Y]\) contributes the two cross terms. In (C.11) the block \((x^s)^{-1}x^{-3}\) contributes the two cross terms but nothing in the squaring direction, and \([y,y^s]\) is inert altogether, its first-order terms cancelling in pairs because both of its slots carry the same letter. In each shape exactly one generator is twisted: it occupies the coupled slot \(v^2+[v,\cdot]\text{,}\) while the other two carry the plain bracket slots.
    🔗
    Remark C.14.
    These are the transported analogues, at \(q=2\) and in the conventions of this paper, of the defect homomorphism of [Ser63, Lemme 6.3], which is stated for the normal form available when \(q\neq2\) and is surjective there. At \(q=2\) it is not: the cokernel of \(\bar d_k\) is two-dimensional at every level. That failure is the whole difficulty of this subsection, and it is repaired by Theorem C.15 together with the congruence clause of (C.14).
    🔗
    🔗
    Theorem C.15. Span theorem.
    Let \(F\) be the free pro-\(2\) group on three generators, filtered by (C.9), and let \(\bar d_k\) be either (C.10) or (C.11) evaluated at the generators. For every \(k\ge3\text{,}\)
    \begin{equation} Z_k(F)=\im\bar d_k +\angles{g_i^{2^{k-1}},\,g_j^{2^{k-1}}},\tag{C.12} \end{equation}
    where \(g_i,g_j\) are the two untwisted generators: \(\notnfar{Sgen}{S},\notn{Ygen}{Y}\) for \(\notn{r0}{r_0}\) and \(s,x\) for \(r_2\text{.}\) The corresponding power of the twisted generator already lies in \(\im\bar d_k\text{.}\) The same identity holds in \(Z_k(D)\) for any quotient \(D\) of \(F\) and any generating triple, because the filtration (C.9) is verbal.
    🔗
    Lean (free form, first shape)Lean (free form, second shape)Lean (descent)
    🔗
    Proof.
    Because the filtration is verbal, \(Z_k\) is generated by the classes of \(v^2\) and \([v,g]\) with \(v\in\lambda_{k-1}\) and \(g\in F\text{.}\) We reduce both families into the right-hand side of (C.12).
    🔗
    Bracket atoms. For fixed \(v\) the class of \([v,g]\) is multiplicative in \(g\) and central, so \(g\) may be taken to be a generator. Against either untwisted generator, \([v,g_i]\) is by definition a value of \(\bar d_k\text{,}\) namely the one with \(v\) in the corresponding slot and \(1\) in the others. Against the twisted generator \(t\) one has, also by definition, \([v,t]=(v^2)^{-1}\bar d_k(v,1,1)\text{.}\) So the bracket atoms lie in \(\im\bar d_k\) together with the square atoms.
    🔗
    Square atoms, by induction on \(k\text{.}\) Let \(v\in\lambda_{k-1}\text{.}\) By the statement one level down, the image of \(v\) in \(Z_{k-1}\) is a product of values of \(\bar d_{k-1}\) and of the two level-\((k-1)\) powers. Lift that factorization back into \(\lambda_{k-1}\text{;}\) the ambiguity is an element of \(Z_k\text{,}\) a central involution, which dies on squaring. Squaring is multiplicative on \(\lambda_{k-1}\)-classes because \([\lambda_{k-1},\lambda_{k-1}]\subseteq\lambda_{k+1}\text{,}\) so it suffices to square each factor. A lifted power \(g_i^{2^{k-2}}\) squares to the level-\(k\) power \(g_i^{2^{k-1}}\text{,}\) and a lifted value of \(\bar d_{k-1}\) squares to a value of \(\bar d_k\) by the transport identity
    \begin{equation} \bar d_k(w)^2=\bar d_k(w^2),\tag{C.13} \end{equation}
    read slotwise. Its proof is the same layer calculus: the four factors of \(\bar d_k(w)\) lie one step deeper, squares of products of such elements are products of squares, and the correction term in \([u,g]^2=[u^2,g]\) is \([[u,g],u]\in[\lambda_{k-1},\lambda_{k-2}]\subseteq\lambda_{2k-3}\text{,}\) which is trivial in \(Q_{k+1}\) as soon as \(k\ge4\text{.}\) This closes the induction, and no termination measure beyond \(k\) is needed, because the recursion is exactly the statement one level down.
    🔗
    Base case. For \(k=3\) the computation takes place in \(Q_4\text{,}\) where the layer calculus is exact: \((uv)^4=u^4v^4[v,u]^2\text{,}\) and \([u,v]^2\) is bimultiplicative. Both atom families then close under the same reductions, using \([u^2,z]=[u,z][[u,z],u][u,z]\) for the squares of bracket atoms, and the diagonal identity \(t^4=\bar d_3(t^2,1,1)\text{,}\) valid because \(t\) commutes with \(t^2\text{,}\) for the twisted generator’s fourth power.
    🔗
    🔗
    Remark C.16.
    The spanning statement is asserted for \(q=2\) in [Ser63, Section 7], where the generator powers are printed with exponent \(2^h\) at level \(h\text{.}\) The level-\(h\) classes are those of the \(2^{h-1}\)-st powers; the \(2^h\)-th powers lie one step deeper and are zero in \(Z_h\text{.}\) With the exponents corrected, (C.12) is that statement, and Theorem C.15 supplies a proof of it, for the two relator shapes at issue, in the form needed here. Which pair of generators carries the powers is not a matter of choice: it is determined by the relator, and the wrong pair fails already at \(k=3\text{.}\)
    🔗
    🔗
    Fix now one of the two directions: a target group \(D\) with its orientation \(\chi\text{,}\) and the relator of the other group as the tested word. For \(k\ge2\) one has \(\chi(\lambda_k)\subseteq1+2^{k+1}\mathbb{Z}_2\text{,}\) so \(\chi\) has a well-defined level-\(k\) shadow \(\hat\chi_k\) on \(Q_k\text{.}\) Let \(t_1,t_2,t_3\) be the orientation values of the tested group’s own generators: \(-1,1,\notn{eta}{\eta}\) with \(\notn{eta}{\eta}=(-3)^{-1}\) for \(\notn{r0}{r_0}\text{,}\) and \(S,X,Y\) as in (C.8) for \(r_2\text{.}\) Put
    \begin{equation} S_k=\left\{T:\{1,2,3\}\to Q_k \;\middle|\; \begin{array}{l} \text{the tested relator vanishes at }T,\\ T\text{ generates }Q_k,\\ \hat\chi_k(T_i)\equiv t_i\ \bmod\ 2^k\ \ (i=1,2,3) \end{array}\right\}.\tag{C.14} \end{equation}
    The third clause is what makes the induction work. It is a condition on the trajectory rather than on the level, and it is where the invariant that distinguishes the possible orientation images enters.
    🔗
    Lemma C.17. Stage lemma.
    Let \(k\ge3\) and \(T\in S_k\text{.}\) Then
    🔗
    1. reachability: \(\delta_k(T)\in\im\bar d_k\text{;}\)
      🔗
      🔗
    2. digit adjustment: the map from \(\ker\bar d_k\) to \((\mathbb{Z}/2)^2\) recording the two fresh orientation digits of the corrected triple is surjective.
      🔗
      🔗
    Consequently some modification of \(T\) lifts into \(S_{k+1}\text{,}\) and \(S_k\neq\emptyset\) for every \(k\ge3\text{.}\)
    🔗
    Lean (reachability)Lean (digit adjustment)Lean (stage step)Lean (the levelwise sets)
    🔗
    Proof.
    (i) By Theorem C.15, applied at the generating triple \(T\text{,}\)
    \begin{equation*} \delta_k(T)=\bar d_k(w)\cdot t_p^{\alpha}t_q^{\beta}, \qquad \alpha,\beta\in\F_2, \end{equation*}
    where \(t_p,t_q\) are the two power classes. For each untwisted generator \(z\) let \(D_z\) be the \(\chi\)-crossed derivation of the free pro-\(2\) group taking the value \(1\) at \(z\) and \(0\) at the other two generators. Every \(\chi\)-crossed derivation kills the relator of \(D\) (that is exactly the statement that \(\chi\) is an orientation), so \(D_z\) descends to \(D\text{.}\) Reducing \(D_z\) modulo a suitable power of \(2\text{,}\) which may be done inside the finite semidirect product \(\mathbb{Z}/2^N\rtimes(\mathbb{Z}/2^N)^\times\text{,}\) gives an additive functional \(\varphi^z\) on \(Z_k\) that kills \(\im\bar d_k\text{;}\) and the \(2\times2\) matrix formed by the two functionals on the two power classes is invertible over \(\F_2\text{,}\) by the generation clause alone. Finally the congruence clause forces \(\varphi^z(\delta_k(T))=0\text{:}\) written out, this vanishing is the orientation identity of the tested group at its own generator values, namely \(3+\notn{eta}{\eta}^{-1}=0\) for \(\notn{r0}{r_0}\) and the relation among \(S,X,Y\) of (C.8) for \(r_2\text{.}\) Hence \(\alpha=\beta=0\text{.}\)
    🔗
    (ii) The digit in the twisted slot is automatic. Applying \(\chi\) to the relator clause one level up, and using \(\chi(\lambda_j)\subseteq1+2^{j+1}\mathbb{Z}_2\) at \(j=k+1\text{,}\) gives a relation modulo \(2^{k+2}\) among the orientation values of the lifted triple; the corresponding identity holds exactly at the targets, since \((-1)^2\cdot1^4=1\) and \(X^{-4}Y^2=1\text{.}\) Comparing the two forces the fresh digit of the twisted slot to vanish, with no adjustment and with no data from level \(k+2\text{.}\) The remaining two digits are moved by explicit elements of \(\ker\bar d_k\text{:}\) modifications whose slots are \(2^{k-2}\)-nd powers of the canonical lifts themselves, so that the brackets they would contribute vanish because an element commutes with its own powers. The digit each such modification carries is computed by lifting the exponent from the exact valuations
    \begin{equation*} v_2(\notn{eta}{\eta}-1)=v_2(X-1)=v_2(S-1)=2, \end{equation*}
    which place a nonzero digit at position exactly \(k\text{.}\) Two such moves span \((\mathbb{Z}/2)^2\text{.}\)
    🔗
    For the last assertion, combine (i) and (ii): correct \(T\) by a modification realizing the inverse of \(\delta_k(T)\text{,}\) then adjust inside \(\ker\bar d_k\text{.}\) Generation survives because modifications lie in \(\lambda_{k-1}\subseteq\notn{Frattini}{\Phi}(Q_k)\text{.}\) The base case \(S_3\neq\emptyset\) is checked directly in \(Q_3\text{,}\) a group of order \(2^8\text{:}\) the triples \((y,sx,x)\) and \((SY,Y,\notn{Agen}{A})\) serve in the two directions.
    🔗
    🔗
    Remark C.18.
    The congruence clause is necessary and not merely convenient. Its two cokernel coordinates measure exactly the top orientation deviation digits of \(T\) in the two untwisted slots, with the slots transposed, so the defect is reachable precisely when the clause holds. The sharpest illustration is the group \(\angles{A,S,Y\;\middle|\;A^2S^8[S,Y]}\text{,}\) which has the same rank, the same \(q\) and the same abelianization as \(\notn{D0}{D_0}\text{,}\) and whose orientation differs only in the image. For it the analogue of \(S_4\) is empty, because the relevant orientation value is \((1-8)^{-1}\equiv1\) rather than \(\notn{eta}{\eta}\equiv5\) modulo \(8\text{,}\) so no triple can achieve the required congruence depth. This is the point at which the surjectivity hypothesis of Proposition C.11 is consumed.
    🔗
    🔗
    We can now prove Proposition C.11. Each \(S_k\) is a finite set, the restriction maps \(S_{k+1}\to S_k\) are defined because all three clauses weaken, and each \(S_k\) is nonempty by Lemma C.17. Compactness of an inverse limit of nonempty finite sets, exactly as in the proof of Lemma 2.5, supplies a compatible family. Such a family is a continuous homomorphism from the free pro-\(2\) group on three generators to \(D\) that kills the tested relator and is surjective at every level, hence a continuous epimorphism from the tested group onto \(D\text{.}\) Running the construction in both directions and composing gives a continuous surjective endomorphism of a topologically finitely generated profinite group, which is an isomorphism by Hopficity. Hence \(D\cong \notn{D0}{D_0}\text{.}\)
    🔗
    Applied to \(D=D_R\text{,}\) which satisfies the hypotheses by Lemma C.9 and Proposition C.10, this yields \(D_R\cong \notn{D0}{D_0}\) and completes the proof of Proposition C.12, hence of Proposition C.5 and of Theorem C.3.
    🔗
    🔗

    Subsection C.6 Inputs

    Theorem C.3 rests on the same classical inputs as Theorem 1.2 and on no others. The two places where a further input might have been expected are the classification of Demushkin groups and the identification of the pro-\(2\) quotient. The first is used only through Proposition C.11, which is proved in Subsection C.5 from the filtration (C.9) and the orientation calculus rather than quoted; the second reduces to it. Everything else is either an item of Corollary 6.19, re-verified for (C.2) in Proposition C.5, or a part of the induction that never sees the wild word.
    🔗
    In the formalization this is checked mechanically rather than asserted: the axiom set reported for the formalized form of Theorem C.3 is identical to the one reported for Theorem 1.2, and the formalized form of Proposition C.11 reports no classical input at all. The whole chain is formalized without gaps.

    🔗

    Appendix D Worked examples: three small targets

    The presentation turns extension-counting questions into finite computations: by Proposition 2.3, surjections \(\GA\twoheadrightarrow G\) are exactly the generating quadruples \((\sigma,\tau,x_0,x_1)\in G^4\) satisfying the tame relation (1.5), the wild relation (1.6), and \(x_0,x_1\in O_2(G)\text{,}\) while \(|\Sur(\GQ,G)|=|\operatorname{Aut}(G)|\cdot\#\{G\)-extensions of \(\Qtwo\}\text{.}\) This appendix evaluates the auxiliary words (1.1)–(1.3) on three small targets, identifies the branch of the induction that each exercises, and compares the resulting counts with the known extension counts, as tabulated in the LMFDB’s database of \(2\)-adic fields [bib-LMFDB]; the same counts are the ground truth used by the finite-quotient verifier. Throughout, recall \(x^g=g^{-1}xg\text{,}\) \([x,y]=x^{-1}y^{-1}xy\text{,}\) and that exponentiation by \(\w\) extracts the \(2\)-primary part of an element of finite order: \(g^{\w}=g\) when \(g\) has \(2\)-power order, and \(g^{\w}=1\) when \(g\) has odd order.
    🔗
    One observation applies to every finite \(2\)-group target and explains why such targets probe exactly the maximal pro-\(2\) quotient: the tame relation forces \(\tau\mapsto1\text{.}\) Indeed, conjugate elements have equal orders, so \(\tau^\sigma=\tau^2\) forces \(|\tau|=|\tau^2|\text{,}\) which for an element of \(2\)-power order gives \(\tau=1\text{.}\)
    🔗

    Subsection D.1 A \(2\)-group target: the cyclic group of order four

    Let \(G=\mathbb Z/4\text{,}\) written multiplicatively as \(\langle g\rangle\text{.}\) Here \(O_2(G)=G\text{,}\) and \(\tau\mapsto1\) by the observation above. Since every element has \(2\)-power order, \(\sigma_2=\sigma^{\w}=\sigma\) and \(u_i=(x_i\tau)^{\w}=x_i\text{.}\) The word ledger collapses:
    \begin{equation*} u_0=x_0,\quad d_0=u_0x_0^{-1}=1,\quad z_0=x_0^{\sigma_2}=x_0,\quad c_0=[d_0,z_0]=1,\quad d_g=1,\quad h_c=1, \end{equation*}
    and, because \(G\) is abelian,
    \begin{equation*} h_0=x_0^{g_0}\,x_0\,d_gd_0d_0^2h_c=x_0^2. \end{equation*}
    The wild relation (1.6) therefore reads \(x_0^2\,u_1^{-1}\,x_1^{\sigma}\,c_0=x_0^2\,x_1^{-1}x_1=x_0^2=1\text{:}\) on this target the relator sees only the elementary shadow \(x_0^2\) of \(h_0\text{,}\) exactly as in Lemma 5.3. An admissible quadruple is thus \((\sigma,\tau,x_0,x_1)=(g,1,x_0,x_1)\) with \(x_0\in\{1,g^2\}\) and \(x_1\) arbitrary, or any quadruple with \(x_1\) a generator. Counting generating triples \((\sigma,x_0,x_1)\) with \(x_0^2=1\text{:}\) the pair \((\sigma,x_1)\) must contain a generator of \(G\) (\(16-4=12\) ways) and \(x_0\) is one of \(2\) elements, so
    \begin{equation*} |\Sur(\GA,\mathbb Z/4)|=2\cdot12=24. \end{equation*}
    On the Galois side, local class field theory gives \(\Qtwo^\times\cong 2^{\mathbb Z}\times\{\pm1\}\times(1+4\mathbb Z_2)\text{,}\) so \(\Qtwo\) has exactly \(12\) cyclic quartic extensions and \(|\Sur(\GQ,\mathbb Z/4)|=12\cdot|\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb Z/4)|=24\text{.}\) The counts agree. (For \(G=\mathbb Z/2\) the same collapse makes the relator vacuous and yields \(2^3-1=7\) surjections: the seven quadratic extensions of \(\Qtwo\text{.}\))
    🔗
    🔗

    Subsection D.2 A tame target: the symmetric group \(S_3\)

    Let \(G=S_3\text{,}\) so \(O_2(G)=1\) and admissibility forces \(x_0,x_1\mapsto1\text{.}\) Every auxiliary word then evaluates to the identity: \(u_i=\tau^{\w}=1\) because \(\tau\) has odd order (it is conjugate to its square), and consequently \(d_0=z_0=c_0=d_g=h_c=h_0=1\text{,}\) so (1.6) holds automatically. The count is governed entirely by the \((\sigma,\tau)\)-frame: we need generating pairs with \(\tau^\sigma=\tau^2\text{.}\) Taking \(\tau=(123)\text{,}\) the condition \(\sigma^{-1}(123)\sigma=(132)\) holds exactly for the three transpositions \(\sigma\in\{(12),(13),(23)\}\text{;}\) with the two choices of \(3\)-cycle \(\tau\) this gives
    \begin{equation*} |\Sur(\GA,S_3)|=6, \end{equation*}
    and each such pair does generate \(S_3\text{.}\) On the Galois side there is exactly one \(S_3\)-extension of \(\Qtwo\) (the splitting field of \(x^3-2\text{,}\) the Galois closure of the tamely ramified cubics), so \(|\Sur(\GQ,S_3)|=1\cdot|\operatorname{Aut}(S_3)|=6\text{.}\) This target illustrates the tame frame of Section 3: \(\sigma\) maps to geometric Frobenius in the residue extension and \(\tau\) to a tame generator, with \(\tau^\sigma=\tau^q\text{,}\) \(q=2\text{.}\)
    🔗
    🔗

    Subsection D.3 A mixed target: the symmetric group \(S_4\)

    Let \(G=S_4\text{.}\) Now \(L=O_2(G)=V_4=\{1,(12)(34),(13)(24),(14)(23)\}\) with \(G/L\cong S_3\text{,}\) so a surjection carries a nontrivial elementary \(2\)-layer over a tame frame. Consider the quadruple
    \begin{equation*} \sigma=(12),\qquad \tau=(123),\qquad x_0=(12)(34),\qquad x_1=1. \end{equation*}
    Both tame data are as in the \(S_3\) example (lifted along \(S_4\to S_3\)), and \(x_0,x_1\in O_2(G)\text{.}\) The words evaluate as follows. Since \(\sigma\) has order \(2\text{,}\) \(\sigma_2=\sigma\) and \(g_0=\sigma_2^2=1\text{.}\) The product \(x_0\tau=(12)(34)(123)=(134)\) has odd order, so \(u_0=(x_0\tau)^{\w}=1\) and likewise \(u_1=\tau^{\w}=1\text{.}\) Then
    \begin{equation*} d_0=u_0x_0^{-1}=x_0,\qquad z_0=x_0^{\sigma_2}=((12)(34))^{(12)}=(12)(34)=x_0, \end{equation*}
    so \(c_0=[d_0,z_0]=[x_0,x_0]=1\text{,}\) \(d_g=d_0^{g_0}=d_0\text{,}\) \(h_c=[d_g,d_0]=1\text{,}\) and
    \begin{equation*} h_0=x_0^{g_0}\,x_0\,d_gd_0d_0^2h_c =x_0^2\,d_0^2\,d_0^2=1. \end{equation*}
    The wild relation \(h_0u_1^{-1}x_1^\sigma c_0=1\) holds, the four elements generate \(S_4\) (the frame generates a copy of \(S_3\) and \((12)\cdot(12)(34)=(34)\) supplies the fourth point), and the quadruple is admissible.
    🔗
    This target exercises the first genuinely mixed branch of the induction. In the tower (7.1) the marked kernel is \(L_Y=V_4\text{,}\) whose unique chief factor is the standard two-dimensional simple \(\F_2[S_3]\)-module, which is non-scalar, so the recursion of Theorem 8.17 applies with \(K=V_4\) and \(R=\Phi(V_4)=1\text{:}\) only the elementary stage (8.13) is active, with no Frattini or scalar-phase layer. The exact-image bookkeeping is visible concretely: maps whose image is a proper subgroup containing the frame (for example the four point-stabilizer copies of \(S_3\text{,}\) with \(x_0,x_1\mapsto1\)) are subtracted by Lemma 8.12, leaving the count of surjections with image exactly \(S_4\text{.}\) Summing the resulting counts over the six tame frames as in Lemma 10.1 gives
    \begin{equation*} |\Sur(\GA,S_4)|=72=3\cdot|\operatorname{Aut}(S_4)|, \end{equation*}
    matching the three \(S_4\)-extensions of \(\Qtwo\text{,}\) the Galois closures of the three quartic fields with Galois group \(S_4\).
    🔗
    🔗

    Subsection D.4 The finite-quotient verifier’s input

    The same comparisons, run mechanically over a battery of 5,402 potentially \(2\)-realizable finite groups, constitute the finite-quotient verification described at github.com/roed314/padicIGP. The verifier consumes the presentation as the following relation file, whose lines are exactly the words (1.1)–(1.3) and the relator (1.6); the integer \(40491355905\) represents \(\w\) modulo \(85667662080=2^8\cdot3^2\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13\cdot17\cdot19\cdot23\text{,}\) which suffices for every group in the battery:
    🔗
    sigma,tau,x0,x1

sigma2 = sigma^40491355905
g0 = sigma2^2
u0 = (x0*tau)^40491355905
u1 = (x1*tau)^40491355905
d0 = u0*x0^-1
z0 = x0^sigma2

Passing all 5,402 comparisons is strong evidence for the presentation but is not a proof; the proof is the body of this paper.

    Appendix E Background

    This appendix collects short background summaries for the external inputs of the paper. Each subsection states the facts in the form they are used, with citations to specific locations in the references, and points back to the statements that use them.
    🔗

    Subsection E.1 Profinite group preliminaries

    A profinite group is an inverse limit of finite groups, and the single topological input we use is compactness, in the following combinatorial form: the inverse limit of an inverse system of nonempty finite sets over a directed poset is nonempty [RZ, Proposition 1.1.4]. The proof is exactly the finite intersection property of closed subsets of the compact product: partial compatible families form nonempty closed sets, any finitely many of which meet, so a fully compatible family exists. This is the argument invoked in Lemma 2.5 to assemble a single epimorphism out of epimorphisms onto the members of a directed system of finite quotients. The sets being intersected there are finite because a continuous homomorphism from a topologically finitely generated profinite group to a finite group is determined by its values on a fixed finite generating set; in particular a finitely generated profinite group has only finitely many open normal subgroups of each index [RZ, Proposition 2.5.1].
    🔗
    Finitely generated profinite groups are Hopfian: every continuous epimorphism \(\varphi:G\to G\) of a topologically finitely generated profinite group \(G\) onto itself is an isomorphism [RZ, Proposition 2.5.2]. The mechanism is again finiteness: \(\varphi^{-1}\) induces an injection of the finite set of open normal subgroups of index at most \(n\) into itself, hence a bijection, so \(\ker\varphi\) lies in every open normal subgroup. Hopficity is used twice in this paper: in Lemma 2.5, where the composite of the two constructed epimorphisms \(P\twoheadrightarrow Q\twoheadrightarrow P\) is a surjective endomorphism and therefore an isomorphism, and in Lemma 3.8, where endomorphisms already known to be surjective are upgraded to automorphisms. (Continuity of the inverse is automatic for compact groups.)
    🔗
    The Frattini subgroup \(\PhiG(G)\) of a profinite group is the intersection of its maximal open subgroups. A closed subgroup \(H\) with \(H\PhiG(G)=G\) equals \(G\) [RZ, Corollary 2.8.5], and for a pro-\(p\) group \(\PhiG(G)=\overline{G^p[G,G]}\text{,}\) so that the Frattini quotient \(G/\PhiG(G)\) is a vector space over \(\F_p\) [RZ, Lemma 2.8.7]; for a finite \(2\)-group \(K\) this is the formula \(\PhiG(K)=K^2[K,K]\) used at the head of Section 7. Together these give the pro-\(p\) Burnside basis theorem: a subset of a pro-\(p\) group generates it if and only if its image spans the Frattini quotient, and minimal generating sets correspond to bases of \(G/\PhiG(G)\text{;}\) this is the “Frattini argument” of [NSW, Proposition (3.9.1)], where it is expressed as \(d(G)=\dim H^1(G,\F_p)\text{.}\) In Lemma 3.8 this is how surjectivity is checked: the endomorphism \(\theta_u\) sends a free basis to a set that is again a basis modulo the Frattini subgroup, and the images of the three generators under \(\Psi_u\) form a triangular basis of the Frattini quotient; Hopficity then converts surjectivity into automorphy.
    🔗
    Fibre products of profinite groups exist and are computed naively: the pullback of \(\beta_1:H_1\to H\) and \(\beta_2:H_2\to H\) is the closed subgroup of \(H_1\times H_2\) of pairs with equal image in \(H\) [RZ, Section 2.10]. Two facts about them are used in Section 4, where the boundary (4.1) is such a fibre product. First, for closed normal subgroups \(U,V\) of \(\Gamma\) the natural square exhibits \(\Gamma/(U\cap V)\) as the fibre product of \(\Gamma/U\) and \(\Gamma/V\) over \(\Gamma/UV\) [RZ, Exercise 2.10.1]; consequently, the image of a pair of epimorphisms is the fibre product of the two targets over their largest common quotient compatible with the pair. Second, and equivalently, a pair of epimorphisms \(\varphi_i:\Gamma\to H_i\) with \(\beta_1\varphi_1=\beta_2\varphi_2\) maps onto the fibre product precisely when \(\ker(\beta_1\varphi_1) =\ker(\varphi_1)\ker(\varphi_2)\) [RZ, Lemma 2.10.2]. This is the content of the phrase profinite Goursat in Section 4: surjectivity of \(b_\Gamma\) reduces to the statement that the largest common quotient of \(\TA\) and \(\Pi\) glued by the pair is \(\mathbb{Z}_2\) itself, which holds because every common quotient is pro-\(2\text{,}\) hence a quotient of the maximal pro-\(2\) quotient \(\mathbb{Z}_2\) of \(\TA\text{,}\) and the full \(\mathbb{Z}_2\) occurs.
    🔗
    Sylow theory extends to profinite groups by the compactness argument of the first paragraph: \(p\)-Sylow subgroups exist and are conjugate [RZ, Corollary 2.3.6], and likewise \(\pi\)-Hall subgroups of prosolvable groups [RZ, Corollary 2.3.7]. The form we use is the Schur–Zassenhaus theorem: a closed normal Hall subgroup \(K\) of a profinite group \(G\) admits a complement, and any two complements are conjugate [RZ, Theorem 2.3.15]. In Lemma 9.2 and Lemma 7.2 it is applied to finite targets: the preimage of the odd-order kernel \(N=\ker(H\to H_2)\) in \(Y\) is an extension of \(N\) by the finite \(2\)-group \(L_Y\text{,}\) so Schur–Zassenhaus provides an odd-order complement \(\widetilde N\text{,}\) the odd Hall lift, mapping isomorphically onto \(N\text{.}\) Since the preimage is the product of \(L_Y\) and \(\widetilde N\text{,}\) the conjugating element between two complements may be taken in \(L_Y\text{;}\) this is the \(L_Y\)-conjugacy used to pin \(\widetilde N\) down as normal once it is known to centralize \(L_Y\text{.}\)
    🔗
    Free pro-\(2\) groups enter through three standard facts. A free pro-\(C\) group on a finite set is characterized by the usual universal property [RZ, Lemma 3.3.4], and any generating set of the same finite cardinality is again a basis [RZ, Lemma 3.3.5]; combined with the Frattini criterion above, this is the change-of-basis principle behind the substitution \(P=S^3\text{,}\) \(T=S^{-3}A^{-2}\) in Lemma 3.8 and the Nielsen change (3.16) of Proposition 3.11. Next, powers with profinite exponents: for \(x\) in a profinite group and \(\lambda\in\Zhat\text{,}\) the power \(x^\lambda\) is defined through the unique continuous epimorphism from \(\Zhat\) onto the closed procyclic subgroup generated by \(x\text{,}\) and the exponent laws follow from the integer case by continuity [RZ, Section 4.1]. On a pro-\(2\) group the exponent acts through \(\mathbb{Z}_2\text{,}\) so for odd \(m\) the power map \(x\mapsto x^m\) is a bijection with inverse \(x\mapsto x^{m^{-1}}\text{,}\) \(m^{-1}\in\mathbb{Z}_2^\times\text{;}\) this is the unique-cube-root step of Lemma 3.8. Finally, HNN extensions exist in the pro-\(2\) category: for a variety \(\mathcal C\) of finite groups (such as finite \(2\)-groups) and a continuous isomorphism \(f:A\to B\) of closed subgroups of a pro-\(\mathcal C\) group \(H\text{,}\) there is a unique pro-\(\mathcal C\) HNN extension \(\mathrm{HNN}(H,A,f)\text{,}\) characterized by the universal property that continuous homomorphisms out of it correspond to pairs consisting of a homomorphism on \(H\) and an image of the stable letter intertwining \(A\) and \(B\) [RZ, Section 9.4, Proposition 9.4.1]. The relation (3.9) exhibits \(D_0\) as such an extension of the free pro-\(2\) group \(F_{S,A}\) with stable letter \(Y\text{,}\) and it is through this universal property that the automorphism \(\theta_u\) of the base is extended over \(Y\) in Lemma 3.8.
    🔗
    🔗

    Subsection E.2 The Hochschild–Serre spectral sequence and low-degree exact sequence

    To an extension of profinite groups \(1\to N\to G\to Q\to 1\text{,}\) with \(N\) a closed normal subgroup, and a discrete \(G\)-module \(A\text{,}\) the Lyndon–Hochschild–Serre spectral sequence associates
    \begin{equation*} E_2^{pq}=H^p(Q,H^q(N,A))\Longrightarrow H^{p+q}(G,A). \end{equation*}
    For profinite \(G\) and continuous cochain cohomology this is [NSW, Theorem 2.4.1]; for abstract groups it is constructed in [Bro, Chapter VII, §6]. All coefficient modules used in this paper (\(\F_2\text{,}\) \(V\text{,}\) \(V^\vee\)) are finite and discrete, so the continuous theory of [NSW] applies verbatim over \(G_{\Qtwo}\text{,}\) and the two theories agree on the finite quotients where the normalized-cochain calculations of Lemma 6.1 and Lemma 6.4 take place.
    🔗
    The bottom of the spectral sequence is summarized by the five-term exact sequence of low degree
    \begin{equation} 0\to H^1(Q,A^N)\xrightarrow{\operatorname{inf}} H^1(G,A)\xrightarrow{\operatorname{res}} H^1(N,A)^{Q}\xrightarrow{\operatorname{tg}} H^2(Q,A^N)\xrightarrow{\operatorname{inf}} H^2(G,A),\tag{E.1} \end{equation}
    valid for closed normal \(N\) [NSW, Proposition 1.6.7]; it is the edge-morphism sequence of any first-quadrant \(E_2\)-spectral sequence [NSW, Proposition 2.1.1]. The homological version for abstract groups is [Bro, Corollary VII.6.4]. The transgression \(\operatorname{tg}\) has a direct cochain description (extend a \(Q\)-invariant cocycle on \(N\) to a cochain on \(G\) and take its coboundary [NSW, Proposition 1.6.6]) and coincides with the differential \(d_2^{0,1}\) [NSW, Theorem 2.4.3]. When \(H^i(N,A)=0\) for \(0<i<n\text{,}\) the same sequence holds with \(H^1\) and \(H^2\) replaced by \(H^n\) and \(H^{n+1}\) (inflation–restriction) [NSW, Proposition 1.6.7]; degree-one instances underlie the descent of the radical edge class in Lemma 8.6 and the identification of \(H^1(\Qtwo,V)\) in the unramified case of Proposition 6.18.
    🔗
    The spectral sequence refines (E.1) to a decreasing filtration \(H^2(G,A)\supseteq F^1\supseteq F^2\supseteq 0\) on \(H^2\text{:}\) the quotient \(H^2/F^1\) embeds in \(E_2^{0,2}=H^2(N,A)^Q\text{,}\) so \(F^1\) consists exactly of the classes restricting to zero on the fibre \(N\text{;}\) the bottom piece is \(F^2=\operatorname{im}(\operatorname{inf})\text{;}\) and the intermediate graded piece \(F^1/F^2\) embeds in \(E_2^{1,1}=H^1(Q,H^1(N,A))\) [NSW, §§2.1-2.2]. Consequently there is an exact segment
    \begin{equation} H^2(Q,A^N) \xrightarrow{\operatorname{inf}} \ker\bigl(H^2(G,A)\to H^2(N,A)\bigr) \longrightarrow H^1(Q,H^1(N,A)),\tag{E.2} \end{equation}
    which for \(1\to V\to G\to H\to 1\) with \(A=\F_2\) is the sequence (6.22) used to prove uniqueness of the normalized base class in Lemma 6.4. A class in \(F^1\) is said to have filtration one; its leading term is its image in \(E_2^{1,1}\text{.}\) For the split extension \(1\to V\to V\rtimes C\to C\to 1\) with central coefficients, a filtration-one class is represented at normalized-cochain level by a “linear-in-the-fibre” cocycle \(\Gamma_\gamma\) together with an inflated scalar term, and this normalized representative is the difference decomposition (6.5) of Lemma 6.1. In the split case inflation is a split injection and all differentials into the horizontal edge vanish [NSW, Proposition 2.4.5].
    🔗
    Degree-two classes with central coefficients are the same thing as central extensions: choosing a set-theoretic section \(s\) with \(s(1)=1\) turns an extension of \(G\) by \(A\) into a normalized factor set \(f(g,h)\) defined by \(s(g)s(h)=f(g,h)\,s(gh)\text{,}\) and cohomologous normalized factor sets classify the extension up to equivalence [Bro, Chapter IV, §3]. Every class of a profinite group with finite discrete coefficients contains a normalized continuous \(2\)-cocycle [NSW, Chapter I, §2]. The equivariant factor sets, correction functions \(m_c\text{,}\) and square maps attached to the quadratic modules of this paper are all built in this normalized framework; see Lemma 6.1 and the convention audit in Appendix A. The transgression obstruction computed relative to a fixed equivariant class in Lemma 6.21 is the analogous differential \(d_2^{0,2}\) on the fibre \(H^2\text{,}\) evaluated by the same section-comparison method; its role in the Gauss-sum comparison appears in Subsection 6.4.
    🔗
    The vanishing arguments in this paper follow a single coprimality pattern. If \(U\le G\) has finite index then \(\operatorname{cor}\circ\operatorname{res}\) is multiplication by \((G:U)\text{,}\) so positive-degree cohomology of a finite group is annihilated by the group order [Bro, III.10.1-10.2], [NSW, Propositions 1.6.1-1.6.2]. Hence an odd-order group has no higher cohomology with characteristic-\(2\) coefficients. Feeding this into the Hochschild–Serre spectral sequence of \(1\to I\to H\to H/I\to 1\) with \(I\) of odd order and \((V^\vee)^I=0\) collapses every \(E_2\)-term and gives \(H^*(H,V^\vee)=0\text{.}\) This is the argument used for the ramified case in Lemma 6.4 and Proposition 7.4, and, combined with Kummer theory and Shapiro’s lemma, for the unit-filtration computation of \(H^1(\Qtwo,V)\) in Lemma 6.17.
    🔗
    🔗

    Subsection E.3 Shapiro’s lemma, corestriction, and the normalized bar resolution

    Shapiro’s lemma states that for a closed subgroup \(H\) of a profinite group \(G\) and a discrete \(H\)-module \(A\) there is a canonical isomorphism
    \begin{equation*} H^n(G,\operatorname{Ind}_H^G A)\;\cong\;H^n(H,A) \end{equation*}
    for all \(n\ge 0\) [NSW, Proposition 1.6.4], [Bro, Proposition III.6.2]. In this paper the standing instance is a Galois extension \(K/F\) with finite group \(H\) and the coinduced module \(\F_2[H]\text{:}\) Shapiro identifies \(H^1(G_F,\F_2[H])\) with \(H^1(G_K,\F_2)\text{,}\) whose elements are the Kummer “scalar coordinates” \(\alpha_r\) of Lemma 6.15. What the classical statement does not fix is a cochain-level realization; the choice-audited normalized Shapiro cochain map \(\operatorname{Sh}\) used throughout Lemma 6.13, Lemma 6.14, and Lemma 6.15 is constructed in Appendix A (see (A.11) and its degree-one form (A.12)), together with the exact normalized coboundaries produced by any change of section.
    🔗
    For an open subgroup \(H\le G\) (index \(l\)), restriction is supplemented by the wrong-way corestriction (transfer) \(\operatorname{cor}_H^G:H^n(H,A)\to H^n(G,A)\text{,}\) with \(\operatorname{cor}\circ\operatorname{res}=l\text{;}\) it can be defined by dimension shifting, by Shapiro’s lemma applied to the canonical surjection \(\operatorname{Ind}_H^G A\to A\text{,}\) or directly on resolutions [Bro, Chapter III, §9]. On cochains it is a sum over a chosen coset transversal of translated arguments: for homogeneous continuous cochains this explicit formula is given in [NSW, Chapter I, §5.4], and [NSW, Proposition 1.6.5] identifies it as the coordinate-sum map under Shapiro. The inhomogeneous normalized version with transversal transition elements \(\ell_\omega(\gamma)=t_\omega^{-1}\gamma t_{\gamma^{-1}\omega}\text{,}\) its compatibility \(d\operatorname{cor}=\operatorname{cor}d\text{,}\) and the exact cup-product identity \(\operatorname{cor}(\alpha\smile\beta)=\sum_h \operatorname{Sh}(\alpha)_h\,\operatorname{Sh}(\beta)_{\bar\gamma^{-1}h}\) are written out in Appendix A ((A.20), (A.24)); these are the “normalized bar corestriction” formulas invoked in Lemma 6.15 and Lemma 6.14, and, through Kummer theory, in Lemma 6.17.
    🔗
    Normalization refers to the normalized (reduced) standard resolution: the bar resolution of [Bro, Chapter I, §5] modulo its degenerate subcomplex, whose cochains are the inhomogeneous cochains vanishing whenever some argument equals \(1\text{;}\) every \(H^2\)-class of a profinite group with finite coefficients is represented by a normalized continuous cocycle [NSW, Chapter I, §2]. Working systematically with normalized representatives is what makes the zero-section and fibre normalizations of Lemma 6.4 meaningful at cochain level rather than only in cohomology; the paper’s conventions are fixed once and for all in Appendix A.
    🔗
    The multiplicative companion of the additive transfer is the Evens norm \(N_H^{G,\mathrm{Ev}}\text{,}\) defined via the monomial embedding of \(G\) into the wreath product \(S_l\wr H\) and a resolution of the form \(W\otimes X^{\otimes l}\) [Eve, §§2, 4-5]. Its low-degree expansion
    \begin{equation*} N_{H\to G}(1+\chi)=1+\operatorname{tr}_{H\to G}(\chi)+\cdots +N_{H\to G}(\chi) \end{equation*}
    exhibits the ordinary transfer as the linear term [Eve, §7, Theorem 1], which at index two is the normalization identity (6.41) of Lemma 6.13. Instantiating Evens’s construction on normalized bar resolutions yields the explicit degree-two cochains recorded in Appendix A and evaluated on involution orbits in Lemma 6.15.
    🔗
    🔗

    Subsection E.4 Local Tate duality and the Euler–Poincaré characteristic

    For a \(p\)-adic local field \(k\text{,}\) local class field theory provides the invariant map, a canonical isomorphism \(\inv_k:H^2(G_k,\ol{k}^\times)\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;}\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}\text{;}\) see [NSW, Corollary (7.1.4)]. For every \(n\ge1\) (the hypothesis \(\operatorname{char}(k)\nmid n\) is vacuous in characteristic zero, so \(n\) may share the residue characteristic), the Kummer sequence computes \(H^1(k,\mu_n)\cong k^\times/k^{\times n}\) and \(H^2(k,\mu_n)\cong\tfrac{1}{n}\mathbb{Z}/\mathbb{Z}\text{,}\) with \(H^i(k,\mu_n)=0\) for \(i\ge 3\text{;}\) see [NSW, Theorem (7.1.8)]. In particular \(H^2(\GQ,\mu_2)\cong\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{Z}/\mathbb{Z}\) is the group of order two, which we identify with \(\F_2\text{.}\) Since \(\mu_2=\{\pm1\}\subset\Qtwo\text{,}\) the module \(\mu_2\) carries the trivial Galois action, so \(\mu_2\cong\F_2\) as \(\GQ\)-modules: the mod-\(2\) cyclotomic twist is trivial, as used in Proposition 5.16. Composing a cup product with \(\inv\) is what turns a degree-two class into a scalar; this is the step “applying the invariant map” in the variation formula of Lemma 8.6.
    🔗
    Local Tate duality is the statement that this scalar pairing is perfect. Let \(A\) be a finite \(G_k\)-module and set \(A'=\Hom(A,\mu)\text{,}\) where \(\mu\) is the group of all roots of unity in \(\ol{k}\text{,}\) the dualizing module of \(G_k\) ([NSW, Theorem (7.2.4)]). Then the cup product
    \begin{equation*} H^i(k,A')\times H^{2-i}(k,A)\longrightarrow H^2(k,\mu)\cong\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z} \end{equation*}
    induces, for \(0\le i\le 2\text{,}\) isomorphisms of finite abelian groups \(H^i(k,A')\cong H^{2-i}(k,A)^*\text{;}\) see [NSW, Theorem (7.2.6)] and, in the form \(H^r(G,M^D)\cong H^{2-r}(G,M)^*\) with \(M^D=\Hom(M,K_s^\times)\text{,}\) [Mil, Theorem I.2.1 and Corollary I.2.3]. When \(A\) is killed by two, every homomorphism from \(A\) to \(\mu\) or to \(K_s^\times\) takes values in \(\mu_2\text{,}\) so \(A'=\Hom(A,\mu_2)=A^\vee:=\Hom(A,\F_2)\) with the contragredient action, and duality becomes a perfect \(\F_2\)-valued pairing \(H^i(\Qtwo,A)\times H^{2-i}(\Qtwo,A^\vee)\to H^2(\Qtwo,\mu_2)=\F_2\text{.}\) This is the pairing of Proposition 5.16; its case \(i=1\) is the perfect degree-one duality invoked in Lemma 8.6, where nonvanishing of a class in \(H^1(\Qtwo,T^\vee)\) is detected by pairing it against \(H^1(\Qtwo,T)\text{.}\)
    🔗
    The local Euler–Poincaré characteristic computes the alternating product of the (finite) orders \(h^i(k,A)=\#H^i(k,A)\text{:}\)
    \begin{equation*} \chi(k,A)=\frac{h^0(k,A)\,h^2(k,A)}{h^1(k,A)}=\|\#A\|_k, \end{equation*}
    where \(\|x\|_k=q^{-v(x)}\) is the normalized absolute value of \(k\) (\(q\) the residue cardinality); see [NSW, Theorem (7.3.1)]. Equivalently \(\chi(G,M)=(R:mR)^{-1}\) with \(R\) the ring of integers and \(m=\#M\text{;}\) see [Mil, Theorem I.2.8]. For \(k=\Qtwo\) and an \(\F_2[\GQ]\)-module \(V\) of dimension \(d\) this reads \(\|2^d\|_{\Qtwo}=(\mathbb{Z}_2:2^d\mathbb{Z}_2)^{-1}=2^{-d}\text{,}\) that is,
    \begin{equation*} \dim H^1(\Qtwo,V)=\dim H^0(\Qtwo,V)+\dim H^2(\Qtwo,V)+d. \end{equation*}
    This dimension count is the input cited in the inductive step of Subsection 2 and in the numerical formula of Proposition 5.16.
    🔗
    The paper applies these two facts together to self-dual modules. Suppose \(V\) is a nontrivial simple \(\F_2\)-module of dimension \(d\) on which \(\GQ\) acts through a finite quotient, and \(V\cong V^\vee\text{.}\) Simplicity gives \(H^0(\Qtwo,V)=V^{\GQ}=0\text{;}\) duality in degree zero gives \(H^2(\Qtwo,V)\cong H^0(\Qtwo,V^\vee)^*=0\) because \(V^\vee\cong V\) is again nontrivial simple; and the Euler–Poincaré formula then yields \(\dim H^1(\Qtwo,V)=d\text{.}\) This is the count used in both cases of Proposition 6.18: in the ramified case it produces the \(d\)-dimensional local quadratic space, and in the unramified case the same \(d\)-dimensional space is identified with a line over the Schur field \(F_V\text{.}\) For self-dual \(V\) the degree-one pairing is a perfect pairing of \(H^1(\Qtwo,V)\) with itself; it is this self-duality that stands behind the cardinal identity \(|X_+|^2=|H^1(\Qtwo,V)|\) of Lemma 6.17. The finer statement used there, that under the Kummer description of \(H^1\) the pairing matches depth-\(j\) and depth-\((2e-j)\) layers of the unit filtration (“Hilbert duality”), is a computation in local class field theory and is discussed with the dyadic square-class background.
    🔗
    🔗

    Subsection E.5 Local reciprocity, Kummer theory, and the dyadic Hilbert symbol

    Local class field theory furnishes the reciprocity map \(\rec:\Qtwo^\times\to G_{\Qtwo}^{\mathrm{ab}}\text{,}\) an isomorphism onto a dense subgroup under which norm subgroups of finite abelian extensions correspond to the open subgroups of finite index; see [NSW, Corollary (7.1.5) and Theorem (7.2.3)] and [Ser79, Chapters XI--XIII]. Two normalizations are in circulation, differing by inversion. We use the classical (arithmetic) one: a uniformizer acts on the maximal unramified extension as the Frobenius substitution \(x\mapsto x^q\text{,}\) and the units map onto inertia; this is [Ser79, Chapter XIII, §4, Proposition 13 and its Corollary], and likewise the convention of [Neu, Chapter V, §2]. Thus \(\rec(2)\) is arithmetic Frobenius, exactly the normalization fixed in Lemma 3.5; because the unramified character \(\nu_{\mathrm{ur}}\) of that lemma is normalized by geometric Frobenius (the inverse generator), one gets \(\nu_{\mathrm{ur}}(\rec(2))=-1\text{.}\) On the multiplicative side, \(\Qtwo^\times\cong 2^{\mathbb Z}\times\{\pm1\}\times(1+4\mathbb Z_2)\) with \(1+4\mathbb Z_2\cong\mathbb Z_2\text{,}\) topologically generated by any unit \(u\) with \(v_2(u-1)=2\text{;}\) see [Ser73, Chapter II, §3.2--3.3, Proposition 8 and Theorem 2] and [Ser79, Chapter XIV, §4, Examples after Proposition 10]. Since \(-3\equiv5\pmod 8\text{,}\) the unit \(-3\) is such a generator, which is why the marked basis \(\rec(-4),\rec(1/2),\rec(-3)\) of Lemma 3.5 and the abelianized relation in Subsection 3.4 present the pro-\(2\) completion of \(\Qtwo^\times\) as \(\langle2\rangle_{\mathbb Z_2}\oplus\langle-1\rangle_{C_2}\oplus\langle-3\rangle_{\mathbb Z_2}\text{.}\)
    🔗
    The \(2\)-adic cyclotomic character \(\chi:G_{\Qtwo}\to\mathbb Z_2^\times\) is the action on \(\mu_{2^\infty}\text{.}\) The maximal abelian extension of \(\Qtwo\) is the compositum of the unramified tower with the totally ramified cyclotomic tower \(\Qtwo(\mu_{2^\infty})\text{;}\) see [Ser79, Chapter XIV, §7, Theorem 2]. Under the arithmetic normalization the norm residue symbol acts on \(2^{n}\)-th roots of unity by \((u\,2^{v_2(a)},\Qtwo(\zeta)/\Qtwo)\,\zeta=\zeta^{u^{-1}}\text{:}\) units act by the inverse, and \(\rec(2)\) fixes the cyclotomic tower; see [Neu, Chapter V, Theorem (2.4)] and [Ser79, Chapter XIV, §7, Remark and Exercise]. This is the computation \(\chi(\rec(u))=u^{-1}\text{,}\) \(\chi(\rec(2))=1\) behind the orientation row of Lemma 3.5, and it explains why the pair \((\nu_{\mathrm{ur}},\chi)\) sees the unramified and cyclotomic coordinates of \(G_{\Qtwo}^{\mathrm{ab}}\) separately.
    🔗
    For any field \(K\) of characteristic different from \(2\text{,}\) Kummer theory identifies \(H^1(G_K,\mu_2)\cong K^\times/K^{\times2}\text{,}\) the class of \(a\) corresponding to the cocycle \(s\mapsto s(\sqrt a)/\sqrt a\text{;}\) see [Ser79, Chapter X, §3(b)] and, for local fields together with \(H^2(G_K,\mu_2)\cong\tfrac12\mathbb Z/\mathbb Z\text{,}\) [NSW, Theorem (7.1.8)(ii) and Corollary (7.1.4)]. Under this identification the cup product of two Kummer classes is the class of the symbol \((a,b)\text{,}\) and applying the invariant map gives the Hilbert symbol: \((a,b)=1\) if and only if \(b\) is a norm from \(K(\sqrt a)\text{;}\) see [Ser79, Chapter XIV, §2, Propositions 5 and 7] and [Neu, Chapter V, Proposition (3.1)]. For a local \(K\) the pairing is a nondegenerate bilinear form on the \(\F_2\)-vector space \(K^\times/K^{\times2}\text{;}\) see [Ser79, Chapter XIV, §2, Proposition 7(vi)] and, for \(\mathbb R\) and \(\mathbb Q_p\text{,}\) [Ser73, Chapter III, Theorem 2]; this is the mod-\(2\) instance of local Tate duality [NSW, Theorem (7.2.6)]. Cohomological squares are Bockstein values, whence \((a,a)=(a,-1)\text{;}\) see [Ser79, Chapter XIV, §2, Exercise 1]. This is the precise sense of “under Kummer theory, cup product is the Hilbert symbol” in Lemma 3.5, and of the scalar cup/Bockstein ledger (3.18) in Subsection 3.4.
    🔗
    Over \(\Qtwo\) everything is explicit. A unit is a square exactly when it is congruent to \(1\) modulo \(8\text{,}\) so \(\Qtwo^\times/\Qtwo^{\times2}\) is of type \((2,2,2)\) with representatives \(\{\pm1,\pm5,\pm2,\pm10\}\text{;}\) see [Ser73, Chapter II, §3.3, Theorem 4 and Corollary] and [Ser79, Chapter XIV, §4, Lemma 3]. Writing \(\epsilon(u)=\tfrac{u-1}{2}\) and \(\omega(u)=\tfrac{u^2-1}{8}\) modulo \(2\text{,}\) the dyadic Hilbert symbol is
    \begin{equation*} (2^\alpha u,2^\beta v)_2=(-1)^{\epsilon(u)\epsilon(v)+\alpha\omega(v)+\beta\omega(u)}, \end{equation*}
    which is [Ser73, Chapter III, §1.2, Theorem 1]; the same values appear generator by generator in [Ser79, Chapter XIV, §4, Case (ii)]. Evaluated on the square-class basis \((-1,2,-3)\) of Lemma 3.5 (recall \(-3\equiv5\pmod8\)), the only nontrivial pairings are \((-1,-1)_2=-1\) and \((2,-3)_2=-1\text{,}\) which is the table producing the quadratic initial form \(\alpha^2+\beta\gamma+\gamma\beta\) there and the pairing matrix of (3.18).
    🔗
    For a general dyadic field \(k\) with \(e=v_k(2)\text{,}\) write \(U_i\) for the image of \(1+\mathfrak p^i\) in \(k^\times/k^{\times2}\text{.}\) The graded pieces of the unit filtration itself are \(U^{(0)}/U^{(1)}\cong\bar k^\times\) and \(U^{(i)}/U^{(i+1)}\cong\bar k\text{;}\) see [Ser79, Chapter IV, §2, Proposition 6]. Squares are governed by the quadratic defect: the defect of a unit is \(0\text{,}\) or \(4\mathfrak o\text{,}\) or \(\mathfrak p^d\) with \(d\) odd and \(4\mathfrak o\subset\mathfrak p^d\subset\mathfrak o\text{,}\) every such value occurs, and the defect-\(4\mathfrak o\) class is precisely the class generating the unramified quadratic extension; see [OMe, 63:2 through 63:6]. Deep units are squares: \(1+4\mathfrak p\subseteq k^{\times2}\text{,}\) i.e. \(U_{2e+1}=1\text{,}\) by the Local Square Theorem [OMe, 63:1], equivalently by the isomorphism \(x\mapsto x^2:U^{(m)}\to U^{(m+e)}\) for \(m>e\) of [Ser79, Chapter XIV, §4, Proposition 9]; the quantitative Hensel statement behind it (a root exists once \(v(f(a_0))>2v(f'(a_0))\)) is [FV, Chapter II, (1.3), Corollaries 3--4], and it is in exactly this form that Hensel’s lemma extracts the square root of \(n/(2u-1)\in U_{2e+2}\) in the proof of Lemma 6.16. Consequently only the odd depths below \(2e\) and the unramified layer at depth \(2e\) carry square classes, the stratification recorded at (6.35); and since \(v_k(-1-1)=e\text{,}\) one has \(-1\in U_e\text{.}\) The complementary-depth orthogonality \(U_i^\perp=U_{2e-i+1}\) of (6.36) is the standard duality bookkeeping for this stratification: it combines the norm criterion for the vanishing of a symbol with the conductor filtration of norm groups [Ser79, Chapter XV, §2, Corollary 2 to Theorem 1] and the square-class count against nondegeneracy [OMe, 63:9 and 63:13].
    🔗
    Two further classical inputs drive the cancellations in Lemma 6.16 and Lemma 6.17. First, the Steinberg relations \((a,-a)=1\) and \((a,1-a)=1\) hold for any Hilbert symbol; see [Ser79, Chapter XIV, §2, Proposition 4(iv) and Proposition 7(iv)], [Ser73, Chapter III, Proposition 2], or [Neu, Chapter V, Proposition (3.2)(v)]. They yield the moves used there: \((x,x)=(x,-1)\text{,}\) and \((2u,2u-1)=(2u,-1)\) from \(1-2u=-(2u-1)\text{.}\) Second, in an unramified extension the norm is surjective on principal units, level by level: \(N(U_L^{(n)})=U_K^{(n)}\) for \(n\ge1\text{;}\) see [Ser79, Chapter V, §2, Propositions 1--3]. For the unramified quadratic extension \(E=k(\sqrt d)\) of a dyadic local field, every unit of \(k\) is a norm: \(N(E^\times)=\mathcal O_k^\times\,k^{\times2}\) and \(N(\mathcal O_E^\times)=\mathcal O_k^\times\text{,}\) hence \((u,d)=1\) for all units \(u\text{;}\) see [OMe, 63:16 and 63:11a]. These are precisely the two uses of unramifiedness isolated in the proof of Lemma 6.16 (the depth estimate for Hensel’s lemma and the killing of the symbols involving the unramified class) and, through the Kummer-theoretic identification \(H^1(\Qtwo,V)\cong\Hom_{H_V}(V^\vee,M_K)\text{,}\) they feed the unit-filtration computation of Lemma 6.17.
    🔗
    🔗

    Subsection E.6 Demushkin groups and Labute’s classification

    A pro-\(p\) group \(G\) is a Demushkin group if \(H^1(G,\F_p)\) is finite dimensional, \(H^2(G,\F_p)\) is one dimensional, and the cup product \(H^1(G,\F_p)\times H^1(G,\F_p)\to H^2(G,\F_p)\) is a non-degenerate bilinear form; see [Lab, p. 106] and [NSW, Definition (3.9.9)]. The first two conditions say that \(G\) is a one-relator pro-\(p\) group: \(G\cong F/(r)\text{,}\) where \(F\) is a free pro-\(p\) group of rank \(n=\dim_{\F_p}H^1(G,\F_p)\) and \((r)\) is the closed normal subgroup generated by a single relator. Two invariants are read off from the abelianization \(G^{\mathrm{ab}}\cong \mathbb{Z}_p^{\,n-1}\times \mathbb{Z}_p/q\mathbb{Z}_p\text{:}\) the rank \(n\) and the power \(q=q(G)\) of \(p\) (with \(q=0\) when \(G^{\mathrm{ab}}\) is torsion free); see [NSW, p. 232]. The only finite Demushkin group is \(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}\text{,}\) the absolute Galois group of \(\mathbb{R}\) ([NSW, Proposition (3.9.10)]); all others are infinite of cohomological dimension \(2\text{.}\) The example that drives Section 3 is the maximal pro-\(2\) quotient \(G_{\Qtwo}(2)\text{,}\) a Demushkin group with \(n=3\) and \(q=2\) ([NSW, Theorem (7.5.11)(ii) and Chapter VII §5, p. 417]).
    🔗
    The classification is by normal forms for the relator. Write \([x,y]=x^{-1}y^{-1}xy\text{.}\) For \(q\neq2\) (the case treated by Demushkin) the rank \(n\) is even and one can choose a basis \(x_1,\dots,x_n\) of \(F\) with
    \begin{equation*} r=x_1^{q}[x_1,x_2][x_3,x_4]\cdots[x_{n-1},x_n], \end{equation*}
    so \(G\) is determined by \((n,q)\text{;}\) see [NSW, Theorem (3.9.11)]. For \(q=2\) this fails, and Serre introduced a finer invariant, the image of a canonical character \(\chi\colon G\to\mathbb{Z}_2^\times\) described below. When \(q=2\) and \(n\) is odd there is a basis with
    \begin{equation*} r=x_1^{2}\,x_2^{2^f}\,[x_2,x_3][x_4,x_5]\cdots[x_{n-1},x_n], \qquad f\in\{2,3,\dots,\infty\}, \end{equation*}
    and then \(\im(\chi)=\{\pm1\}\times(1+2^f\mathbb{Z}_2)\text{;}\) this case is due to Serre, see [Ser63, Théorème 3.2, p. 147], [Lab, p. 107 and Theorem 3], and [NSW, Theorem (3.9.19)(i)]. (For \(q=2\) and \(n\) even there are two further families, Labute’s main theorem; see [Lab, Theorem 1].) The invariants are complete: two Demushkin groups with the same \(n\) and \(\im(\chi)\) are isomorphic, and indeed any two relators in \(F\) yielding such groups differ by an automorphism of \(F\) ([Lab, Theorem 2]). Basis changes of this kind are the Nielsen transformations used in Proposition 3.11. Taking \(n=3\text{,}\) \(q=2\text{,}\) \(f=2\) gives the relator \(A^2S^4[S,Y]\text{,}\) that is, the standard rank-three dyadic Demushkin group \(D_0\) of (3.1) studied in Subsection 3.1.
    🔗
