    Every Demushkin group carries a canonical character \(\chi\colon G\to\mathbb{Z}_p^\times\text{,}\) called its orientation in this paper. Serre defined it as the unique continuous homomorphism such that, letting \(I(\chi)\) denote \(\mathbb{Z}_p\) with \(G\) acting through \(\chi\text{,}\) the maps \(H^1(G,I/p^{j+1}I)\to H^1(G,I/p^{j}I)\) are surjective for all \(j\ge1\) ([Lab, §3, Proposition 6 and Theorem 4]). Conceptually, an infinite Demushkin group has cohomological dimension \(2\) and is precisely a Poincaré duality group of dimension \(2\) ([NSW, p. 231 and Theorem (3.9.15)]): its dualizing module is isomorphic to \(\mathbb{Q}_p/\mathbb{Z}_p\) as an abelian group, \(G\) acts on it through \(\Aut(\mathbb{Q}_p/\mathbb{Z}_p)=\mathbb{Z}_p^\times\text{,}\) and the resulting character is \(\chi\) ([NSW, Definition (3.7.1)]; the identification of Serre’s invariant with the dualizing-module character is due to Tate, see [Lab, p. 107, Remark 1] and [Ser63, no. 9.3, pp. 153-154]). Since the dualizing module is constructed directly from the cohomology of the open subgroups of \(G\text{,}\) namely as a direct limit of the duals \(H^n(U,-)^\ast\) ([NSW, Theorem (3.4.1) and Chapter III §7]), every isomorphism of Demushkin groups intertwines the orientations and every automorphism preserves them. This functoriality is exactly what is invoked in Proposition 3.9 and in Subsection 3.3. On the odd-rank \(q=2\) normal form above, the orientation takes the values \(\chi(x_1)=-1\text{,}\) \(\chi(x_2)=1\text{,}\) \(\chi(x_3)=(1-2^f)^{-1}\text{,}\) and \(\chi(x_i)=1\) for \(i>3\) ([Lab, Theorem 4, proof, case (2)]); for \(D_0\) (where \(f=2\)) this is the character \((-1,\,1,\,(-3)^{-1})\) on \((A,S,Y)\) appearing in Lemma 3.4. The invariant \(q(G)\) is recovered from \(\chi\) as the largest power of \(p\) with \(\im(\chi)\subseteq 1+q\mathbb{Z}_p\) ([Lab, Corollary to Theorem 4]).
    🔗
    The arithmetic source of these groups is local. Let \(K\) be a \(p\)-adic field of degree \(N\) over \(\mathbb{Q}_p\) containing the \(p\)-th roots of unity, and let \(G_K(p)\) be the Galois group of its maximal pro-\(p\) extension \(K(p)\text{.}\) Then \(G_K(p)\) is a Demushkin group of rank \(N+2\) whose dualizing module is the group \(\mu_{p^\infty}\) of all \(p\)-power roots of unity in \(K(p)\) ([NSW, Theorem (7.5.11)(ii)]); consequently its canonical orientation is the \(p\)-adic cyclotomic character (see also [Lab, §5, p. 131]). By local class field theory \(G_K(p)^{\mathrm{ab}}\) is the pro-\(p\) completion of \(K^\times\text{,}\) so \(q(G_K(p))=\#\mu(K)(p)\) ([Lab, §5, p. 130]), and under the Kummer identification \(H^1(G_K(p),\F_p)\cong K^\times/K^{\times p}\) the cup product is the Hilbert symbol ([Lab, §5, p. 131]; [Ser79, Chapter XIV §§1-2]), which is how the dyadic Hilbert-symbol table enters Lemma 3.5. For \(K=\Qtwo\) one has \(N=1\) odd and \(q=2\text{,}\) and the classification yields three generators \(x,y,z\) with the single relation \(x^2y^4[y,z]=1\) ([Lab, Theorem 8]; [NSW, Chapter VII §5, p. 417]), with \(\im(\chi)=\{\pm1\}\times(1+4\mathbb{Z}_2)=\mathbb{Z}_2^\times\) ([Lab, §5, pp. 131-132]). This is the abstract identification \(G_{\Qtwo}(2)\cong D_0\) of Lemma 3.4, with cyclotomic orientation.
    🔗
    It is worth isolating what the classification does not provide. It guarantees some isomorphism \(G_{\Qtwo}(2)\to D_0\text{,}\) unique at best up to composition with automorphisms, and it retains no memory of the arithmetic marking: the full unramified character \(\nu_{\mathrm{ur}}\colon G_{\Qtwo}(2)\twoheadrightarrow\mathbb{Z}_2\) is not among the classifying invariants. The boundary construction of this paper requires the pair \((G_{\Qtwo}(2),\nu_{\mathrm{ur}})\) up to isomorphism of pairs, a strictly finer datum: see Remark 3.15, and see Remark 3.13 for a familiar Labute-style presentation that admits no compatible marking even though the underlying abstract group is correct. Remark 3.6 shows that the abelianized relation together with the quadratic initial form still does not pin down the marked identification. The canonical orientation restores the missing rigidity: because every abstract isomorphism intertwines the canonical orientations, its effect on the abelianization automatically preserves the orientation character, and Proposition 3.9 shows that all such automorphisms of the abelianization lift to \(\Aut(D_0)\text{,}\) so an arbitrary abstract isomorphism can be corrected to a marked one (Subsection 3.3).
    🔗
    Finally, the phrase quadratic initial form refers to the leading term of a relator along a central filtration of the free group. For a power \(q\) of \(p\text{,}\) the descending \(q\)-central series of a free pro-\(p\) group \(F\) is defined by \(F^1=F\) and \(F^{i+1}=(F^i)^q[F^i,F]\) ([NSW, Definition (3.8.1)]; [Lab, §2, p. 112]). Every relator \(\rho\in F^2=F^q[F,F]\) has a representation
    \begin{equation*} \rho\equiv \prod_{j=1}^{n} x_j^{\,q a_j}\; \prod_{1\le k<l\le n}[x_k,x_l]^{\,a_{kl}} \pmod{F^3}, \end{equation*}
    with the exponents \(a_{kl}\) (and, for \(q\neq0\text{,}\) the \(a_j\)) uniquely determined in \(\mathbb{Z}_p/q\mathbb{Z}_p\) ([NSW, Proposition (3.9.13)(i)]); this collection of exponents is the quadratic initial form of \(\rho\text{.}\) It computes the degree-two cohomology of \(G=F/(\rho)\text{:}\) in the dual basis \(\chi_1,\dots,\chi_n\) of \(H^1(G,\mathbb{Z}/q)\) and with the trace isomorphism \(\mathrm{tr}_\rho\) on \(H^2(G,\mathbb{Z}/q)\text{,}\) the cup products are \(\mathrm{tr}_\rho(\chi_k\cup\chi_l)=-a_{kl}\) for \(k<l\) and the Bockstein satisfies \(\mathrm{tr}_\rho(B\chi_j)=-a_j\) ([NSW, Propositions (3.9.13)(ii) and (3.9.14)]; [Lab, §2, Proposition 3]); for \(q=2\) the diagonal cup squares \(\mathrm{tr}_\rho(\chi_j\cup\chi_j)\) read off the same exponents \(a_j\), which is why Lemma 3.5 speaks of a single Bockstein/cup form such as \(\alpha^2+\beta\gamma+\gamma\beta\text{.}\) For the standard relator \(r_0=A^2S^4[S,Y]\) the factor \(S^4=(S^2)^2\) lies in \(F^3\text{,}\) so the initial form is \(A^2+[S,Y]\text{,}\) as used in Remark 3.6. Section 3 states such reductions modulo the third term of the Zassenhaus filtration \(F_{(n)}=\{g\mid g-1\in I^n\}\text{,}\) where \(I\) is the augmentation ideal of \(\F_p[[F]]\) ([NSW, p. 230]; proved in [Koc, §7.4, Theorems 7.11 and 7.12]). From the two containments \((F_{(i)})^p\subseteq F_{(ip)}\) and \([F_{(i)},F]\subseteq F_{(i+1)}\) recorded there, one checks by induction that \(F^i\subseteq F_{(i)}\) (the containment is also recorded in the proof of [Koc, Theorem 7.13]), so a congruence modulo \(F^3\) implies the corresponding congruence modulo the third Zassenhaus term.
    🔗
    🔗

    Subsection E.7 Extraspecial groups, Heisenberg models, and the square-map correspondence

    Commutators are normalized as \([x,y]=x^{-1}y^{-1}xy\text{,}\) so that \(xy=yx[x,y]\text{;}\) this is the convention of [Asc, Section 8] and the one fixed in Lemma 5.2. The general expansion identities are \([ab,c]=[a,c]^b[b,c]\) and \([a,bc]=[a,c][a,b]^c\) [Asc, (8.5.4)]. In a group of class at most two the conjugations act trivially on commutators, so the commutator map becomes bimultiplicative; more precisely, if \(z=[x,y]\) centralizes \(x\) and \(y\text{,}\) then \([x^n,y^m]=z^{nm}\) and
    \begin{equation} (yx)^n=z^{n(n-1)/2}y^nx^n \qquad (n\ge 0)\tag{E.3} \end{equation}
    [Asc, (8.6)]. For \(n=2\) this is the collector identity \((xy)^2=x^2y^2[y,x]\) used throughout the class-two calculations; when commutators are central involutions the direction of the commutator is immaterial. A central extension of an elementary abelian \(2\)-group by an elementary abelian \(2\)-group is exactly this setting: squares and commutators land in the central subgroup [Asc, (23.2)], so the group has class at most two, commutators have order at most two, and fourth powers vanish; these are the hypotheses under which Lemma 5.2 rearranges (E.3) into its exact collector form. The same commutator toolkit supplies the three-subgroup lemma [Asc, (8.7)] invoked in Lemma 7.2.
    🔗
    A central extension \(1\to\F_2\to\widetilde V\to V\to 1\) of an elementary abelian \(2\)-group \(V\) is described by a normalized factor set \(f:V\times V\to\F_2\text{,}\) and its equivalence class by the cohomology class of \(f\text{:}\) this is the classical dictionary between extensions with abelian kernel and \(H^2\) [Bro, Chapter IV, Theorem 3.12]. Two functions on \(V\) are extracted from the group \(\widetilde V\text{.}\) The squaring map \(\widetilde v\mapsto\widetilde v^2\) takes central values and depends only on the image \(v\in V\text{,}\) defining \(q:V\to\F_2\text{;}\) the commutator induces a pairing \(b(v,w)=[\widetilde v,\widetilde w]\text{,}\) bilinear by the class-two expansions above. The collector identity \((xy)^2=x^2y^2[x,y]\) says precisely that
    \begin{equation*} q(v+w)=q(v)+q(w)+b(v,w), \end{equation*}
    so \(q\) is a quadratic map whose polar form is the commutator pairing, the computation carried out in [Asc, (23.10), proof]. Conversely, any factor set with \(f(v,v)=q(v)\) realizes a prescribed quadratic map \(q\text{,}\) as in the explicit models of Lemma 6.1. Cohomologous factor sets yield the same \(q\text{,}\) a class with \(q=0\) is split (all lifts are then commuting involutions, so a basis of \(V\) lifts to a complement), and every quadratic map arises; the resulting bijection
    \begin{equation*} H^2(V,\F_2)\;\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;}\; \{\text{quadratic maps } V\to\F_2\} \end{equation*}
    is the square-map correspondence of Lemma 6.4: the polarization recovers the commutator form, and the square and commutator data determine the extension class.
    🔗
    A finite \(p\)-group is special if its Frattini subgroup, center, and derived subgroup coincide, and extraspecial if in addition the center is cyclic, hence of order \(p\) [Asc, Section 23 and (23.7)]. Extraspecial \(2\)-groups are exactly the fibre extensions above whose commutator pairing is nondegenerate [Asc, (23.10)]: on \(V=E/Z\) the commutator form is symplectic, the squaring map is a quadratic form \(q\) polarizing to it, \(\dim V=2n\) is even, and \(|E|=2^{1+2n}\text{.}\) Under this dictionary a subgroup between \(Z\) and \(E\) is elementary abelian exactly when its image in \(V\) is totally singular [Asc, (23.10.4)]. Over \(\F_2\) a nondegenerate quadratic space of dimension \(2n\) is isometric to exactly one of \(D^n\) (hyperbolic) or \(D^{n-1}Q\) (one definite plane) [Asc, (21.2)], and correspondingly there are exactly two extraspecial groups of order \(2^{1+2n}\text{:}\) the central products \(D_8^n\) and \(D_8^{n-1}Q_8\text{,}\) distinguished by their \(2\)-rank [Asc, (23.14)], with central products taken with identified centers [Asc, (11.1), (11.2)]. The building blocks are the two-dimensional cases: the hyperbolic plane \(q_{\mathrm{hyp}}(x_1,x_2)=x_1x_2\) corresponds to the dihedral group \(D_8\) (the two coordinate lifts are involutions, their commutator is the central involution, and their product has order four), while the definite plane corresponds to \(Q_8\text{,}\) all of whose noncentral elements have order four [Asc, (23.14), proof, and (21.1)]. The dihedral case is exactly the fibre extension computed in Lemma 6.13.
    🔗
    The coefficient group in which the paper computes cup products is the finite Heisenberg model of Subsection 5.2: for an elementary module \(A\text{,}\)
    \begin{equation*} \mathcal H(A)=A\times A^\vee\times\F_2, \qquad (a,\lambda,z)(a',\lambda',z') =(a+a',\lambda+\lambda',z+z'+\lambda(a')), \end{equation*}
    with diagonal action of the acting group. In the language above, \(\mathcal H(A)\) is the central extension of \(V=A\oplus A^\vee\) given by the factor set \(((a,\lambda),(a',\lambda'))\mapsto\lambda(a')\text{;}\) its square map is the hyperbolic quadratic form \(q(a,\lambda)=\lambda(a)\text{,}\) and its commutator pairing is the evaluation pairing \(\lambda(a')+\lambda'(a)\text{.}\) Since that pairing is nondegenerate, \(\mathcal H(A)\) is extraspecial of hyperbolic type, a central product of \(\dim A\) copies of \(D_8\) by the classification just recalled [Asc, (23.10), (23.14)]; the Heisenberg presentation is its standard polarized form, adapted to the splitting \(V=A\oplus A^\vee\text{.}\) This finiteness is what the deformation section exploits: the Stokes identities of Lemma 5.7 and Proposition 5.8 are proved by conjugating finite word evaluations in \(\mathcal H(A)\rtimes C\text{,}\) with no cellular diagonal approximation, and coefficient naturality is checked in the mixed model \(A\times A'^\vee\times\F_2\) of Lemma 5.6.
    🔗
    The splitting theory used for the odd part of finite targets is classical. The Schur–Zassenhaus theorem states that a normal Hall subgroup \(H\) of a finite group \(G\) has a complement, and that all complements are conjugate; the solvability hypothesis in the standard statement can be removed by the odd order theorem [Asc, (18.1) and Remarks]. For solvable groups, Hall’s theorem provides Hall \(\pi\)-subgroups for every set of primes \(\pi\text{,}\) again conjugate and containing every \(\pi\)-subgroup [Asc, (18.2), (18.5)]. In Lemma 7.2 and Lemma 9.2 these are applied to the preimage of the odd-order kernel \(N=\ker(H\to H_2)\text{,}\) an extension of \(N\) by a finite \(2\)-group: Schur–Zassenhaus furnishes the odd Hall lift \(\widetilde N\text{,}\) and conjugacy of complements combines with the centralizing argument to make the lift unique and normal. The accompanying coprime-action identity \([G,A]=[G,A,A]\) for a \(2'\)-group of automorphisms of a \(2\)-group [Asc, (24.5)] is what collapses the chief-series commutator chains in both lemmas. The profinite form of Schur–Zassenhaus, used when the same splitting is needed before passage to a finite quotient, is recalled in Subsection E.1 with the Ribes–Zalesskii reference.
    🔗
    🔗

    Subsection E.8 Quadratic forms over \(\F_2\) and the Arf invariant

    Over a field of characteristic \(2\text{,}\) a quadratic form on a vector space \(V\) is a function \(q:V\to F\) satisfying \(q(ax+by)=a^2q(x)+b^2q(y)+ab\,b_q(x,y)\) for a (then unique) bilinear form \(b_q\text{;}\) equivalently \(b_q(x,y)=q(x+y)+q(x)+q(y)\text{,}\) the polar form of \(q\text{,}\) which is symmetric and alternating [Gro, Chapter 12, pp. 113--114] [Wal, §1.5, (1.5.1)]. In contrast with odd characteristic, \(q\) is not determined by \(b_q\text{.}\) The radical \(\operatorname{rad}V\) is the kernel of \(b_q\text{;}\) following Grove, \(q\) is nondefective when the radical is zero, which forces \(\dim V\) to be even [Gro, Chapter 12, p. 114]. Nondefectiveness is what this paper calls nonsingularity of \(q\text{.}\) A vector \(v\ne0\) with \(q(v)=0\) is singular, and a subspace on which \(q\) vanishes identically is totally singular; a totally singular subspace is in particular totally isotropic for \(b_q\) [Gro, Chapter 12, p. 114]. In the equivariant setting of Section 6 the radical is the pivot: for a form invariant under a group acting irreducibly, the radical of a nonzero invariant polar form is a proper submodule, hence zero. This step closes both Lemma 6.20 and the nonsingularity argument of Proposition 7.4.
    🔗
    A hyperbolic pair is a pair \((u,v)\) of singular vectors with \(b_q(u,v)=1\text{,}\) spanning a hyperbolic plane; this is stronger than a hyperbolic pair for the alternating form alone, for which we reserve the term symplectic plane [Gro, Chapter 12, p. 115]. Every singular vector outside the radical lies in a hyperbolic pair [Gro, Proposition 12.1], and a nondefective plane with no singular vector (an anisotropic plane) has, in a suitable basis, the form \(q(a_1v_1+a_2v_2)=a_1^2+a_1a_2+ba_2^2\) with \(x^2+x+b\) irreducible [Gro, Proposition 12.7]. Witt theory holds in characteristic \(2\text{:}\) isometries between subspaces of a nondefective space extend to the whole space, all maximal totally singular subspaces have a common dimension, the Witt index, and over a perfect field every nondefective form of even dimension is an orthogonal sum of hyperbolic planes with at most one anisotropic plane [Gro, Theorems 12.9 and 12.10, Corollaries 12.11 and 12.12]. Moreover a totally singular subspace of dimension \(k\) always sits inside an orthogonal sum of \(k\) hyperbolic planes, so a nondefective space of dimension \(2m\) containing a totally singular subspace of dimension \(m\) is hyperbolic [Gro, Proposition 14.6 and Corollary 14.8]. This Lagrangian criterion is how the ramified case of Proposition 6.18 pins down the local determinant form: a totally singular subgroup of the maximal possible size forces the hyperbolic (plus) type without any choice of symplectic basis.
    🔗
    For a nondefective quadratic space with symplectic basis \(\{u_i,v_i\}_{i\le m}\text{,}\) the class of \(\sum_{i}q(u_i)q(v_i)\) in \(F/\{a^2+a:a\in F\}\) is independent of the chosen symplectic basis; it is the Arf invariant of \(q\) [Gro, Theorem 13.13 and p. 124]. Since concatenating symplectic bases of orthogonal summands gives a symplectic basis of the sum, the defining expression is additive over orthogonal sums, the additivity invoked in Lemma 6.8. Over a finite field the subgroup \(\{a^2+a\}\) has index \(2\text{,}\) so the Arf invariant is a bit, and for \(F=\F_2\) it is literally an element of \(\F_2\) [Gro, p. 124]. It is the complete invariant in even dimension over a perfect field: the hyperbolic normal form has Arf invariant \(0\text{,}\) the form with an anisotropic plane \(x^2+x+b\) has Arf invariant \(b\text{,}\) and two such forms are equivalent exactly when the invariants agree [Gro, Proposition 13.14]. Wall calls this invariant the pseudo-discriminant, computes it as \(\sum_i b_{2i-1}b_{2i}\) in normalized coordinates, and records the same classification, attributing it to Arf [Wal, §3.6, Lemma 3.6.2]. The two even-dimensional types over \(\F_q\) are the plus type (hyperbolic, Witt index \(n/2\)) and the minus type (Witt index \(n/2-1\)), with orthogonal groups \(O_+\) and \(O_-\) [Gro, Chapter 14, p. 150] [Wal, §3.7, (3.7.1)].
    🔗
    The zero counts behind the paper’s Gauss signs are classical. Writing \(s_n\) for the number of vectors with \(q(v)=0\) (including \(0\)) in a nondefective space of even dimension \(n\) over \(\F_q\text{,}\) one has \(s_n=q^{n-1}+q^{m}-q^{m-1}\) for the hyperbolic type with \(n=2m\text{,}\) and \(s_n=q^{n-1}-q^{m+1}+q^{m}\) for the minus type with \(n=2m+2\) [Gro, Proposition 14.47(b),(c)]. For \(q=2\) and \(d=\dim V\) this reads
    \begin{equation*} \#q^{-1}(0)=2^{d-1}+(-1)^{\Arf(q)}2^{d/2-1}, \end{equation*}
    since the hyperbolic type is the type of Arf invariant \(0\text{;}\) equivalently, the quadratic Gauss sum \(\sum_{x\in V}(-1)^{q(x)}=2\,\#q^{-1}(0)-2^{d}\) equals \((-1)^{\Arf(q)}2^{d/2}\text{.}\) This is the identity used in Proposition 6.9 and Proposition 6.18, where the paper also re-derives the minus-type count directly on a Hermitian line by fibring over the norm map, giving \(1+(2^m+1)(2^{m-1}-1)=2^{2m-1}-2^{m-1}\) zeros.
    🔗
    An isometry of \((V,q)\) preserves \(b_q\text{,}\) so the orthogonal group \(O(V,q)\) is a subgroup of the symplectic group of \(b_q\text{,}\) and in particular every isometry has determinant \(1\) [Gro, Chapter 14, p. 127]; the determinant is replaced by Dickson’s pseudodeterminant, a surjective homomorphism \(\delta:O(V,q)\to\F_2\text{,}\) independent of all choices, which takes the value \(1\) on every orthogonal transvection and whose kernel is by definition \(SO(V,q)\) [Gro, Corollary 14.4, Proposition 14.5 and pp. 130--131]. For an isometry \(\mathsf U\) write \(N=1+\mathsf U\text{.}\) Wall attaches to \(\mathsf U\) the subspace \(R=NV\text{,}\) its space, and the form \(\omega\) on \(R\) defined by \(\omega(Nx,Ny)=b_q(x,Ny)\text{;}\) this form is well defined and nondegenerate, and the orthogonal complement of \(R\) is the fixed space \(\ker N\) [Wal, §1.1, (1.1.2), Lemma 1.1.1 and Corollary]. In the characteristic-\(2\) orthogonal case the invariance of \(q\) strengthens this to \(b_q(x,Nx)=q(Nx)\text{,}\) so \(\omega(u,u)=q(u)\) for \(u\in R\text{:}\) the Wall form remembers the quadratic form on \(R\) [Wal, §1.5, (1.5.5)--(1.5.6) and Lemma 1.5.1], and equivalence of Wall forms detects conjugacy in the orthogonal group [Wal, §1.5, Theorem 1.5.2]. This is exactly the structure exploited by Lemma 6.6: the doubled form \(q_{\mathsf U}(x)=q(x)+b_q(x,\mathsf U^{-1}x)=q(x)+q(Nx)\) is compared with \(q\) through the Wall form of \(\mathsf U\text{,}\) and an induction on \(\omega\text{,}\) splitting an anisotropic plane or a symplectic plane at each step, shows that the Arf invariant shifts by \(\dim R=\operatorname{rank}(1+\mathsf U)\) modulo \(2\text{.}\) The proof is self-contained, so the classical identification of this rank parity with \(\delta(\mathsf U)\) is never needed.
    🔗
    Hermitian forms enter through the unramified and ramified models of the invariant form. For a quadratic extension \(F/F_0\) with involution \(x\mapsto x^*\text{,}\) every Hermitian space has an orthogonal basis with diagonal entries in \(F_0\text{,}\) over a finite field even an orthonormal one, so all Hermitian spaces of a given dimension over a finite field are equivalent [Gro, Theorems 10.2 and 10.3, Corollary 10.4]; moreover the trace \(F\to F_0\) is onto [Gro, Proposition 10.6] and the norm \(F^\times\to F_0^\times\) is onto with all fibres of size \(q+1\) [Gro, Chapter 11, p. 109]. Composing a Hermitian form with the trace gives the \(\F_2\)-valued quadratic trace forms \(q_c(x)=\Tr_{F_0/\F_2}(c\,xx^*)\text{;}\) Lemma 6.7 shows these are the only nonsingular quadratic forms on a line invariant under the norm-one circle group, and Lemma 6.8 diagonalizes the invariant Hermitian matrix to split the ramified form into such lines, each of Arf invariant \(1\) by the zero count above. Finally, the algebraic normal form of a quadratic map over \(\F_2\text{,}\) the unique reduced polynomial representative determined by the values on coordinate vectors together with the polar form, is established where it is used, in Lemma 6.3, whose orbit polynomials are its invariant incarnation.
    🔗
    🔗

    Subsection E.9 Modular representations, Clifford theory, and Schur fields

    Representation theory over \(\F_2\) is governed by the interplay between the odd part and the \(2\)-part of the acting group. If a finite group \(H\) has odd order, then \(|H|\) is invertible in \(\F_2\) and Maschke’s theorem applies: every invariant subspace of an \(\F_2[H]\)-module is a direct summand [Web, Theorem 1.2.1], so every finite-dimensional \(\F_2[H]\)-module is semisimple [Web, Corollary 1.2.5]; the same averaging over \(H\) shows that \(|H|\) annihilates positive-degree cohomology, so \(H^n(H,M)=0\) for \(n>0\) when \(|H|\) is odd and \(M\) is an \(\F_2[H]\)-module [Bro, Corollary III.10.2]. At the opposite pole, a \(2\)-group has only the trivial simple module in characteristic \(2\) [Web, Proposition 6.2.1], and consequently the largest normal \(2\)-subgroup \(O_2(H)\) is the common kernel of the action of \(H\) on all simple \(\F_2[H]\)-modules [Web, Corollary 6.2.2]. The paper’s recurring unramified reduction combines the two poles: the \(2\)-primary subgroup of a cyclic unramified image acts trivially on every simple characteristic-\(2\) module, so the faithful image \(H_V\) of a simple unramified module has odd order, and semisimplicity together with the cohomological vanishing is available. This is the form in which Maschke’s theorem enters Lemma 6.3, Lemma 6.4, Proposition 7.4, and Proposition 6.18.
    🔗
    For a finite-dimensional module \(U\) over \(\F_2[H]\text{,}\) with \(H\) now arbitrary, the radical \(\rad U\) is the intersection of the maximal submodules, equivalently the smallest submodule with semisimple quotient, and the socle \(\soc U\) is the sum of the simple submodules, the largest semisimple submodule [Web, Lemma 6.3.1 and Proposition 6.3.4]. The largest semisimple quotient \(U/\rad U\) is called the head (or top) of \(U\text{;}\) Webb says “radical quotient”. We say \(U\) has simple head \(V\) when \(U/\rad U\cong V\) is simple, that is, when \(\rad U\) is the unique maximal submodule. These notions organize Section 7: a chief series of the finite \(2\)-kernel \(L_Y\text{,}\) i.e. a maximal chain of subgroups normal under the full ambient action, has elementary abelian factors admitting no proper nonzero invariant subgroups; each chief factor is thus a simple \(\F_2[H]\)-module for the tame quotient \(H\text{,}\) called scalar exactly when it is the trivial module. Isolating the first non-scalar chief factor produces the simple-head sequence \(0\to T\to M\to V\to 0\) of Lemma 7.1, with \(T=\rad M\) and \(\Hom_C(M,\F_2)=0\text{;}\) the trivial action of odd Hall lifts along chief series with scalar factors below drives Lemma 7.2, and the same sequence carries the radical-edge descent of Lemma 8.6 and the inductive step in Subsection 9.2.
    🔗
    Clifford’s theorem controls restriction to a normal subgroup \(N\triangleleft H\text{:}\) over any field, the restriction to \(N\) of a simple module \(U\) is semisimple [Web, Theorem 5.3.1], and it decomposes into isotypic homogeneous components \(S_1^{a_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus S_r^{a_r}\) which \(H\) permutes transitively, with equal multiplicities and dimensions; moreover \(U\) is induced from the stabilizer of a component [Web, Theorem 5.3.2]. When \(N\) is abelian and the field algebraically closed, every simple \(N\)-module is a one-dimensional character [Web, Theorem 5.3.3], so the restriction splits into \(\chi\)-weight spaces indexed by characters \(\chi\) of \(N\text{,}\) permuted by conjugation; the stabilizer of a weight is its inertia group in the classical terminology adopted here (Webb writes \(\operatorname{Stab}_G\)). Lemma 6.11 runs this analysis over \(\overline{\F}_2\) for the odd cyclic tame-inertia subgroup \(I\triangleleft H_V\text{:}\) the inertia characters occurring in an absolutely irreducible constituent have one-dimensional weight spaces, they are permuted in orbits by \(H_V\) and by Frobenius, and the Sylow-\(2\) subgroup moves the weights freely in blocks of \(2\)-power size. The same weight picture, with self-duality exchanging \(\chi\) and \(\chi^{-1}\text{,}\) underlies the Hermitian model of Lemma 6.8.
    🔗
    A module is projective if and only if it is a direct summand of a free module, if and only if every epimorphism onto it splits [Web, Proposition 7.1.3]. Over \(\F_2[P]\) with \(P\) a \(2\)-group, finitely generated projective modules are free [Web, Theorem 8.1.1]: this is the regularity established block-by-block on Sylow-\(2\) weight orbits in Lemma 6.11. Restriction and induction preserve projectivity [Web, Lemma 8.1.2], and when the index of a subgroup \(P\le H\) is odd (for instance \(P\) a Sylow \(2\)-subgroup, or \(P=1\) in an odd-order group), every module is relatively \(P\)-projective, so that \(U\) is projective over \(\F_2[H]\) if and only if the restriction \(U|_P\) is projective [Web, Proposition 11.3.5 and Corollary 11.3.6]. Projectivity is likewise insensitive to the ground field: for a field extension \(E/F\text{,}\) a module \(U\) is projective if and only if \(E\otimes_F U\) is projective [Web, Chapter 9, Exercise 17], and by the Noether–Deuring theorem an isomorphism of modules established after an arbitrary extension of scalars already holds over the ground field [Web, Theorem 9.2.8]. Together these descend the free Sylow-block structure from \(\overline{\F}_2\) back to \(\F_2\text{,}\) completing Lemma 6.11. For a simple module \(V\) that is either projective (ramified case) or semisimple with all its \(\F_2[H]\)-companions (unramified case, odd \(|H|\)), every embedding into and surjection from a free module splits; this produces the \(H\)-split pairs \(V\to\F_2[H]^N\to V\) with \(pi=1\) of Lemma 6.3, whose left-regular coordinates (the basis of the regular representation indexed by the elements of \(H\) [Web, Section 1.1]) carry the orbit polynomials of the base determinant class.
    🔗
    By Schur’s lemma the endomorphism ring of a simple module is a division ring [Web, Theorem 2.1.1]; simplicity survives every extension of scalars precisely when the endomorphisms reduce to the scalars [Web, Proposition 9.2.5], and any field containing enough roots of unity is a splitting field [Web, Theorem 9.2.7]. All the endomorphism rings used in this paper are taken over cyclic groups, where the division ring is automatically commutative: for \(C\) cyclic and \(S\) a simple \(F[C]\)-module, \(\End_{F[C]}(S)\) is a field, and extending scalars to it splits \(S\) into absolutely simple summands [Web, Chapter 9, Exercise 3]. Over \(\F_2\) this yields the finite Schur fields \(F_V\) of the paper: a simple module \(W\) of an odd-order cyclic group with \(\dim_{\F_2}W=f\) is a one-dimensional vector space over \(F_V=\End(W)\cong\F_{2^f}\text{,}\) a generator acting as multiplication by a primitive character value \(\zeta\text{,}\) and the \(f\) weights of \(W\otimes_{\F_2}\overline{\F}_2\) form a single Frobenius orbit \(\{\zeta^{2^i}\}\text{.}\) Self-duality \(V\cong V^\vee\) ([Web, p. 28] for the dual module) places \(\zeta^{-1}\) in this orbit, forcing the orbit length \(f=2m\) to be even and making \(x\mapsto x^*=x^{2^{m}}\) the involutive automorphism of \(F_V\) with fixed field \(F_{V,0}\cong\F_{2^{m}}\text{;}\) on endomorphisms this involution is the adjoint with respect to the invariant polar form. The norm and trace of \(F_V/F_{V,0}\text{,}\) and the norm-one unitary scalars \(\mathcal U\le F_V^\times\) acting by isometries, carry the Hermitian-line computations of Lemma 6.8, Proposition 6.9, and Proposition 6.18, and feed the isometry invariance of the normalized base class in Lemma 6.4.
    🔗
    🔗

    Subsection E.10 Free differential calculus and the Fox Jacobian

    Free differential calculus is Fox’s calculus of derivations in the group ring of a free group. A derivation of a group ring is an additive map \(D\) satisfying \(D(u\cdot v)=Du\cdot v^{o}+u\cdot Dv\text{,}\) where \(v^{o}\) denotes the coefficient sum; on group elements this reads \(D(gh)=Dg+g\,Dh\) [Fox, §1, (1.1)-(1.2)]. For a free group with basis \(x_1,\dots,x_d\text{,}\) each generator carries a partial derivative \(\partial/\partial x_j\text{,}\) characterized by \(\partial x_k/\partial x_j=\delta_{jk}\text{,}\) and every derivation of the free group ring is uniquely of the form \(f\mapsto\sum_j(\partial f/\partial x_j)\,h_j\) with prescribed values \(h_j\) on the generators [Fox, §2, Theorem, (2.1)-(2.2)]. The fundamental formula
    \begin{equation*} f\;=\;f(1)+\sum_{j}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_j}\,(x_j-1) \end{equation*}
    recovers an element of the free group ring from its augmentation and its derivatives [Fox, (2.3)]; the augmentation-zero elements form what Fox calls the fundamental ideal, the modern augmentation ideal [Fox, §1].
    🔗
    On words the product rule takes the recursive form \(\partial(uv)/\partial x_j =\partial u/\partial x_j+u\,\partial v/\partial x_j\text{,}\) with \(\partial(u^{-1})/\partial x_j=-u^{-1}\,\partial u/\partial x_j\) [Fox, (1.2)', (1.5), (1.6)], and the derivative of a power is a power sum:
    \begin{equation*} \frac{\partial x^{p}}{\partial x}=1+x+\cdots+x^{p-1}, \qquad p\ge 1, \end{equation*}
    the norm element of the cyclic group generated by the base [Fox, (2.4)], with a practical rule and a chain rule for substituted words [Fox, (2.5)-(2.6)]. Evaluated through a homomorphism to a finite semidirect product \(C\ltimes A\text{,}\) so that the group-ring coefficients act on the kernel \(A\text{,}\) these identities become exactly the finite Fox rules \(D_{uv}=D_u+\bar uD_v\text{,}\) \(D_{u^{-1}}=-\bar u^{-1}D_u\text{,}\) \(D_{u^{n}}=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\bar u^{\,j}D_u\) of Appendix B (see (B.1)) and the raw finite Fox rules of Lemma 5.4: identities of literal finite word evaluations, for which no calculus over a completed group ring need be invoked. In particular, for an \(\w\)-power the evaluated power sum collapses: an integer representative of \(\w\) modulo the relevant finite exponent is odd and divisible by the odd order \(e\) of the lower operator \(\mathsf T\text{,}\) so over \(\F_2\) the power rule yields \(P=1+\mathsf T+\cdots+\mathsf T^{e-1}\text{;}\) as \(e\) is odd, \(P\) is an idempotent projecting onto the \(\mathsf T\)-invariants, the norm projector of Lemma 5.5.
    🔗
    For a group presented by generators \(x_1,\dots,x_d\) and relators \(r_1,\dots,r_m\text{,}\) the array \((\partial r_i/\partial x_j)\) is the Jacobian matrix of the presentation. Fox already observed that the derivatives are the degree-one cocycles of the free group and that the computation of the cohomology of a presented group in dimensions \(1,2,3,\dots\) rests on its Jacobian matrices, as carried out by Lyndon for one-relator groups and by Artin and Tate for certain finite groups [Fox, pp. 547-548]. This is the linearization used in Section 5: varying the generators of a lift to \(C\ltimes A\) by \((a_1,\dots,a_d)\in A^d\) changes each relator defect to first order by the evaluated row \(\sum_j(\partial r_i/\partial x_j)^{\rho}\,a_j\text{,}\) and the fundamental formula applied to \(r_i\) gives \(\sum_j(\partial r_i/\partial x_j)^{\rho}(\mathsf X_j-1) =\rho(r_i)-1=0\text{,}\) so the relator rows annihilate the simultaneous conjugations and the three terms of (5.1) form a complex whose degree-one cohomology classifies first-order lifts; the rows displayed in Lemma 5.5 are these evaluated derivatives for the tame and wild relators. In degree two the relator values retain full information by the classical pro-\(p\) facts: a minimal system of relations has cardinality \(\dim_{\F_p}H^2(G,\F_p)\) [Koc, Theorem 6.13], and for a minimal presentation \(1\to R\to F\to G\to 1\) the transgression \(H^1(R)^{G}\to H^2(G,\mathbb{Z}/q)\) is an isomorphism, so a degree-two class is determined by the values at the relators of the corresponding homomorphism on \(R\) [Koc, §7.8]. In the completed setting the same derivative map is the boundary of the relation-module sequence
    \begin{equation*} 0\longrightarrow R^{\mathrm{ab}}(p) \longrightarrow \mathbb{Z}_p[[G]]^{d} \longrightarrow \mathbb{Z}_p[[G]] \longrightarrow \mathbb{Z}_p\longrightarrow 0, \end{equation*}
    the profinite analogue of Lyndon’s theorem: a relation maps to its differential, whose coordinates in the free module on \(dx_1,\dots,dx_d\) are its partial derivatives, and \(dx_j\mapsto x_j-1\) realizes the fundamental formula [NSW, Proposition (5.6.4) and Theorem (5.6.6)].
    🔗
    The pro-\(p\) version of the calculus, which the finite ledgers of Appendix B shadow, lives in the complete group algebra \(\F_p[[G]]=\varprojlim \F_p[G/N]\) [Koc, Definition 7.1]. For a free pro-\(p\) group \(F\) on \(s_1,\dots,s_m\text{,}\) the Magnus embedding identifies \(\F_p[[F]]\) with the algebra of formal noncommutative power series in variables \(x_i\) via \(s_i\mapsto 1+x_i\) [Koc, Theorem 7.16, with Definition 4.3], matching Fox’s identification of the formal Taylor expansion by higher derivatives with the Magnus representation on \(x_j=s_j-1\) [Fox, §3, (3.4)]; a system of relations \(\{r_i\}\) generates the kernel of \(\F_p[[F]]\to\F_p[[G]]\) as the closed ideal on the \(r_i-1\) [Koc, Theorem 7.17]. Second-order word coefficients compute cup products: writing a relator in collected normal form \(r_i\equiv\prod_\nu s_\nu^{a_\nu q}\prod_{\nu<\mu} [s_\nu,s_\mu]^{a_{\nu\mu}}\) modulo the third step of the \((q)\)-filtration, evaluation at \(r_i\) through the inverse transgression sends \(\chi_\nu\cup\chi_\mu\) to \(-a_{\nu\mu}\) for \(\nu<\mu\) [Koc, Theorems 7.22-7.23]; this is the classical prototype for extracting cup products from central word coordinates, the mechanism behind the finite Fox recursion formulas and Heisenberg central coordinate of Subsection 5.2. A systematic topological version of Fox’s calculus for completed group rings (continuous derivations of \(\mathbb{Z}_p[[G]]\) into compact modules, the differential module, its freeness of rank \(d\) over a free pro-\(p\) group) is developed in [NSW, Chapter V, §6, (5.6.1)-(5.6.4)]. This body of results is what makes free differential calculus the established pro-\(p\) tool invoked in Subsection 1.2; the deformation section’s device is to evaluate the resulting Jacobian on each finite tame module and read off lifting counts.
    🔗
    🔗

    Subsection E.11 Peripheral inertia and the arithmetic action on fundamental groups

    For a geometrically connected curve \(U\) over a field \(k\) of characteristic zero, the étale fundamental group sits in an extension
    \begin{equation*} 1\longrightarrow\pi_1(\overline U)\longrightarrow\pi_1(U) \longrightarrow\operatorname{Gal}(\bar k/k)\longrightarrow 1, \end{equation*}
    where \(\overline U\) is the base change to an algebraic closure, and conjugation in this extension induces the arithmetic outer action \(\operatorname{Gal}(\bar k/k)\to\operatorname{Out}(\pi_1(\overline U))\) of the absolute Galois group on the geometric fundamental group [Sti, Section 1.1, (1.1)]. For \(X=\mathbb{P}^1_{\mathbb{Q}}\setminus\{0,1,\infty\}\) and a prime \(\ell\) the same applies to the maximal pro-\(\ell\) quotient of the geometric fundamental group, a free pro-\(\ell\) group of rank \(2\text{:}\) Ihara realizes it as \(\pi_1=\operatorname{Gal}(M/\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(t))\) with \(M\) the maximal pro-\(\ell\) extension of \(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(t)\) unramified outside \(\{0,1,\infty\}\text{,}\) and obtains the outer representation \(\varphi_{\mathbb{Q}}\colon G_{\mathbb{Q}}\to\operatorname{Out}\pi_1\) from the extension \(1\to\pi_1\to\operatorname{Gal}(M/\mathbb{Q}(t))\to G_{\mathbb{Q}}\to1\) [Iha, Section 1(A), (1.1) and (1.2)].
    🔗
    The cusps carry the peripheral structure of this action. A cusp \(y\) of an affine hyperbolic curve, that is, a point of the boundary divisor \(Y=X\setminus U\text{,}\) gives rise to inertia subgroups \(I_{\tilde y}\subset\pi_1(\overline U)\text{,}\) one for each prolongation \(\tilde y\) of \(y\) to the universal pro-étale cover. They satisfy \(I_{\gamma\tilde y}=\gamma I_{\tilde y}\gamma^{-1}\text{,}\) and the prolongations of a fixed cusp form a single orbit, so \(y\) determines a well-defined conjugacy class of peripheral subgroups, and this class is preserved by the arithmetic action whenever the cusp is \(k\)-rational [Sti, Definition 10 and Section 3.3]. Each inertia group is free procyclic, its normalizer in \(\pi_1(U)\) is the decomposition group \(D_{\tilde y}\text{,}\) an extension of \(\operatorname{Gal}(\bar k/\kappa(y))\) by \(I_{\tilde y}\text{,}\) and the conjugation action of \(D_{\tilde y}\) on \(I_{\tilde y}\) is through the cyclotomic character: the inertia group acts on the tower obtained by extracting compatible roots of a local parameter at the cusp, and the resulting identification \(I_{\tilde y}\cong\Zhat(1)\) is equivariant for conjugation and for the cyclotomic character [Sti, Section 3.3, Proposition 11, Corollary 15, Proposition 16, and Definitions 34 and 37].
    🔗
    For \(\mathbb{P}^1_{\mathbb{Q}}\setminus\{0,1,\infty\}\) all three cusps are rational, and one may choose inertia generators \(x,y,z\) above \(0,1,\infty\) with \(xyz=1\) such that \(x,y\) freely generate the pro-\(\ell\) fundamental group; the arithmetic action then satisfies Ihara’s formula
    \begin{equation*} \varphi_{\mathbb{Q}}(\sigma)x\sim x^{\chi(\sigma)},\qquad \varphi_{\mathbb{Q}}(\sigma)y\sim y^{\chi(\sigma)},\qquad \varphi_{\mathbb{Q}}(\sigma)z\sim z^{\chi(\sigma)}, \end{equation*}
    with \(\sim\) denoting conjugacy in \(\pi_1\) and \(\chi\) the \(\ell\)-adic cyclotomic character [Iha, Section 1(A), (1.4)]. Taking \(\ell=2\text{,}\) this is exactly the input to Lemma 3.7, whose generators \(P,T,C\) with \(C=(PT)^{-1}\) play the roles of \(x,y,z\text{:}\) surjectivity of the \(2\)-adic cyclotomic character onto \(\mathbb{Z}_2^\times\) supplies, for every unit \(u\text{,}\) an outer automorphism of the geometric pro-\(2\) fundamental group sending each of the three peripheral generators to a conjugate of its \(u\)-th power.
    🔗
    🔗

    Subsection E.12 Complexes, cones, and cup products at the cochain level

    All homological algebra in this section is finite-dimensional linear algebra over \(\F_2\text{,}\) carried by three-term complexes such as the word complex (5.1). Two standard devices organize it. First, a chain map \(f:X^\bullet\to Y^\bullet\) of complexes (a degreewise linear map commuting with the differentials) has a mapping cone \(\Cone(f)\text{,}\) formed degree by degree: its degree-\(n\) term is \(X^{n+1}\oplus Y^n\text{,}\) and over \(\F_2\) its differential is simply \((x,y)\mapsto(d_Xx,\,f(x)+d_Yy)\text{,}\) the sign in the general formula being invisible because \(2=0\text{.}\) Second, a degreewise short exact sequence of complexes yields a long exact cohomology sequence whose connecting homomorphism is natural; applied to the degreewise-split sequence \(0\to Y^\bullet\to\Cone(f)\to X^\bullet[1]\to0\text{,}\) it shows that \(f\) is a quasi-isomorphism (it induces isomorphisms on all cohomology; Brown says weak equivalence) exactly when \(\Cone(f)\) is acyclic, meaning its cohomology vanishes in every degree. See [Bro, Chapter I, Section 0].
    🔗
    The long exact sequence gives a two-out-of-three principle: in a degreewise short exact sequence of complexes, if two of the three complexes are acyclic, then so is the third. Since cones are formed degree by degree, a map of degreewise short exact sequences of complexes produces a degreewise short exact sequence of cones. These two remarks are the entire homological content of the exact cone dévissage of Lemma 5.11: a short exact sequence of coefficient modules induces compatible short exact sequences of word complexes and of their duals, hence of the cones \(K(-)\text{,}\) and acyclicity of \(K(V)\) for the simple modules \(V\) propagates along a composition series to every elementary module, with no semisimplicity hypothesis.
    🔗
    Duality enters through the exact functor \(\Hom_{\F_2}(-,\F_2)\text{.}\) For a three-term complex \(X^0\to X^1\to X^2\) of finite-dimensional \(\F_2\)-vector spaces, the shifted dual \(\Hom_{\F_2}(X^\bullet,\F_2)[-2]\) is again a three-term complex in degrees \(0\) through \(2\text{,}\) with the transposed differentials in reversed order, and its degree-\(i\) cohomology is \(H^{2-i}(X^\bullet)^\vee\text{:}\) over a field the \(\operatorname{Ext}\)-term of the universal coefficient sequence vanishes [Bro, Chapter I, Section 0]. Consequently a chain map from \(X^\bullet\) to a shifted dual, such as (5.17) of Proposition 5.10, is a quasi-isomorphism if and only if the induced pairings \(H^i\times H^{2-i}\to\F_2\) are perfect; equivalently, by the cone criterion above, if and only if the cone (5.20) is acyclic. This is the form in which Proposition 5.15 is stated and proved.
    🔗
    Finally, the cup products. At cochain level the cup product of inhomogeneous cochains is given by the explicit formula
    \begin{equation*} (f\smile g)(g_1,\ldots,g_{p+q}) =f(g_1,\ldots,g_p)\cdot(g_1\cdots g_p)\,g(g_{p+1},\ldots,g_{p+q}), \end{equation*}
    as in [NSW, Chapter I, Section 4, Proposition (1.4.8)] and, for continuous cochains on profinite groups, [NSW, Chapter II, Section 7]. Classically this formula is not an ansatz but the shadow of a diagonal approximation: an augmentation-preserving equivariant chain map \(\Delta:F\to F\otimes F\) on a projective resolution \(F\text{,}\) unique up to equivariant homotopy, through which the cup product is defined as the cross product followed by \(\Delta\text{.}\) On the bar resolution the standard choice is the Alexander–Whitney map \(\Delta(g_0,\ldots,g_n)=\sum_{p}(g_0,\ldots,g_p)\otimes(g_p,\ldots,g_n)\text{,}\) the algebraic form of a cellular approximation to the diagonal of the classifying space; see [Bro, Chapter V, Sections 1 and 3]. The remark opening Subsection 5.2 is to be read against this background: the Stokes identities feeding Proposition 5.10 are identities of finite word evaluations, proved by conjugation in the finite Heisenberg group before any passage to cohomology, so no resolution, and in particular no choice of cellular diagonal approximation, enters the candidate side. The displayed cochain formula is needed only on the Galois side, where the classical cup product supplies the pairing of Proposition 5.16.
    🔗
    🔗

    Subsection E.13 The Evens norm and the Evens–Kahn formula

    Let \(H\le G\) be a subgroup of finite index \(l\text{.}\) A transversal of \(H\) in \(G\) determines Frobenius’s monomial embedding \(\Phi\colon G\to \mathcal S_l\wr H\) into the wreath product with the symmetric group, and Evens’s multiplicative transfer, or norm map, sends a class \(\alpha\in H^n(H,\F_2)\) to the pullback along \(\Phi\) of its Nakaoka wreath power on \(\mathcal S_l\wr H\text{;}\) the resulting class \(N_H^G(\alpha)\in H^{ln}(G,\F_2)\) does not depend on the transversal [Eve, §§2, 4--5]. The norm is multiplicative, \(N_H^G(\alpha\smile\beta)=N_H^G(\alpha)\smile N_H^G(\beta)\) [Eve, Proposition 4], but it is neither additive nor degree-preserving. With integral coefficients sign problems confine the construction to even degrees; with \(\F_2\)-coefficients, the only case used in this paper, it is available in every degree [Kah, I.2].
    🔗
    For an index-two subgroup \(N\triangleleft G\) and a class \([\alpha]\in H^1(N,\F_2)\text{,}\) the norm of the unit \(1+[\alpha]\) expands into homogeneous components as
    \begin{equation*} N_N^G(1+[\alpha]) =1+\cor_N^G[\alpha]+N_N^{G,\mathrm{Ev}}([\alpha]), \end{equation*}
    where the degree-one term is the ordinary additive transfer and the degree-two term is the index-two Evens norm appearing throughout Section 6. This is the two-sheeted case of the general expansion of \(N(1+x)\) into partial norms, whose first term is the transfer and whose top term is the norm [Eve, Theorem 1], [Kah, Proposition I.2.4]. Lemma 6.13 makes this class explicit: on the universal two-point model \(E_2\rtimes J\) (the swap module over \(J\cong C_2\)) the norm of the coordinate character is represented by a normalized \(2\)-cocycle whose fibre extension is the dihedral group \(D_8\text{,}\) and the general index-two case is recovered by pulling this model back along a graph homomorphism, using naturality of the norm in index-preserving pullback squares [Eve, Proposition 3].
    🔗
    Restrictions of the norm are computed by Evens’s double-coset rule, the multiplicative analogue of Mackey’s formula: for \(K\le G\text{,}\) with \(\F_2\)-coefficients,
    \begin{equation*} \res_K\,N_H^G(\alpha) =\prod_{KgH\in K\backslash G/H} N_{K\cap {}^{g}H}^{K}\bigl(\res_{K\cap {}^{g}H}({}^{g}\alpha)\bigr) \end{equation*}
    [Eve, Proposition 2]. In the two-point model the two instances used in Lemma 6.13 read: restriction to the index-two subgroup itself is the product of the two conjugates, \(\res_{E_2}N_{E_2}^{E_2\rtimes J,\mathrm{Ev}}(e_1^\vee) =e_1^\vee e_s^\vee\text{,}\) while restriction to a complement passes through the trivial intersection subgroup and vanishes. Since \(H^1(J,E_2^\vee)=0\text{,}\) the low-degree exact sequence shows that these two restrictions already determine a class on \(E_2\rtimes J\text{;}\) this uniqueness device is how Lemma 6.13 identifies the explicit cocycle with the Evens norm.
    🔗
    A real representation \(\rho\) of a finite group carries Stiefel–Whitney classes \(w_i(\rho)\text{,}\) those of the associated vector bundle on the classifying space; for a real representation of a Galois group with open kernel one inflates from a finite quotient [Kah, II.1.2], and for a quadratic form \(q\simeq\langle a_1,\dots,a_r\rangle\) one has Delzant’s classes \(w(q)=\prod_i(1+(a_i))\text{,}\) with \(w_1\) the discriminant and \(w_2\) the Hasse–Witt invariant [Kah, II.1.3]. The Evens–Kahn formula, named after the total Chern class formula of Evens and D. S. Kahn for induction from prime-index subgroups, computes the total Stiefel–Whitney class of an induced representation along an index-two subgroup through the norm: Kozlowski constructs a multiplicative transfer for double coverings on the units of mod-\(2\) cohomology and proves that the total Stiefel–Whitney class intertwines it with the \(KO\)-transfer [Koz, Theorem 1.1], while B. Kahn, working algebraically in Evens’s framework, obtains
    \begin{equation*} w(\operatorname{Ind}\rho) =N(w(\rho)) +\sum_{i\ge0}N(w_i(\rho))\bigl((1+\mu)^{r-i}+1\bigr), \end{equation*}
    where \(r\) is the rank and \(\mu\in H^1(G,\F_2)\) classifies the double covering [Kah, Théorème I.4.2], [Gui, Appendix A.1]. Over the absolute Galois group of a field of characteristic not two the correction terms vanish and the formula becomes exact: \(w(\operatorname{Ind}\rho)=N(w(\rho))\cdot w(\operatorname{Ind}1)^{r}\text{,}\) and likewise for trace forms \(w(\Tr_{E/F}q)=N(w(q))\cdot w(\Tr_{E/F}\langle1\rangle)^{r}\) [Kah, Théorèmes 1--2]. For a rank-one character \(\ell\) the relative class \(w(\operatorname{Ind}\ell)/ w(\operatorname{Ind}1)\) is thereby normalized to \(N(1+\ell)=1+\cor\ell+\Evens(\ell)\text{;}\) its degree-two component is exactly the index-two Evens norm. This is the Evens–Kahn normalization in which Lemma 6.13 identifies the universal two-point class.
    🔗
    For a quadratic extension of fields \(L/k\) of characteristic different from \(2\text{,}\) writing \(\Evens_{L/k}\) for the index-two Evens norm of the corresponding Galois groups, the rank-one case of the trace-form comparison reads
    \begin{equation*} w(\Tr_{L/k}\langle a\rangle) =w(\Tr_{L/k}\langle1\rangle) \bigl(1+\cor_{L/k}[a]+\Evens_{L/k}([a])\bigr), \end{equation*}
    the degree-two Evens–Kahn identity invoked in Lemma 6.16. Both trace forms are binary and explicitly diagonalizable, so isolating the degree-two component expresses \(\Evens_{L/k}([a])\) as a sum of Hilbert symbols in the diagonal entries; compare Kahn’s closed formula \(N((a))=(\Tr_{L/k}a,\,-d\,N_{L/k}a)+(2,d)\text{,}\) valid when \(\Tr_{L/k}a\ne0\text{,}\) with \(d\) the discriminant of \(L/k\) [Kah, Lemme II.2.1]. Section Section 6 runs this reduction inside the orbit decomposition of the regular module, where involution orbits contribute \(\cor_{K_0/F}\Evens_{K/K_0}(\alpha_r)\) (Lemma 6.15, via Lemma 6.14): Lemma 6.16 shows that over dyadic local fields the norm \(\Evens_{L/k}\) annihilates the deep units \(U_{e+1}(L)\) of an unramified quadratic extension, which is what makes the involution-orbit contributions vanish on the deep half in Lemma 6.17.
    🔗
    🔗

    Subsection E.14 Characters of finite abelian groups and Fourier inversion

    A character of a finite abelian group \(G\) is a homomorphism from \(G\) to the multiplicative group \(\mathbb{C}^*\text{;}\) the characters form the dual group \(\widehat G=\Hom(G,\mathbb{C}^*)\) [Ser73, Ch. VI, §1.1, Definition 1]. The dual is again a finite abelian group, of the same order as \(G\text{,}\) and the evaluation map \(x\mapsto(\chi\mapsto\chi(x))\) is an isomorphism of \(G\) onto its bidual [Ser73, Ch. VI, §1.1, Propositions 2 and 3]. When \(G\) is a finite \(\F_2\)-vector space every character takes values in \(\{\pm1\}\text{,}\) so \(\widehat G\) is identified with the \(\F_2\)-linear dual \(G^\vee=\Hom(G,\F_2)\text{,}\) the character attached to \(\lambda\in G^\vee\) being \(x\mapsto(-1)^{\langle\lambda,x\rangle}\text{.}\)
    🔗
    The orthogonality relations state that for a fixed character \(\chi\in\widehat G\) the sum \(\sum_{x\in G}\chi(x)\) equals \(|G|\) if \(\chi=1\) and \(0\) otherwise, and dually that for a fixed element \(x\in G\) the sum \(\sum_{\chi\in\widehat G}\chi(x)\) equals \(|G|\) if \(x=1\) and \(0\) otherwise [Ser73, Ch. VI, §1.2, Proposition 4 and its Corollary]. The second relation is a finite Fourier inversion: averaging all characters at \(x\) yields the indicator of \(x=1\text{.}\) In the \(\pm1\)-valued form used in this paper (Lemma 8.4), if \(\Lambda\) is the character group of a finite \(\F_2\)-obstruction space and \(o:X\to\Lambda^\vee\) is defined on a finite set \(X\text{,}\) then
    \begin{equation*} \#\{x\in X: o(x)=0\} =\frac1{|\Lambda|}\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda}\bigl(2m_\lambda-|X|\bigr), \end{equation*}
    where \(m_\lambda=\#\{x\in X:\langle\lambda,o(x)\rangle=0\}\text{;}\) each summand \(2m_\lambda-|X|\) is the signed character sum \(\sum_{x\in X}(-1)^{\langle\lambda,o(x)\rangle}\text{.}\)
    🔗
    In the exact-image recursion of Subsection 8.1 the set \(X\) consists of boundary-framed exact-image maps, and \(o\) is the obstruction to lifting them one Frattini layer up the target tower. The recursion separates \(o\) into scalar tests, one invariant scalar character at a time, each nonzero character being realized by a central double cover of the target. In the same way a scalar class \(\zeta\in H^2(C,\F_2)\) is represented by a central double cover of the lower target \(C\text{,}\) the phase cover, whose splitting indicator realizes the sign \((-1)^{\iota_\Gamma(\rho^*\zeta)}\) appearing in the Fourier sum. Averaging these signed splitting indicators over the scalar phases isolates exactly the maps with vanishing obstruction, and the phase-cover transform (Lemma 8.15) converts each signed sum back into ordinary exact-image counts: writing \(n_{\Gamma,0}(\zeta)\) for the number of lower maps for which the phase cover is unobstructed, so that its pullback cover splits, the signed sum equals \(2n_{\Gamma,0}(\zeta)-e_\Gamma(C)\text{,}\) and the eight scalar twists of each unobstructed lift (Lemma 8.2) are partitioned by their exact images inside the cover. In this way every Fourier coefficient of the lifting count becomes an exact-image count for a strictly smaller target, closing the recursion.
